root.title: Smooth Nonconvex Criticality and Landscape Theory
root.top_down_role: Local and approximate stationarity for smooth nonconvex objectives, the geometry and dynamics of saddle points, and method families for detecting or escaping nonminimizing stationary regions. General constrained optimality theory and full globalization frameworks remain in their owning chapters.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Nonconvex Criticality Landscape Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Core unconstrained first- and second-order criticality classes, including approximate stationarity and strict saddles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(x\). The point \(x\) is first-order critical when \(
abla f(x)=0\), and it is second-order critical when additionally \(
abla^2 f(x)\succeq 0\). For tolerances \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H\ge 0\), the point \(x\) is an \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\)-second-order stationary point when \(\lVert
abla f(x)Vert_2\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2 f(x))\ge-\varepsilon_H\). A first-order critical point is a strict saddle when \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2 f(x))<0\), and it is nondegenerate when \(\det(
abla^2 f(x))
e0\). Negative curvature rules out exact second-order criticality; it rules out \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\)-second-order stationarity when \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2 f(x))<-\varepsilon_H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point is first-order critical when its gradient vanishes and second-order critical when, in addition, its Hessian is positive semidefinite. It is approximately second-order stationary when its gradient is small and its negative curvature does not exceed the specified tolerance. A first-order critical point is a strict saddle when its Hessian has a negative eigenvalue, and it is nondegenerate when its Hessian is nonsingular. Negative curvature beyond the allowed tolerance excludes approximate second-order stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The local criticality class is determined by \(
abla f(x)\), \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2 f(x))\), and, for nondegeneracy, \(\det(
abla^2 f(x))\), with approximate second-order stationarity allowing curvature down to \(-\varepsilon_H\).

notation.meaning: smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix H

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth Nonconvex Problem and Information Regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open, and \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) is not assumed convex. The unconstrained problem is \(\inf_{x\in U}f(x)\), usually with \(U=\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, deterministic, unconstrained smooth optimization; the definition separates regularity assumptions from the information supplied to an algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A smooth nonconvex problem-information regime is a pair \((\mathcal F,\mathcal O)\). The problem class \(\mathcal F\) consists of differentiable objectives \(f:U	o\mathbb R\), possibly restricted by quantitative conditions such as \(\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|^
u\) or \(\|
abla^2f(x)-
abla^2f(y)\|\le M\|x-y\|^\alpha\). The information interface \(\mathcal O_f\) is a query map whose answer at an admissible query contains specified local data, for example \(f(x)\), \(
abla f(x)\), \(
abla^2f(x)\), or \(
abla^2f(x)v\). An algorithm belongs to this regime only when each new query is determined from earlier oracle answers and permitted internal data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime consists of a class of differentiable, not necessarily convex objectives and a specified query interface. The class records first- or second-derivative regularity, while the interface states whether an algorithm receives values, gradients, full Hessians, or Hessian–vector products. An algorithm is in the regime when its queries depend only on previously returned permitted information and its internal state.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and every queried point belongs to \(U\).
Each \(f\in\mathcal F\) possesses every derivative requested by \(\mathcal O_f\).
No convexity, global-minimum oracle, or information outside the declared interface is assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal F,\mathcal O)\) fixes both the admissible smooth nonconvex instances and the local information available for stationarity or curvature analysis.
equivalent_formulations_latex: An exact order-\(p\) local oracle may be written \(\mathcal O_f^{(p)}(x)=(f(x),\nabla f(x),\ldots,\nabla^pf(x))\).
A matrix-free second-order interface replaces the full Hessian component by the bilinear query \((x,v)\mapsto\nabla^2f(x)v\).
special_cases_latex: The first-order Lipschitz regime has \(\nu=1\) and supplies \((f(x),\nabla f(x))\).
The explicit second-order regime supplies \((f(x),\nabla f(x),\nabla^2f(x))\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Complexity counts are meaningful only after the oracle interface and regularity constants are fixed.
Two methods acting on the same objective class can inhabit different information regimes if one forms full Hessians and the other uses only Hessian–vector products.
boundary_notes: This definition excludes constrained feasible-set oracles and stochastic sampling oracles.
Smoothness constants may be local to a specified neighborhood or global on the entire domain; the choice must be declared.

knowledge_statements.title: Unconstrained Smooth Nonconvex Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional unconstrained formulation with differential stationarity and no convexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable and not necessarily convex. Unconstrained smooth nonconvex minimization is the problem
\[\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x).\]
A point \(x_*\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is first-order stationary when \(
abla f(x_*)=0\). If \(f\) is twice differentiable at \(x_*\), it is second-order stationary when additionally \(
abla^2 f(x_*)\succeq0\); it is a strict saddle when \(
abla f(x_*)=0\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2 f(x_*))<0\). These conditions classify criticality but do not, without additional assumptions, guarantee global minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize a smooth, possibly nonconvex function over Euclidean space; stationary points have zero gradient, while Hessian curvature distinguishes second-order stationary points from strict saddles.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\) defines first-order stationarity; when defined, Hessian signs refine the local criticality classification.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition for a twice-differentiable finite-dimensional objective, with no convexity assumption and no assertion that a global minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a twice differentiable function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, the unconstrained minimization problem is $\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)$. A point $x^*\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is a local minimizer if there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $x^*$ such that $f(x^*)\le f(x)$ for every $x\in U$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unconstrained minimization seeks to minimize a twice-differentiable objective over Euclidean space. A point is a local minimizer when its value is no greater than the value at every sufficiently nearby point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ is a local minimizer}\iff\exists\,U\ni x^*\text{ a neighborhood such that }\forall x\in U,\ f(x^*)\le f(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Unconstrainedness at an Interior Feasible Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local feasible-set characterization used by unconstrained minimization; it does not require the entire feasible set to equal the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n and x^*\in D. Optimization is locally unconstrained at x^* when x^* is an interior point of D, equivalently when there exists \varepsilon>0 such that B_\varepsilon(x^*)\subseteq D. The condition D=\mathbb{R}^n is sufficient but not necessary. If D is open, every x^*\in D satisfies this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local minimization is unconstrained at a feasible point when the feasible set contains a full neighborhood of that point. The whole space need not be feasible; interiority is enough, and every point of an open feasible set is interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\operatorname{int}D\iff\exists\varepsilon>0\text{ such that }B_\varepsilon(x^*)\subseteq D.

children.title: First-Order Smoothness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regularity levels supporting first-order stationarity, descent analysis, and first-order complexity.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open, \(f:U\to\mathbb R\), and distances and gradient norms use a fixed norm and its dual.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable objectives; regularity may hold globally on a set or locally near a reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The first-order smoothness regime of \(f\) is classified by the continuity modulus of \(
abla f\). The objective is \(C^1\) when \(
abla f\) is continuous. It has a \((L,
u)\)-Hölder gradient on \(D\subseteq U\) when \(L\ge0\), \(
u\in(0,1]\), and \(\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_*\le L\|x-y\|^
u\) for every \(x,y\in D\). The endpoint \(
u=1\) is the Lipschitz-gradient regime. These classes satisfy \(C^{1,1}(D)\subseteq C^{1,
u}(D)\subseteq C^1(D)\) on bounded \(D\), with constants adjusted to the diameter of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First-order regimes are determined by how continuously the gradient varies. Continuous differentiability requires only continuity. Hölder-gradient smoothness bounds gradient changes by a constant times distance to a power between zero and one. Power one is Lipschitz-gradient smoothness.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq U\) contains every point at which the regularity inequality is invoked.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((L,\nu)\), together with its validity set \(D\), specifies the quantitative first-order regularity available to descent and stationarity analyses.
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(\nu=1\), the condition is \(\nabla f\in\operatorname{Lip}(D;\mathbb R^n)\).
Local \(C^{1,\nu}\) regularity at \(\bar x\) means that the Hölder inequality holds on some neighborhood of \(\bar x\).
special_cases_latex: \(\nu=1\) gives Lipschitz continuity of the gradient.
Dropping a quantitative modulus leaves the qualitative \(C^1\) regime.
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(x,x+s\in D\) with the intervening segment in \(D\), Hölder-gradient regularity yields a first-order Taylor remainder of order \(\|s\|^{1+\nu}\).
boundary_notes: Continuity of the gradient alone does not supply a global Hölder constant.
The definition does not imply convexity or boundedness below.

notation.meaning: Differentiable functions with a locally or globally Hölder-continuous gradient of exponent \(\nu\).

children.top_down_role: The classical qualitative first-order stationarity regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuously Differentiable Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualitative first-order regularity on an open Euclidean domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open. An objective \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable, written \(f\in C^1(U)\), when every first partial derivative exists on \(U\) and the gradient mapping \(\nabla f:U\to\mathbb{R}^n\) is continuous. Consequently, for every \(x\in U\),
\[f(x+s)=f(x)+\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}s+o(\lVert s\rVert)\quad\text{as }s\to0,\]
with \(x+s\in U\). This regime supplies qualitative first-order models but imposes no uniform gradient modulus or associated global descent constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable objective has a continuous gradient and a first-order Taylor expansion with a remainder negligible relative to the step length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in C^1(U)\) and the displayed first-order expansion holds at every \(x\in U\).

notation.meaning: a remainder whose ratio to the step norm tends to zero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines first-order differentiability and the gradient, then identifies the continuously differentiable objective regime and its local Lipschitz consequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A function $f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}$ is differentiable at $x$ if there exist $
abla f(x)\in\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\varepsilon:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}$ such that $f(x+d)=f(x)+
abla f(x)^Td+\|d\|\varepsilon(d)$ for all $d\in\mathbb{R}^n$, where $\varepsilon(d)	o0$ as $\|d\|	o0$. The components of $
abla f(x)$ are the partial derivatives of $f$ at $x$. A differentiable function whose partial derivatives are continuous is continuously differentiable, or $C^1$; every $C^1$ function is locally Lipschitz continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Differentiability means that the gradient supplies a linear approximation with an error that is little-o of the displacement norm. Continuous partial derivatives define the C1 regime, and C1 functions are locally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x+d)=f(x)+\nabla f(x)^Td+o(\|d\|),\qquad f\in C^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\implies f\text{ is locally Lipschitz continuous}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mean Value Theorem on an Open Sphere
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar mean-value identity along a segment contained in an open Euclidean sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be an open sphere, let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} be continuously differentiable on S, and let x\in S. For every y\in\mathbb{R}^n such that x+y\in S, there exists \alpha\in[0,1] such that f(x+y)=f(x)+\nabla f(x+\alpha y)^\top y.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a scalar function is continuously differentiable on an open sphere and both endpoints of a displacement lie in that sphere, its increment equals the displacement dotted with the gradient at some point on the intervening segment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\alpha\in[0,1]\;\text{such that}\;f(x+y)=f(x)+\nabla f(x+\alpha y)^\top y.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional derivative, line-integral, and mean-value identities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order identities for a continuously differentiable scalar function on an open convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\mathbb{R}$ be continuously differentiable on an open convex set $D\subset\mathbb{R}^n$. For $x\in D$ and $p\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$, the directional derivative exists and satisfies $ rac{\partial f}{\partial p}(x)=\lim_{\varepsilon	o0} rac{f(x+\varepsilon p)-f(x)}{\varepsilon}=
abla f(x)^Tp$. If $x,x+p\in D$, then $f(x+p)-f(x)=\int_0^1
abla f(x+tp)^Tp\,dt$, and there exists $z$ in the open segment $(x,x+p)$ such that $f(x+p)=f(x)+
abla f(z)^Tp$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a C1 scalar function on an open convex set, the directional derivative is the gradient inner product. Its change along a contained segment is the integral of these inner products and equals one such inner product at an intermediate point.

rac{\partial f}{\partial p}(x)=
abla f(x)^Tp,\qquad f(x+p)-f(x)=\int_0^1
abla f(x+tp)^Tp\,dt=
abla f(z)^Tp	ext{ for some }z\in(x,x+p).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-valued first-order smoothness at a point and throughout an open set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuously differentiable at $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ if each partial derivative $\partial f/\partial x_i$ exists and is continuous at $x$, for $i=1,\ldots,n$. The gradient is $\nabla f(x)=[\partial f/\partial x_1(x),\ldots,\partial f/\partial x_n(x)]^T$. For an open set $D\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, $f\in C^1(D)$ means that $f$ is continuously differentiable at every point of $D$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous scalar function is continuously differentiable at a point when all first partial derivatives exist and are continuous there; these derivatives form its gradient. It is C1 on an open set when this holds at every point of that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla f(x)=\left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(x),\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(x)\right]^T,\qquad f\in C^1(D)\iff f\text{ is continuously differentiable at every point of }D.

children.title: Lipschitz-Gradient Objectives
children.top_down_role: The standard quantitative first-order model and complexity regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz-Gradient Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform first-order smoothness on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f\) be differentiable on an open set containing \(D\). The objective has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(D\) when \(L\ge0\) and
\[\lVert\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\rVert\le L\lVert x-y\rVert\qquad(x,y\in D).\]
Under this condition, every \(x,y\in D\) satisfy the quadratic model bound
\[\left|f(y)-f(x)-\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y-x)\right|\le \frac{L}{2}\lVert y-x\rVert^2.\]
No convexity of \(f\) is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradient changes at most linearly with distance, yielding a uniform quadratic error bound for first-order Taylor models even when the objective is nonconvex.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Lipschitz-gradient inequality implies the displayed quadratic Taylor-remainder bound on \(D\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Lipschitz-gradient condition and two-sided quadratic Taylor-remainder bound are mathematically standard and fit the condition container, but the record has no citation. An authoritative source with a section, theorem, lemma, or page locator is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(f\) is differentiable on an open set containing \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic finite-dimensional first-order smoothness on a declared convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The objective \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(D\), or is \(L\)-smooth there, if \(L\ge0\) and \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in D\). The constant \(L\) is any valid upper Lipschitz bound; the least such bound is the gradient Lipschitz modulus on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective is Lipschitz-gradient smooth on a set when the norm of the difference between gradients at any two points is at most a fixed constant times the distance between those points.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(D\).
The same norm is used on the domain and gradient range in the displayed Euclidean formulation.
Convexity of \(D\) is imposed when invoking segmentwise Taylor bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f\) is an \(L\)-Lipschitz map on \(D\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(x,y\in D\), \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|^2\le L^2\|x-y\|^2\).
If \(f\in C^2\) on a convex neighborhood of \(D\), the condition follows from \(\|\nabla^2f(z)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L\) there; conversely it implies this Hessian bound wherever the Hessian exists.
special_cases_latex: \(L=0\) means that \(f\) is affine on each connected component of \(D\).
For a quadratic \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+b^Tx+c\) with symmetric \(Q\), one may take \(L=\|Q\|_{\mathrm{op}}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(x,y\in D\), \(|f(y)-f(x)-\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)|\le\tfrac L2\|y-x\|^2\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Twice continuous differentiability and the Hessian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar-valued second-order smoothness at a point and throughout an open set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuously differentiable function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is twice continuously differentiable at $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ if every second partial derivative $\partial^2f/(\partial x_i\partial x_j)$ exists and is continuous at $x$, for $1\le i,j\le n$. Its Hessian is the matrix $\nabla^2f(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ with $[\nabla^2f(x)]_{ij}=\partial^2f(x)/(\partial x_i\partial x_j)$. For an open set $D\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, $f\in C^2(D)$ means that $f$ is twice continuously differentiable at every point of $D$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable scalar function is twice continuously differentiable when all second partial derivatives exist and are continuous. These derivatives form its Hessian, and C2 on an open set means this holds everywhere on that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [\nabla^2f(x)]_{ij}=\frac{\partial^2f(x)}{\partial x_i\partial x_j},\quad 1\le i,j\le n,\qquad f\in C^2(D)\iff f\text{ is twice continuously differentiable at every point of }D.

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz-Hessian Objectives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform second-order smoothness on a convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f\) be twice differentiable on an open set containing \(D\). The Hessian is \(M\)-Lipschitz on \(D\) when
\[\lVert\nabla^2f(x)-\nabla^2f(y)\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le M\lVert x-y\rVert\qquad(x,y\in D).\]
It follows that every \(x,y\in D\), with \(s=y-x\), satisfy
\[\left|f(y)-f(x)-\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}s-\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x)s\right|\le\frac{M}{6}\lVert s\rVert^3.\]
Thus quadratic models have a uniform cubic function-value remainder.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Lipschitz Hessian changes at most linearly with distance and gives a cubic bound on the error of the quadratic Taylor model.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Hessian Lipschitz condition implies the displayed cubic Taylor-remainder bound.

notation.meaning: operator norm induced by the Euclidean norm

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) has the derivatives required by the selected interface.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic exact or controlled-error local information; query cost is separate from mathematical availability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A derivative-information interface for \(f\) is a query map \(\mathcal O_f:Q	o A\) whose input contains a point \(x\in U\) and, when appropriate, a direction \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), and whose output contains declared derivative data. Canonical exact interfaces are \(x\mapsto(f(x),
abla f(x))\), \(x\mapsto(f(x),
abla f(x),
abla^2f(x))\), and \((x,v)\mapsto(f(x),
abla f(x),
abla^2f(x)v)\). A controlled-error interface returns \(\widetilde g(x)\) or \(\widetilde H(x)v\) together with stated error bounds relative to the exact quantities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A derivative interface specifies the legal queries and exactly which local derivatives, derivative actions, or controlled approximations are returned. Full Hessian and Hessian–vector interfaces are distinct even though they encode the same linear map after sufficiently many queries.
assumptions_latex: Every query point belongs to the differentiability domain of \(f\).
Exact interfaces return the mathematical derivative without approximation.
An inexact interface declares the norm and tolerance governing each error.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The query domain, answer type, and accuracy relation define the derivative information available to an algorithm.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A full Hessian answer represents the linear operator \(v\mapsto\nabla^2f(x)v\) by its matrix.
An automatic-differentiation interface is exact up to arithmetic effects when it evaluates derivatives by applying the chain rule to the computational graph.
special_cases_latex: Gradient-only, explicit-Hessian, and Hessian–vector product interfaces are canonical instances.
Finite differences produce constructed, generally inexact derivative interfaces.
immediate_consequences_latex: Oracle-complexity statements must specify which query type counts as one call.
Matrix-free access permits Krylov operations without materializing \(\nabla^2f(x)\).
boundary_notes: The interface does not assert that returned information is cheap to compute.
Stochastic unbiased estimators require additional probabilistic specifications and are outside this deterministic definition.

children.title: Gradient-Oracle Interface

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Oracle Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact deterministic first-order information interface.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a differentiable objective \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\), an exact gradient oracle is a mapping \(\mathcal{O}_g:D\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying
\[\mathcal{O}_g(x)=\nabla f(x)\qquad(x\in D).\]
One oracle query at \(x\) returns the full gradient vector. The query supports the stationarity measure \(\lVert\mathcal{O}_g(x)\rVert\); in particular, \(x\) is first-order stationary exactly when \(\mathcal{O}_g(x)=0\). When function values are also returned, the combined first-order oracle may be written \(\mathcal{O}_{f,g}(x)=(f(x),\nabla f(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact gradient oracle returns the full gradient at a queried point, enabling descent directions and the norm-based test for first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}_g(x)=\nabla f(x)\), and \(\lVert\mathcal{O}_g(x)\rVert=0\) exactly characterizes first-order stationarity.

children.title: Explicit-Hessian Interface
children.top_down_role: Direct matrix access for inertia, factorization, and spectral certification.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit-Hessian Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact deterministic access to the full Hessian matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a twice differentiable objective \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\), an explicit-Hessian oracle is a mapping \(\mathcal{O}_H:D\to\mathbb{S}^n\) satisfying
\[\mathcal{O}_H(x)=\nabla^2f(x)\qquad(x\in D).\]
A query materializes all matrix entries, permitting matrix factorizations, inertia computations, and direct eigenvalue tests. Together with an exact gradient oracle, the returned pair certifies second-order stationarity at \(x\) precisely when \(\mathcal{O}_g(x)=0\) and \(\mathcal{O}_H(x)\succeq0\); a negative eigenvalue of \(\mathcal{O}_H(x)\) supplies a direction of negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit-Hessian oracle returns the entire Hessian matrix, allowing direct factorization, inertia computation, and spectral tests for second-order stationarity or negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}_H(x)=\nabla^2f(x)\), enabling direct verification of \(\mathcal{O}_H(x)\succeq0\) or detection of negative curvature.

notation.meaning: real symmetric n by n matrices

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The full-Hessian interface and its stationarity and negative-curvature uses are mathematically appropriate, and definition is the correct content kind. The record supplies no citation for the oracle interface or its asserted capabilities.

The matrix entries are available for arbitrary matrix operations, including factorization, inertia computation, Rayleigh quotients, and multiplication by chosen vectors.

children.top_down_role: Matrix-free curvature access for Krylov and truncated-Newton methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Hessian–Vector Product Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact matrix-free curvature interface at a queried point and direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a twice differentiable objective \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\), a Hessian–vector product oracle is a mapping \(\mathcal{O}_{Hv}:D\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying
\[\mathcal{O}_{Hv}(x,v)=\nabla^2f(x)v.\]
The interface returns the action of the Hessian without requiring its entries to be formed or stored. Repeated products at fixed \(x\) permit Krylov-subspace constructions
\[\mathcal{K}_k(\nabla^2f(x),v)=\operatorname{span}\{v,\nabla^2f(x)v,\ldots,(\nabla^2f(x))^{k-1}v\},\]
which support approximate linear solves and extremal-eigenvalue estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hessian–vector oracle returns curvature applied to a chosen vector without forming the matrix, supporting Krylov, truncated-Newton, and spectral procedures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each query returns \(\nabla^2f(x)v\), and repeated queries generate the displayed Krylov subspace.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A constructed derivative interface is a map whose returned derivative data are computed from more primitive representations rather than supplied independently. A finite-difference Hessian action is \(\widetilde H(x;h)v=[\nabla f(x+hv)-\nabla f(x)]/h\). An automatic-differentiation interface applies the chain rule to the elementary-operation graph and returns analytic derivatives of the represented computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constructed interfaces obtain derivatives from function evaluations, gradient differences, or a computational graph. Finite differences are inexact and step-size dependent; automatic differentiation evaluates derivatives of the represented computation up to arithmetic effects.

The required derivatives exist with enough regularity for the stated truncation bounds.

With Lipschitz Hessian, forward Hessian–vector differences have truncation error \(O(h\|v\|^2)\).

Automatic differentiation is distinct from symbolic differentiation and finite differencing.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Difference Derivative Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward and centered coordinate differences constructed from function evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be defined near \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(e_i\) be the \(i\)-th coordinate vector, and let \(h>0\). The forward and centered finite-difference gradient components are
\[(g_h^{\mathrm F}(x))_i=\frac{f(x+he_i)-f(x)}{h},\qquad (g_h^{\mathrm C}(x))_i=\frac{f(x+he_i)-f(x-he_i)}{2h}.\]
If \(f\in C^2\) locally, then \((g_h^{\mathrm F}(x))_i=\partial_i f(x)+O(h)\). If the one-dimensional restriction along \(e_i\) has a bounded third derivative locally, then \((g_h^{\mathrm C}(x))_i=\partial_i f(x)+O(h^2)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Function evaluations at coordinate perturbations approximate gradient components; forward differences are first-order accurate, while centered differences are second-order accurate under stronger smoothness.
assumptions_latex: \(h>0\), and every displayed evaluation point lies in the domain of \(f\).
The stated local derivative regularity holds along each sampled coordinate line.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_h^{\mathrm F}(x)=\nabla f(x)+O(h)\) componentwise, while \(g_h^{\mathrm C}(x)=\nabla f(x)+O(h^2)\) under bounded third directional derivatives.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounds the componentwise and infinity-norm errors of a coordinate central-difference gradient approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:D\subset\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R} satisfy the conditions referenced as Theorem 1.2.23, with constant \gamma. Let the relevant norm satisfy \|e_i\|=1 for i=1,\ldots,n, let h\ne0, and assume x+h e_i,x-h e_i\in D for every i. Define a\in\mathbb{R}^n by
\[
a_i=\frac{f(x+h e_i)-f(x-h e_i)}{2h}.
\]
Then, for every i=1,\ldots,n,
\[
|a_i-[\nabla f(x)]_i|\le\frac{\gamma}{6}h^2.
\]
If the \ell_\infty norm is used, then
\[
\|a-\nabla f(x)\|_\infty\le\frac{\gamma}{6}h^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the smoothness conditions referenced by the source and with both coordinate perturbations in the domain, each central-difference gradient component has error at most gamma h squared divided by six. With the infinity norm, the full gradient error has the same bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate Forward- and Central-Difference Derivative Approximations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives coordinate finite-difference formulas, the forward-difference evaluation count, and the stated first-order forward-error boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}, let h>0, and suppose the required perturbed points are in the domain. Define the coordinate forward difference by
\[
g_i^{\mathrm{FD}}(x;h)=\frac{f(x+h e_i)-f(x)}{h}.
\]
All n coordinates can be constructed from evaluations at x and x+h e_i for i=1,\ldots,n, requiring n+1 evaluation points. Under the derivative-remainder condition invoked in the extract with constant \gamma,
\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(x)=g_i^{\mathrm{FD}}(x;h)+\delta_{i,h},\qquad |\delta_{i,h}|\le\frac{\gamma}{2}h,
\]
so the coordinate forward-difference error is O(h). The coordinate central difference is
\[
g_i^{\mathrm{CD}}(x;h)=\frac{f(x+h e_i)-f(x-h e_i)}{2h}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The i-th forward-difference derivative approximation is [f(x+h e_i)-f(x)]/h. Constructing all n coordinates uses function values at n+1 points. Under the remainder condition invoked by the source, each coordinate error is at most gamma h/2 and hence is O(h). The corresponding central difference is [f(x+h e_i)-f(x-h e_i)]/(2h).
assumptions_latex: x+h e_i\text{ and, for the central formula, }x-h e_i\text{ are in the domain}
\text{The derivative-remainder condition invoked in the extract holds with constant }\gamma
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g_i^{\mathrm{FD}}(x;h)=\frac{f(x+h e_i)-f(x)}{h},\quad \left|\partial_i f(x)-g_i^{\mathrm{FD}}(x;h)\right|\le\frac{\gamma}{2}h=O(h),\quad g_i^{\mathrm{CD}}(x;h)=\frac{f(x+h e_i)-f(x-h e_i)}{2h},\quad N_{\mathrm{FD}}=n+1.

children.title: Automatic-Differentiation Derivative Access
children.top_down_role: Derivative information produced through automatic-differentiation systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Automatic-Differentiation Derivative Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact chain-rule differentiation of a finite computational graph in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose a scalar objective is represented by a finite acyclic computational graph whose elementary nodes \(z_j=\phi_j(z_{p_1},\ldots,z_{p_r})\) are differentiable. Forward-mode automatic differentiation propagates tangents by
\[\dot z_j=\sum_{\ell=1}^r \partial_\ell\phi_j\,\dot z_{p_\ell},\]
so seeding an input tangent \(v\) returns the directional derivative \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}v\). Reverse mode propagates adjoints from the scalar output by
\[\bar z_{p_\ell}\mathrel{+}=\bar z_j\,\partial_\ell\phi_j,\]
and returns every component of \(\nabla f(x)\). In exact arithmetic these are chain-rule derivatives of the represented program, not finite-difference approximations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Automatic differentiation applies the chain rule through a computational graph: forward mode returns directional derivatives, and reverse mode returns the gradient of a scalar output.
assumptions_latex: The objective is represented by a finite acyclic graph of differentiable elementary operations.
All operations are evaluated where their derivatives exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Forward propagation returns \(\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}v\), while reverse propagation returns \(\nabla f(x)\) in exact arithmetic.

notation.meaning: forward-mode tangent at graph node j
reverse-mode adjoint at graph node j

abla f(x)\|_2\le\delta_g,\qquad \|\widetilde H(x)-
abla^2f(x)\|_2\le\delta_H.\] The reported tolerances are part of the oracle output or are fixed certified bounds. Consequently, \(\|\widetilde g(x)\|_2\le\varepsilon-\delta_g\) implies \(\|

knowledge_statements.title: Uncontrolled Inexactness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of stationarity certification when derivative errors have no valid bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f_a(t)=\tfrac12(t-a)^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), where \(a\in\mathbb{R}\). At \(t=0\), the true derivative is \(f_a'(0)=-a\). An uncontrolled inexact oracle may nevertheless report \(\widetilde g(0)=0\), with unreported error \(a\). Thus the reported residual is zero while \(|f_a'(0)|=|a|\) can be arbitrarily large. Hence no implication of the form \(\|\widetilde g(x)\|\le\varepsilon\Rightarrow\|\nabla f(x)\|\le C\varepsilon\), with finite universal \(C\), is valid without an error bound or another structural relation between \(\widetilde g\) and \(\nabla f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With unbounded derivative error, an oracle may report zero residual at points whose true gradient is arbitrarily large, so stationarity cannot be certified.
assumptions_latex: \widetilde g(0)=0\text{ is permitted without an error bound}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{a\in\mathbb{R}}|f_a'(0)|=\infty\text{ while }|\widetilde g(0)|=0

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact unconstrained differential criticality through second order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(x\) is a first-order stationary point when \(
abla f(x)=0\). If \(f\) is twice differentiable at \(x\), then \(x\) is a second-order stationary point when \(
abla f(x)=0\) and \(
abla^2f(x)\succeq0\). A twice differentiable critical point is nondegenerate when \(\det
abla^2f(x)
e0\); a nondegenerate second-order stationary point therefore has \(
abla^2f(x)\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First-order stationarity means zero gradient. Second-order stationarity additionally requires a positive-semidefinite Hessian. A critical point is nondegenerate when its Hessian has no zero eigenvalue.
assumptions_latex: The derivatives appearing in each level exist at \(x\).
The Hessian is symmetric in the Euclidean coordinates used.
Criticality is assessed for unconstrained perturbations in every direction.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained smooth stationarity in finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A point \(x_\star\in U\) is first-order stationary, or critical, when \[\nabla f(x_\star)=0.\] Equivalently, every directional derivative vanishes: \(Df(x_\star)[d]=0\) for all \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Every unconstrained local minimizer or local maximizer lying in \(U\) is first-order stationary, although stationarity alone does not distinguish minima, maxima, and saddle points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior point is first-order stationary exactly when its gradient, equivalently every directional derivative, vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla f(x_\star)=0\iff Df(x_\star)[d]=0\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n

knowledge_statements.title: Nondegenerate Criticality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Morse-type nondegeneracy for unconstrained smooth critical points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:U	o\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A critical point \(x_\star\in U\) is nondegenerate when \[
abla f(x_\star)=0,\qquad \det
abla^2f(x_\star)
e0.\] Equivalently, every eigenvalue of \(
abla^2f(x_\star)\) is nonzero. The Morse index is the number of negative Hessian eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. Index zero characterizes a strict local minimum; index \(n\) characterizes a strict local maximum; intermediate index characterizes a strict saddle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical point is nondegenerate when its Hessian is nonsingular; its negative-eigenvalue count classifies it as a minimum, maximum, or saddle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \det\nabla^2f(x_\star)\ne0

notation.meaning: number of negative Hessian eigenvalues counted with multiplicity

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Criticality Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Taylor-decrement formulation of finite-order unconstrained criticality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\ge1\), let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be \(p\)-times continuously differentiable, and define the order-\(p\) Taylor polynomial at \(x\) by \[T_p(x,d)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^p\frac{1}{j!}\nabla^jf(x)[d]^j.\] For a radius \(\Delta>0\), define \(\phi_{f,p}(x;\Delta)=f(x)-\min_{\|d\|_2\le\Delta}T_p(x,d)\). The point \(x\) satisfies the order-\(p\) Taylor criticality condition at scale \(\Delta\) precisely when \(\phi_{f,p}(x;\Delta)=0\); approximate order-\(p\) criticality replaces zero by a prescribed nonnegative tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order criticality can be measured by the greatest decrease predicted by the order-p Taylor model within a specified radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi_{f,p}(x;\Delta)=0

notation.meaning: j-th derivative tensor applied j times to d
order-p Taylor polynomial of f at x
maximum Taylor-model decrement within radius Delta

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Taylor-decrement construction is mathematically coherent and the content kind fits an interface condition, but higher-order criticality has multiple conventions. The claim that approximate criticality merely replaces zero by a tolerance also omits any convention-dependent radius or tolerance scaling. A specific authoritative source is required to establish the intended formulation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximate First- and Second-Order Stationarity Certificates
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), \(x\in U\), and tolerances \(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-accuracy unconstrained stationarity targets in the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x\) is an \(\epsilon_g\)-first-order stationary point when \(\|
abla f(x)\|\le\epsilon_g\). If \(f\) is twice differentiable at \(x\), it is an \((\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\)-second-order stationary point when \(\|
abla f(x)\|\le\epsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x))\ge-\epsilon_H\). A certificate consists of the point, tolerances, evaluated residuals, and enough derivative information to validate both inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate first-order stationarity requires a gradient norm no larger than its tolerance. Approximate second-order stationarity additionally permits negative curvature only down to a declared Hessian-eigenvalue tolerance.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) for the first-order certificate.
\(f\) is twice differentiable at \(x\) for the second-order certificate.
The norm, matrix inner product, and scaling conventions are fixed before tolerances are interpreted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate is valid exactly when \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\epsilon_g\) and, at second order, \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq-\epsilon_HI\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The curvature inequality is equivalent to \(v^T\nabla^2f(x)v\ge-\epsilon_H\|v\|^2\) for every \(v\in\mathbb R^n\).
Using residuals \(r_1=\|\nabla f(x)\|\) and \(r_2=\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\}\), validity is \(r_1\le\epsilon_g\) and \(r_2\le\epsilon_H\).
special_cases_latex: \((\epsilon_g,)\) imposes exact nonnegative curvature but approximate first-order stationarity.
\((0,0)\) recovers exact second-order stationarity.
immediate_consequences_latex: A first-order stopping rule based only on \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\) cannot exclude a strict saddle.
The pair \((\epsilon_g,epsilon_H)\) makes the requested accuracy explicit for complexity comparisons.
boundary_notes: Absolute tolerances are not invariant under arbitrary rescaling of variables or the objective.
The supplied sources contain a numerical gradient-norm termination criterion but not a complete authoritative statement of the paired gradient-and-eigenvalue convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate First-Order Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute Euclidean first-order residual for unconstrained smooth optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:U	o\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\varepsilon_g\ge0\). A point \(x\in U\) is an \(\varepsilon_g\)-first-order stationary point when \[\|
abla f(x)\|_2\le\varepsilon_g.\] The residual \(r_1(x)=\|
abla f(x)\|_2\) is directly computable under exact gradient access. When only \(\widetilde g(x)\) with certified error \(\|\widetilde g(x)-
abla f(x)\|_2\le\delta_g\) is available, the verifiable condition \(\|\widetilde g(x)\|_2+\delta_g\le\varepsilon_g\) suffices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate first-order stationarity requires the gradient norm to be no larger than a prescribed tolerance, with oracle error included when necessary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\nabla f(x)\|_2\le\varepsilon_g

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The absolute gradient-norm definition and the certified-oracle sufficient condition follow correctly from the error bound and match the leaf. No source with a specific locator is supplied for the selected approximate-stationarity convention.

children.title: Approximate Second-Order Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Joint finite-accuracy gradient and curvature targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Second-Order Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint gradient and minimum-Hessian-eigenvalue accuracy criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H\ge0\). A point \(x\in U\) is an \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\)-second-order stationary point when \[\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\le\varepsilon_g,\qquad \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\ge-\varepsilon_H.\] Thus the first inequality bounds first-order criticality error, while the second excludes curvature more negative than \(-\varepsilon_H\). At \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)=(0,0)\), this definition reduces to exact second-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate second-order stationarity jointly bounds the gradient norm and the magnitude of the Hessian's most negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\nabla f(x)\|_2\le\varepsilon_g,\quad \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\ge-\varepsilon_H

notation.meaning: smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The joint gradient and minimum-eigenvalue criterion is a standard, precise approximate second-order stationarity convention and correctly reduces to exact second-order stationarity at zero tolerances. Because conventions can couple or rescale these tolerances, the absent authoritative locator prevents acceptance.

children.title: Scale-Aware Stationarity Measures
children.top_down_role: Criticality measures adjusted for norms, variable scaling, or local magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable at \(x\). Let \(s_i>0\) be a typical magnitude for variable \(x_i\), and let \(F>0\) be a typical objective magnitude.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, smooth, unconstrained first-order stationarity with fixed componentwise variable scales and an objective-value scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}(x;s,F):=\max_{1\le i\le n}\frac{|\nabla_i f(x)|\max\{|x_i|,s_i\}}{\max\{|f(x)|,F\}}.\] For \(\varepsilon\ge0\), the point \(x\) is scale-aware \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when \(\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}(x;s,F)\le\varepsilon\). The positive floors \(s_i\) and \(F\) make the measure well-defined when a coordinate or the objective value is near zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a differentiable objective, scale each gradient component by the larger of the current coordinate magnitude and its typical magnitude, divide by the larger of the current objective magnitude and its typical magnitude, and take the largest resulting component. A point is scale-aware \(\varepsilon\)-stationary exactly when this maximum is at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) satisfies the scale-aware stationarity certificate precisely when \(\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}(x;s,F)\le\varepsilon\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(D(x;s)=\operatorname{diag}(\max\{|x_i|,s_i\})\), \(\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}(x;s,F)=\|D(x;s)\nabla f(x)\|_\infty/\max\{|f(x)|,F\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(s_i=1\) and \(F=1\), the measure uses the conventional floors \(\max\{|x_i|,1\}\) and \(\max\{|f(x)|,1\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Because every denominator is positive, \(\mu_{\mathrm{sc}}(x;s,F)=0\) if and only if \(\nabla f(x)=0\).
When units are changed together with the corresponding typical magnitudes, the componentwise relative-gradient interpretation is preserved.
boundary_notes: This definition is not invariant under adding an arbitrary constant to \(f\), because its objective scale uses \(|f(x)|\).
It is a first-order certificate and does not exclude maxima or saddle points.

notation.meaning: Positive typical magnitude of the objective.

children.title: Relative Stationarity Measures

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Stationarity Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensionless first-order residual relative to an explicit positive reference scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r(x)\ge0\) be an absolute stationarity residual and let \(s(x)>0\) be a declared reference scale having the same units as \(r(x)\). The associated relative stationarity measure is \[r_{\mathrm{rel}}(x)=\frac{r(x)}{s(x)}.\] The point \(x\) is relatively \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when \(r_{\mathrm{rel}}(x)\le\varepsilon\). For first-order unconstrained criticality one may take \(r(x)=\|\nabla f(x)\|_*\), where the dual norm matches the chosen variable norm. The scale rule \(s\) is part of the certificate and must be reported for comparisons to be meaningful.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative stationarity divides an absolute residual by a positive declared reference scale; the scale rule is an essential part of the certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_{\mathrm{rel}}(x)=r(x)/s(x)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The ratio definition is internally consistent, dimensionless under the stated units assumption, and appropriately requires disclosure of the scale rule. Relative stationarity normalizations are convention-dependent, however, and no inspectable source locator is supplied.

children.title: Scaling-Invariance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes where stationarity assessments remain stable under admissible rescaling.

knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Invariance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate invariance of metric-scaled first-order residuals under invertible linear reparameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x=Sy\) for an invertible matrix \(S\), define \(\widehat f(y)=f(Sy)\), and equip the \(x\)-coordinates with a symmetric positive-definite metric \(M_x\). Transport the metric by \(M_y=S^	op M_xS\). Since \(
abla\widehat f(y)=S^	op
abla f(x)\), \[\|
abla\widehat f(y)\|_{M_y^{-1}}=\|
abla f(x)\|_{M_x^{-1}}.\] Thus metric-scaled stationarity is invariant under invertible linear coordinate changes when both the gradient and metric are transformed consistently. Using the untransformed Euclidean norm generally destroys this invariance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A metric-scaled gradient residual is unchanged by invertible linear reparameterization when the metric is transported with the coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|\nabla\widehat f(y)\|_{M_y^{-1}}=\|\nabla f(Sy)\|_{M_x^{-1}}

notation.meaning: primal metrics in the two coordinate systems

children.title: Normalization Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of practical certificates on normalization choices or vanishing reference magnitudes.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative dependence of relative stationarity certificates on the chosen normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r(x)\ge0\) be an absolute stationarity residual, and let \(s_1(x),s_2(x)>0\) be two normalization rules. Define \(\rho_i(x)=r(x)/s_i(x)\). If constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) satisfy \(c\,s_1(x)\le s_2(x)\le C\,s_1(x)\) throughout a comparison region, then \[\frac{1}{C}\rho_1(x)\le\rho_2(x)\le\frac{1}{c}\rho_1(x).\] Without such uniform comparability, one normalization can declare a sequence approximately stationary while another does not; therefore numerical tolerances attached to normalized residuals are not interpretable independently of the normalization rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Comparable normalizations yield equivalent residuals up to fixed factors; incomparable normalizations can produce conflicting approximate-stationarity judgments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C^{-1}\rho_1(x)\le\rho_2(x)\le c^{-1}\rho_1(x)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The comparison inequalities follow correctly from the assumed bounds on the two positive normalizations, and the content is properly classified as a property. The broader sensitivity conclusion is sound, but the record supplies neither an external source nor an explicit standard-field rationale meeting the evidence contract.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q\ge1\), let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be \(q\)-times continuously differentiable near \(x\), and let \(T_{f,j}(x;d)=f(x)+\sum_{\ell=1}^j\nabla^\ell f(x)[d]^\ell/\ell!\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth unconstrained approximate local minimality, formulated through radius-restricted Taylor-model decrements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(j\in\{1,\ldots,q\}\) and \(\delta>0\), define \[\phi_{f,j}^{\delta}(x):=f(x)-\min_{\|d\|\le\delta}T_{f,j}(x;d).\] Given tolerances \(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_q\ge0\), a radius \(\delta>0\), and normalization constants \(c_j>0\), call \(x\) a \((q,\boldsymbol\epsilon,\delta)\)-Taylor-certified point when \[\phi_{f,j}^{\delta}(x)\le c_j\epsilon_j\delta^j\qquad(j=1,\ldots,q).\] The certificate-strength hierarchy is the nested family obtained by appending the order-\(q\) inequality while retaining every lower-order inequality with the same norm, radius, and tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The order-\(j\) certificate measures the largest predicted decrease of the degree-\(j\) Taylor model inside a ball of radius \(\delta\). An order-\(q\) certified point must pass every test from order one through order \(q\). Consequently, a higher-level certificate is stronger by definition when it contains the unchanged lower-level tests.
assumptions_latex: The minimum defining \(\phi_{f,j}^{\delta}(x)\) is taken over a compact norm ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The hierarchy level \(q\) is the conjunction \(\bigwedge_{j=1}^q\{\phi_{f,j}^{\delta}(x)\le c_j\epsilon_j\delta^j\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\phi_{f,j}^{\delta}(x)=\max_{\|d\|\le\delta}\bigl(f(x)-T_{f,j}(x;d)\bigr)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(j=1\) and the Euclidean norm, \(\phi_{f,1}^{\delta}(x)=\delta\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\).
For \(j=2\), the decrement is the optimal predicted reduction of the quadratic Taylor model on the radius-\(\delta\) ball.
immediate_consequences_latex: With identical lower-order parameters, every level-\(q\) certificate implies the level-\((q-1)\) certificate.
Failure at any order \(j\le q\) prevents certification at level \(q\).
boundary_notes: No supplied source locator was found that fixes the normalization constants or this exact hierarchy; the constants are therefore left explicit.
Different higher-order approximate-minimizer families need not be equivalent when they use different radii, norms, tolerances, or derivative tests.

notation.meaning: Degree-\(j\) Taylor polynomial of \(f\) at \(x\) in displacement \(d\).
Maximum degree-\(j\) Taylor-model decrement in the radius-\(\delta\) ball.

children.title: Strong Higher-Order Certificates
children.top_down_role: Higher-order approximate-minimizer certificates using stronger local requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Higher-Order Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Taylor-model certificate combining accessible first- and second-order tests with uniform order-p model control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p\ge 3\), and define \(T_p(x;s)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{1}{j!}D^j f(x)[s]^j\). A point \(x\) has a strong \((p,\Delta,\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H,\eta)\)-certificate when
\[\|\nabla f(x)\|\le \varepsilon_g,\qquad \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(x))\ge-\varepsilon_H,\qquad \min_{\|s\|\le\Delta}\bigl(T_p(x;s)-f(x)\bigr)\ge-\eta.\]
Thus no step in the radius-\(\Delta\) ball yields Taylor-model decrease exceeding \(\eta\), while the usual approximate first- and second-order conditions also hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong certificate bounds the gradient, excludes substantial negative curvature, and verifies that the full order-p Taylor model has no significant decrease in a prescribed ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) satisfies uniform order-\(p\) Taylor-model control together with approximate first- and second-order stationarity.

notation.meaning: Order-p Taylor polynomial of f at x evaluated at displacement s.
The jth derivative tensor applied to j copies of s.
Smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally precise and fits the strong-certificate leaf, but the proposed strong higher-order convention and its tolerance normalization have no cited source. Source support is required before treating this particular combination of Taylor-model, gradient, and Hessian conditions as established terminology.

children.title: Weak Higher-Order Certificates
children.top_down_role: Higher-order certificates based on less restrictive local requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Higher-Order Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Derivative-accessible relaxation retaining only approximate first- and second-order consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any declared order \(p\ge2\), a point \(x\) has a weak \((p,\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\)-certificate when
\[\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon_g\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(x))\ge-\varepsilon_H.\]
The order label records the surrounding higher-order analysis, but this weak certificate imposes no uniform condition on \(D^j f(x)\) for \(j\ge3\) and no global minimization condition on an order-\(p\) Taylor model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weak higher-order certificate checks only a small gradient and nearly positive-semidefinite Hessian, without controlling higher derivatives or the full Taylor model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is an approximate second-order stationary point, independently of derivatives of orders \(3,\ldots,p\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formula is a valid approximate second-order stationarity condition, but calling it a weak order-p certificate while imposing no order-p condition is a convention requiring evidence. No source supports the terminology or the role of the otherwise inert order label.

children.title: Certificate Implication Hierarchy
children.top_down_role: Logical relationships among higher-order certificate strengths.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Implication Hierarchy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implications under the strong and weak certificate conventions used in this shard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p\ge3\). Every strong \((p,\Delta,\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H,\eta)\)-certificate is a weak \((p,\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\)-certificate. Moreover, strong certification is monotone under radius reduction and tolerance relaxation: if \(0<\Delta'\le\Delta\), \(\varepsilon'_g\ge\varepsilon_g\), \(\varepsilon'_H\ge\varepsilon_H\), and \(\eta'\ge\eta\), then the strong certificate at \((\Delta,\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H,\eta)\) implies the strong certificate at \((\Delta',\varepsilon'_g,\varepsilon'_H,\eta')\). The reverse implication from weak to strong does not follow without additional higher-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong certification implies weak certification and survives smaller radii or looser tolerances; weak first- and second-order checks alone do not imply Taylor-model control.
assumptions_latex: The strong and weak certificates are defined as in the preceding records.
\(0<\Delta'\le\Delta\) and all primed tolerances are no smaller than their unprimed counterparts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathrm{Strong}_p\Rightarrow\mathrm{Weak}_p\), while \(\mathrm{Weak}_p\not\Rightarrow\mathrm{Strong}_p\) in general.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The forward implication and monotonicity follow from the shard's proposed definitions, and the property fits the implication-hierarchy leaf. However, those definitions are themselves unsourced, and the general failure of the reverse implication needs an inspectable source or explicitly sourced counterexample.

children.title: Computational Accessibility Gap
children.top_down_role: Differences in the information or computational effort needed to assess certificate families.

knowledge_statements.title: Computational Accessibility Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation between derivative-level checks and uniform Taylor-model verification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a twice differentiable objective, the weak certificate can be tested from \(\nabla f(x)\) and the smallest eigenvalue of \(\nabla^2 f(x)\). In contrast, the strong order-\(p\) certificate requires evaluating
\[\min_{\|s\|\le\Delta}\bigl(T_p(x;s)-f(x)\bigr).\]
When \(p\ge3\), this is generally a nonconvex polynomial optimization problem, even though every derivative tensor at \(x\) is explicitly available. Consequently, efficient verification of the weak certificate does not by itself provide an efficient procedure for verifying the strong certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient and minimum-eigenvalue tests are directly computable, whereas strong certification requires solving a generally nonconvex polynomial problem over a ball.
assumptions_latex: The derivative tensors defining \(T_p(x;\cdot)\) are available explicitly.
Computational accessibility refers to deterministic finite-dimensional derivative evaluation and optimization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Efficient weak-certificate verification does not imply efficient strong-certificate verification for general \(p\ge3\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly identifies a qualitative accessibility gap, but the assertions that the eigenvalue test is efficient and that strong verification is generally a nonconvex polynomial-optimization task depend on an explicit computational model and supporting source. The failure-boundary content kind otherwise fits the leaf.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Classical First- and Second-Order Local Optimality System
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\), and let \(x_*\in D\). A local minimizer satisfies \(f(x_*)\le f(x)\) throughout some neighborhood of \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional unconstrained minimization at an interior point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The classical local optimality system consists of three derivative principles. If \(f\in C^1\) and \(x_*\) is a local minimizer, then \(
abla f(x_*)=0\). If \(f\in C^2\) and \(x_*\) is a local minimizer, then additionally \(d^	op
abla^2f(x_*)d\ge0\) for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\). Conversely, if \(f\in C^2\), \(
abla f(x_*)=0\), and \(d^	op
abla^2f(x_*)d>0\) for every \(d
e0\), then \(x_*\) is a strict isolated local minimizer. These implications are respectively the first-order necessary, second-order necessary, and second-order sufficient principles.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a smooth interior local minimum the gradient must vanish. With two continuous derivatives, the Hessian must also be positive semidefinite. Conversely, a stationary point with a positive-definite Hessian is a strict isolated local minimum. Together these implications form the classical derivative-based local optimality system.
assumptions_latex: The first-order implication assumes \(f\in C^1(D)\); the second-order implications assume \(f\in C^2(D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(x_*	ext{ local minimum}\Rightarrow
abla f(x_*)=0\), and under \(C^2\), \(x_*	ext{ local minimum}\Rightarrow
abla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\), while \(
abla f(x_*)=0\) and \(
abla^2f(x_*)\succ0\Rightarrow x_*	ext{ strict isolated local minimum}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\) means \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_*))\ge0\).
\(\nabla^2f(x_*)\succ0\) means \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_*))>0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the conditions become \(f'(x_*)=0\), necessary \(f''(x_*)\ge0\), and sufficient \(f''(x_*)>0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A stationary point with an indefinite Hessian is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum.
A singular positive-semidefinite Hessian leaves the local-minimum question unresolved by the classical second-order tests.
boundary_notes: The system is local and gives no global-optimality conclusion for a nonconvex objective.
The positive-definite condition is sufficient but not necessary for a strict local minimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(x^*\in X\), and suppose \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(x^*\). If \(x^*\in\operatorname{int}X\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) over \(X\), then \(

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained finite-dimensional condition for an interior local minimum.

Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable at \(x_*\in U\). If \(x_*\) is a local minimizer of \(f\), then every directional derivative vanishes:
\[Df(x_*)[d]=0\quad\text{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
Equivalently,
\[\nabla f(x_*)=0.\]

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(x_*\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact first-order necessary condition for a smooth unconstrained interior local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The first-order necessary-condition certificate at \(x_*\) is \[
abla f(x_*)=0.\] The associated necessary-condition principle is the implication \[ igl[\exists r>0\  orall x\in D:\ \|x-x_*\|<r\Rightarrow f(x_*)\le f(x) igr]\Longrightarrow
abla f(x_*)=0.\] Equivalently, every directional derivative at \(x_*\) vanishes: \(f'(x_*;d)=
abla f(x_*)^	op d=0\) for all \(d\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable objective at an interior point, local minimality requires the gradient to be zero. This is equivalent to requiring zero first directional derivative in every direction. Passing this test only identifies a first-order stationary point; it does not by itself establish local minimality.
assumptions_latex: \(x_*\) is a local minimizer of \(f\) for the necessary implication.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\iff \nabla f(x_*)^\top d=0\) for every \(d\in\mathbb R^n\).
\(\nabla f(x_*)=0\iff\|\nabla f(x_*)\|=0\) for any norm.
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the condition is \(f'(x_*)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\nabla f(x_*)\ne0\), then \(x_*\) cannot be an unconstrained interior local minimizer.
The condition also holds at smooth interior local maxima.
boundary_notes: Boundary points of constrained domains need not have zero gradient.
Stationarity alone does not distinguish minima, maxima, or saddles.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Necessary Condition Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hessian restriction at an unconstrained twice differentiable local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and let \(f:U	o\mathbb{R}\) be twice differentiable at a local minimizer \(x_*\in U\). Then
\[
abla f(x_*)=0\qquad	ext{and}\qquad d^{\mathsf T}
abla^2 f(x_*)d\ge0\quad	ext{for every }d\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
Equivalently, the Hessian \(
abla^2 f(x_*)\) is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior twice differentiable local minimizer, the gradient vanishes and the Hessian is positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\) and \(\nabla^2 f(x_*)\succeq0\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, and let \(x_*\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact second-order necessary conditions for a smooth unconstrained interior local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The second-order necessary-condition certificate at \(x_*\) is the conjunction \[
abla f(x_*)=0,\qquad d^	op
abla^2f(x_*)d\ge0\quad	ext{for every }d\in\mathbb R^n.\] Thus every \(C^2\) interior local minimizer is a second-order critical point. The curvature condition is equivalently \(
abla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\), or \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x_*))\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice continuously differentiable objective can have an unconstrained interior local minimum only at a stationary point whose Hessian is positive semidefinite. Equivalently, the second directional derivative is nonnegative in every direction, or the smallest Hessian eigenvalue is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\iff d^\top\nabla^2f(x_*)d\ge0\) for all \(d\in\mathbb R^n\).
For a symmetric Hessian, \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\iff\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_*))\ge0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(n=1\), the conditions are \(f'(x_*)=0\) and \(f''(x_*)\ge0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A stationary point admitting \(d\) with \(d^\top\nabla^2f(x_*)d<0\) is not a local minimum.
A zero Hessian eigenvalue is permitted by the necessary condition.
boundary_notes: Positive semidefiniteness is not sufficient for local minimality.
The unconstrained condition must be replaced by a tangent- or critical-cone condition in constrained optimization.

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue of the symmetric matrix \(H\).

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Sufficient Condition Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite Hessian test for a strict unconstrained local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, let \(f\in C^2(U)\), and let \(x_*\in U\). If
\[\nabla f(x_*)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\nabla^2 f(x_*)\succ0,\]
then there exist \(r>0\) and \(c>0\) such that
\[f(x)\ge f(x_*)+c\|x-x_*\|^2\quad\text{whenever }\|x-x_*\|<r.\]
Hence \(x_*\) is a strict local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary point with positive-definite Hessian is a strict local minimizer and satisfies a local quadratic-growth bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exist \(r,c>0\) giving local quadratic growth, so \(x_*\) is a strict local minimizer.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, and let \(x_*\in D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact second-order sufficient condition for a strict isolated local minimum in smooth unconstrained optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The second-order sufficient-condition certificate at \(x_*\) is \[
abla f(x_*)=0,\qquad d^	op
abla^2f(x_*)d>0\quad	ext{for every }d\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}.\] Equivalently, \(
abla^2f(x_*)\succ0\), or \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x_*))>0\). A point satisfying this certificate is a strict isolated local minimizer: there exists \(r>0\) such that \(f(x)>f(x_*)\) whenever \(0<\|x-x_*\|<r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary point with a positive-definite Hessian is a strict isolated local minimum. Positive definiteness means strictly positive quadratic curvature in every nonzero direction, equivalently a strictly positive smallest Hessian eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists r>0\ \forall x:\ 0<\|x-x_*\|<r\Rightarrow f(x)>f(x_*)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\succ0\iff\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_*))>0\).
In finite dimensions, positive definiteness is equivalent to the existence of \(m>0\) such that \(d^\top\nabla^2f(x_*)d\ge m\|d\|_2^2\) for every \(d\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The certified minimizer is isolated from other local minimizers in a sufficiently small neighborhood.
The Hessian is nonsingular at a certified point.
boundary_notes: The condition is not necessary: a strict local minimum may have a singular Hessian.
Positive semidefiniteness without positive definiteness does not supply this certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict local extremum from definite curvature on a punctured neighborhood
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Neighborhood-based second-order sufficiency in which curvature may become semidefinite at the stationary point by continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:D	o\mathbb R\), where \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(x^*\in\operatorname{int}D\). Suppose \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable near \(x^*\) and \(
abla f(x^*)=0\). If there exists a neighborhood \(N\) of \(x^*\) such that \(z^T
abla^2 f(x)z>0\) for every \(x\in(N\cap D)\setminus\{x^*\}\) and every \(z
e0\), then \(x^*\) is a strict local minimum. If instead \(z^T
abla^2 f(x)z<0\) throughout that punctured neighborhood for every \(z
e0\), then \(x^*\) is a strict local maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary point is a strict local minimum when the Hessian is positive definite at every distinct nearby point. Negative definiteness throughout the punctured neighborhood similarly gives a strict local maximum.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is twice continuously differentiable near }x^*
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\ \forall x\in(N\cap D)\setminus\{x^*\}\bigr]\Rightarrow x^*\text{ is a strict local minimum};\quad \bigl[\nabla^2f(x)\prec0\ \forall x\in(N\cap D)\setminus\{x^*\}\bigr]\Rightarrow x^*\text{ is a strict local maximum}

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Local-Optimality Tests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional higher-order exclusion test when the Hessian is singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in C^r(U)\), let \(x_*\in U\) satisfy \(
abla f(x_*)=0\), and fix \(d
e0\). Define \(k(d)\) as the least \(j\in\{2,\ldots,r\}\) for which \(D^j f(x_*)[d]^j
e0\), when such an index exists. If \(x_*\) is a local minimizer, then
\[k(d)	ext{ is even}\qquad	ext{and}\qquad D^{k(d)}f(x_*)[d]^{k(d)}>0.\]
Therefore an odd first nonzero directional derivative, or a negative even one, certifies that \(x_*\) is not a local minimizer. If all tested derivatives vanish, the test is inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along every direction, a local minimum's first nonzero derivative must have even order and positive value; otherwise local minimality is excluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the first nonzero derivative along \(d\) is odd or negative, then \(x_*\) is not a local minimizer.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Null-Space Higher-Order Test at a Degenerate Stationary Point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be \(C^p\) near a stationary point \(x_*\), let \(H=\nabla^2f(x_*)\succeq0\) be singular, and let \(N=\ker H\ne\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth unconstrained local discrimination when the first-order condition holds and the semidefinite singular Hessian makes the classical second-order tests inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\in\{3,\ldots,p\}\), define the degree-\(m\) null-space form \[P_m(v):=\frac1{m!}\nabla^m f(x_*)[v]^m,\qquad v\in N.\] Let \(m_*\) be the least \(m\ge3\) for which \(P_m\) is not identically zero on \(N\), when such an order exists. The leading null-space test classifies the sign of \(P_{m_*}\) on \(N\cap\{\|v\|=1\}\): uniform positivity is a positive higher-order certificate, while a negative value is a nonminimality certificate. If no finite \(m_*\) is available, or if the leading form is nonnegative but vanishes in some null direction, this test remains inconclusive.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a stationary point with a singular positive-semidefinite Hessian, second-order curvature does not resolve directions in the Hessian null space. The degenerate test restricts successive higher derivatives to that null space and examines the first nonzero homogeneous form. Its sign supplies the higher-order local diagnostic; unresolved zeros require still finer analysis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The degenerate certificate is the sign classification of the first nonzero restricted form \(P_{m_*}|_N\).
special_cases_latex: If \(n=1\), \(f'(x_*)=f''(x_*)=0\), and the first nonzero derivative has even order and positive value, the leading-form test is positive.
If the first nonzero restricted order is odd, \(P_{m_*}(-v)=-P_{m_*}(v)\), so the form cannot be positive on every nonzero null direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: A negative value of the leading null-space form identifies a direction incompatible with local minimality.
A positive-semidefinite Hessian alone does not settle a degenerate point.
boundary_notes: Mixed terms coupling null and positive-curvature subspaces may require a reduced or splitting analysis; the restricted-form test is not asserted as universally sufficient here.
No supplied locator supports this exact multivariate higher-order formulation.

notation.meaning: Hessian null space at the stationary point.
Degree-\(m\) derivative form restricted to Hessian-null directions.

children.title: Practical Stationarity Test System
children.top_down_role: Practical organization of stationarity tests under scaling, finite precision, and inexact local information.
