children.title: Stationary Manifolds
children.top_down_role: Smooth families of stationary points with tangent and transverse geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth critical families together with their tangent-null and transverse Hessian geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)\). A stationary manifold is an embedded \(C^1\) submanifold \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) such that \(
abla f(x)=0\) for every \(x\in M\). The restriction of \(f\) to each connected component of \(M\) is constant, and \(T_xM\subseteq\ker
abla^2f(x)\). It is Morse--Bott at \(x\) when \(T_xM=\ker
abla^2f(x)\), so the Hessian is nondegenerate on a complementary normal space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary manifold is a smooth family of critical points; its tangent directions are Hessian-null, while Morse–Bott nondegeneracy acts transversely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f)\) and \(T_xM\subseteq\ker\nabla^2f(x)\) for every \(x\in M\).

notation.meaning: set of points where the gradient vanishes
tangent space of M at x

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stationary-manifold and tangent-kernel claims are mathematically coherent under the stated regularity, and the definition fits the topic. The Morse–Bott equality and transverse-nondegeneracy terminology require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Smooth stationary manifold and transverse Hessian
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(M\) be a finite-dimensional smooth Riemannian manifold and \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) a \(C^2\) function. Let \(S\subseteq M\) be a connected embedded submanifold of positive dimension.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonisolated families of stationary points. No transverse nondegeneracy is imposed, so the definition is broader than Morse–Bott geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The submanifold \(S\) is a stationary manifold of \(f\) if \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\) for every \(x\in S\). For each \(x\in S\), differentiation of stationarity along \(S\) gives \(T_xS\subseteq\ker\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\). The transverse Hessian is the induced quadratic form on a chosen normal space \(N_xS=(T_xS)^\perp\); it may be positive definite, negative definite, indefinite, or singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary manifold is a positive-dimensional smooth embedded manifold consisting entirely of critical points. Every tangent direction lies in the Hessian kernel. The Hessian restricted to normal directions describes transverse curvature, but it is allowed to be singular; requiring it to be nonsingular would specialize the definition to Morse–Bott geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f),\qquad T_xS\subseteq\ker\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\quad(\forall x\in S).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The defining stationarity condition is \(df_x=0\) for all \(x\in S\).
For an embedded Euclidean submanifold, \(\nabla f(x)=0\) on \(S\).
special_cases_latex: If the transverse Hessian is positive definite, \(S\) has local-minimum type in normal directions.
If the transverse Hessian is indefinite, \(S\) is a manifold of saddles.
If its kernel equals \(T_xS\) everywhere, \(S\) is Morse–Bott.
immediate_consequences_latex: The objective is constant on connected \(S\).
Stationary manifolds necessarily create Hessian-null tangent modes.
boundary_notes: A nonmanifold stationary set or a union of crossing stationary strata is not a stationary manifold at its singular points.
The inclusion of tangent directions in the Hessian kernel need not be equality.
The definition concerns exact stationarity and does not cover merely small-gradient valleys.

notation.meaning: Normal space used to describe transverse curvature.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: embedded submanifold contained in the critical set, with tangent directions in the Hessian kernel.
A precise source locator supporting this general definition was not inspected.
knowledge_statements.title: Smooth stationary manifold and transverse Hessian

children.title: Symmetry Orbits of Critical Points
children.top_down_role: Equivalent critical points generated by objective invariances.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Orbits of Critical Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical-point families generated by smooth invariance under a group action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) by diffeomorphisms, and suppose \(f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\) for all \(g\in G\) and \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(x_\star\) is critical, then every point of its orbit \(G\cdot x_\star\) is critical. Moreover, when the orbit is an embedded submanifold, \(T_{x_\star}(G\cdot x_\star)\subseteq\ker\nabla^2f(x_\star)\). Thus continuous symmetries produce Hessian-null directions and nonisolated equivalent critical points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Objective invariance transports a critical point along its entire symmetry orbit, and continuous orbit directions lie in the Hessian kernel.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\star\in\operatorname{Crit}(f)\Longrightarrow G\cdot x_\star\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f)\).

notation.meaning: orbit of x under the group action
tangent space to the symmetry orbit

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For a smooth invariant objective, diffeomorphic group actions transport critical points along an orbit, and differentiating the stationary family gives Hessian-null orbit directions. The property fits the leaf, but neither the equivariant-criticality claim nor the orbit-kernel claim has a cited source.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical-point orbit under an objective symmetry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act smoothly on a finite-dimensional smooth manifold \(M\), written \((g,x)\mapsto g\cdot x\). Let \(f:M\to\mathbb R\) be \(C^2\) and \(G\)-invariant: \(f(g\cdot x)=f(x)\) for all \(g\in G\) and \(x\in M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous or discrete objective invariances. Smooth orbit and tangent-space assertions apply to the Lie-group orbit with its standard immersed-submanifold structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a critical point \(x_\star\in\operatorname{Crit}(f)\), its symmetry orbit is \(G\cdot x_\star=\{g\cdot x_\star:g\in G\}\). Invariance makes every point of this orbit critical and gives \(f|_{G\cdot x_\star}\equiv f(x_\star)\). If the orbit is an embedded submanifold, then \(T_x(G\cdot x_\star)\subseteq\ker\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\) for every \(x\in G\cdot x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An objective symmetry maps a critical point to an orbit of equivalent critical points having the same objective value. For a smooth positive-dimensional orbit, infinitesimal symmetry directions are tangent stationary directions and therefore are Hessian-null. Discrete symmetries may produce several equivalent isolated critical points without tangent null directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_\star\in\operatorname{Crit}(f)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad G\cdot x_\star\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f),\qquad f(g\cdot x_\star)=f(x_\star).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The orbit is the equivalence class of \(x_\star\) under \(x\sim y\) when \(y=g\cdot x\) for some \(g\in G\).
Its tangent space is generated by infinitesimal action vectors \(\xi_M(x)\) for \(\xi\) in the Lie algebra of \(G\).
special_cases_latex: A finite group generates a discrete collection of equivalent critical points.
A free continuous group action produces positive-dimensional orbits.
If transverse Hessian nondegeneracy holds, the orbit is a Morse–Bott critical manifold.
immediate_consequences_latex: Continuous nontrivial symmetries prevent Hessian nonsingularity in the unreduced parameterization along the orbit.
Optimization solutions are naturally identified modulo the group action.
boundary_notes: A group orbit may be immersed rather than embedded, and orbit dimension can change at points with different stabilizers.
Hessian covariance under the group action depends on the chosen metric or coordinate representation; the invariant statement is the preservation of criticality and objective value.
Not every stationary manifold is generated by a symmetry.

notation.meaning: Orbit of a point under the group action.
Infinitesimal vector field generated by a Lie-algebra element.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard group-action orbit and invariance-induced preservation of criticality.
No inspected source locator supports all stated smooth-orbit and Hessian-kernel clauses.
knowledge_statements.title: Critical-point orbit under an objective symmetry

children.title: Singular Stationary Sets
children.top_down_role: Nonmanifold critical sets and intersections of stationary strata.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Stationary Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Critical sets that fail local smooth-manifold regularity at a point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f\in C^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\), write \(S=\{x:\nabla f(x)=0\}\). A point \(x_\star\in S\) is singular for the stationary set if no neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_\star\) makes \(S\cap U\) an embedded \(C^1\) submanifold of fixed dimension. The stationary set is singular when it contains such a point. Typical mechanisms include intersections of stationary strata, branches of different dimensions, cusps, and rank changes in the gradient equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular stationary set is a gradient-zero set that is not locally a smooth manifold of fixed dimension at some critical point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\star\in S\) is singular precisely when \(S\) lacks local embedded-manifold structure at \(x_\star\).

notation.meaning: neighborhood of the point under classification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a coherent local nonmanifold definition matching the stated role, with variables and regularity specified. A source from differential topology, singularity theory, or stratified critical-set analysis is required to support the terminology and listed mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular point of a stationary set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be \(C^2\) on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(S=\{x\in U:\nabla f(x)=0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local geometric definition for critical sets that fail to be smooth manifolds, including intersections, cusps, and points where stationary-stratum dimension changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x_\star\in S\) is a singular stationary-set point if there is no neighborhood \(V\) of \(x_\star\) for which \(S\cap V\) is a \(C^1\) embedded submanifold of \(\mathbb R^n\). The stationary set is singular if it contains at least one such point. When \(S\) admits a local stratification \(S\cap V=\bigcup_{\alpha}S_\alpha\) into smooth stationary strata, singular points include intersections or frontier points at which no single stratum describes the entire local germ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary set is singular at a critical point when, in every sufficiently small neighborhood, the critical set fails to look like one smooth embedded manifold of fixed dimension. Typical mechanisms include crossings of stationary branches, cusps, self-intersections, and changes in local dimension. Smooth stratifiability does not remove the singularity of the union at a junction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x_\star\in S\text{ is singular}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\nexists V\ni x_\star\text{ such that }S\cap V\text{ is a }C^1\text{ embedded submanifold}.\]
special_cases_latex: The union of two transverse smooth stationary curves is singular at their intersection.
A smooth stationary manifold is nonsingular as a set even when its transverse Hessian is degenerate.
An isolated stationary point is a zero-dimensional embedded submanifold and is therefore not set-singular merely because its Hessian is singular.
immediate_consequences_latex: A single tangent bundle and normal bundle cannot describe the entire stationary germ at a singular point.
Morse–Bott geometry fails at a set-singular point.
boundary_notes: Set singularity and Hessian degeneracy are distinct: either can occur without the other under the corresponding local definitions.
The definition does not require an algebraic or analytic structure and does not guarantee existence of a finite stratification.
A boundary point created only by restricting the domain requires a relative-manifold convention and is outside this open-domain formulation.

notation.meaning: A smooth local stationary stratum when a stratification exists.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: local failure of embedded-submanifold structure is the standard geometric meaning of set singularity.
A source is needed for the application of this general geometric definition specifically to stationary sets.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular point of a stationary set

children.title: Extended Flat Stationary Geometry
children.top_down_role: Extended regions with weak or vanishing local differential signals.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be \(C^2\) on an open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(F\subseteq U\) be a connected set containing more than one point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact extended flatness: a nontrivial connected stationary set on which the entire ambient Hessian vanishes. Approximate plateaus and tangent-only flatness are nearby but weaker notions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(F\) is an extended Hessian-flat stationary set of \(f\) if \[\nabla f(x)=0\quad\text{and}\quad\nabla^2f(x)=0\qquad\text{for every }x\in F.\] It is a flat stationary region when, additionally, \(F\) has nonempty interior. More generally, for \(f\in C^r\), it is stationary-flat through order \(r\) if \(D^kf(x)=0\) for every \(x\in F\) and every \(1\leq k\leq r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended Hessian-flat stationary set is a nontrivial connected family of points at which both the gradient and the entire Hessian vanish. If the set has interior, it is a flat stationary region. Higher-order flatness requires every derivative through a declared order to vanish on the set. This exact definition is stronger than a stationary manifold, where only tangent directions must be Hessian-null.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[F\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f),\qquad |F|>1,\qquad \nabla^2f(x)=0\quad(\forall x\in F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Hessian flatness is equivalent to \(v^\top\nabla^2f(x)w=0\) for all \(v,w\in\mathbb R^n\) and all \(x\in F\).
special_cases_latex: If \(F\) is open, then the objective is constant on each connected component of \(F\).
A line or surface of points with zero gradient and zero ambient Hessian is extended flat even when it has empty interior in \(\mathbb R^n\).
Order-two stationary flatness is exactly the gradient-plus-Hessian condition stated above.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point of \(F\) is a degenerate critical point.
No first- or second-order local differential signal distinguishes points or directions at a point of \(F\).
boundary_notes: A stationary manifold with nonzero transverse curvature is not Hessian-flat.
A small-gradient or small-Hessian plateau is approximate flatness and requires explicit tolerances rather than the exact equalities used here.
Vanishing derivatives through a finite order does not imply local constancy outside the set.

notation.meaning: The full derivative tensor of order k.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact vanishing of gradient and Hessian formalizes the blueprint's extended regions with vanishing differential signals.
The node title is not a standardized term; an inspected source is required to confirm whether exact, approximate, tangent, or higher-order flatness is intended.
knowledge_statements.title: Extended Hessian-flat stationary set

children.title: Stationary Plateaus
children.top_down_role: Extended regions with vanishing or nearly vanishing local differential signals.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Plateaus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Open regions on which all first-order objective information vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\). A stationary plateau is a nonempty connected open set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfying \(\nabla f(x)=0\) for every \(x\in U\). The objective is therefore constant on \(U\). If \(f\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)\), then \(\nabla^2f(x)=0\) throughout \(U\) as well. A lower-dimensional stationary family is not a plateau in this sense because it has empty interior in the ambient space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary plateau is a nonempty connected open region on which the gradient vanishes everywhere. The objective is constant on that region, and if it is twice continuously differentiable, its Hessian is zero throughout the region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f|_U=0\Longrightarrow f|_U\) is constant.

children.title: Flat Valleys
children.top_down_role: Elongated low-curvature regions associated with weak transverse or longitudinal variation.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat Valleys
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Manifolds of equivalent minima with zero tangential and positive transverse curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)\). A flat valley is a connected embedded submanifold \(M\) consisting of local minimizers such that \(f|_M\) is constant, \(T_xM=\ker\nabla^2f(x)\), and \(v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x)v>0\) for every nonzero \(v\in(T_xM)^\perp\) and every \(x\in M\). Hence motion tangent to \(M\) is flat to second order, whereas every normal displacement has strictly positive quadratic curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flat valley is a connected manifold of equal local minima, with Hessian-null tangent directions and strictly positive curvature in every normal direction.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a connected embedded submanifold of local minimizers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_xM=\ker\nabla^2f(x)\) and \(\nabla^2f(x)|_{(T_xM)^\perp}\succ0\) for every \(x\in M\).

notation.meaning: tangent space to the valley manifold
Euclidean normal space to the valley

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition consistently describes a Morse–Bott-type manifold of minima with Hessian-null tangent directions and positive normal curvature, and the definition content kind fits the leaf. No citation supports either the transverse condition or the potentially variable term “flat valley.”

children.title: Plateau-to-Valley Transitions
children.top_down_role: Local transitions between broadly stationary regions and directionally confined flat regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Plateau-to-Valley Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A polynomial family exhibiting loss of a stationary plateau and emergence of a flat valley.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the parameterized smooth function \(f_\mu:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) defined by \(f_\mu(x,y)=\mu y^2\), one has \(\nabla f_\mu(x,y)=(0,2\mu y)\). At \(\mu=0\), every point is stationary and \(f_0\) is constant, so the whole plane is a stationary plateau. For \(\mu>0\), the stationary set becomes \(\{(x,0):x\in\mathbb R\}\), which is a flat valley of global minimizers with positive curvature in the normal direction and zero curvature tangentially. For \(\mu<0\), the same stationary line is instead a flat ridge. Thus an arbitrarily small parameter change can alter both the dimension and normal type of stationary geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The family μy² changes from an entirely stationary plateau at μ=0 to a flat valley for μ>0 and a flat ridge for μ<0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu=0\) is the degeneracy boundary separating flat-valley and flat-ridge normal geometry.

children.title: Local-Signal Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Limits on distinguishing plateaus, valleys, and nearby saddles from weak derivative information.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Signal Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order local data need not determine the type of a degenerate stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f_+,f_-:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(f_+(x)=x^4\) and \(f_-(x)=-x^4\). At the origin, \(f_+(0)=f_-(0)=0\), \(f_+'(0)=f_-'(0)=0\), and \(f_+''(0)=f_-''(0)=0\). Hence the objective value, gradient, and Hessian give identical local signals at the two stationary points. Nevertheless, \(0\) is a strict local minimum of \(f_+\) and a strict local maximum of \(f_-\). Consequently, when the Hessian is singular, first- and second-order information alone cannot generally distinguish valley, ridge, saddle, or higher-order flat behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The functions x⁴ and −x⁴ have identical value, gradient, and Hessian at zero, yet zero is respectively a strict minimum and maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigl(f(0),f'(0),f''(0)\bigr)\) does not determine degenerate critical-point type.

children.top_down_role: Continuous- and discrete-time stability structures governing attraction to or avoidance of saddle points.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open, let \(f\in C^2(X)\), and let the dynamics be either a forward flow \(\Phi_t:X\to X\), \(t\geq0\), or iterates of a map \(G:X\to X\). Let \(\mathcal S\subseteq\{x:\nabla f(x)=0\}\) be a specified family of saddle points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, deterministic, smooth dynamics. This definition concerns asymptotic attraction to saddles, not a finite-time escape rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The dynamics is called \(\mathcal S\)-saddle-avoiding relative to a reference measure \(\mu\) if its saddle-attraction set
\[
B(\mathcal S)=\{x\in X:\operatorname{dist}(\Phi_t(x),\mathcal S)\to0\text{ as }t\to\infty\}
\]
for a flow, or
\[
B(\mathcal S)=\{x\in X:\operatorname{dist}(G^k(x),\mathcal S)\to0\text{ as }k\to\infty\}
\]
for a map, is \(\mu\)-null. Pointwise avoidance of \(x^\star\in\mathcal S\) means that its basin \(B(x^\star)\) is null. A stable-manifold saddle-avoidance structure additionally requires that, locally at each saddle, all convergent initial conditions lie in an invariant stable set whose dimension is strictly smaller than \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow or iteration is saddle-avoiding when the set of initial states whose trajectories approach the designated saddle family has reference measure zero. Pointwise avoidance applies the condition to one saddle. The stable-manifold form additionally represents locally convergent initial states by a lower-dimensional invariant stable set.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is open and the relevant trajectories remain defined for all forward times or iterations.
\(f\in C^2(X)\), and \(\mathcal S\) consists of critical points having at least one dynamically unstable direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient flow and its solution semiflow
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open and let \(f\in C^1(X)\) have locally Lipschitz gradient. For every initial state \(x_0\in X\), consider the maximal solution of an autonomous ordinary differential equation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean gradient flow for an unconstrained smooth objective; projected, Riemannian, differential-inclusion, and stochastic flows are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The continuous-time gradient dynamics generated by \(f\) is the initial-value problem
\[
\dot x(t)=-\nabla f(x(t)),\qquad x(0)=x_0.
\]
Whenever the solution exists at time \(t\), define \(\Phi_t(x_0)=x(t;x_0)\). Uniqueness gives \(\Phi_0=\operatorname{id}\) and \(\Phi_{t+s}=\Phi_t\circ\Phi_s\) on their common domain. A complete gradient flow has \(\Phi_t(x_0)\) defined for every \(x_0\in X\) and every \(t\geq0\). Along each classical trajectory,
\[
\frac{d}{dt}f(\Phi_t(x_0))=-\|\nabla f(\Phi_t(x_0))\|^2,
\]
so the objective is nonincreasing and is constant on a time interval exactly when that trajectory is stationary there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous-time gradient dynamics is the ordinary differential equation whose velocity is the negative gradient of the objective. Its solution maps form a semiflow wherever solutions exist uniquely. The objective decreases along every nonstationary trajectory, with instantaneous derivative equal to minus the squared gradient norm.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^1(X)\) and \(\nabla f\) is locally Lipschitz, ensuring local existence and uniqueness.
Only times before a trajectory exits \(X\) or its maximal existence interval are included unless completeness is separately assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dynamics is \(\dot x=-\nabla f(x)\), with solution operator \(\Phi_t\) and energy identity \(\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=-\|\nabla f(x(t))\|^2\leq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every classical solution satisfies the integral equation \(x(t)=x_0-\int_0^t\nabla f(x(s))\,ds\).
A time-rescaled flow \(\dot x=-c\nabla f(x)\), \(c>0\), has the same oriented trajectories with time parameter multiplied by \(c\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Hx+b^\top x\), the flow is the affine linear system \(\dot x=-Hx-b\).
If \(\nabla f\) is globally Lipschitz on \(\mathbb R^d\), the forward flow is globally defined.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every equilibrium is a critical point of \(f\), and every critical point generates a constant trajectory.
A noncritical periodic orbit cannot occur because \(f\) strictly decreases whenever \(\nabla f\neq0\).
boundary_notes: Local Lipschitz continuity gives uniqueness but does not by itself prevent finite-time escape from an open domain.
For nonsmooth objectives, the corresponding object is generally a differential inclusion rather than this classical flow.
The identity is an asymptotic structural fact and contains no convergence-rate assertion.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Flow Equilibria
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equilibrium characterization for unconstrained Euclidean gradient flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable and consider the autonomous gradient flow \(\dot x(t)=-
abla f(x(t))\). A point \(x_*\in\mathbb R^n\) is an equilibrium precisely when the constant trajectory \(x(t)\equiv x_*\) satisfies the differential equation, which is equivalent to \(
abla f(x_*)=0\). Along every differentiable solution, \( rac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=-\|
abla f(x(t))\|^2\leq0\). Therefore the objective is a Lyapunov function, and it is constant along a trajectory on an interval exactly when that trajectory consists of critical points on that interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient-flow equilibria are exactly stationary points, and the objective decreases along every trajectory except while the trajectory remains in the critical set.
assumptions_latex: \(x(\cdot)\) is a differentiable solution of \(\dot x=-\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_*\text{ is an equilibrium}\iff\nabla f(x_*)=0\), and \(\frac{d}{dt}f(x(t))=-\|\nabla f(x(t))\|^2\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open, let \(f\in C^1(X)\) have locally Lipschitz gradient, and let \(\Phi_t\) denote the local flow of \(\dot x=-\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional classical gradient flow. This definition identifies equilibria with first-order critical points but does not classify their stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x^\star\in X\) is a gradient-flow equilibrium if its trajectory is constant:
\[
\Phi_t(x^\star)=x^\star
\]
for every time \(t\) for which the flow is defined. Equivalently, the generating vector field vanishes at \(x^\star\):
\[
-\nabla f(x^\star)=0.
\]
Thus the equilibrium set is
\[
\operatorname{Eq}(\Phi)=\operatorname{crit}(f):=\{x\in X:\nabla f(x)=0\}.
\]
If \(f\in C^2(X)\), an equilibrium is nondegenerate when \(\det\nabla^2f(x^\star)\neq0\), and it is hyperbolic for the gradient flow when the linearization \(-\nabla^2f(x^\star)\) has no eigenvalue with zero real part. Because the Hessian is symmetric, these two conditions coincide in Euclidean gradient flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient-flow equilibrium is an initial state whose solution remains fixed for all time. It is exactly a critical point of the objective. For a twice continuously differentiable objective, nondegeneracy of the Hessian is equivalent to hyperbolicity of the corresponding gradient-flow equilibrium.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^1(X)\) and its gradient is locally Lipschitz near \(x^\star\).
The flow is generated by the negative Euclidean gradient without constraints or preconditioning.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(x^\star\in\operatorname{Eq}(\Phi)\iff
abla f(x^\star)=0\), and for \(f\in C^2\), \(x^\star\) is hyperbolic iff \(0
otin\operatorname{spec}(
abla^2f(x^\star))\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x^\star\) is an equilibrium iff the constant curve \(x(t)\equiv x^\star\) solves \(\dot x=-\nabla f(x)\).
\(x^\star\) is an equilibrium iff \(\left.\frac{d}{dt}\Phi_t(x^\star)\right|_{t=0}=0\).
special_cases_latex: A strict local minimizer with positive-definite Hessian is a hyperbolic equilibrium whose linearization has only negative eigenvalues.
A strict saddle with a negative Hessian eigenvalue has a positive eigenvalue in the flow linearization.
immediate_consequences_latex: Equilibrium is a first-order notion and therefore includes local minima, local maxima, saddles, and degenerate critical points.
An isolated nondegenerate critical point is an isolated equilibrium.
boundary_notes: A critical point on the boundary of a constrained domain is not covered by this unconstrained definition.
Equilibrium does not imply Lyapunov stability or attraction.
Degenerate equilibria require nonlinear analysis because the linearization has a zero eigenvalue.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Time Stability Types
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hessian-based local stability classification for an isolated gradient-flow equilibrium.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)\), let \(x_*\) satisfy \(
abla f(x_*)=0\), and linearize \(\dot x=-
abla f(x)\) at \(x_*\). The linearization is \(\dot z=-
abla^2f(x_*)z\). If \(
abla^2f(x_*)\) is positive definite, then \(x_*\) is a locally asymptotically stable equilibrium. If \(
abla^2f(x_*)\) has a negative eigenvalue, then the linearization has a positive eigenvalue and \(x_*\) is unstable. If the Hessian is positive semidefinite but singular, the linearization has neutral directions; linearization alone then does not determine Lyapunov stability or attraction, which depend on higher-order terms or nearby stationary geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive Hessian eigenvalues imply local attraction, a negative Hessian eigenvalue implies instability, and zero eigenvalues leave stability undecided by linearization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The signs of the eigenvalues of \(\nabla^2f(x_*)\) determine hyperbolic stability, while zero eigenvalues create an inconclusive neutral case.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lyapunov, asymptotic, unstable, and neutral equilibria
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Phi_t\) be a forward flow on an open subset \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and let \(x^\star\) be an equilibrium. Distances are Euclidean unless another metric is specified.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local continuous-time stability of a single equilibrium. The spectral terminology requires a continuously differentiable vector field.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The equilibrium \(x^\star\) is Lyapunov stable if
\[
\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall x_0\in X:\ \|x_0-x^\star\|<\delta\Rightarrow\|\Phi_t(x_0)-x^\star\|<\varepsilon\quad\forall t\geq0.
\]
It is locally attractive if some \(r>0\) satisfies \(\Phi_t(x_0)\to x^\star\) for every \(x_0\in B_r(x^\star)\). It is locally asymptotically stable when it is both Lyapunov stable and locally attractive. It is unstable when it is not Lyapunov stable. For \(\dot x=h(x)\) with \(h\in C^1\), a nonhyperbolic equilibrium—one for which \(Dh(x^\star)\) has an eigenvalue with zero real part—is called spectrally neutral; this label alone makes no claim of Lyapunov stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lyapunov stability means that every sufficiently close initial condition remains close for all future time. Local attraction means all initial conditions in some neighborhood converge to the equilibrium. Asymptotic stability combines both properties, while instability is failure of Lyapunov stability. Spectral neutrality means that the linearization has a center eigenvalue and does not by itself determine nonlinear stability.
assumptions_latex: All initial conditions quantified in the definition have forward trajectories defined for every \(t\geq0\).
Spectral classifications assume \(\dot x=h(x)\) with \(h\in C^1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The four types are determined by the displayed quantified stability condition, neighborhood convergence, their conjunction, or failure of stability; neutrality is \(\operatorname{spec}(Dh(x^\star))\cap i\mathbb R\neq\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Lyapunov stability is equivalent to: every neighborhood \(U\) of \(x^\star\) contains a neighborhood \(V\) such that \(\Phi_t(V)\subseteq U\) for all \(t\geq0\).
special_cases_latex: If every eigenvalue of \(Dh(x^\star)\) has negative real part, then the equilibrium is locally exponentially stable.
For gradient flow, \(Dh(x^\star)=-\nabla^2f(x^\star)\), so a positive-definite Hessian gives linear asymptotic stability.
immediate_consequences_latex: Local attraction without Lyapunov stability is not, by definition, asymptotic stability.
A center eigenvalue makes linearization inconclusive; higher-order terms may produce stability, instability, or continua of equilibria.
boundary_notes: Neutrality is a spectral descriptor, not the logical negation of asymptotic stability.
Global asymptotic stability additionally quantifies over all initial states in the state space.
Finite-time numerical stability and conditioning are different notions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient-descent iteration as a discrete dynamical system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(f\in C^1(X)\), and let \((\alpha_k)_{k\geq0}\) be positive stepsizes chosen so that every update remains in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic Euclidean gradient descent. Constant-stepsize dynamics is autonomous; varying stepsizes produce a nonautonomous system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The discrete gradient dynamics of \(f\) is
\[
x_{k+1}=G_{\alpha_k}(x_k),\qquad G_\alpha(x):=x-\alpha\nabla f(x),\qquad k=0,1,\ldots.
\]
For a constant stepsize \(\alpha>0\), the orbit from \(x_0\) is \(x_k=G_\alpha^k(x_0)\), and \(G_\alpha\) is the gradient map. For varying stepsizes,
\[
x_k=G_{\alpha_{k-1}}\circ\cdots\circ G_{\alpha_0}(x_0).
\]
A more general preconditioned gradient dynamics has \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kD_k\nabla f(x_k)\) with symmetric positive-definite \(D_k\); the canonical unpreconditioned system is obtained with \(D_k=I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Discrete gradient dynamics repeatedly subtracts a positive stepsize times the gradient. With a fixed stepsize, one gradient map is iterated and the system is autonomous. With changing stepsizes, the orbit is a composition of different gradient maps. Positive-definite preconditioning gives a broader gradient-like family.
assumptions_latex: Each update belongs to \(X\); if \(X=\mathbb R^d\), this domain condition is automatic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state evolution is \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k\nabla f(x_k)\), or \(x_k=G_\alpha^k(x_0)\) for constant \(\alpha\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The increment equation is \((x_{k+1}-x_k)/\alpha_k=-\nabla f(x_k)\), the forward-Euler discretization of gradient flow.
For constant \(\alpha\), the orbit satisfies the semigroup identity \(G_\alpha^{k+\ell}=G_\alpha^k\circ G_\alpha^\ell\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Hx+b^\top x\), \(G_\alpha(x)=(I-\alpha H)x-\alpha b\).
Steepest descent is the choice \(D_k=I\) in the preconditioned family.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every critical point is unchanged by every positive-stepsize gradient map.
The stepsize changes the discrete dynamics even though it only rescales time in the corresponding continuous gradient flow.
boundary_notes: A large stepsize need not decrease the objective and may destabilize a local minimizer.
Projected gradient methods use a projection after the gradient step and have a different fixed-point condition.
Stochastic gradients produce a random dynamical system rather than the deterministic map defined here.

notation.meaning: Gradient update map at stepsize alpha.
k-fold composition of the constant-stepsize gradient map.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Map Fixed Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point characterization of stationarity for constant-stepsize gradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, choose a nonzero stepsize \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), and define the gradient map \(T_\alpha(x)=x-\alpha
abla f(x)\). Then \(x_*\) is a fixed point of \(T_\alpha\) if and only if \(T_\alpha(x_*)=x_*\), equivalently \(\alpha
abla f(x_*)=0\), and hence if and only if \(
abla f(x_*)=0\). Thus, for every nonzero constant stepsize, the fixed-point set of gradient descent equals the critical set of \(f\), although the stability type of each fixed point may depend on \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every nonzero constant stepsize, the fixed points of the gradient-descent map are exactly the stationary points of the objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Fix}(T_\alpha)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\nabla f(x)=0\}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed point of a gradient update map
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), let \(f\in C^1(X)\), and fix \(\alpha>0\). Define \(G_\alpha(x)=x-\alpha\nabla f(x)\) wherever the update lies in \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained, unpreconditioned, constant-stepsize gradient descent. The equivalence changes for projected or proximal maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x^\star\in X\) is a fixed point of the gradient map if
\[
G_\alpha(x^\star)=x^\star.
\]
Since \(\alpha>0\), this condition is equivalent to
\[
x^\star-\alpha\nabla f(x^\star)=x^\star
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\nabla f(x^\star)=0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{Fix}(G_\alpha)=\operatorname{crit}(f)
\]
for every positive stepsize for which the map is defined. If \(f\in C^2\), the derivative at a fixed point is
\[
DG_\alpha(x^\star)=I-\alpha\nabla^2f(x^\star),
\]
which determines its linear discrete-time stability but not its membership in the fixed-point set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient-map fixed point is a state left unchanged by one gradient-descent step. For every positive stepsize, fixed points are exactly the critical points of the objective. When the objective is twice differentiable, the derivative of the update map at a fixed point is the identity minus the stepsize times the Hessian.
assumptions_latex: The derivative formula assumes \(f\in C^2\) near \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname{Fix}(G_\alpha)\iff\nabla f(x^\star)=0\), with \(DG_\alpha(x^\star)=I-\alpha\nabla^2f(x^\star)\) when \(f\in C^2\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x^\star\) is fixed iff the orbit initialized at \(x^\star\) is constant: \(G_\alpha^k(x^\star)=x^\star\) for all \(k\geq0\).
\(x^\star\) is fixed iff the gradient-step residual \(R_\alpha(x):=\alpha^{-1}(x-G_\alpha(x))\) vanishes at \(x^\star\).
special_cases_latex: For a quadratic objective with Hessian \(H\), fixed points solve \(Hx+b=0\).
If \(\alpha=0\), every point is fixed; this excluded case demonstrates why positivity is essential.
immediate_consequences_latex: Changing a positive constant stepsize does not change the fixed-point set.
Local minima, local maxima, saddles, and degenerate critical points can all be fixed points.
boundary_notes: For projected gradient, fixed points encode constrained first-order stationarity rather than \(\nabla f=0\).
A fixed point need not attract nearby iterates.
If the update is undefined outside a restricted domain, the fixed-point equality is asserted only on the map's domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local invertibility of a gradient update
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be open, let \(f\in C^2(X)\), fix \(\alpha>0\), and define \(G_\alpha(x)=x-\alpha\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean gradient maps. Local invertibility is distinguished from global injectivity or global diffeomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gradient map \(G_\alpha\) is locally invertible at \(x\in X\) if there are open neighborhoods \(U\ni x\) and \(V\ni G_\alpha(x)\) such that the restriction \(G_\alpha|_U:U\to V\) is bijective and has a continuous inverse. It is a local \(C^1\)-diffeomorphism at \(x\) when this inverse is continuously differentiable. Since
\[
DG_\alpha(x)=I-\alpha\nabla^2f(x),
\]
the inverse-function criterion is
\[
\det(I-\alpha\nabla^2f(x))\neq0.
\]
Under this condition, \(G_\alpha\) is a local \(C^1\)-diffeomorphism at \(x\). If the condition holds at every point, the map is a local diffeomorphism everywhere, although it need not be globally one-to-one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient map is locally invertible at a state when it restricts to a bijection between neighborhoods of that state and its image. It is locally a continuously differentiable diffeomorphism whenever the identity minus the stepsize times the Hessian is nonsingular. Pointwise local invertibility does not imply global invertibility.
assumptions_latex: \(G_\alpha(x)=x-\alpha\nabla f(x)\) maps the selected neighborhood into \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonsingularity of \(DG_\alpha(x)=I-\alpha\nabla^2f(x)\) makes \(G_\alpha\) a local \(C^1\)-diffeomorphism at \(x\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Jacobian condition is equivalent to \(1/\alpha\notin\operatorname{spec}(\nabla^2f(x))\).
Local \(C^1\)-invertibility means that some neighborhood admits a unique local backward iterate \(G_\alpha^{-1}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\|\nabla^2f(x)\|<1/\alpha\), then \(I-\alpha\nabla^2f(x)\) is nonsingular.
If \(\nabla f\) is globally \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(0<\alpha<1/L\), then every Hessian eigenvalue lies below \(1/\alpha\) in magnitude wherever the Hessian exists.
immediate_consequences_latex: Near a locally invertible point, preimages of local invariant sets can be transported by a smooth inverse branch.
At a fixed point, loss of local invertibility occurs exactly when a multiplier of the linearized map equals zero.

Local diffeomorphism does not imply surjectivity or global injectivity.
The common bound \(\alpha<1/L\) is sufficient, not necessary, for pointwise nonsingularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Stepsize-Dependent Fixed-Point Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Spectral stability of a gradient-map fixed point as the stepsize varies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^n)\), let \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\), and set \(T_\alpha(x)=x-\alpha\nabla f(x)\) with \(\alpha>0\). If the Hessian eigenvalues at \(x_*\) are \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\), then the eigenvalues of \(DT_\alpha(x_*)\) are \(1-\alpha\lambda_i\). The fixed point is linearly attracting exactly when \(0<\alpha\lambda_i<2\) for every \(i\). For a positive-definite Hessian this is equivalent to \(0<\alpha<2/\lambda_{\max}\). Any negative Hessian eigenvalue produces a multiplier greater than one, while \(\alpha\lambda_i\in\{0,2\}\) produces a neutral multiplier of modulus one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient-map stability depends on α through multipliers 1−αλ: attraction requires every multiplier to have modulus below one, while negative curvature is unstable for α>0.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\rho(DT_\alpha(x_*))<1\iff 0<\alpha\lambda_i<2\) for every \(i\).

notation.meaning: Eigenvalues of the Hessian at the fixed point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Spectral stability of a gradient-map fixed point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in C^2\) near a critical point \(x^\star\in\mathbb R^d\). For \(\alpha>0\), let \(G_\alpha(x)=x-\alpha\nabla f(x)\), and write \(H=\nabla^2f(x^\star)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local linear stability for constant-stepsize, deterministic Euclidean gradient descent. Nonlinear conclusions at unit-modulus multipliers are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The stepsize-dependent linear type of the fixed point \(x^\star\) is defined by the multipliers of
\[
DG_\alpha(x^\star)=I-\alpha H.
\]
If \(\lambda_1(H),\ldots,\lambda_d(H)\) are the Hessian eigenvalues, the multipliers are \(m_i(\alpha)=1-\alpha\lambda_i(H)\). The fixed point is linearly attracting when
\[
\rho(I-\alpha H)=\max_i|1-\alpha\lambda_i(H)|<1,
\]
linearly unstable when at least one multiplier has modulus greater than one, hyperbolic when no multiplier has modulus one, and spectrally neutral when at least one multiplier has modulus one. These classifications explicitly depend on \(\alpha\), although the fixed-point equation does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The local discrete-time type of a critical point is determined by the eigenvalues of the gradient map's derivative. Each Hessian eigenvalue is transformed into the multiplier one minus the stepsize times that eigenvalue. Attraction requires every multiplier to lie strictly inside the unit disk; instability occurs if one lies outside; a multiplier on the unit circle is neutral and requires nonlinear analysis.
assumptions_latex: The stepsize is constant and positive.
The terms attracting, unstable, hyperbolic, and neutral in the formal core refer to the linearized map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stability type is determined by \(\{|1-\alpha\lambda_i(H)|\}_{i=1}^d\), with attraction exactly when their maximum is less than one.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Linear attraction is equivalent to \(0<\alpha\lambda_i(H)<2\) for every \(i\).
If \(H\succ0\), linear attraction is equivalent to \(0<\alpha<2/\lambda_{\max}(H)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(H\) has a negative eigenvalue, then \(1-\alpha\lambda_i(H)>1\) for every \(\alpha>0\), so the strict saddle is linearly unstable.
At a positive-definite local minimum, increasing \(\alpha\) through \(2/\lambda_{\max}(H)\) changes an attracting multiplier through \(-1\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A positive stepsize cannot make a strict saddle linearly attracting.
A stepsize that is harmless for a flat direction may destabilize a direction of large positive curvature.
boundary_notes: When a multiplier has modulus one, linearization alone does not decide nonlinear stability.
For varying stepsizes there is no single fixed derivative matrix controlling the orbit.
At a degenerate critical point, a zero Hessian eigenvalue produces the neutral multiplier one for every stepsize.

notation.meaning: Multiplier associated with the ith Hessian eigenvalue.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local invariant-manifold decomposition at an equilibrium
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let either \(\dot x=h(x)\) with local flow \(\Phi_t\), or \(x_{k+1}=G(x_k)\), be \(C^1\) near an equilibrium or fixed point \(x^\star\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local smooth dynamics near one stationary state. Existence of all listed manifolds requires the corresponding invariant-manifold hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A local invariant manifold through \(x^\star\) is an embedded \(C^1\) submanifold \(W_{\mathrm{loc}}\) containing \(x^\star\) such that trajectories remain in it while they remain in a chosen neighborhood. For a flow this means \(\Phi_t(W_{\mathrm{loc}})\cap U\subseteq W_{\mathrm{loc}}\) for the admissible times; for a map it means \(G(W_{\mathrm{loc}})\cap U\subseteq W_{\mathrm{loc}}\), with backward invariance when an inverse branch is used. If the linearization admits the invariant splitting
\[
\mathbb R^d=E^s\oplus E^c\oplus E^u,
\]
then stable, center, and unstable local manifolds are invariant manifolds tangent at \(x^\star\) to \(E^s,E^c,E^u\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local invariant manifold is a smooth surface through the stationary state that locally carries complete trajectory segments. The linearized stable, center, and unstable spectral subspaces prescribe the tangent spaces of the corresponding local invariant manifolds when the relevant manifold theorem applies.
assumptions_latex: The vector field or map is at least \(C^1\) near \(x^\star\).
For discrete backward invariance, \(G\) has a specified local inverse near \(x^\star\).
The spectral splitting uses negative, zero, and positive real parts for flows, and modulus below, equal to, and above one for maps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The local geometry consists of invariant submanifolds \(W^s_{\mathrm{loc}},W^c_{\mathrm{loc}},W^u_{\mathrm{loc}}\) satisfying \(T_{x^\star}W^\sigma_{\mathrm{loc}}=E^\sigma\) for \(\sigma\in\{s,c,u\}\), whenever those manifolds exist.
special_cases_latex: At a hyperbolic equilibrium, \(E^c=\{0\}\), so only stable and unstable directions occur.
For gradient flow, the eigenspaces of \(-\nabla^2f(x^\star)\) provide the linear stable, center, and unstable splitting.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonzero unstable subspace makes the local stable manifold lower-dimensional than the ambient state space.
Center manifolds capture directions not decided by exponential linear contraction or expansion.
boundary_notes: Center manifolds generally are not unique, unlike the local stable and unstable manifolds in the hyperbolic setting.
Forward invariance alone is weaker than two-sided invariance.
Tangency to a spectral subspace does not make the manifold globally linear.

notation.meaning: Stable, center, and unstable spectral subspaces of the linearization.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local stable-manifold theorem for a hyperbolic fixed point of a smooth gradient map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:U\to\mathbb R^n\) be a \(C^r\) local diffeomorphism, with \(r\geq1\), and let \(x_*\in U\) be a hyperbolic fixed point. Write \(\mathbb R^n=E^s\oplus E^u\), where the eigenvalues of \(DT(x_*)|_{E^s}\) have modulus less than one and those of \(DT(x_*)|_{E^u}\) have modulus greater than one. Then a neighborhood of \(x_*\) contains a \(C^r\) embedded local stable manifold \(W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)\), tangent to \(E^s\) at \(x_*\), locally forward invariant, and consisting exactly of points whose forward iterates remain local and converge to \(x_*\). Its dimension is \(\dim E^s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a hyperbolic fixed point, the points converging forward to it form a smooth invariant manifold tangent to the contracting eigenspace.
assumptions_latex: \(DT(x_*)\) has no eigenvalue of modulus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)\) with \(T_{x_*}W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}=E^s\) and \(\dim W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}=\dim E^s\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stable set and local stable manifold
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x^\star\) be an equilibrium of a \(C^1\) flow \(\Phi_t\), or a fixed point of a \(C^1\) map \(G\), on an open subset of \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local and global stable objects for finite-dimensional smooth dynamics. Manifold regularity is asserted only under stable-manifold hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The global stable set of \(x^\star\) is
\[
W^s(x^\star)=\{x:\Phi_t(x)\to x^\star\text{ as }t\to\infty\}
\]
for a flow, and
\[
W^s(x^\star)=\{x:G^k(x)\to x^\star\text{ as }k\to\infty\}
\]
for a map. Given a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x^\star\), the local stable set consists of points whose forward trajectories remain in \(U\) and converge to \(x^\star\). A local stable manifold \(W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(x^\star)\) is such a local stable set when it is an embedded invariant submanifold tangent at \(x^\star\) to the stable spectral subspace \(E^s\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The stable set contains exactly the initial states converging to the stationary point in forward time. Its local version also requires the trajectory to remain in a chosen neighborhood. Under the stable-manifold hypotheses, the local stable set is a smooth invariant manifold tangent to the contracting spectral subspace.
assumptions_latex: The flow or map is defined along every forward orbit included in the stable set.
For the manifold clause, the dynamics is sufficiently smooth and has the required spectral separation at \(x^\star\).
For a flow, \(E^s\) is spanned by generalized eigendirections with negative real part; for a map, by multipliers of modulus below one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W^s(x^\star)\) is the forward basin converging to \(x^\star\), while \(T_{x^\star}W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(x^\star)=E^s\) when the local stable manifold exists.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a flow, \(x\in W^s(x^\star)\) iff \(\operatorname{dist}(\Phi_t(x),x^\star)\to0\).
For a map, \(x\in W^s(x^\star)\) iff the omega-limit set of its orbit is \(\{x^\star\}\).
special_cases_latex: If every linearized direction is stable, the local stable manifold has dimension \(d\) and contains a neighborhood of \(x^\star\).
At a strict saddle of gradient flow, the stable manifold excludes Hessian-negative directions and therefore has codimension at least one.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any trajectory converging to \(x^\star\) eventually enters every neighborhood of \(x^\star\).
A stable manifold of dimension below \(d\) has empty interior in \(\mathbb R^d\).
boundary_notes: A stable set need not be a manifold at nonhyperbolic points.
The global stable set may have folds or multiple components even when the local stable manifold is smooth.
Stability of the equilibrium and membership in its stable set are distinct notions.

Stable spectral subspace of the linearization.

knowledge_statements.title: Unstable Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local unstable-manifold theorem for a hyperbolic fixed point of a smooth gradient map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:U\to\mathbb R^n\) be a \(C^r\) local diffeomorphism, with \(r\geq1\), and let \(x_*\) be a hyperbolic fixed point with splitting \(\mathbb R^n=E^s\oplus E^u\). Then a neighborhood of \(x_*\) contains a \(C^r\) embedded local unstable manifold \(W^u_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)\), tangent to \(E^u\) at \(x_*\) and locally backward invariant. It consists of points admitting backward iterates that remain in the neighborhood and converge to \(x_*\). Its dimension is \(\dim E^u\). Equivalently, \(W^u_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)\) is the local stable manifold of \(x_*\) for the inverse map \(T^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Points converging to a hyperbolic fixed point under backward iteration form a smooth manifold tangent to the expanding eigenspace.
assumptions_latex: \(DT(x_*)\) has no eigenvalue of modulus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(W^u_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)\) with \(T_{x_*}W^u_{\mathrm{loc}}=E^u\) and \(\dim W^u_{\mathrm{loc}}=\dim E^u\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unstable set and local unstable manifold
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x^\star\) be an equilibrium of a complete local \(C^1\) flow \(\Phi_t\), or a fixed point of a locally invertible \(C^1\) map \(G\), on an open subset of \(\mathbb R^d\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward-time attraction and forward-time departure near a stationary state. For noninvertible maps, a backward history must be specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The unstable set of \(x^\star\) is the stable set for reversed time:
\[
W^u(x^\star)=\{x:\Phi_t(x)\to x^\star\text{ as }t\to-\infty\}
\]
for a flow. For an invertible map,
\[
W^u(x^\star)=\{x:G^{-k}(x)\to x^\star\text{ as }k\to\infty\}.
\]
A local unstable manifold \(W^u_{\mathrm{loc}}(x^\star)\) is a locally invariant embedded submanifold contained in this backward basin and tangent at \(x^\star\) to the unstable spectral subspace \(E^u\). Forward trajectories starting on it, other than the equilibrium, depart along dynamically expanding directions while they remain in the local neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unstable set consists of points that approach the stationary state in backward time. For an invertible discrete map, it is defined by repeated inverse iteration. Under the unstable-manifold hypotheses, the local unstable set is a smooth invariant manifold tangent to the expanding spectral subspace.
assumptions_latex: The continuous trajectory is defined for the required negative times, or the map has a selected local inverse branch.
The dynamics is sufficiently smooth and has the spectral separation required for an unstable manifold.
For flows, \(E^u\) corresponds to positive real parts; for maps, to multipliers of modulus above one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W^u(x^\star)\) is the backward-time basin, and \(T_{x^\star}W^u_{\mathrm{loc}}(x^\star)=E^u\) whenever the local unstable manifold exists.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(W^u\) for the original dynamics is \(W^s\) for the reversed flow or inverse map.
For a flow, \(x\in W^u(x^\star)\) iff \(\operatorname{dist}(\Phi_{-t}(x),x^\star)\to0\) as \(t\to\infty\).
special_cases_latex: For gradient flow at a strict saddle, each negative Hessian eigenvalue produces an unstable eigenvalue of \(-\nabla^2f(x^\star)\).
At a strict local maximum with negative-definite Hessian, the unstable manifold has full dimension.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nontrivial unstable manifold certifies that the equilibrium cannot be locally asymptotically stable.
The dimension of the local unstable manifold equals the dimension of the unstable spectral subspace in the hyperbolic setting.
boundary_notes: A forward map that is not locally invertible may admit multiple backward histories, so its unstable set requires a history-based definition.
Forward departure need not be monotone in Euclidean distance.
The unstable manifold is not the complement of the stable manifold.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a \(C^r\) flow or locally invertible \(C^r\) map, \(r\geq1\), have a fixed point \(x^\star\) and a linear spectral splitting \(\mathbb R^d=E^s\oplus E^c\oplus E^u\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local nonhyperbolic dynamics, including degenerate saddles. Center manifolds are generally nonunique and encode behavior unresolved by linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A local center manifold is a locally invariant embedded \(C^r\) manifold \(W^c_{\mathrm{loc}}(x^\star)\) satisfying
\[
x^\star\in W^c_{\mathrm{loc}}(x^\star),\qquad T_{x^\star}W^c_{\mathrm{loc}}(x^\star)=E^c,
\]
where \(E^c\) corresponds to eigenvalues with zero real part for a flow or multipliers of modulus one for a map. A local center-stable manifold is tangent to \(E^s\oplus E^c\), and a local center-unstable manifold is tangent to \(E^c\oplus E^u\). The neutral invariant-manifold family is the collection of such locally invariant manifolds carrying the directions for which the linearization gives neither strict exponential contraction nor strict exponential expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A center manifold is a locally invariant smooth manifold tangent to the neutral spectral subspace. Center-stable and center-unstable manifolds also include the contracting or expanding directions. These manifolds organize degenerate or nonhyperbolic behavior that cannot be classified from strict linear contraction and expansion alone.
assumptions_latex: The dynamics has the regularity and spectral splitting required by a center-manifold theorem.
For a discrete map, the relevant local inverse exists when backward invariance is asserted.
The center spectrum is separated from the strictly stable and unstable spectra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The neutral family consists of locally invariant manifolds tangent to \(E^c\), \(E^s\oplus E^c\), or \(E^c\oplus E^u\) at \(x^\star\).
special_cases_latex: For gradient flow, zero Hessian eigenvalues generate the center subspace because the linearization is \(-\nabla^2f(x^\star)\).
A continuum of equilibria may itself form a center manifold when its tangent space equals \(E^c\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonlinear stability along neutral directions must be determined from the reduced dynamics on a center manifold.
A center-stable manifold can contain all trajectories that remain near a nonhyperbolic equilibrium for forward time, under suitable local hypotheses.
boundary_notes: Center manifolds are generally not unique away from the equilibrium, although their tangent space is fixed.
A neutral eigenvalue does not imply constant motion along the center manifold.
The regularity of a center manifold may be lower than that of the dynamics without stronger spectral assumptions.

children.title: Center Manifolds

knowledge_statements.title: Center Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local center-manifold theorem for a nonhyperbolic fixed point of a smooth discrete map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be \(C^r\), with \(r\geq2\), and let \(T(x_*)=x_*\). Suppose \(DT(x_*)\) admits an invariant splitting \(E^s\oplus E^c\oplus E^u\), with eigenvalue moduli respectively less than, equal to, and greater than one. Then there exists a local \(C^{r-1}\) center manifold \(W^c_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)\) through \(x_*\), tangent to \(E^c\) at \(x_*\), and locally invariant under \(T\). The center manifold need not be unique, but every sufficiently small orbit that remains near \(x_*\) for all forward and backward times is contained in a center manifold. Local neutral dynamics reduce to the restriction of \(T\) to this manifold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Neutral eigendirections generate a locally invariant center manifold; nearby bounded two-sided dynamics are governed by the map restricted to that manifold.
assumptions_latex: \(DT(x_*)\) has an invariant stable-center-unstable spectral splitting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a locally invariant \(W^c_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)\) satisfying \(T_{x_*}W^c_{\mathrm{loc}}=E^c\).

knowledge_statements.title: Center-Stable Manifolds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local center-stable manifold for a partially hyperbolic fixed point of a discrete map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n\) be a \(C^r\) local diffeomorphism, with \(r\geq2\), fixing \(x_*\). Suppose \(DT(x_*)\) has an invariant splitting \(E^s\oplus E^c\oplus E^u\), with eigenvalue moduli less than one on \(E^s\), equal to one on \(E^c\), and greater than one on \(E^u\). Then there exists a local center-stable manifold \(W^{cs}_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)\), tangent at \(x_*\) to \(E^s\oplus E^c\) and locally forward invariant. Every point whose forward orbit remains in a sufficiently small neighborhood of \(x_*\) lies in \(W^{cs}_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)\). Its codimension equals \(\dim E^u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All sufficiently local forward-trapped orbits lie in a center-stable manifold tangent to the stable and neutral eigendirections.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(W^{cs}_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)\) with tangent space \(E^s\oplus E^c\) and codimension \(\dim E^u\).

children.title: Neutral-Mode Persistence

knowledge_statements.title: Neutral-Mode Persistence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit linear multipliers do not determine persistence, attraction, or repulsion of neutral modes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the smooth one-dimensional maps \(T_-(x)=x-x^3\) and \(T_+(x)=x+x^3\). Both fix the origin and have the same neutral linearization, \(T_-'(0)=T_+'(0)=1\). For every sufficiently small nonzero \(x\), iteration of \(T_-\) decreases \(|x|\) and converges to \(0\), whereas iteration of \(T_+\) increases \(|x|\) until it leaves any prescribed sufficiently small neighborhood. Thus a unit multiplier records a persistent linear neutral mode but does not determine nonlinear stability. The leading nonzero term in the center-manifold reduced map can convert the neutral direction into attraction, repulsion, or more complicated local behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two maps with the same unit multiplier can be respectively attracting and repelling, so neutral linear modes do not determine nonlinear persistence or stability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_-'(0)=T_+'(0)=1\), but \(0\) attracts locally for \(T_-\) and repels locally for \(T_+\).

notation.meaning: Map with an attracting cubic correction.
Map with a repelling cubic correction.

children.title: Degenerate-Saddle Attraction Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of saddle-avoidance conclusions near neutral or weakly stable structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate-Saddle Attraction Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows why a zero Hessian spectrum alone cannot determine attraction to a degenerate critical point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the gradient flows generated on \(\mathbb{R}^2\) by \(f_{+}(x,y)=x^4+y^4\) and \(f_{-}(x,y)=x^4-y^4\). Both functions satisfy \(\nabla f_{\pm}(0,0)=0\) and \(\nabla^2 f_{\pm}(0,0)=0\). For \(f_{+}\), every trajectory converges to the origin. For \(f_{-}\), a trajectory converges to the origin exactly when its initial condition satisfies \(y_0=0\); otherwise its \(y\)-component moves away and may escape in finite forward time. Thus identical degenerate linearizations can have full-dimensional or measure-zero attraction sets, so strict-saddle stable-manifold conclusions do not extend from Hessian data alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two functions with identical zero Hessians have radically different attraction sets, demonstrating that degenerate critical-point avoidance requires higher-order information.
assumptions_latex: Trajectories solve \(\dot z=-\nabla f_{\pm}(z)\) on their maximal forward intervals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_{f_+}(0)=\mathbb{R}^2\), whereas \(\mathcal A_{f_-}(0)=\{(x,0):x\in\mathbb{R}\}\).

notation.meaning: Initial points whose gradient-flow trajectories exist globally and converge to the origin.

children.title: Stable-Manifold Saddle-Avoidance Principles
children.top_down_role: Measure-theoretic avoidance families for strict saddles under suitable gradient-like dynamics.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(Z\) denote either a smooth flow or an iterated smooth map on \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and let \(\mathcal S\) be a family of strict saddles or other stationary points having unstable directions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal measure-theoretic principle, not a finite-time escape theorem. The countability and inverse-image hypotheses are explicit because they are essential to null-set propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The stable-manifold saddle-avoidance principle applies to \((Z,\mathcal S)\) when, for every \(s\in\mathcal S\), there is a neighborhood \(U_s\) and an embedded local stable manifold \(W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(s)\subset U_s\) of dimension less than \(d\) such that every orbit converging to \(s\) eventually enters \(W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(s)\). For a discrete map, the relevant inverse branches must preserve Lebesgue-null sets. If \(\mathcal S\) is countable, the resulting exceptional set is contained in
\[
\bigcup_{s\in\mathcal S}\bigcup_{k\geq0}Z^{-k}(W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(s)),
\]
with the analogous time-slice construction for a flow, and is required to be Lebesgue-null.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The principle represents every saddle-convergent orbit by eventual entry into a lower-dimensional local stable manifold. Countability of the saddle family and preservation of null sets under backward transport then make the total saddle-convergence set negligible. The definition records these structural ingredients without asserting an escape time.
assumptions_latex: Each \(s\in\mathcal S\) has at least one unstable direction, so \(\dim W^s_{\mathrm{loc}}(s)<d\).
Every trajectory converging to \(s\) eventually belongs to the corresponding local stable manifold.
The saddle family is countable, or an alternative argument establishes nullity of the uncountable union.
For a map, inverse images under the applicable local diffeomorphisms preserve null sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The saddle basin \(B(\mathcal S)=\{x:Z_t(x)\to s\text{ for some }s\in\mathcal S\}\) is Lebesgue-null.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For any initialization law \(\nu\ll\operatorname{Leb}_d\), nullity is equivalent to \(\nu(B(\mathcal S))=0\).
special_cases_latex: A single hyperbolic strict saddle has a local stable manifold of codimension at least one.
A finite saddle family automatically satisfies the countability requirement.
immediate_consequences_latex: Absolutely continuous random initialization converges to the designated saddle family with probability zero.
The principle remains purely asymptotic and allows arbitrarily long residence near a saddle.
boundary_notes: An uncountable union of null stable manifolds need not be null.
A map lacking suitable local invertibility may fail to transport local nullity backward.
Initial laws singular with respect to Lebesgue measure can place positive mass on stable manifolds.

children.title: Gradient-Flow Saddle Avoidance
children.top_down_role: Continuous-time avoidance organized through stable-set geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient-Flow Saddle Avoidance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local continuous-time avoidance at a critical point possessing at least one strictly unstable direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n)\), let \(x_*\) satisfy \(
abla f(x_*)=0\), and suppose \(
abla^2 f(x_*)\) has \(r\geq 1\) negative eigenvalues. For the gradient flow \(\dot x=-
abla f(x)\), there is a neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_*\) and a local center-stable manifold of dimension \(n-r\) containing every initial point in \(U\) whose forward trajectory remains in \(U\) and converges to \(x_*\). Consequently, this local attraction set has \(n\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a strict saddle, all convergent gradient-flow trajectories lie in a lower-dimensional center-stable manifold and therefore form a null set.
assumptions_latex: \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\) and \(\nabla^2 f(x_*)\) has \(r\geq1\) negative eigenvalues.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim W^{cs}_{\mathrm{loc}}(x_*)=n-r<n\) and \(\operatorname{Leb}_n(\mathcal A_U(x_*))=0\).

notation.meaning: Local center-stable manifold of the gradient flow.
Points whose forward trajectories stay in the local neighborhood and converge to the critical point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local theorem is correctly scoped: the r negative Hessian eigenvalues give r unstable flow directions, and the local attraction set lies in an (n-r)-dimensional center-stable manifold. An authoritative stable/center-stable manifold source with a specific locator is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Measure-zero saddle avoidance by gradient flow
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^d)\) have a complete gradient flow \(\Phi_t\), and let \(\mathcal S\subseteq\operatorname{crit}(f)\) be a designated family of strict saddles.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous-time asymptotic avoidance in finite dimensions. Completeness, countability, and strict-saddle geometry are part of the regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gradient flow is said to avoid \(\mathcal S\) in the stable-manifold sense if
\[
B_{\mathrm{flow}}(\mathcal S):=\{x_0:\Phi_t(x_0)\to s\text{ for some }s\in\mathcal S\}
\]
has \(d\)-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero, and this nullity is organized locally by stable manifolds. At a nondegenerate strict saddle \(s\), the flow linearization is \(-\nabla^2f(s)\); each negative Hessian eigenvalue is therefore an unstable flow eigenvalue, so the local stable manifold has dimension strictly smaller than \(d\). For a countable saddle family, continuous-time saddle avoidance means \(\operatorname{Leb}_d(B_{\mathrm{flow}}(\mathcal S))=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient-flow saddle avoidance means that almost no initial state converges to a designated strict saddle. Negative Hessian curvature becomes an unstable direction of the negative-gradient flow, making the stable manifold lower-dimensional. The formal property is nullity of the union of the saddle basins.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^d)\), and \(\nabla f\) generates a complete unique flow.
Every \(s\in\mathcal S\) is a nondegenerate critical point with at least one negative Hessian eigenvalue.
The family \(\mathcal S\) is countable, or its basin union is independently known to be measurable and null.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Leb}_d\{x_0:\Phi_t(x_0)\to s\text{ for some }s\in\mathcal S\}=0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every random initialization \(X_0\) with law absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, \(\mathbb P(\Phi_t(X_0)\to\mathcal S)=0\).
special_cases_latex: For one hyperbolic strict saddle, its basin is locally contained in a stable manifold of codimension at least one.
At a strict local maximum with negative-definite Hessian, the stable subspace is trivial.
immediate_consequences_latex: Almost-sure nonconvergence to strict saddles holds for absolutely continuous initialization whenever the stated avoidance property is established.
The objective may still decrease very slowly near a saddle with weak curvature.
boundary_notes: The definition does not cover degenerate saddles with zero Hessian eigenvalues.
Avoidance does not imply convergence to a local minimum unless trajectories themselves converge to critical points.
It supplies no quantitative exit-time or complexity bound.

notation.meaning: Initial states whose gradient-flow trajectories converge to the saddle family.
