knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Eigenpair Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-controlled certificate for a symmetric matrix and a normalized approximate eigenpair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), let \(\lVert v\rVert_2=1\), set \(\theta=v^{\mathsf T}Hv\), and define \(r=Hv-\theta v\). The tuple \((v,\theta,r)\) is verifiable using one product with \(H\). There exists an eigenvalue \(\lambda_i(H)\) satisfying \(|\lambda_i(H)-\theta|\le\lVert r\rVert_2\). Independently of the residual size, \(\theta<0\) certifies strict negative curvature because \(v^{\mathsf T}Hv<0\). If \(\theta+\lVert r\rVert_2<0\), the residual enclosure additionally certifies that at least one eigenvalue of \(H\) is strictly negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A normalized Ritz vector, its Rayleigh quotient, and its residual give checkable negative curvature and an eigenvalue enclosure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Some \(\lambda_i(H)\) lies in \([\theta-\lVert r\rVert_2,\theta+\lVert r\rVert_2]\), and \(\theta<0\) directly certifies negative curvature.

notation.meaning: Rayleigh quotient of the candidate vector.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The residual enclosure for a normalized approximate eigenpair of a real symmetric matrix is precise, and the Rayleigh-quotient negativity test is independently valid, but the eigenvalue enclosure has no cited supporting source.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), let \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(\theta\in\mathbb R\), and choose residual and normalization tolerances \(\varepsilon_r,\varepsilon_n\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic certificate for approximate spectral curvature; extremality requires a separate bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((\theta,v)\) is an \((\varepsilon_r,\varepsilon_n)\)-approximate eigenpair certificate for \(H\) when \[\bigl|\|v\|_2-1\bigr|\le\varepsilon_n,\qquad \|Hv-\theta v\|_2\le\varepsilon_r.\] If \(\|v\|_2=1\), its Rayleigh value is \(\rho(v)=v^THv\). It is a certified negative-curvature direction at threshold \(\gamma\ge0\) when \(v^THv\le-\gamma\). It is an approximate minimum-eigenpair certificate only if it also includes a lower spectral bound \(\ell\le\lambda_{\min}(H)\) satisfying \(\theta-\ell\le\varepsilon_\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate eigenpair certificate consists of an almost unit vector and scalar with a small eigen-residual. Negative curvature is certified directly by a negative Rayleigh quotient. Calling the pair an approximation to the smallest eigenpair additionally requires a lower bound showing that its value is close to the bottom of the spectrum.
assumptions_latex: All norms and tolerances are specified; the extremal variant supplies a valid lower spectral bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual inequality certifies approximate eigenpair consistency, while the Rayleigh and lower-bound conditions separately certify negative curvature and spectral extremality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For unit \(v\), \(v^T(Hv-\theta v)=\rho(v)-\theta\), hence \(|\rho(v)-\theta|\le\varepsilon_r\).
special_cases_latex: When \(\varepsilon_r=\varepsilon_n=0\), \((\theta,v)\) is an exact normalized eigenpair.
If \(\theta+\varepsilon_r<0\) and \(\|v\|_2=1\), then \(v^THv<0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For symmetric \(H\) and unit \(v\), the residual bound implies that some eigenvalue \(\lambda_i(H)\) satisfies \(|\lambda_i(H)-\theta|\le\varepsilon_r\).
boundary_notes: A small residual can correspond to any eigenvalue and does not alone prove proximity to \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\).
The definition assumes exact evaluation of the displayed residual; inexact products require an additional oracle-error allowance.

notation.meaning: Rayleigh quotient for a unit vector.

review_flags: An inspected authoritative source explicitly supporting the residual-to-spectrum and extremality distinctions is required.

children.title: Probabilistic Curvature Certificates
children.top_down_role: High-probability detection or exclusion of negative curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Probabilistic Curvature Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided randomized certificates distinguish detected curvature from high-probability spectral exclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\), tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and failure probability \(\delta\in(0,1)\). A randomized curvature procedure is a probabilistic certificate at level \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) if it returns either a nonzero vector \(v\) with the deterministically checkable inequality \(v^{\mathsf T}Hv\le-\varepsilon\lVert v\rVert^2\), or the outcome \(\mathsf{NO\text{-}NEG}\), and satisfies \(\Pr\{\mathsf{NO\text{-}NEG}\text{ and }\lambda_{\min}(H)<-\varepsilon\}\le\delta\). Thus a returned vector certifies negative curvature without probability qualification, while \(\mathsf{NO\text{-}NEG}\) supports \(H\succeq-\varepsilon I\) only with failure probability at most \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Detection is verified by a Rayleigh quotient; nondetection excludes eigenvalues below the threshold only up to a declared failure probability.
assumptions_latex: The probability is over the procedure's internal randomness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: False exclusion of curvature below \(-\varepsilon\) occurs with probability at most \(\delta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a coherent definition of a one-sided probabilistic curvature certificate and correctly separates deterministic detection from probabilistic exclusion. However, no source supports this certificate convention or connects the stated failure event to an actual randomized procedure.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), let \(\gamma\ge0\), let \(0<\delta<1\), and let \(\mathcal A(H;\omega)\) be a randomized procedure on probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional randomized detection or exclusion of curvature below a declared threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A \((\gamma,\delta)\)-probabilistic curvature certificate is a random output taking one of two forms: a unit vector \(v\) with \(v^THv\le-\gamma\), or the declaration \(\mathrm{NoNC}(\gamma)\). Soundness requires \[\mathbb P\!\left[\text{an output vector violates }v^THv\le-\gamma\right]\le\delta.\] If exclusion is supported, it additionally requires \[\mathbb P\!\left[\mathrm{NoNC}(\gamma)\ \text{and}\ \lambda_{\min}(H)<-\gamma\right]\le\delta.\] The probability is over the internal randomness, conditional on the fixed matrix and declared oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probabilistic curvature certificate either returns a unit vector whose Rayleigh quotient is sufficiently negative or declares that no curvature below the threshold exists. Its failure probability bounds false vector certificates and, when exclusion is claimed, false no-negative-curvature declarations.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) and the oracle data are fixed independently of the internal random seed.
The probability space, threshold, and whether the guarantee is detection-only or also exclusion-capable are stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: With failure probability at most \(\delta\), the certificate's declared detection or exclusion predicate is correct.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exclusion guarantee is \(\mathbb P[\mathrm{NoNC}(\gamma)\Rightarrow\lambda_{\min}(H)\ge-\gamma]\ge1-\delta\).
special_cases_latex: For \(\delta=0\), the definition reduces to a deterministic certificate.
A one-sided detector may omit \(\mathrm{NoNC}(\gamma)\) and certify only returned directions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Repeated independent runs with failure probabilities \(\delta_i\) have total failure probability at most \(\sum_i\delta_i\).
boundary_notes: A high probability of finding a direction under a spectral-gap assumption is not an unconditional exclusion certificate.
The probability guarantee does not account for floating-point or oracle error unless those sources are included in the probability model.

notation.meaning: Declaration excluding eigenvalues below minus the threshold.

review_flags: No inspected source precisely supported both randomized detection and exclusion guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Precision Curvature Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Backward-error margin for validating computed negative curvature in floating-point arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\), and suppose floating-point computation produces \(\widehat v\ne0\) and \(\widehat q\) together with certified bounds \(|\widehat q-\widehat v^{\mathsf T}H\widehat v|\le\eta_q\) and \(|\lVert\widehat v\rVert_2^2-\widehat n|\le\eta_n\), where \(\widehat n>\eta_n\). If \(\widehat q+\eta_q<0\), then \(\widehat v^{\mathsf T}H\widehat v<0\), so \(\widehat v\) is a strict negative-curvature direction despite rounding. More quantitatively, if \(\widehat q+\eta_q\le-\varepsilon(\widehat n+\eta_n)\), then \(\widehat v^{\mathsf T}H\widehat v/\lVert\widehat v\rVert_2^2\le-\varepsilon\). Weak separation is inconclusive whenever the error interval crosses zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified error bounds validate negative curvature only when the computed quadratic form remains negative after the full rounding margin is added.
assumptions_latex: \(\eta_q\) and \(\eta_n\) are rigorous absolute error bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The margin test \(\widehat q+\eta_q<0\) rigorously certifies strict negative curvature; an interval crossing zero is inconclusive.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interval-margin tests are internally correct when eta_q and eta_n are rigorous bounds, and the certificate content kind matches the leaf. A source is still required for the finite-precision validation framework and construction of certified error bounds.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb S^n\) be exact, let \(u\) denote unit roundoff, and let a computation return certificate data \(\widehat C\) using floating-point arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional certificate that explicitly separates backward error, conditioning, and spectral separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite-precision curvature certificate with backward-error radius \(\eta\ge0\) is an exact certificate for some symmetric perturbed matrix \(H+E\) satisfying \[E=E^T,\qquad \|E\|_2\le\eta.\] A reported negative direction \(\widehat v\ne0\) is sign-stable at margin \(m>0\) when \[\frac{\widehat v^TH\widehat v}{\|\widehat v\|_2^2}\le-m\quad\text{and}\quad m>\eta.\] An inertia claim is sign-stable only when the certified perturbed spectrum is separated from zero by more than \(\eta\); otherwise zero and weakly signed eigenvalues are classified as unresolved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-precision certificate is interpreted as an exact certificate for a nearby symmetric matrix. Its conclusion transfers to the exact matrix only when the negative-curvature or spectral-separation margin exceeds the backward-error radius. Eigenvalues too close to zero remain unresolved.
assumptions_latex: A normwise backward-error bound \(\eta\), including rounding and inexact-oracle effects, is available.
The perturbation is symmetric and measured in the spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Certificate conclusions are asserted for \(H\) only when their sign margin is larger than the admissible perturbation \(\eta\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A negative Rayleigh conclusion for \(H+E\) with value at most \(-m\) transfers to \(H\) whenever \(m>\|E\|_2\).
special_cases_latex: When \(\eta=0\), the definition reduces to an exact-arithmetic certificate.
If all eigenvalues satisfy \(|\lambda_i(H+E)|>\eta\), their signs are stable under every allowed perturbation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Weak spectral separation forces a three-way outcome: certified positive, certified negative, or unresolved.
boundary_notes: A small residual without a backward-error analysis is not a finite-precision certificate.
Componentwise and normwise error models are not interchangeable without additional scaling information.
review_flags: A precise numerical-linear-algebra source for the backward-error and spectral-separation formulation is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Backward-Stable Finite-Precision Curvature Certificate

children.title: Curvature-Certificate Cost Models
children.top_down_role: Matrix, factorization, Hessian–vector, gradient, memory, and communication costs.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Certificate Cost Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive resource accounting for direct and matrix-free curvature-certificate procedures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a curvature-certificate algorithm, let \(N_H,N_g,N_s,N_f\) denote its numbers of Hessian–vector products, gradient evaluations, preconditioner solves, and matrix factorizations. If their respective unit costs are \(c_H,c_g,c_s,c_f\), and all remaining arithmetic costs \(c_a\), then its serial work is bounded by \(T\le N_Hc_H+N_gc_g+N_sc_s+N_fc_f+c_a\). If peak storage is \(S\), the resource record is \((T,S)\). In a distributed implementation with \(R\) synchronization rounds, communicated volume \(V\), latency \(\alpha\), and inverse bandwidth \(\beta\), the communication contribution is bounded by \(R\alpha+V\beta\). Every reported complexity must specify which primitive counts, accuracy tolerance, and probability of failure are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificate cost is reported through explicit primitive-operation counts, peak memory, and latency-bandwidth communication terms at a stated accuracy and reliability.
assumptions_latex: Primitive costs and counts are defined for one fixed computational architecture.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Total modeled cost is bounded by the stated additive work and communication expressions, with peak memory reported separately.

notation.meaning: Communication rounds, volume, latency, and inverse bandwidth.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resource categories fit the cost-model leaf, but the additive work inequality requires the unit costs to be defined as valid upper bounds, and the latency-bandwidth expression needs an authoritative architecture-model source. No citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be a curvature-certification procedure applied to a problem of dimension \(n\), with explicitly declared matrix, oracle, memory, and distributed-computing primitives.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A multiresource cost definition; it does not collapse unlike resources into one scalar unless weights are declared.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The curvature-certificate cost of \(\mathcal A\) is the resource vector \[\operatorname{Cost}(\mathcal A)=(N_{\mathrm{asm}},N_{\mathrm{fac}},N_{Hv},N_g,N_f,F,M,B,R),\] where the components count matrix assemblies, factorizations, Hessian–vector products, gradient evaluations, function evaluations, scalar arithmetic operations, peak memory, communicated words or bytes, and synchronization rounds. A scalarized cost is defined only after choosing nonnegative weights \(w\): \[C_w(\mathcal A):=w^T\operatorname{Cost}(\mathcal A).\] Expected or high-probability costs must be labeled separately when \(\mathcal A\) is randomized.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cost of curvature certification is a vector of matrix, factorization, Hessian–vector, gradient, function, arithmetic, memory, bandwidth, and synchronization resources. A single numerical cost exists only after weights and a computational platform are specified.
assumptions_latex: The primitive operations and whether base-point gradients may be reused are declared.
For randomized procedures, the statistic used for each cost component is stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Cost}(\mathcal A)\) provides a platform-aware accounting of all principal resources used to produce the certificate.
special_cases_latex: For forward finite-difference Hessian actions with a cached base gradient, each product contributes one additional gradient evaluation.
An explicit dense factorization model records \(N_{\mathrm{fac}}>0\), whereas a matrix-free Krylov model may have \(N_{\mathrm{fac}}=N_{\mathrm{asm}}=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Methods cannot be totally ordered by cost without weights or componentwise dominance.
boundary_notes: Oracle complexity and floating-point operation complexity measure different resources.
Communication and memory costs may dominate arithmetic on distributed or accelerator-based systems.

notation.meaning: Weighted scalarization of the resource vector.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable, and let an iterative method generate \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) using local derivative or oracle information.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional taxonomy based on the mechanism that prevents indefinite stationary points from becoming terminal states.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A saddle-escape method family is a class of update rules equipped with an escape trigger for points satisfying \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\le-\varepsilon_H\). Its defining requirement is that the triggered step is not zero and is selected through at least one of: an explicit negative-curvature direction; minimization of an indefinite trust-region model; minimization of a regularized local model; a deliberate perturbation; or injected stochastic noise. The family specification includes the trigger, step-generation map, and acceptance rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle-escape family consists of iterative methods that detect or respond to a small-gradient region with sufficiently negative curvature and generate a nonzero step using explicit curvature, a restricted or regularized model, a perturbation, or noise. The definition includes how escape is triggered and accepted.
assumptions_latex: The method declares gradient and curvature thresholds \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H>0\).
The information regime used to evaluate or approximate the trigger is stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update mechanism supplies a nonzero escape step whenever its declared strict-saddle trigger is certified.
special_cases_latex: A deterministic negative-curvature line-search method and a randomized perturbed-gradient method belong to different mechanism subfamilies.
Trust-region and cubic-regularization steps qualify through their local-model subproblems even without a separately returned eigenvector.
immediate_consequences_latex: A method that terminates solely because the gradient is small is not, by that fact alone, a saddle-escape method.
boundary_notes: The definition classifies mechanisms and does not itself assert convergence time or escape probability.
Degenerate saddles with no negative eigenvalue are outside the stated strict-negative-curvature trigger.
review_flags: A single authoritative source for the complete cross-family taxonomy was not inspected.
knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Escape Method Family

children.title: Explicit Negative-Curvature Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods directly incorporating a computed negative-curvature direction.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable and let \(x_k\) be a current iterate with gradient \(g_k\) and symmetric curvature model \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic or randomized methods that explicitly compute and use a negative-curvature vector, rather than exploiting indefiniteness only implicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An explicit negative-curvature method is an iterative scheme that, whenever its curvature routine returns \(d_k\ne0\) with \[d_k^TB_kd_k\le-\gamma_k\|d_k\|_2^2\quad(\gamma_k>0),\] constructs the trial step with a nonzero curvature component, \[s_k=p_k+\beta_k\sigma_kd_k,\qquad \beta_k>0,\] where \(p_k\) is an optional descent component and the sign \(\sigma_k\in\{-1,1\}\) is chosen so that \(g_k^T(\sigma_kd_k)\le0\). The globalization rule then accepts or scales this explicitly curvature-bearing step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit negative-curvature method computes a vector with a sufficiently negative quadratic form and places a nonzero multiple of that vector in the trial step. Its sign is chosen not to oppose first-order descent, and a line search or another globalization mechanism controls its length.
assumptions_latex: The returned vector satisfies the displayed negative-curvature inequality.
The acceptance mechanism permits a nonzero curvature component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every triggered trial step contains \(\beta_k\sigma_kd_k\ne0\), so detected negative curvature is directly exploited.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For unit \(d_k\), the certificate is \(d_k^TB_kd_k\le-\gamma_k\).
special_cases_latex: Taking \(p_k=0\) gives a pure negative-curvature step.
Taking \(p_k=-g_k\) gives a composite descent–curvature step.
immediate_consequences_latex: At an exact stationary point with \(d_k^TB_kd_k<0\), either sign of \(d_k\) has zero first-order term and negative quadratic model curvature.
boundary_notes: A positive-definite Hessian modification that discards all negative-curvature information is not explicit curvature exploitation.
The definition does not prescribe how the vector is computed or guarantee a particular decrease rate.

notation.meaning: Optional first-order or Newton descent component.

children.title: Composite Descent-Curvature Direction Methods
children.top_down_role: Families combining first-order descent with separate curvature exploitation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(g\in\mathbb R^n\) be a gradient and \(B\in\mathbb S^n\) a curvature model at the same point. Let \(p\) be a descent direction and \(d\) a negative-curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional methods that retain separate first-order and curvature components in one trial direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A composite descent–curvature direction is \[s(\alpha,\beta)=\alpha p+\beta\sigma d,\qquad \alpha\ge0,\ \beta>0,\] where \[g^Tp<0,\qquad d^TBd<0,\qquad \sigma\in\{-1,1\},\qquad g^T(\sigma d)\le0.\] A composite direction method is an iteration that computes such components, chooses \(\alpha,\beta\), and globalizes the combined direction without forcing \(\beta=0\) whenever the negative-curvature trigger is active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite descent–curvature direction is a nonnegative combination of an ordinary descent direction and a nonzero, suitably signed negative-curvature direction. A method in this family computes and preserves both roles in the trial step when negative curvature is active.
assumptions_latex: \(g\ne0\) when strict first-order descent is required.
The direction \(d\) has a strictly negative quadratic form under \(B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composite step has \(g^Ts<0\) whenever \(\alpha>0\), while retaining the explicitly nonzero curvature component \(\beta\sigma d\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g=0\), the method may set \(\alpha=0\) and use the pure curvature component.
If \(p=-g\), the first-order component is steepest descent.
immediate_consequences_latex: The sign convention prevents the curvature component from increasing the linear model term.
boundary_notes: The sum need not itself have negative quadratic form because cross terms and the descent component may dominate.
Alternating separate descent and curvature iterations are related but are not composite directions in the literal same-step sense.
review_flags: A precise source for this same-step composite-direction definition is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Composite Descent–Curvature Direction

children.title: Descent-Direction Components
children.top_down_role: First-order direction components targeting objective decrease away from stationary regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Descent-Direction Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative admissibility condition for the descent component of a composite descent–curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable at \(x\), with \(g=\nabla f(x)\). A vector \(d_g\) is an admissible descent-direction component with constants \(c_g>0\) and \(C_g>0\) if \(g^{\mathsf T}d_g\le-c_g\lVert g\rVert^2\) and \(\lVert d_g\rVert\le C_g\lVert g\rVert\). When \(g\ne0\), the first inequality makes \(d_g\) a strict descent direction; when \(g=0\), the norm condition forces \(d_g=0\), leaving any composite step's motion to its curvature component. For a composite direction \(d=d_g+d_c\), descent compatibility additionally requires \(g^{\mathsf T}d_c<c_g\lVert g\rVert^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The descent component must yield gradient-proportional decrease and have controlled norm; any added curvature component must not cancel that decrease.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(g\ne0\) and \(g^{\mathsf T}d_c<c_g\lVert g\rVert^2\), then \(g^{\mathsf T}(d_g+d_c)<0\).

notation.meaning: Descent component of the composite direction.
Curvature component added to the descent component.

children.title: Negative-Curvature Components
children.top_down_role: Direction components exploiting locally unstable curvature.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Curvature Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a curvature component for a composite direction at a smooth unconstrained iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable, and set \(g=\nabla f(x)\) and \(H=\nabla^2 f(x)\). A nonzero vector \(v\) is a negative-curvature component with margin \(\gamma>0\) if \(v^{\mathsf T}Hv\le -\gamma\lVert v\rVert^2\). Its sign may be chosen so that \(g^{\mathsf T}v\le0\). Consequently, for every \(\beta\ge0\), the quadratic model \(m(s)=f(x)+g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Hs\) satisfies \(m(0)-m(\beta v)\ge\tfrac12\gamma\beta^2\lVert v\rVert^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-curvature component has uniformly negative Hessian curvature and can be oriented so every nonnegative step along it decreases the local quadratic model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m(0)-m(\beta v)\ge\tfrac12\gamma\beta^2\lVert v\rVert^2\) for every \(\beta\ge0\).

notation.meaning: Gradient and Hessian of f at the current iterate.

knowledge_statements.title: Direction-Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A second-order regime rule selecting descent, curvature, or approximate-stationarity output.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(x\), tolerances \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H>0\), a descent candidate \(d\), and a unit curvature candidate \(v\), compute \(g=\nabla f(x)\) and \(H=\nabla^2 f(x)\). If \(\lVert g\rVert>\varepsilon_g\), select \(p=d\), where \(g^{\mathsf T}d<0\). Otherwise, if \(v^{\mathsf T}Hv< -\varepsilon_H\), orient \(v\) so that \(g^{\mathsf T}v\le0\) and select \(p=v\). If neither test holds and \(v^{\mathsf T}Hv\) certifies \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\ge-\varepsilon_H\), stop and return \(x\) as an \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\)-second-order point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use descent when the gradient is large, negative curvature near first-order stationarity, and stop only when both residual tests pass.
assumptions_latex: \(v\) supplies a valid smallest-eigenvalue certificate when termination is considered
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The rule returns a descent direction, a negative-curvature direction, or a point satisfying \(\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\ge-\varepsilon_H\).

children.title: Component-Compatibility Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where descent and curvature components interfere or provide insufficient joint progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Component-Compatibility Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when descent and curvature components combine without losing their separate model reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the quadratic model \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Hs\), let \(d\) satisfy \(g^{\mathsf T}d<0\), and let \(v\) satisfy \(g^{\mathsf T}v\le0\) and \(v^{\mathsf T}Hv<0\). For \(\alpha,\beta\ge0\), the composite step \(p=\alpha d+\beta v\) obeys \(q(0)-q(p)=[q(0)-q(\alpha d)]+[q(0)-q(\beta v)]-\alpha\beta d^{\mathsf T}Hv\). Hence \(d^{\mathsf T}Hv\le0\) is a compatibility condition guaranteeing at least additive predicted decrease; \(d^{\mathsf T}Hv=0\) is its boundary, while a positive cross-curvature can reduce the combined decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The components combine additively when their Hessian cross-term is nonpositive; a positive cross-term can cancel predicted decrease.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^{\mathsf T}Hv\le0\) implies \(q(0)-q(\alpha d+\beta v)\ge[q(0)-q(\alpha d)]+[q(0)-q(\beta v)]\).

notation.meaning: Quadratic model without its constant term.

knowledge_statements.title: Modified-Newton Negative-Curvature Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A spectral modified-Newton step coupled to explicit extraction of an indefinite Hessian direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iterate \(x_k\), form \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) and a symmetric Hessian model \(H_k=Q_k\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{k,i})Q_k^{\mathsf T}\). Given \(\delta>0\), define \(B_k=Q_k\operatorname{diag}(\max\{|\lambda_{k,i}|,\delta\})Q_k^{\mathsf T}\) and the descent component \(d_k=-B_k^{-1}g_k\). If \(\lambda_{\min}(H_k)<0\), retain a corresponding unit eigenvector \(v_k\), oriented by \(g_k^{\mathsf T}v_k\le0\). Select or combine \(d_k\) and \(v_k\), choose a globalization step length, and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\); terminate only after prescribed first- and second-order tests hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Modify the Newton matrix to obtain descent while separately retaining an eigenvector that exposes negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_k^{\mathsf T}d_k=-g_k^{\mathsf T}B_k^{-1}g_k<0\) when \(g_k\ne0\), while \(v_k^{\mathsf T}H_kv_k=\lambda_{\min}(H_k)<0\) when negative curvature exists.

notation.meaning: Positive-definite spectral modification of the Hessian model.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable, with \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\) or a symmetric approximation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Newton-type families that modify the Newton equations for descent while separately retaining or extracting indefinite-curvature information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A modified-Newton negative-curvature method constructs a descent system \[(B_k+E_k)p_k=-g_k,\qquad B_k+E_k\succ0,\] and, whenever \(B_k\) is detected to be indefinite, also obtains \(d_k\ne0\) satisfying \(d_k^TB_kd_k<0\). Its trial step is either a composite \(s_k=p_k+\beta_k\sigma_kd_k\) with \(\beta_k>0\), or a declared choice between \(p_k\) and a nonzero multiple of \(d_k\). Thus modification secures a descent Newton component but does not erase the detected negative-curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family modifies an indefinite Newton matrix to obtain a stable descent equation while also retaining a direction of negative curvature from the original matrix. The accepted trial step either combines the two directions or selects explicitly between them.
assumptions_latex: \(B_k\) and \(E_k\) are symmetric and \(B_k+E_k\) is positive definite.
An indefinite-curvature branch returns a vector with negative quadratic form under the unmodified \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method has a well-defined descent Newton component and an explicit mechanism for exploiting rather than discarding detected indefiniteness.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A shifted system uses \(E_k=\mu_kI\) with \(\mu_k> -\lambda_{\min}(B_k)\).
special_cases_latex: A modified Cholesky factorization can supply the positive-definite system.
When \(B_k\succ0\), the method may take \(E_k=0\) and omit the curvature branch.
immediate_consequences_latex: For \(g_k\ne0\), the solution of the positive-definite modified system satisfies \(g_k^Tp_k<0\).
boundary_notes: A method that replaces \(B_k\) by a positive-definite matrix and discards all information about its negative eigenspace is modified Newton but not a negative-curvature-retaining method.
The definition does not prescribe the magnitude of the modification.

knowledge_statements.title: Newton–CG Negative-Curvature Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Truncated conjugate gradients simultaneously approximates a Newton step and detects nonpositive curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given symmetric \(H_k\), gradient \(g_k\), radius \(\Delta_k>0\), and residual tolerance \(\eta_k\), initialize \(p_0=0\), \(r_0=g_k\), and \(z_0=-r_0\). Apply conjugate-gradient recurrences to \(H_kp=-g_k\). If a search vector satisfies \(z_j^{\mathsf T}H_kz_j\le0\), choose \(\tau_j\ge0\) with \(\lVert p_j+\tau_jz_j\rVert=\Delta_k\) and output that boundary step. If the next CG step first reaches the boundary, truncate there. If \(\lVert r_j\rVert\le\eta_k\lVert g_k\rVert\), output \(p_j\). Thus Hessian-vector products produce either an inexact Newton step or an explicit nonpositive-curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Truncated CG returns an approximate Newton step unless a Krylov direction reveals nonpositive curvature or reaches the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output lies in \(\{p:\lVert p\rVert\le\Delta_k\}\) and is obtained either by residual convergence, boundary truncation, or detection of \(z_j^{\mathsf T}H_kz_j\le0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Truncated Newton–CG Method with Curvature Detection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(B_k\in\mathbb S^n\). Conjugate gradients is applied from \(z_0=0\) to the Newton system \(B_kp=-g_k\), using residuals \(r_j\) and search directions \(d_j\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Large-scale, matrix-free Newton family in which Krylov iterations serve both as an inexact linear solver and a curvature detector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Newton–CG negative-curvature method generates CG iterates until one of the following occurs: \[\|r_{j+1}\|_2\le\varepsilon_k,\qquad d_j^TB_kd_j\le-\gamma_k\|d_j\|_2^2,\qquad\text{or a globalization boundary is reached}.\] The first event returns an inexact Newton step. The second returns or records \(d_j\) as a curvature direction and terminates or truncates the linear solve. The outer method then globalizes the returned step by line search or a trust-region rule. Only products \(B_kd_j\) are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Newton–CG negative-curvature method approximately solves the Newton equations in a Krylov subspace. It stops when the residual is sufficiently small, when a CG direction has nonpositive or sufficiently negative curvature, or when a globalization boundary is reached. The detected direction is used by the outer method.
assumptions_latex: A product oracle supplies \(B_kd\), exactly or with a separately declared error bound.
The outer globalization rule specifies how a curvature termination is converted into a trial step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inner iteration returns either an inexact Newton step or an explicit Krylov direction satisfying the declared curvature test.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The classical nonpositive-curvature test is the case \(\gamma_k=0\): \(d_j^TB_kd_j\le0\).
special_cases_latex: Line-search Newton–CG returns a descent direction and applies an Armijo, Wolfe, or Goldstein search.
CG–Steihaug follows a detected curvature direction to the trust-region boundary.
immediate_consequences_latex: The method can be Hessian-free when each product is replaced by a gradient finite difference.
boundary_notes: Standard CG is a positive-definite linear solver; the truncation rule is essential when \(B_k\) is indefinite.
A line-search variant may return the accumulated iterate rather than the curvature direction itself, so explicit curvature exploitation must be checked at the outer interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Search Negative-Curvature Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A backtracking line search globalizes directions that exploit gradient descent or negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x_k\), choose \(p_k\) with either \(g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k<0\), or \(g_k^{\mathsf T}p_k\le0\) and \(p_k^{\mathsf T}H_kp_k<0\), where \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(H_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\). Given \(\bar\alpha>0\), \(\rho\in(0,1)\), and \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), select the smallest \(j\ge0\) for which \(\alpha_k=\bar\alpha\rho^j\) satisfies \(f(x_k+\alpha_kp_k)\le f(x_k)+\sigma\alpha_kg_k^{\mathsf T}p_k\). Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_kp_k\), and stop only when the chosen first- and second-order tolerances hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtracking globalizes either a descent direction or an oriented negative-curvature direction using sufficient decrease.
assumptions_latex: The selected direction satisfies one of the stated descent-curvature alternatives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted step satisfies \(f(x_{k+1})\le f(x_k)+\sigma\alpha_kg_k^{\mathsf T}p_k\le f(x_k)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Line-Search Method with a Negative-Curvature Branch
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, and suppose an iteration supplies a direction \(s_k\) that may contain a negative-curvature component from a symmetric model \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature-exploiting methods globalized by a one-dimensional sufficient-decrease or Wolfe-type search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A line-search negative-curvature method chooses a nonzero direction \(s_k\) satisfying \(g_k^Ts_k<0\), where, upon a curvature trigger, \(s_k\) contains or is constructed from \(d_k\) with \(d_k^TB_kd_k<0\). It selects \(\alpha_k>0\) by a line search and sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_ks_k\). For Armijo globalization, the accepted step obeys \[f(x_k+\alpha_ks_k)\le f(x_k)+c_1\alpha_kg_k^Ts_k,\qquad 0<c_1<1.\] Wolfe variants additionally impose a derivative-curvature condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A line-search negative-curvature method forms a descent direction that explicitly contains or derives from detected negative curvature, then chooses its length through a sufficient-decrease or Wolfe-type line search. The iterate is updated only after the one-dimensional acceptance condition holds.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) are defined along the trial ray.
The chosen search direction is strict descent before line search.
When the curvature branch is active, its source vector has negative quadratic form under \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted update is \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\alpha_ks_k\) with \(\alpha_k>0\) satisfying the declared line-search conditions.
special_cases_latex: A Newton–CG line-search method truncates CG on nonpositive curvature and globalizes the returned descent direction.
A composite implementation line-searches a direction containing both gradient-descent and curvature components.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Armijo inequality gives strict objective decrease whenever \(g_k^Ts_k<0\).
boundary_notes: A line search cannot generally accept a direction with \(g_k^Ts_k>0\) under the standard Armijo condition for sufficiently small positive steps.
Near an exact saddle where \(g_k=0\), specialized curvature steps may require a higher-order decrease condition rather than ordinary strict-descent Armijo globalization.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At iterate \(x_k\), let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), let \(B_k\in\mathbb S^n\), and let \(\Delta_k>0\). Define \(m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^Ts+\tfrac12s^TB_ks\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddle-relevant interface to trust-region algorithms: model restriction, negative-curvature boundary handling, and acceptance by actual-to-predicted reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region escape interface returns a step \(s_k\) satisfying \(\|s_k\|_2\le\Delta_k\) and a prescribed approximate-minimization condition for \[\min_{\|s\|_2\le\Delta_k}m_k(s).\] When an inner direction \(d\) satisfies \(d^TB_kd\le0\), the interface follows the current Krylov path along \(d\) to a point on \(\|s\|_2=\Delta_k\) that minimizes the model on that line. It reports predicted reduction \(m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)>0\) and the ratio \[\rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)}{m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)},\] which the outer trust-region controller uses for acceptance and radius adjustment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A trust-region escape interface approximately minimizes an indefinite quadratic model inside a radius. If nonpositive curvature is encountered, it returns a boundary point along that curvature direction. It also supplies predicted reduction and the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio used by the full trust-region controller.
assumptions_latex: The returned step yields positive predicted reduction before the ratio is formed.
The outer controller declares acceptance and radius-update thresholds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The interface returns a feasible model-reducing step, handles detected nonpositive curvature at the boundary, and supplies \(\rho_k\) for globalization.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For CG–Steihaug, curvature termination takes \(s_k=z_j+\tau d_j\) with \(\|s_k\|_2=\Delta_k\) and \(\tau\) chosen to minimize \(m_k\) along the boundary intersection.
special_cases_latex: If \(g_k=0\) and \(B_k\) has a negative eigenvalue, the global trust-region solution lies on the boundary and has strictly lower model value.
If the Hessian is positive definite and the Newton step lies inside the region, the interface may return the Newton step.
immediate_consequences_latex: A negative-curvature boundary step prevents an indefinite stationary model point from being treated as an interior minimizer.
boundary_notes: The interface does not contain the full convergence or radius-update theory of trust-region methods.
A solver that stops at the first nonpositive-curvature direction may exploit weak rather than most-negative curvature.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Cauchy, Eigenpoint, and Accepted Trust-Region Step Roles
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q(s)=q(0)+g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\) on \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\), and let \(\Delta>0\). Write \(\lambda_{\min}(B)\) for the leftmost eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Euclidean trust-region models, including indefinite quadratic models; the definition separates first-order and negative-curvature model-decrease roles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g\ne0\), the Cauchy point is \(s^{\mathrm C}\in\arg\min\{q(-tg):t\ge0,\ t\|g\|\le\Delta\}\). If \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), choose a unit vector \(u\) satisfying \(u^{\mathsf T}Bu\le\kappa_{\mathrm{eig}}\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), where \(\kappa_{\mathrm{eig}}\in(0,1]\), orient it so that \(g^{\mathsf T}u\le0\), and define an eigenpoint by \(s^{\mathrm E}\in\arg\min\{q(tu):0\le t\le\Delta\}\). A model-decrease trial point of quality \(\kappa_{\mathrm{md}}\in(0,1]\) is any \(s\) with \(\|s\|\le\Delta\) and \(q(0)-q(s)\ge\kappa_{\mathrm{md}}\max\{q(0)-q(s^{\mathrm C}),q(0)-q(s^{\mathrm E})\}\), omitting the eigenpoint term when \(B\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a quadratic model on a trust-region ball, the Cauchy point minimizes the model along the feasible negative-gradient ray. When the model Hessian has negative curvature, an eigenpoint minimizes the model along a feasible, suitably oriented direction whose curvature captures a fixed fraction of the most negative eigenvalue. A model-decrease trial point is any feasible point whose predicted reduction is at least a fixed fraction of the larger reduction supplied by these first-order and second-order reference points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s^{\mathrm C}\) certifies gradient-related decrease, \(s^{\mathrm E}\) certifies negative-curvature decrease, and an admissible trial point preserves a fixed fraction of the better certificate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Cauchy point can be written \(s^{\mathrm C}=-t_{\mathrm C}g\), where \(t_{\mathrm C}\in\arg\min_{0\le t\le\Delta/\|g\|}q(-tg)\).
For an exact leftmost eigenvector, one may take \(u^{\mathsf T}Bu=\lambda_{\min}(B)\), corresponding to \(\kappa_{\mathrm{eig}}=1\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g=0\) and \(B\) is indefinite, the Cauchy point supplies no decrease, while the eigenpoint remains nonzero and lies on the trust-region boundary.
If \(B\succeq0\), only the Cauchy decrease is required by this two-role definition.
immediate_consequences_latex: The predicted reduction of a model-decrease trial point is nonnegative.
The definition prevents a second-order trust-region method from accepting only gradient-related decrease when substantial negative curvature is present.
boundary_notes: The definition does not prescribe the acceptance ratio comparing actual and predicted reduction.
Approximate Cauchy and eigenpoints may use comparable sufficient-decrease inequalities, but their constants must be stated separately.

children.title: Cauchy-Point Role
children.top_down_role: First-order model-decrease role of Cauchy-type trial points.

knowledge_statements.title: Cauchy-Point Role
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The Cauchy point guarantees trust-region model decrease controlled by the gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, let \(\Delta>0\), and define \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\). If \(g\ne0\), define \(s_C=-t_Cg\), where \(t_C\) minimizes \(q(-tg)\) over \(0\le t\le\Delta/\lVert g\rVert\); if \(g=0\), set \(s_C=0\). Then \(s_C\) is feasible. Moreover, if \(g\ne0\), \(q(0)-q(s_C)\ge\tfrac12\lVert g\rVert\min\{\Delta,\lVert g\rVert/\lVert B\rVert\}\), where \(\lVert g\rVert/\lVert B\rVert\) is interpreted as \(+\infty\) when \(B=0\); if \(g=0\), the decrease is zero. Thus the Cauchy point supplies a computable gradient-driven baseline for approximate trust-region solutions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Cauchy point minimizes the quadratic model along the negative-gradient ray and supplies the standard gradient-based decrease guarantee, with zero decrease when the gradient is zero.
assumptions_latex: The matrix norm is the Euclidean operator norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(g\ne0\), then \(q(0)-q(s_C)\ge\tfrac12\lVert g\rVert\min\{\Delta,\lVert g\rVert/\lVert B\rVert\}\), with the stated zero-matrix convention; if \(g=0\), then \(q(0)-q(s_C)=0\).

children.title: Eigenpoint Role
children.top_down_role: Negative-curvature model-decrease role of eigenvector-oriented trial points.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenpoint Role
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The eigenpoint guarantees trust-region model decrease controlled by the most negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), let \(u\) be a unit eigenvector associated with \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), oriented so that \(g^{\mathsf T}u\le0\). The boundary eigenpoint \(s_E=\Delta u\) is feasible for radius \(\Delta>0\) and satisfies \(q(0)-q(s_E)=-\Delta g^{\mathsf T}u-\tfrac12\Delta^2\lambda_{\min}(B)\ge\tfrac12[-\lambda_{\min}(B)]\Delta^2\). Thus it supplies a curvature-driven decrease baseline even when the gradient is small or orthogonal to the most-negative eigenspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A boundary step along the most-negative eigenvector guarantees decrease proportional to negative curvature times the squared radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(0)-q(s_E)\ge\tfrac12[-\lambda_{\min}(B)]\Delta^2\).

notation.meaning: Oriented unit eigenvector for the smallest eigenvalue.
Smallest eigenvalue of the model Hessian.

children.title: Model-Decrease Comparison
children.top_down_role: Comparison of first-order and curvature-driven decrease mechanisms.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Decrease Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compares gradient-driven and curvature-driven sufficient-decrease benchmarks for trust-region steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, let \(\Delta>0\), and define \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\). Let \(s_C\) be the Cauchy point. When \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), let \(s_E\) be a boundary eigenpoint for the same model and radius. If a feasible step \(s\) satisfies \(q(0)-q(s)\ge\kappa\max\{q(0)-q(s_C),q(0)-q(s_E)\}\) for some \(\kappa\in(0,1]\), then it satisfies both \(q(0)-q(s)\ge\tfrac\kappa2\lVert g\rVert\min\{\Delta,\lVert g\rVert/\lVert B\rVert\}\) and \(q(0)-q(s)\ge\tfrac\kappa2[-\lambda_{\min}(B)]\Delta^2\). In the first bound, the right-hand side is defined as zero when \(g=0\), and \(\lVert g\rVert/\lVert B\rVert\) is interpreted as \(+\infty\) when \(g\ne0\) and \(B=0\). If \(\lambda_{\min}(B)\ge0\), only the Cauchy benchmark is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible step matching a fixed fraction of the better Cauchy or eigenpoint decrease inherits both the gradient and negative-curvature bounds; only the Cauchy benchmark applies when there is no negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The comparison condition implies the Cauchy decrease bound and, when \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), the eigenpoint decrease bound, each scaled by \(\kappa\).

notation.meaning: Feasible approximate trust-region step being assessed.

children.title: Dominance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Local model regimes favoring one trial-point mechanism over the other.

knowledge_statements.title: Dominance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partitions trust-region model-decrease behavior by comparing gradient and negative-curvature lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and let \(\Delta>0\). Define \(L_C=0\) when \(g=0\); when \(g\ne0\), define \(L_C=\tfrac12\lVert g\rVert\min\{\Delta,\lVert g\rVert/\lVert B\rVert\}\), interpreting \(\lVert g\rVert/\lVert B\rVert\) as \(+\infty\) if \(B=0\). Define \(L_E=\tfrac12\max\{0,-\lambda_{\min}(B)\}\Delta^2\). The gradient-dominant regime is \(L_C>L_E\), the curvature-dominant regime is \(L_E>L_C\), and their transition boundary is \(L_C=L_E\). A step attaining a fixed fraction of \(\max\{L_C,L_E\}\) adapts to the larger of these two model-decrease guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict comparison of the Cauchy and eigenpoint lower bounds identifies gradient-dominant and curvature-dominant regimes, while equality defines their transition boundary.
assumptions_latex: The matrix norm is the Euclidean operator norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_C>L_E\) characterizes strict gradient dominance, \(L_E>L_C\) characterizes strict curvature dominance, and \(L_C=L_E\) is the transition boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Trust-Region Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global optimality representation for a quadratic trust-region subproblem with an indefinite Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{\lVert s\rVert\le\Delta} g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), where \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\) may be indefinite and \(\Delta>0\). A vector \(s_*\) is a global minimizer if and only if there exists \(\lambda_*\ge0\) such that \((B+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g\), \(B+\lambda_*I\succeq0\), \(\lVert s_*\rVert\le\Delta\), and \(\lambda_*(\Delta-\lVert s_*\rVert)=0\). When \(B\) is indefinite, positive semidefiniteness forces \(\lambda_*\ge-\lambda_{\min}(B)>0\), so every global solution lies on the trust-region boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A global trust-region solution is characterized by a shifted positive-semidefinite Hessian, stationarity, feasibility, and complementary slackness.
assumptions_latex: The trust region uses the Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_*\) is globally optimal exactly when the displayed shifted-system and complementarity conditions hold.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), let \(B\in\mathbb S^n\), and let \(\Delta>0\). The feasible set is the closed Euclidean ball \(\mathcal B_\Delta=\{s\in\mathbb R^n:\|s\|_2\le\Delta\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, Euclidean, exact quadratic trust-region subproblems with a symmetric but not necessarily positive-semidefinite Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An indefinite trust-region subproblem is \[\min_{\|s\|_2\le\Delta}q(s),\qquad q(s)=q(0)+g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs,\] with \(\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\). A vector \(s_*\) is a global solution exactly when there exists \(\lambda_*\ge0\) such that \((B+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g\), \(B+\lambda_*I\succeq0\), \(\|s_*\|_2\le\Delta\), and \(\lambda_*(\Delta-\|s_*\|_2)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An indefinite trust-region subproblem minimizes a quadratic function over a Euclidean ball when the symmetric quadratic coefficient has a negative eigenvalue. Its global minimizers are characterized by a nonnegative shift that makes the shifted Hessian positive semidefinite, satisfies the shifted stationarity equation, preserves feasibility, and obeys complementary slackness with the ball boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_*\in\arg\min_{\|s\|_2\le\Delta}q(s)\) if and only if \(\exists\lambda_*\ge0\) satisfying the shifted stationarity, positive-semidefiniteness, feasibility, and complementarity conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The positive-semidefiniteness condition is equivalent to \(\lambda_*\ge-\lambda_{\min}(B)\).
Since \(B\) is indefinite, every global minimizer lies on the boundary: \(\|s_*\|_2=\Delta\), and hence \(\lambda_*>0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g=0\), any boundary vector in a leftmost eigenspace minimizes the quadratic term.
If \(B+\lambda_*I\succ0\), the solution is uniquely \(s_*=-(B+\lambda_*I)^{-1}g\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The ball constraint makes the problem bounded below despite negative curvature.
A local minimizer satisfying only first-order constrained conditions need not be global unless the shifted Hessian is positive semidefinite.
boundary_notes: This definition uses the Euclidean norm; general ellipsoidal trust regions require replacing \(I\) by the metric matrix.
The associated secular equation and numerical solution method are not part of the definition.

notation.meaning: smallest eigenvalue of the symmetric model Hessian

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hard-Case Spectral Degeneracy in a Trust-Region Subproblem
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{\|s\|_2\le\Delta}g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), with \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\), and let \((s_*,\lambda_*)\) satisfy the global optimality conditions \((B+\lambda_*I)s_*=-g\) and \(B+\lambda_*I\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Euclidean trust-region subproblems; the boundary describes the classical hard case caused by a singular optimal spectral shift.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The trust-region subproblem is at its spectral degeneracy boundary, or in the hard case, when \(B+\lambda_*I\) is singular. Equivalently, \(\lambda_*=-\lambda_{\min}(B)\) and solvability requires \(g\perp\ker(B-\lambda_{\min}(B)I)\). Every global solution then has the form \[s_*=-(B+\lambda_*I)^\dagger g+v,\qquad v\in\ker(B+\lambda_*I),\qquad \|s_*\|_2=\Delta.\] The null-space component is chosen to meet the boundary equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The spectral degeneracy boundary, traditionally called the hard case, occurs when the positive-semidefinite shift associated with a global trust-region solution is singular. The gradient must be orthogonal to the leftmost eigenspace, and a solution consists of the pseudoinverse solution plus a component in that eigenspace whose magnitude enforces the trust-region boundary.
assumptions_latex: \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\), \(\Delta>0\), and \((s_*,\lambda_*)\) satisfies the global trust-region optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_*=-\lambda_{\min}(B)\), \(g\perp\ker(B+\lambda_*I)\), and \(s_*\) has the pseudoinverse-plus-null-space representation with \(\|s_*\|_2=\Delta\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(U_{\min}\) spans the leftmost eigenspace, the orthogonality condition is \(U_{\min}^{\mathsf T}g=0\).
Writing \(p=-(B+\lambda_*I)^\dagger g\), one has \(p\perp\ker(B+\lambda_*I)\), so the boundary condition becomes \(\|v\|_2^2=\Delta^2-\|p\|_2^2\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g=0\) and \(B\) is indefinite, \(p=0\) and every \(s_*=v\) with \(v\) in the leftmost eigenspace and \(\|v\|_2=\Delta\) is optimal.
For a simple leftmost eigenvalue, the null-space correction has two possible signs whenever \(\|p\|_2<\Delta\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The optimal solution may be nonunique.
A Krylov space initialized by \(g\) can miss the leftmost eigenspace under exact orthogonality.
boundary_notes: An almost-hard case, where the gradient has a very small rather than zero component in the leftmost eigenspace, is ill-conditioned but is not spectrally singular in this exact sense.
Singularity at an arbitrary nonoptimal shift does not define the hard case.

notation.meaning: leftmost eigenspace at the optimal shift

children.title: Hard-Case Spectral Geometry

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Case Spectral Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes trust-region hard-case geometry through a singular leftmost-eigenvalue shift and gradient orthogonality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{\lVert s\rVert\le\Delta}g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), where \(B\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) is symmetric, \(\Delta>0\), and \(\lambda_1=\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\). Let \(E_1=\ker(B-\lambda_1I)\). In the hard-case regime, \(g\perp E_1\), the optimal shift is \(\lambda_*=-\lambda_1\), and \(\widehat s=-(B+\lambda_*I)^{\dagger}g\) satisfies \(\lVert\widehat s\rVert\le\Delta\). Then \(B+\lambda_*I\) is singular and the global minimizers are exactly \(s_*=\widehat s+z\), where \(z\in E_1\) and \(\lVert\widehat s+z\rVert=\Delta\). If \(\lVert\widehat s\rVert<\Delta\), a nonzero eigenspace component supplies the missing boundary norm; if \(\lVert\widehat s\rVert=\Delta\), the only admissible component is \(z=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the trust-region hard case, the gradient is orthogonal to the leftmost eigenspace and the singular shifted solution is completed, when necessary, by a component in that eigenspace to reach the boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\lVert\widehat s\rVert\le\Delta\), the global minimizers are exactly \(\widehat s+z\) with \(z\in E_1\) and \(\lVert\widehat s+z\rVert=\Delta\).

notation.meaning: Eigenspace associated with the smallest eigenvalue.
Minimum-norm solution of the singular shifted system.

children.title: Singular Subproblem Geometry
children.top_down_role: Trust-region subproblem geometry arising from singular or nearly singular curvature models.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Subproblem Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudoinverse representation of global solutions at the trust-region spectral-degeneracy boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider the trust-region subproblem 
\[\min_{\|p\|\leq \Delta}\; g^{\mathsf T}p+\tfrac12p^{\mathsf T}Bp,\]
where \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\Delta>0\). If a global multiplier \(\lambda_*\geq0\) makes \(M=B+\lambda_*I\succeq0\) singular, then a global solution exists exactly when \(g\in\operatorname{Range}(M)\) and some \(z\in\ker(M)\) satisfies \(\|-M^\dagger g+z\|\leq\Delta\) together with \(\lambda_*(\|-M^\dagger g+z\|-\Delta)=0\). Every global solution has the form
\[p_*=-M^\dagger g+z,\qquad z\in\ker(M),\]
subject to these feasibility and complementarity conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a singular multiplier, every trust-region minimizer is a pseudoinverse solution plus a nullspace vector, with feasibility and complementary slackness determining the admissible vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_*=-\bigl(B+\lambda_*I\bigr)^\dagger g+z\) for an admissible \(z\in\ker(B+\lambda_*I)\).

notation.meaning: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of the shifted Hessian matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Hard-Case Resolution Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact boundary-completion regimes for the classical symmetric trust-region hard case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta=\lambda_{\min}(B)<0\), \(E=\ker(B-\theta I)\), and suppose \(g\perp E\). Set \(M=B-\theta I\succeq0\), \(q=-M^\dagger g\), and \(\lambda_*=-\theta\). The singular hard case is resolvable at this multiplier precisely when \(\|q\|\leq\Delta\). If \(\|q\|<\Delta\), every boundary solution is \(p_*=q+z\), where \(z\in E\) and \(\|z\|=(\Delta^2-\|q\|^2)^{1/2}\). If \(\|q\|=\Delta\), then \(p_*=q\). If \(\|q\|>\Delta\), no solution uses \(\lambda_*=-\theta\); the global multiplier must satisfy \(\lambda_*>-\theta\), making \(B+\lambda_*I\) positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The hard case is completed by a minimum-eigenvalue eigenvector when the pseudoinverse step is short, is unique at equality, and otherwise requires a larger nonsingular shift.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|q\|<\Delta\), \(\|q\|=\Delta\), and \(\|q\|>\Delta\) determine respectively nullspace completion, boundary equality, and a nonsingular larger-shift regime.

notation.meaning: Eigenspace associated with the smallest eigenvalue of the model Hessian.
Minimum-norm solution of the singular shifted stationarity equation.
Smallest eigenvalue of the symmetric Hessian matrix.

children.title: Near-Singularity Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity of curvature exploitation near singular spectral configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Singularity Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditioning of shifted trust-region stationarity equations near spectral degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M(\lambda)=B+\lambda I\succ0\) and \(p(\lambda)=-M(\lambda)^{-1}g\). For perturbations \(e\in\mathbb R^n\) and symmetric \(E\) satisfying \(\|E\|_2<\delta\), where \(\delta=\lambda_{\min}(M(\lambda))\), define \(\widetilde p=-(M(\lambda)+E)^{-1}(g+e)\). Then
\[\|\widetilde p-p(\lambda)\|_2\leq \frac{\|e\|_2+\|E\|_2\|p(\lambda)\|_2}{\delta-\|E\|_2}.\]
Moreover, wherever \(M(\lambda)\) is nonsingular,
\[p'(\lambda)=-M(\lambda)^{-1}p(\lambda).\]
Thus both data sensitivity and multiplier sensitivity can grow proportionally to the reciprocal spectral gap as \(\delta\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The shifted trust-region step becomes ill-conditioned as its smallest shifted eigenvalue approaches zero; perturbation amplification is controlled by the reciprocal spectral gap.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\widetilde p-p(\lambda)\|_2\leq(\|e\|_2+\|E\|_2\|p(\lambda)\|_2)/(\delta-\|E\|_2)\).

notation.meaning: Smallest eigenvalue, hence spectral gap from singularity, of the shifted Hessian.
Perturbations of the shifted matrix and gradient vector.

knowledge_statements.title: Truncated-Krylov Trust-Region Escape
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lanczos–Krylov solution of an indefinite quadratic model with explicit negative-curvature truncation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(g\), a symmetric Hessian operator \(B\), radius \(\Delta>0\), and tolerance \(\tau\geq0\), generate an orthonormal Lanczos basis \(Q_j\) for \(\mathcal K_j(B,g)=\operatorname{span}\{g,Bg,\ldots,B^{j-1}g\}\). At iteration \(j\), solve
\[y_j\in\arg\min_{\|y\|\leq\Delta}\;(Q_j^{\mathsf T}g)^{\mathsf T}y+\tfrac12y^{\mathsf T}(Q_j^{\mathsf T}BQ_j)y,
\qquad p_j=Q_jy_j.\]
Stop when the projected first-order residual is at most \(\tau\), the boundary is reached along detected nonpositive curvature, or the Krylov space ceases to expand. Output \(p_j\); if \(d^{\mathsf T}Bd<0\) is detected, select the feasible sign along \(d\) giving the smaller quadratic-model value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lanczos reduces the indefinite trust-region model to expanding Krylov subspaces and truncates at adequate stationarity, the boundary, or detected negative curvature.
assumptions_latex: \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\) is available through matrix-vector products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(p_j\in\mathcal K_j(B,g)\) satisfies \(\|p_j\|\leq\Delta\) and exploits any detected direction \(d\) with \(d^{\mathsf T}Bd<0\).

notation.meaning: Order-j Krylov subspace generated by the Hessian and gradient.
Orthonormal Lanczos basis for the current Krylov subspace.
Lifted solution of the projected trust-region problem.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q(s)=g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Bs\), let \(B=B^{\mathsf T}\), let \(W\succ0\), and impose \(\|s\|_W=(s^{\mathsf T}Ws)^{1/2}\le\Delta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Large-scale finite-dimensional trust-region subproblems solved through matrix-vector products and truncated preconditioned conjugate-gradient or Lanczos recurrences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A truncated-Krylov trust-region escape step is generated in nested spaces \(\mathcal K_j=\operatorname{span}\{W^{-1}g,(W^{-1}B)W^{-1}g,\ldots,(W^{-1}B)^{j-1}W^{-1}g\}\). Starting at \(s_0=0\), the recurrence is truncated when either a search direction \(d_j\) satisfies \(d_j^{\mathsf T}Bd_j\le0\), or the next interior iterate would violate \(\|s\|_W\le\Delta\). In either event the returned step is \(s=s_j+\tau d_j\), where \(\tau>0\) is chosen so that \(\|s_j+\tau d_j\|_W=\Delta\). A Lanczos continuation may instead minimize the projected quadratic over \(\mathcal K_j\cap\{s:\|s\|_W\le\Delta\}\) to expose an extreme Ritz direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A truncated-Krylov escape step approximately solves a large trust-region subproblem in expanding preconditioned Krylov spaces. The conjugate-gradient recurrence stops at nonpositive curvature or upon crossing the trust-region boundary, and returns the intersection of its current search line with that boundary. A Lanczos continuation can refine the projected subproblem and reveal an approximate leftmost eigenvector when stronger negative-curvature detection is needed.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm accesses \(B\) through products with Krylov vectors and uses the \(W\)-norm trust region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned step belongs to a generated Krylov space, is feasible, and lies on the trust-region boundary whenever truncation is caused by nonpositive curvature or boundary crossing.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under the change of variables \(z=W^{1/2}s\), the method is an ordinary Euclidean Krylov method for the transformed matrix \(W^{-1/2}BW^{-1/2}\).
The nonpositive-curvature test is the failure of positive definiteness of the quadratic model along the current conjugate direction.
special_cases_latex: With \(W=I\), this is the unpreconditioned Steihaug–Toint truncated conjugate-gradient construction.
If \(g=0\), a Krylov space started from the gradient is trivial; a separate, typically random Lanczos starting vector is required to seek negative curvature.
immediate_consequences_latex: No matrix factorization of \(B\) is required.
A detected negative-curvature direction is converted into a feasible boundary step that decreases the quadratic for a suitable orientation.
boundary_notes: The basic truncated conjugate-gradient method can miss negative curvature orthogonal to its starting vector.
Residual termination at an interior point is distinct from saddle escape and need not produce a boundary step.

notation.meaning: preconditioned Krylov subspace at iteration j
norm induced by the positive-definite preconditioner

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable, let \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and write \(g=\nabla f(x)\) and \(H=\nabla^2f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth unconstrained optimization; this is an interface definition covering model stabilization without fixing an acceptance or parameter-update rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A regularization-based escape interface assigns to \((x,g,H)\) a coercive model \[m_{x,\sigma}(s)=f(x)+g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Hs+R_\sigma(s),\] where \(R_\sigma(0)=0\), \(R_\sigma(s)>0\) for \(s\ne0\), and \(R_\sigma(s)/\|s\|_2^2\to\infty\) as \(\|s\|_2\to\infty\). The interface returns a global minimizer \(s_\sigma\in\arg\min_s m_{x,\sigma}(s)\). It is saddle-relevant when \(g=0\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(H)<0\) imply \(s_\sigma\ne0\) and \(m_{x,\sigma}(s_\sigma)<m_{x,\sigma}(0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularization-based escape interface augments the local quadratic model by a positive, superquadratically coercive term and returns a global minimizer of the resulting model. It is saddle-relevant when an exactly stationary point with an indefinite Hessian produces a nonzero step and strict model decrease.
assumptions_latex: The regularizer is positive away from zero and dominates quadratic growth at infinity.
The model subproblem is solved to global optimality for this canonical interface.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regularized model has a global minimizer, and the saddle-relevance condition converts negative curvature at a stationary point into a nonzero model-decreasing step.
special_cases_latex: Cubic regularization uses \(R_\sigma(s)=\sigma\|s\|_2^3/3\), up to coefficient convention.
A shifted-Hessian model uses quadratic regularization, but it is outside the superquadratic coercivity clause unless the shifted quadratic is positive definite.
immediate_consequences_latex: The step length is controlled by the regularization parameter rather than an explicit trust-region constraint.
A global minimizer cannot remain at the origin when the quadratic term has a negative-curvature direction.
boundary_notes: The inspected source supports cubic and Levenberg–Marquardt regularization but does not state this umbrella interface verbatim.
Acceptance ratios and adaptive updates of \(\sigma\) belong to more specific method definitions.

children.title: Cubic-Regularization Methods
children.top_down_role: Second-order regularized-model families with saddle-escape capability.

knowledge_statements.title: Cubic-Regularization Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-step cubic regularization using gradient and Hessian models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\sigma>0\), and a stopping tolerance \(\varepsilon\geq0\), repeat with \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\): choose a global minimizer
\[s_k\in\arg\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n}\;m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}B_ks+\tfrac{\sigma}{3}\|s\|^3,
\]
and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). Stop and output \(x_k\) when the prescribed criticality test, such as \(\|g_k\|\leq\varepsilon\) together with a required lower bound on \(\lambda_{\min}(B_k)\), is met. The cubic term makes \(m_k\) coercive and permits steps along negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each iteration globally minimizes a quadratic Taylor model plus a cubic norm penalty, whose coercivity stabilizes the step while retaining negative-curvature escape.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\), where \(s_k\) globally minimizes the coercive cubic model \(m_k\).

notation.meaning: Cubic-regularized second-order model at the current iterate.
Global minimizer of the regularized model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact cubic-model step is standard and algorithm is an appropriate kind, but no source is provided. The stopping rule also leaves the Hessian-eigenvalue threshold unspecified, so the claimed approximate criticality target cannot be assessed without selecting and citing a precise method variant.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable at \(x\), with \(g=\nabla f(x)\), \(H=\nabla^2f(x)\), and regularization parameter \(M>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth unconstrained optimization with an exact Hessian and a globally minimized cubic model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The cubic-regularized Newton model is \[m_{x,M}(s)=f(x)+g^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}Hs+\tfrac{M}{6}\|s\|_2^3.\] A cubic-regularization step is any \(s_M\in\arg\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n}m_{x,M}(s)\), and the next point is \(x^+=x+s_M\). Every such global minimizer satisfies \[g+Hs_M+\tfrac{M}{2}\|s_M\|_2s_M=0,\qquad H+\tfrac{M}{2}\|s_M\|_2I\succeq0.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cubic-regularization method replaces the unrestricted quadratic Newton model by the quadratic model plus a positive cubic norm term. Its step is a global minimizer of this coercive model. The step obeys a shifted Newton equation, and the Hessian shifted by an amount proportional to the step norm is positive semidefinite.
assumptions_latex: \(M>0\), and the Euclidean norm is used.
The cubic model is minimized globally.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_M\) is a globally defined regularized Newton step satisfying the shifted stationarity and positive-semidefiniteness conditions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(\lambda_M=\tfrac{M}{2}\|s_M\|_2\), the conditions become \((H+\lambda_MI)s_M=-g\), \(H+\lambda_MI\succeq0\), and \(\lambda_M=\tfrac{M}{2}\|s_M\|_2\).
Using the convention \(\sigma\|s\|_2^3/3\) gives the same family after setting \(M=2\sigma\).
special_cases_latex: If \(H\succ0\) and the step is small, the cubic step approaches the Newton step as \(M\downarrow0\).
If \(g=0\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(H)<0\), every global minimizer is nonzero and exploits negative curvature.
immediate_consequences_latex: The model is coercive and therefore possesses at least one global minimizer.
The cubic term supplies an implicit step-size control without an explicit trust-region radius.
boundary_notes: This definition does not specify an inexact subproblem criterion.
Global minimization is material when \(H\) is indefinite; an arbitrary local stationary point is not a canonical cubic step.

notation.meaning: positive cubic regularization coefficient in the source convention
global minimizer of the cubic model

children.title: Adaptive Regularization Methods
children.top_down_role: Regularization families adapting model stabilization from observed model agreement.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Regularization Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Acceptance-ratio adaptation of the cubic regularization parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(0<\eta_1\leq\eta_2<1\), \(0<\gamma_-<1<\gamma_+\), and \(\sigma_0>0\). At \(x_k\), compute a step \(s_k\) producing positive predicted decrease for
\[m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}B_ks+\tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3,
\]
and form
\[\rho_k=\frac{f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)}{m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)}.\]
Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) if \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\), and otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=x_k\). Choose \(\sigma_{k+1}\leq\sigma_k\) when \(\rho_k\geq\eta_2\), retain it when \(\eta_1\leq\rho_k<\eta_2\), and choose \(\sigma_{k+1}\geq\gamma_+\sigma_k\) when \(\rho_k<\eta_1\), with a positive lower safeguard.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive regularization accepts steps by actual-to-predicted reduction and decreases or increases stabilization according to how accurately the model predicts the objective.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Acceptance is determined by \(\rho_k\geq\eta_1\), while poor agreement forces an increase of \(\sigma_k\).

notation.meaning: Ratio of actual objective reduction to predicted model reduction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The acceptance ratio expresses the usual adaptive-regularization interface, and algorithm is the correct kind. Nevertheless, no source supports the particular update policy; the allowed ranges for successful-step updates are incomplete, the positive safeguard is not quantified, and the declared parameter gamma-minus is never used.
