knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define predicted and actual reductions by \(\operatorname{pred}_k=T_k(0)-T_k(s_k)\) and \(\operatorname{ared}_k=f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)\), with \(\operatorname{pred}_k>0\), and define \(\rho_k=\operatorname{ared}_k/\operatorname{pred}_k\). Given \(0<\eta_1\le\eta_2<1\), accept \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\) when \(\rho_k\ge\eta_1\), otherwise set \(x_{k+1}=x_k\). The method is adaptive when \(\sigma_{k+1}<\sigma_k\) is permitted for \(\rho_k\ge\eta_2\), \(\sigma_{k+1}\ge\sigma_k\) for intermediate agreement, and \(\sigma_{k+1}>\sigma_k\) for \(\rho_k<\eta_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive regularization method evaluates a regularized-model step using the ratio of actual objective reduction to predicted reduction. It accepts sufficiently accurate steps and weakens regularization after very good agreement, while retaining or strengthening regularization when agreement is poorer.
assumptions_latex: The regularization family is ordered so that larger \(\sigma\) imposes stronger stabilization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iterate and regularization parameter are updated as explicit functions of the model-agreement ratio \(\rho_k\).
special_cases_latex: For adaptive cubic regularization, \(R_{\sigma_k}(s)=\sigma_k\|s\|_2^3/3\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Poor agreement increases model stabilization before a new trial is accepted.
Very successful iterations may permit larger subsequent steps through a smaller regularization parameter.

children.title: Higher-Order Regularization Interface
children.top_down_role: Higher-degree regularized models targeting second- or higher-order criticality.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Regularization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree-p Taylor models stabilized by a degree-p+1 norm term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an integer \(p\geq2\), a point \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\sigma>0\), define the regularized Taylor model
\[m_{x,\sigma}(s)=T_p(x,s)+\frac{\sigma}{p+1}\|s\|^{p+1},\qquad T_p(x,s)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{1}{j!}\nabla^jf(x)[s]^j.\]
A higher-order regularization step is any approximate global minimizer \(s\) satisfying a specified model-decrease and model-criticality accuracy condition; the trial point is \(x+s\). The term of degree \(p+1\) dominates \(T_p(x,s)\) as \(\|s\|\to\infty\), so the model is coercive when its leading Taylor coefficients are finite. For \(p=2\), this interface reduces to cubic regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pth-order Taylor model is stabilized by a positive degree-(p+1) norm term; approximate minimization supplies steps targeting correspondingly higher-order criticality.
assumptions_latex: \(p\geq2\) is an integer and \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is \(p\)-times continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_{x,\sigma}(s)=T_p(x,s)+\sigma\|s\|^{p+1}/(p+1)\) is the higher-order regularized model and is coercive.

notation.meaning: Degree-p Taylor polynomial of the objective at x along s.
jth derivative tensor applied j times to the step.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The degree-p Taylor model plus a positive degree-(p+1) norm term is a suitable representation for this interface, and its coercivity claim is correct in finite dimensions. No source is supplied, however, and the model-decrease and model-criticality requirements defining an admissible approximate step are left unspecified.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p\ge2\), let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be \(p\)-times differentiable at \(x\), and let \(D^jf(x)[s]^j\) denote the \(j\)-linear derivative applied repeatedly to \(s\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth unconstrained optimization using a degree-\(p\) Taylor model regularized by a degree-\(p+1\) norm term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The order-\(p\) Taylor polynomial and its regularized model are \[T_p(x,s)=f(x)+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac1{j!}D^jf(x)[s]^j,\qquad m_{x,\sigma}^{(p)}(s)=T_p(x,s)+\frac{\sigma}{p+1}\|s\|_2^{p+1},\] where \(\sigma>0\). A higher-order regularization step is a global minimizer \(s_\sigma\in\arg\min_{s\in\mathbb R^n}m_{x,\sigma}^{(p)}(s)\), or an explicitly qualified inexact approximation satisfying stated model-decrease and model-criticality tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A higher-order regularization interface forms the degree-p Taylor polynomial and adds a positive degree-(p+1) norm term. Its canonical exact step globally minimizes this coercive model; inexact variants must separately state their decrease and model-criticality requirements.
assumptions_latex: The Euclidean norm is used in the regularizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The regularized Taylor model is coercive and defines at least one global higher-order step \(s_\sigma\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(p=2\), the model is cubic regularization with coefficient \(\sigma/3\).
special_cases_latex: When \(p=2\), the step targets first- and second-order criticality through gradient and Hessian information.
For \(p>2\), additional derivative tensors can encode escape from higher-order degeneracies.
immediate_consequences_latex: The regularization degree exceeds the Taylor degree by one.
The step-size control is implicit in \(\sigma\) rather than imposed by a hard radius.
boundary_notes: No inspected source supports this exact higher-order interface; a dedicated high-order regularization reference is required.
Existence of derivatives alone does not provide evaluation-complexity guarantees; Lipschitz or Hölder assumptions must be added for such results.

children.title: Perturbed Gradient Methods
children.top_down_role: Full-gradient families with explicit randomized escape phases.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Gradient Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient descent with randomized perturbations triggered in small-gradient regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\), step size \(\eta>0\), gradient threshold \(\varepsilon_g>0\), perturbation radius \(r>0\), escape horizon \(T\), and decrease threshold \(F>0\), perform \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta
abla f(x_k)\) while \(\|
abla f(x_k)\|>\varepsilon_g\). When \(\|
abla f(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon_g\), sample \(\xi\) uniformly from \(\{u:\|u\|\leq r\}\), set \(y_0=x_k+\xi\), and run
\[y_{t+1}=y_t-\eta
abla f(y_t),\qquad 0\leq t<T.\]
If \(f(y_T)\leq f(x_k)-F\), continue from \(y_T\); otherwise output \(x_k\) as the method's approximate second-order stationary candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient descent injects a random displacement when the gradient is small, then either records sufficient escape decrease or returns an approximate second-order stationary candidate.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable with Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A small-gradient phase either yields \(f(y_T)\leq f(x_k)-F\) or returns \(x_k\) as an approximate second-order stationary candidate.

notation.meaning: Random perturbation sampled from the radius-r Euclidean ball.
Required objective decrease for declaring escape.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm fits the method-family leaf, but the stated assumptions and arbitrary positive parameters do not justify treating failure of one escape epoch as an approximate second-order stationarity certificate. A precise perturbed-gradient variant, its Hessian regularity assumptions, parameter scaling, escape horizon, and probability guarantee require a primary source.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, with step size \(\eta>0\), perturbation radius \(r>0\), gradient threshold \(\varepsilon_g>0\), and escape horizon \(T\in\mathbb N\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-gradient, discrete-time methods with explicit randomized escape phases; no stochastic gradient oracle is used.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A perturbed gradient method maintains an iterate and a cooldown state. Outside an escape phase it performs \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta\nabla f(x_k)\). If \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2\le\varepsilon_g\) and the cooldown permits a trigger, it samples \(\xi_k\sim\mathsf P\) supported on \(\{u:\|u\|_2\le r\}\), sets \(x_k\leftarrow x_k+\xi_k\), and then performs at most \(T\) full-gradient steps before another perturbation is allowed. An escape test may declare success when \(f\) decreases by at least a prescribed amount or the iterate leaves a prescribed neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbed gradient descent follows ordinary full-gradient descent except when a small-gradient trigger and cooldown rule authorize a bounded random perturbation. It then executes a finite escape phase of gradient steps and may test for sufficient objective decrease or departure from a local neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(\eta,r,\varepsilon_g>0\), \(T\ge1\), and the perturbation law and cooldown rule are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting process is a full-gradient method with separated deterministic descent and randomized saddle-escape phases.
special_cases_latex: Choosing \(\mathsf P\) uniformly on the radius-\(r\) Euclidean ball gives the common isotropic perturbed-gradient template.
immediate_consequences_latex: At most one perturbation occurs within each cooldown window of length \(T\).
The method reduces to ordinary gradient descent when the trigger never fires or \(r=0\).
boundary_notes: No inspected source supports this exact canonical protocol.
Parameters sufficient for high-probability escape from strict saddles are not part of this definition.
review_flags: Needs a primary perturbed-gradient source with an exact algorithm statement.

children.title: Accelerated Perturbed Methods
children.top_down_role: Perturbation families combined with momentum or acceleration.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Perturbed Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Momentum dynamics combined with randomized restarts in small-gradient regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0=v_0\in\mathbb R^n\), step size \(\eta>0\), momentum \(\beta\in[0,1)\), gradient threshold \(\varepsilon_g>0\), and perturbation radius \(r>0\), iterate
\[v_{k+1}=x_k+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=v_{k+1}-\eta\nabla f(v_{k+1}).\]
Whenever the chosen small-gradient and insufficient-progress test holds, sample \(\xi_k\) from a prescribed distribution supported on \(\{u:\|u\|\leq r\}\), reset \(x_k\leftarrow x_k+\xi_k\) and \(x_{k-1}\leftarrow x_k\), and restart the momentum recurrence. Stop when a complete post-perturbation epoch fails its required objective-decrease test; output the corresponding pre-perturbation point as an approximate stationary candidate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accelerated gradient recurrence is restarted after random perturbations in stagnant small-gradient regions, preventing inherited momentum from masking the escape phase.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable with Lipschitz gradient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method alternates momentum-gradient epochs with randomized, momentum-reset escape epochs.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record has the right algorithmic role but does not define x_{-1} before the first momentum recurrence and leaves the perturbation trigger, progress test, epoch length, and decrease test unspecified. Accelerated perturbation methods have materially different recurrences and guarantees, so a specific sourced variant is necessary.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), let \(\eta>0\), and let \(\beta_k\in[0,1)\). Maintain position states \(x_k\) and momentum states \(v_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order perturbation methods whose base dynamics contain momentum; the definition does not select a particular acceleration schedule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An accelerated perturbed method has base recursion \[v_{k+1}=\beta_kv_k+\nabla f(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta v_{k+1}.\] At a prescribed small-gradient or insufficient-progress trigger, it samples a bounded perturbation \(\xi_k\) and applies either a position perturbation \(x_k\leftarrow x_k+\xi_k\), a momentum perturbation \(v_k\leftarrow v_k+\xi_k\), or both, before running a finite momentum-driven escape phase. The perturbation channel and any momentum restart, such as \(v_k\leftarrow0\), are fixed components of the method definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An accelerated perturbed method combines a momentum gradient recursion with explicit randomized escape phases. At a specified trigger it perturbs position, momentum, or both, optionally restarts momentum, and then evolves the accelerated dynamics for a fixed phase.
assumptions_latex: The objective is differentiable and full gradients are available.
\(\eta>0\), \(\beta_k\in[0,1)\), and the trigger, perturbation distribution, channel, restart rule, and escape horizon are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method's state includes both position and momentum, and its saddle-escape mechanism acts through a declared perturbation channel before accelerated evolution resumes.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using \(y_k=x_k+\beta_k(x_k-x_{k-1})\) and \(x_{k+1}=y_k-\eta\nabla f(y_k)\) gives an alternative two-position representation for a Nesterov-type base dynamic.
special_cases_latex: Setting \(\beta_k=0\) and perturbing only position reduces the template to perturbed gradient descent.
immediate_consequences_latex: Momentum can transport a perturbation across multiple subsequent iterations.
A momentum restart changes the escape dynamics and cannot be omitted from a reproducible method specification.
boundary_notes: No inspected source establishes one canonical accelerated perturbation protocol.
Acceleration guarantees for convex objectives do not by themselves imply saddle-escape guarantees in the nonconvex regime.
review_flags: Needs a source identifying a specific accelerated perturbed algorithm and its perturbation/restart convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed Finite-Sum Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized saddle escape using component-gradient or variance-reduced finite-sum estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). Given \(x_0\), step size \(\eta>0\), threshold \(\varepsilon_g>0\), and radius \(r>0\), construct at each iteration a component-gradient estimator \(v_k\) satisfying \(\mathbb E[v_k\mid x_k]=\nabla f(x_k)\), optionally using periodic full-gradient snapshots for variance reduction, and update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta v_k\). When a snapshot or sufficiently accurate estimator satisfies \(\|v_k\|\leq\varepsilon_g\), sample \(\xi_k\) supported on \(\{u:\|u\|\leq r\}\), replace \(x_k\) by \(x_k+\xi_k\), and begin a bounded escape epoch. Accept the epoch if its prescribed objective-decrease test succeeds; otherwise output the pre-perturbation snapshot.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite-sum methods combine component-gradient estimators with explicit small-gradient perturbations and bounded escape epochs, often controlling estimator variance through full-gradient snapshots.
assumptions_latex: \(f=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), with every \(f_i:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) continuously differentiable.
\(v_k\) is conditionally unbiased and has controlled conditional variance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta v_k\), augmented by a randomized escape epoch whenever the finite-sum stationarity estimator is small.

notation.meaning: Component objectives defining the finite-sum problem.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is appropriate for the leaf, but the record merges component-SGD, snapshot variance reduction, and generic bounded escape epochs without specifying one estimator or its variance bound. Conditional unbiasedness also excludes some standard recursive variance-reduced constructions, making the claimed family coverage unreliable without a primary source and specialization.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), and consider a stochastic recursion \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_k(\nabla f(x_k)+\zeta_{k+1})\) adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal F_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete stochastic first-order dynamics in which persistent or state-dependent noise supplies the unstable-direction excitation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A noise-driven escape interface consists of the stochastic-gradient recursion together with conditional noise laws satisfying \(\mathbb E[\zeta_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=0\) and covariance \(\Sigma_k=\mathbb E[\zeta_{k+1}\zeta_{k+1}^{\mathsf T}\mid\mathcal F_k]\). At a strict saddle \(x\) with negative eigenspace \(E_-(x)\), the noise is escape-nondegenerate when \(\operatorname{tr}(P_{E_-(x)}\Sigma_kP_{E_-(x)})>0\) whenever \(x_k\) lies in the designated saddle neighborhood. The interface includes the step-size schedule and any truncation or moment conditions imposed on \(\zeta_{k+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A noise-driven escape interface is a stochastic-gradient recursion equipped with a conditional noise model. Its noise is nondegenerate for a strict saddle when the conditional covariance has positive energy in the saddle's negative-curvature subspace throughout the relevant neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: The process is adapted to \((\mathcal F_k)\), and conditional first and second moments exist.
The negative eigenspace is defined from \(\nabla^2f(x)\) at a twice-differentiable strict saddle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive projected conditional variance supplies a formal interface condition for random excitation of unstable saddle directions.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\Sigma_k\succeq\sigma^2I\) for some \(\sigma>0\), the nondegeneracy condition holds for every nonzero subspace.
special_cases_latex: Stochastic-gradient sampling noise, isotropic Gaussian noise, and state-dependent anisotropic noise fit the covariance interface when their conditional moments exist.
immediate_consequences_latex: Zero covariance on \(E_-(x)\) provides no covariance-level mechanism for leaving the saddle along its unstable directions.
Persistent isotropic noise is nondegenerate at every strict saddle.
boundary_notes: No inspected source supports this exact umbrella covariance condition.
Positive projected variance alone does not state an escape probability or time without tail, smoothness, and step-size assumptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic-Gradient Noise Escape
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional excitation condition enabling intrinsic stochastic-gradient noise to escape strict saddles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose stochastic gradient descent has the form \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta(
abla f(x_k)+\zeta_k)\), with \(\mathbb E[\zeta_k\mid x_k]=0\) and conditional covariance \(\Sigma(x_k)\). At a strict saddle \(x_*\), let \(E_-\) be the negative eigenspace of \(H_*=
abla^2f(x_*)\), and let \(P_-\) be its orthogonal projector. A directional noise-excitation condition is
\[P_-\Sigma(x)P_-\succeq 
u P_-\]
for some \(
u>0\) throughout a neighborhood of \(x_*\). Under the linearized recursion, each Hessian eigenvector \(u\in E_-\) with eigenvalue \(-\gamma<0\) has deterministic amplification factor \(1+\eta\gamma>1\), while the covariance condition continually injects nonzero variance into that unstable direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intrinsic stochastic-gradient noise supports strict-saddle escape only when its covariance injects positive variance into every relevant negative-curvature direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice continuously differentiable near a strict saddle \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_-\Sigma(x)P_-\succeq\nu P_-\) supplies stochastic excitation in every negative-curvature direction.

notation.meaning: Negative eigenspace of the Hessian at the strict saddle.
Orthogonal projector onto the negative eigenspace.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covariance inequality is a clear sufficient excitation condition and condition is the correct content kind. The plain statement overstates it as necessary for escape in every negative-curvature direction, while the mathematical statement only explains local linearized amplification. A source is required to establish the intended sufficiency or necessity claim and any probabilistic escape conclusion.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F(x;\xi)\) be a sample loss, \(f(x)=\mathbb E[F(x;\xi)]\), and \(G(x,\xi)=\nabla_xF(x;\xi)\) be an unbiased stochastic gradient.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation-form smooth nonconvex optimization where sampling variability, rather than an added perturbation, is the proposed escape mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Stochastic-gradient noise escape uses \[x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_kG(x_k,\xi_{k+1})=x_k-\eta_k igl(
abla f(x_k)+\zeta_{k+1} igr),\] where \(\zeta_{k+1}=G(x_k,\xi_{k+1})-
abla f(x_k)\) and \(\mathbb E[\zeta_{k+1}\mid x_k]=0\). It is intrinsically saddle-exciting at a strict saddle \(x\) when the sampling-noise covariance \(\Sigma(x)=\mathbb E[\zeta\zeta^{\mathsf T}\mid x]\) satisfies \(\lambda_{\min}(U_-^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x)U_-)>0\), where the columns of \(U_-\) form an orthonormal basis of the negative eigenspace of \(
abla^2f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic-gradient noise escape is ordinary stochastic gradient descent viewed as gradient descent plus centered sampling noise. The noise is intrinsically exciting at a strict saddle when its covariance is positive definite after restriction to the entire negative-curvature eigenspace.
assumptions_latex: Samples are conditionally independent according to the declared oracle model.
The stochastic gradient is conditionally unbiased and has finite conditional covariance.
The objective is twice differentiable at the strict saddle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restricted covariance condition gives every negative-curvature direction nonzero conditional sampling variance.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The condition is equivalent to \(u^{\mathsf T}\Sigma(x)u>0\) for every nonzero \(u\in E_-(x)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\Sigma(x)\succeq\sigma^2I\), then intrinsic excitation holds uniformly at all strict saddles.
A rank-one noise covariance may excite one negative direction while failing the stated full-subspace condition.
immediate_consequences_latex: No separate perturbation variable is needed when component sampling already satisfies the excitation condition.
Unbiasedness alone does not guarantee saddle excitation.
boundary_notes: No inspected source supports this exact restricted-covariance definition.
Escape guarantees require quantitative lower covariance bounds in a neighborhood, not merely at one point.

children.title: Langevin-Type Escape
children.top_down_role: Diffusive dynamics interacting with saddles and local barriers.

knowledge_statements.title: Langevin-Type Escape
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euler-discretized overdamped Langevin dynamics for diffusion-assisted traversal of saddle neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_0\in\mathbb R^n\), step size \(h>0\), inverse temperature \(\beta>0\), and independent \(\xi_k\sim\mathcal N(0,I_n)\), the unadjusted Langevin iteration is
\[x_{k+1}=x_k-h\nabla f(x_k)+\sqrt{2h/\beta}\,\xi_k.\]
It is the Euler–Maruyama discretization of
\[dX_t=-\nabla f(X_t)\,dt+\sqrt{2/\beta}\,dW_t.\]
Run until a prescribed exit, objective-decrease, or approximate-criticality test is met, and output the corresponding iterate. Near a strict saddle, the drift expands displacement along negative Hessian eigendirections, while the Gaussian term supplies a nondegenerate displacement in every direction at each step.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Langevin escape combines gradient drift with isotropic Gaussian diffusion; negative-curvature drift amplifies displacement while noise prevents confinement to a saddle's stable manifold.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable and its gradient satisfies conditions ensuring the stated diffusion is well posed.
\(h>0\), \(\beta>0\), and \(\xi_k\) are independent standard Gaussian vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}=x_k-h\nabla f(x_k)+\sqrt{2h/\beta}\,\xi_k\) discretizes the overdamped Langevin diffusion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The iteration and its Euler–Maruyama interpretation are standard, and algorithm fits the leaf. No source is supplied, the diffusion well-posedness assumption is circular rather than explicit, and the exit or criticality rule is not specialized. The local drift-and-noise observation does not itself provide an escape-time or probability guarantee.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable, let \(\beta>0\) be an inverse-temperature parameter, and let \((W_t)_{t\ge0}\) be standard \(n\)-dimensional Brownian motion.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous overdamped Langevin diffusion and its unadjusted Euler discretization, interpreted as noise-driven motion near saddles and barriers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The overdamped Langevin dynamics associated with \(f\) and inverse temperature \(\beta\) is the stochastic differential equation \[dX_t=-\nabla f(X_t)\,dt+\sqrt{2\beta^{-1}}\,dW_t.\] Its Euler–Maruyama discretization with step \(h>0\) is \[X_{k+1}=X_k-h\nabla f(X_k)+\sqrt{2h\beta^{-1}}\,Z_{k+1},\qquad Z_{k+1}\sim\mathcal N(0,I_n),\] with independent Gaussian increments. The nondegenerate diffusion term distinguishes Langevin-type escape from deterministic gradient flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overdamped Langevin dynamics follows negative gradient drift plus isotropic Brownian diffusion at a temperature controlled by beta. Its standard unadjusted discretization is a gradient step plus an independent isotropic Gaussian perturbation whose covariance is proportional to the step size and temperature.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable and the stochastic differential equation is well posed under suitable local regularity and growth conditions.
\(\beta>0\); for the discrete scheme, \(h>0\) and the Gaussian increments are independent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diffusion has covariance rate \(2\beta^{-1}I_n\), while each Euler noise increment has covariance \(2h\beta^{-1}I_n\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With temperature \(T=\beta^{-1}\), the diffusion coefficient is \(\sqrt{2T}\).
special_cases_latex: As \(\beta\to\infty\), the noise vanishes formally and the dynamics approaches gradient flow.
Replacing \(I_n\) by a positive-definite mobility matrix yields a preconditioned Langevin variant.
immediate_consequences_latex: The isotropic noise has nonzero variance in every negative-curvature direction.
Finite temperature permits movement that is not monotone in the objective.
boundary_notes: No inspected optimization source supports this exact Langevin escape formulation and scaling convention.
Invariant-distribution and barrier-crossing claims require additional coercivity, regularity, and ergodicity assumptions.
review_flags: Needs an authoritative Langevin optimization or sampling source supporting both the SDE and discretization scaling.

children.title: Anisotropic Noise Design
children.top_down_role: Structured perturbations designed around local geometry or preconditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Anisotropic Noise Design
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry-adapted perturbation interface for escaping strict saddles in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(x\in\mathbb{R}^d\), and choose a symmetric matrix \(M(x)\succeq 0\), a scale \(\sigma>0\), and a centered random vector \(z\) with \(\mathbb{E}[zz^{\mathsf T}]=I\). Generate \(\xi=\sigma M(x)^{1/2}z\), set \(\widetilde x=x+\xi\), and restart the prescribed descent map from \(\widetilde x\). For a unit negative-curvature direction \(u\) satisfying \(u^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2 f(x)u<0\), require \(u^{\mathsf T}M(x)u\geq\mu>0\); then \(\mathbb{E}[(u^{\mathsf T}\xi)^2]\geq\sigma^2\mu\). Stop when the chosen first- or second-order criticality test is met, and output the resulting iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample a covariance-shaped perturbation that retains positive variance along every relevant negative-curvature direction, then restart descent and stop at the selected criticality test.
assumptions_latex: \(z\) is centered, isotropic, and has finite second moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[(u^{\mathsf T}\xi)^2]\geq\sigma^2\mu\) for every protected unit direction \(u\).

notation.meaning: minimum variance-shaping mass on protected directions

review_flags: No supplied locator supports this precise anisotropic saddle-escape interface.
Exact tail assumptions needed for a probabilistic escape theorem remain unspecified.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The covariance calculation is correct and the algorithm kind fits the method-design leaf, but the descent map, protected direction set, criticality test, and distributional conditions needed for an actual saddle-escape guarantee are unspecified. A dedicated anisotropic-perturbation source with a precise theorem or algorithm locator is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), and let \(C(x)\in\mathbb S_+^n\) be a state-dependent covariance or preconditioning matrix with a measurable square root \(C(x)^{1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Discrete stochastic first-order methods using state-dependent, directionally structured noise rather than isotropic perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An anisotropic-noise step has the form \[x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta_kd_k+\sqrt{\eta_k}\,C(x_k)^{1/2}z_{k+1},\qquad \mathbb E[z_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]=0,\quad \mathbb E[z_{k+1}z_{k+1}^{\mathsf T}\mid\mathcal F_k]=I.\] Thus the conditional perturbation covariance is \(\eta_kC(x_k)\). The design is negative-curvature adequate at \(x\) when \(u^{\mathsf T}C(x)u>0\) for every nonzero \(u\) in the negative eigenspace of \(\nabla^2f(x)\); it is uniformly adequate on a region when this quadratic form is bounded below by \(c_-\|u\|_2^2\) for some \(c_->0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An anisotropic-noise method multiplies standardized random noise by a state-dependent covariance square root. Its noise covariance can emphasize directions selected by local geometry or preconditioning. It is adequate for negative-curvature escape when its covariance is positive definite on the complete negative eigenspace, uniformly so when a positive lower bound holds throughout a region.
assumptions_latex: \(C(x)\succeq0\) and a measurable square root is selected.
The standardized noise is conditionally centered with identity conditional covariance.
For saddle adequacy, \(f\) is twice differentiable at the point considered.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbation covariance is \(\eta_kC(x_k)\), and the restricted positive-definiteness condition prevents the design from suppressing any unstable Hessian direction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(U_-\) spans the negative eigenspace, adequacy is equivalent to \(U_-^{\mathsf T}C(x)U_-\succ0\).
special_cases_latex: \(C(x)=\sigma^2I\) gives isotropic noise.
Choosing \(C(x)=P(x)P(x)^{\mathsf T}\) represents noise shaped by a preconditioner \(P(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Rank-deficient noise can still be adequate if its range contains the negative eigenspace.
A covariance concentrated only in positive-curvature directions is inadequate for the stated saddle-escape interface.
boundary_notes: No inspected source supports this exact design criterion.
State-dependent covariance can introduce additional drift in continuous-time formulations; the displayed definition is discrete-time.
Adequacy is not an optimality criterion for allocating a fixed noise budget.

notation.meaning: uniform covariance lower bound on negative-curvature directions

review_flags: Needs a source on geometry-adapted or anisotropic noise for nonconvex saddle escape.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), let \(\mathcal A\) be an algorithm class, and let \(C_A(f,x_0,\omega,t)\) count a specified computational resource used by algorithm \(A\) through time \(t\). The variable \(\omega\) contains any algorithmic or oracle randomness.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth, possibly nonconvex optimization; the definition accommodates deterministic worst-case guarantees, high-probability guarantees, and escape from quantitatively specified saddle regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a target predicate \(P_\theta(f,x)\), the stationarity-or-escape complexity of \(A\) is \[\mathcal C_A(\theta,\delta;\mathcal F)=\inf\!\left\{N\in\mathbb N_0:\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\sup_{x_0\in X_0(f)}\Pr_\omega\!\left(\exists t\;[C_A(f,x_0,\omega,t)\le N\ \wedge\ P_\theta(f,x_t)]\right)\ge1-\delta\right\}.\] Here \(P_\theta\) may require approximate first-order stationarity, approximate second-order stationarity, or departure from a saddle neighborhood with a prescribed objective decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The complexity is the smallest resource budget that makes the probability of reaching the chosen stationarity or saddle-escape target at least one minus the failure probability, uniformly over the function class and admitted initial points.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) and the admissible initialization sets \(X_0(f)\) are fixed before the supremum is taken.
The resource counter \(C_A\) and target predicate \(P_\theta\) are specified independently of the tested instance.
\(\delta\in[0,1)\); deterministic complexity is represented by \(\delta=0\) and a degenerate random variable \(\omega\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_A(\theta,\delta;\mathcal F)=\inf\left\{N:\inf_{f\in\mathcal F,\,x_0\in X_0(f)}\Pr_\omega\bigl(\tau_{P_\theta}\le N\bigr)\ge1-\delta\right\},\qquad \tau_{P_\theta}:=\inf\{C_A(t):P_\theta(f,x_t)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: When the success probability is monotone in the budget, \(\mathcal C_A\le N\) is equivalent to \(\inf_{f,x_0}\Pr_\omega(\tau_{P_\theta}\le N)\ge1-\delta\).
special_cases_latex: First-order stationarity uses \(P_\epsilon(f,x)\equiv\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\epsilon\).
Second-order stationarity may use \(P_{\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H}(f,x)\equiv\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\epsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\ge-\epsilon_H\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Different counters produce iteration, oracle, derivative-evaluation, or linear-algebra complexity for the same target predicate.
A uniform bound over a larger instance class cannot be smaller than the corresponding bound over a subclass.
boundary_notes: The definition does not identify a numerical rate without a specified function class, initialization condition, algorithm, and cost unit.
Expected stopping cost is a different performance criterion and need not follow from a high-probability bound without tail control.

notation.meaning: Target stationarity or saddle-escape predicate with tolerance parameters.

review_flags: No supplied source was inspected; an exact source locator supporting this synthesized umbrella definition is required.

children.title: Complexity Cost Models
children.top_down_role: Distinct units of work used in stationarity and saddle-escape comparisons.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an execution trace \(\xi=(s_0,o_1,s_1,\ldots,o_T,s_T)\) record algorithmic states \(s_t\) and primitive operations \(o_t\) drawn from a fixed operation set \(\mathcal O\). Let \(w:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R_+^q\) assign nonnegative resource charges.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract accounting for smooth nonconvex algorithms; it separates computational resources before any scalar weighting or asymptotic rate is chosen.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A complexity cost model is a pair \((\mathcal O,w)\) inducing the additive vector cost \[C_w(\xi)=\sum_{t=1}^T w(o_t)\in\mathbb R_+^q.\] For a target predicate \(P\), the associated worst-case budget of algorithm \(A\) over \(\mathcal F\) is \[\mathcal C_{A,w}(P;\mathcal F)=\inf\{b\in\mathbb R_+^q:\forall f\in\mathcal F,\ \exists t\text{ with }C_w(\xi_{0:t})\preceq b\text{ and }P(f,x_t)\},\] where \(\preceq\) is componentwise order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost model fixes primitive operations and assigns each a nonnegative resource vector. The cost of a run is the sum of those vectors, and a worst-case target budget is a componentwise budget under which every admitted instance reaches the target.
assumptions_latex: The operation taxonomy and weights are fixed across all compared algorithms and instances.
Costs are additive along a trace and nonnegative in every resource coordinate.
The target predicate and instance class are specified separately from the accounting convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C_w(\xi_{0:T})=\sum_{t=1}^{T}w(o_t),\qquad \mathcal C_{A,w}(P;\mathcal F)=\inf\{b:\forall f\in\mathcal F,\ \tau_P(f)\preceq b\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A scalar cost model is obtained from any price vector \(a\in\mathbb R_+^q\) by \(C_{a,w}(\xi)=a^\top C_w(\xi)\).
special_cases_latex: Unit iteration cost uses \(q=1\) and charges one unit to every outer iteration.
Oracle accounting uses separate coordinates for function, gradient, Hessian, Hessian-vector, or stochastic-oracle calls.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two complexity rates are directly comparable only after their target predicate, instance class, and resource weights have been aligned.
A bound on one coordinate does not by itself bound uncounted computation or communication.
boundary_notes: Wall-clock time generally is not additive or machine-independent and therefore requires an explicitly calibrated model.
Parallel work and critical-path depth are distinct coordinates unless the model deliberately combines them.

notation.meaning: Resource charge assigned to primitive operation.
Accumulated vector cost of an execution trace.

review_flags: No inspected source establishes this vector-cost formalization or a precise locator.

children.title: Iteration Complexity
children.top_down_role: Outer-iteration accounting for criticality targets.

knowledge_statements.title: Iteration Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability outer-iteration count for approximate second-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For iterates \((x_k)_{k\geq0}\) generated for \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), tolerances \(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H>0\), and failure level \(\delta\in[0,1)\), define the stopping time \[\tau_{\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H}=\inf\{k\in\mathbb{N}_0:\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\epsilon_g,\ \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(x_k))\geq-\epsilon_H\}.\] The iteration complexity is \[K(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H,\delta)=\inf\{K\in\mathbb{N}_0:\mathbb{P}(\tau_{\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H}\leq K)\geq1-\delta\},\] with the infimum of the empty set defined as \(+\infty\). For a deterministic method, take \(\delta=0\). Only completed outer updates are counted; inner oracle and linear-algebra work are accounted for separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration complexity is the least outer-update count that reaches approximate second-order stationarity with the prescribed success probability, and it is infinite if no finite count provides that guarantee.
assumptions_latex: \((x_k)_{k\geq0}\) is defined on a common probability space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H,\delta)\in\mathbb{N}_0\cup\{+\infty\}\), and whenever it is finite, \(\mathbb{P}(\tau_{\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H}\leq K(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H,\delta))\geq1-\delta\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable. An algorithm may request exact values of \(f(x)\), \(
abla f(x)\), \(
abla^2f(x)\), or \(
abla^2f(x)v\) at adaptively chosen points and vectors.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic exact-oracle accounting; approximate, stochastic, automatic-differentiation, and finite-difference evaluations require separate declared charges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an execution trace \(\xi\), define its objective-derivative evaluation vector by \[E(\xi)= igl(N_f(\xi),N_g(\xi),N_H(\xi),N_{Hv}(\xi) igr),\] where each coordinate counts completed calls returning respectively \(f(x)\), \(
abla f(x)\), \(
abla^2f(x)\), and \(
abla^2f(x)v\). Given prices \(c_f,c_g,c_H,c_{Hv}\ge0\), its scalar evaluation cost is \[C_E(\xi)=c_fN_f+c_gN_g+c_HN_H+c_{Hv}N_{Hv}.\] Evaluation complexity is the least such budget needed to reach the specified target uniformly over the instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cost model counts objective, gradient, full-Hessian, and Hessian-vector evaluations separately. A scalar evaluation cost is obtained only after fixed nonnegative prices are assigned to those call types.
assumptions_latex: Each oracle call has a declared input-output contract, and repeated calls are counted unless caching is explicitly included.
The prices are fixed independently of the algorithm, instance, and requested accuracy.
Arithmetic performed after an oracle response is not charged unless it is represented by an additional cost coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[E(\xi)=(N_f,N_g,N_H,N_{Hv}),\qquad C_E(\xi)=\langle(c_f,c_g,c_H,c_{Hv}),E(\xi)\rangle.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Separate evaluation bounds retain the partial order \(E(\xi)\preceq b\), whereas a weighted sum projects that vector bound onto one declared price system.
special_cases_latex: A first-order oracle model retains only \((N_f,N_g)\).
A matrix-free second-order model may set \(N_H=0\) while counting \(N_{Hv}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A full-Hessian evaluation cannot be silently identified with one Hessian-vector product.
Joint function-and-gradient calls must be counted according to an explicitly declared bundled-call convention.
boundary_notes: The definition does not account for factorization, storage, or communication costs implicit in using returned derivatives.
Finite-difference gradients have multiple objective-call costs and are not exact gradient calls under this definition.

notation.meaning: Numbers of objective, gradient, full-Hessian, and Hessian-vector calls.

children.title: Objective-Evaluation Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Evaluation Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts scalar objective-oracle calls through the criticality stopping time.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau\) be the algorithm's stopping iteration and let \(q_k^f\in\mathbb{N}_0\) be the number of scalar calls to the oracle \(x\mapsto f(x)\) made while producing outer iteration \(k\), including rejected trials and line-search or trust-region tests. Define \[N_f(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}q_k^f+q_{\mathrm{stop}}^f,\] where \(q_{\mathrm{stop}}^f\) counts any objective calls used solely to certify termination. The objective-evaluation complexity at a prescribed accuracy and success level is the least bound \(B_f\) for which \(\mathbb{P}(N_f(\tau)\leq B_f)\) meets that success level. Batched evaluations are counted pointwise unless declared otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count every scalar objective call, including rejected trials and termination checks, until the criticality target is certified.
assumptions_latex: Each scalar evaluation of \(f\) has unit objective-oracle cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_f(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}q_k^f+q_{\mathrm{stop}}^f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau\) be the stopping iteration and let \(q_k^g\in\mathbb{N}_0\) count calls returning the full vector \(\nabla f(x)\) while producing outer iteration \(k\). Define \[N_g(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}q_k^g+q_{\mathrm{stop}}^g,\] including repeated gradients at distinct trial points and gradients used only for termination. The gradient-evaluation complexity is the least bound \(B_g\) attaining the prescribed deterministic or probabilistic guarantee for \(N_g(\tau)\). knowledge_statements.title: Hessian-Information Evaluation Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts declared second-order information requests without conflating their computational costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\tau\) be the stopping iteration. For each second-order information type \(s\) in a declared set \(\mathcal S\), let \(q_{k,s}\) count requests of type \(s\) during outer iteration \(k\), where types may include a full Hessian, a Hessian–vector product, or an entry or block. Define \[N_s(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}q_{k,s}+q_{\mathrm{stop},s}.\] Hessian-information evaluation complexity is the vector \((N_s(\tau))_{s\in\mathcal S}\), or a stated scalarization of it. A full Hessian evaluation and one Hessian–vector product are distinct oracle events and must not be identified without an explicit conversion model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count each declared form of second-order information separately through termination, unless an explicit cost conversion combines the counts.
assumptions_latex: The oracle types in \(\mathcal S\) are fixed before accounting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_s(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}q_{k,s}+q_{\mathrm{stop},s}\) for every \(s\in\mathcal S\).

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic-Oracle Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counts sampled component, minibatch, or stochastic derivative oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a stochastic oracle queried at \((x,xi)\) return a declared subset of \(f(x;xi)\), \(g(x;xi)\), and second-order information. If iteration \(k\) uses a batch \(B_k\), define the sample-oracle count through stopping time \(\tau\) by \[N_{\mathrm{stoch}}(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}|B_k|+|B_{\mathrm{stop}}|.\] If one sampled index supplies several outputs jointly, it is one call only when the oracle contract declares joint return; otherwise outputs are counted separately. Stochastic-oracle complexity is the least bound \(B_{\mathrm{stoch}}\) attained with the stated success probability, accuracy criterion, sampling rule, and replacement convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Count sampled indices or oracle transactions through termination, explicitly declaring batching, replacement, jointly returned derivatives, accuracy, and success probability.

The batches \(B_k\) and stopping time \(\tau\) are measurable.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f(x)=\mathbb E_\zeta[F(x;\zeta)]\) or \(f(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). A stochastic oracle queried at \(x\) with fresh randomness \(\zeta\) returns a declared random tuple, such as \((F(x;\zeta),G(x;\zeta),H(x;\zeta)v)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic-oracle complexity is the total number of charged sampled component outputs, including all minibatch elements, required to meet a specified target with the prescribed probability.
assumptions_latex: The oracle's conditional bias, variance, independence, and output-type guarantees are part of the instance class.
Every sampled component used in a minibatch contributes to the cost, even when processed in parallel.
The stopping rule is measurable with respect to the information returned by earlier oracle calls.

children.title: Linear-Algebra Resource Complexity
children.top_down_role: Factorization, Krylov, storage, and communication costs hidden by oracle counts.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider an optimization execution in dimension \(d\) that forms or applies matrices, solves linear systems or trust-region subproblems, and possibly communicates distributed vectors or matrix blocks.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-aware accounting supplementing iteration and oracle counts; the primitive resource coordinates must be fixed for the implementation regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear-algebra resource profile of a trace \(\xi\) is \[R_{\mathrm{LA}}(\xi)=\bigl(N_{\mathrm{mv}},N_{\mathrm{fact}},F_{\mathrm{arith}},M_{\mathrm{peak}},W_{\mathrm{comm}},S_{\mathrm{comm}}\bigr),\] counting matrix-vector products, matrix factorizations, arithmetic work, peak stored scalars, communicated words, and synchronization rounds. Each coordinate is the sum or maximum appropriate to that resource: operation and communication work are additive, while \(M_{\mathrm{peak}}=\max_t M_t\). A scalar cost is \(c^\top R_{\mathrm{LA}}\) for a declared nonnegative price vector \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linear-algebra complexity is a multidimensional resource profile recording matrix-vector products, factorizations, arithmetic work, peak memory, communication volume, and synchronization depth. Additive resources are summed, while peak storage is maximized over the execution.
assumptions_latex: Matrix representation, sparsity, precision, and parallel architecture are fixed when asymptotic resource bounds are compared.
Every factorization and matrix-vector application is charged according to the declared representation.
Peak memory and communication depth are not replaced by total arithmetic work.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R_{\mathrm{LA}}(\xi)=\left(\sum_t n_{\mathrm{mv},t},\sum_t n_{\mathrm{fact},t},\sum_t F_t,\max_t M_t,\sum_t W_t,\sum_t S_t\right).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: In a serial dense-arithmetic model, a price vector may convert the profile into flop complexity, but the conversion depends on matrix dimension and operation type.
special_cases_latex: A Krylov implementation is commonly described by Hessian-vector products, stored basis vectors, and orthogonalization work.
A direct Newton implementation additionally records factorization work and matrix storage.
immediate_consequences_latex: Equal oracle complexities do not imply equal arithmetic, memory, or communication complexities.
Matrix-free access can remove full-matrix storage while retaining substantial Krylov and synchronization costs.
boundary_notes: Numerical stability and finite-precision error are quality attributes, not resource coordinates unless explicitly incorporated.
A single universal scalar cost is unavailable without hardware-dependent prices.

notation.meaning: Vector of linear-algebra and communication resources.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorization Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense-arithmetic baseline for explicitly factored second-order systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider solving a dense symmetric linear system \(As=b\) with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) by an explicit \(LDL^{\mathsf T}\) or Cholesky factorization when applicable. In the unit-cost arithmetic RAM model, forming the factorization requires \(O(d^3)\) arithmetic operations and stores \(O(d^2)\) scalars; each subsequent triangular solve with the stored factors requires \(O(d^2)\) operations. If such a fresh dense factorization is performed at each of \(K\) outer iterations, its aggregate factorization work is \(O(Kd^3)\), excluding objective and derivative construction costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fresh dense symmetric factorization costs cubic arithmetic and quadratic storage; repeated over K iterations, the factorization work is cubic times K.
assumptions_latex: Pivoting, when needed, does not change the asymptotic dense bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_{\mathrm{fact}}(K,d)=O(Kd^3)\), with \(O(d^2)\) factor storage and \(O(d^2)\) work per subsequent solve.

notation.meaning: number of fresh factorizations or outer iterations

children.title: Krylov-Space Complexity
children.top_down_role: Computational costs associated with iterative subspace construction.

knowledge_statements.title: Krylov-Space Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-free arithmetic and storage for unrestarted short-recurrence and fully orthogonalized Krylov implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\), let \(r_0\in\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{0\}\), and define the order-\(m\) Krylov space \[\mathcal K_m(A,r_0)=\operatorname{span}\{r_0,Ar_0,\dots,A^{m-1}r_0\}.\] Suppose an unrestarted Krylov implementation performs \(m\) iterations and one application of \(A\) per iteration. If each application costs \(T_A\), an implementation admitting a fixed-length short recurrence requires \(O(mT_A+md)\) arithmetic and \(O(d)\) auxiliary storage. An implementation that stores and fully orthogonalizes an explicit Krylov basis requires \(O(mT_A+m^2d)\) arithmetic and \(O(md)\) storage. These bounds exclude the cost of forming \(A\) explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An m-iteration Krylov implementation uses m matrix–vector products. When a fixed-length recurrence is available it uses linear auxiliary storage, whereas storing and fully orthogonalizing the basis uses order md storage and quadratic orthogonalization work.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}\) is accessed through matrix–vector products costing \(T_A\).
The implementation performs \(m\in\mathbb{N}\) unrestarted iterations and one application of \(A\) per iteration.
The short-recurrence bound applies only when the chosen Krylov method and matrix structure admit a fixed-length recurrence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The short-recurrence implementation has cost \(O(mT_A+md)\) and auxiliary storage \(O(d)\), while the stored, fully orthogonalized implementation has cost \(O(mT_A+m^2d)\) and storage \(O(md)\).

notation.meaning: order-m Krylov space generated from the initial vector; its dimension is at most m

children.title: Memory Complexity

knowledge_statements.title: Memory Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Peak live scalar storage required by an optimization implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an implementation whose run consists of computational steps \(t=0,\dots,T\), where \(T\in\mathbb{N}_0\) is the final step at termination. Let \(L_t\) be the set of simultaneously live scalar storage locations at step \(t\), including iterates, derivative data, factors, Krylov bases, and persistent algorithmic state. Define the memory complexity of the run by \[M(T)=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}|L_t|.\] Read-only problem data may be included or excluded, but the convention must be stated. Thus storing a dense \(d\times d\) Hessian or factor contributes \(\Theta(d^2)\), storing \(m\) vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) contributes \(\Theta(md)\), and storing a constant number of such vectors contributes \(\Theta(d)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Memory complexity is the peak number of simultaneously live scalar words over all computational steps through termination, under a stated convention for read-only problem data.
assumptions_latex: Storage is measured in scalar words.
\(T\in\mathbb{N}_0\) is the final computational-step index at termination.
The set of live algorithmic objects is defined at every computational step \(t\in\{0,\dots,T\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(T)=\max_{0\leq t\leq T}|L_t|\).

knowledge_statements.title: Communication Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributed cost measured by synchronization rounds and transmitted scalar words.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a distributed optimization run with stopping iteration \(\tau\in\mathbb{N}_0\), let \(r_k\in\mathbb{N}_0\) be the number of global communication or synchronization rounds and let \(w_k\in\mathbb{N}_0\) be the total number of scalar words transmitted while producing outer iteration \(k\). Define \[R(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}r_k+r_{\mathrm{stop}},\qquad W(\tau)=\sum_{k=0}^{\tau-1}w_k+w_{\mathrm{stop}}.\] Communication complexity is the ordered pair \((R(\tau),W(\tau))\), or a declared latency-bandwidth scalarization \[C_{\mathrm{comm}}(\tau)=\alpha R(\tau)+\beta W(\tau),\] where \(\alpha,\beta\geq0\). The processor topology, collective-operation charging rule, and treatment of concurrent messages must be fixed before algorithms are compared.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Measure distributed communication through termination by synchronization rounds and transmitted scalar words, optionally combining them with declared nonnegative latency and bandwidth weights under a fixed network convention.
assumptions_latex: The processor topology and collective charging convention are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C_{\mathrm{comm}}(\tau)=\alpha R(\tau)+\beta W(\tau)\).

children.title: First-Order Stationarity Complexity
children.top_down_role: Upper- and lower-bound families for approximate first-order criticality.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), let \(X_0(f)\) specify admitted initial points, and let \(C_A(t)\) be a nondecreasing cost counter for algorithm \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional unconstrained smooth nonconvex optimization; stationarity is measured by the Euclidean gradient norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\epsilon>0\), define the first-order hitting cost \[\tau_\epsilon(A,f,x_0,\omega)=\inf\{C_A(t):\|\nabla f(x_t)\|\le\epsilon\}.\] The high-probability first-order stationarity complexity is \[\mathcal C_A^{(1)}(\epsilon,\delta;\mathcal F)=\inf\left\{N:\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}\inf_{x_0\in X_0(f)}\Pr_\omega(\tau_\epsilon\le N)\ge1-\delta\right\}.\] A method-class upper bound is the infimum over \(A\) in the class; a lower bound asserts that every admitted method has an instance whose hitting cost exceeds the stated budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First-order stationarity complexity is the smallest resource budget within which an algorithm produces a point whose gradient norm is at most the requested tolerance, uniformly over the admitted problems and initializations and with the prescribed confidence.
assumptions_latex: Every \(f\in\mathcal F\) is differentiable at all iterates generated before termination.
The initial-condition restriction and cost unit are fixed as part of the complexity model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_A^{(1)}(\epsilon,\delta;\mathcal F)=\inf\{N:\inf_{f,x_0}\Pr_\omega(\min_{C_A(t)\le N}\|\nabla f(x_t)\|\le\epsilon)\ge1-\delta\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For deterministic \(A\), \(\mathcal C_A^{(1)}(\epsilon,0)\le N\) exactly when every admitted run has some iterate of cost at most \(N\) satisfying \(\|\nabla f(x_t)\|\le\epsilon\).
special_cases_latex: Iteration complexity takes \(C_A(t)=t\).
Gradient-evaluation complexity takes \(C_A(t)\) equal to the cumulative number of gradient calls.
immediate_consequences_latex: Complexity is nonincreasing as \(\epsilon\) is relaxed or \(\delta\) is increased.
A last-iterate guarantee is stronger than this best-visited-iterate definition unless the output rule selects the certified iterate.
boundary_notes: Small gradient does not exclude a local maximum or saddle point.
Constrained problems require a projected-gradient, normal-cone, or other appropriate stationarity residual.

notation.meaning: Cost at first visit to an approximate first-order stationary point.

children.title: Descent-Method Upper-Bound Family
children.top_down_role: Worst-case first-order criticality guarantees for descent methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Descent-Method Upper-Bound Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case gradient-descent bound for an objective with Lipschitz gradient and finite initial optimality gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, bounded below by \(f_{\inf}\), and have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Starting from \(x_0\), define \(x_{k+1}=x_k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(\Delta=f(x_0)-f_{\inf}\). Then, for every integer \(N\geq 1\),
\[
\min_{0\leq k<N}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq \sqrt{\frac{2L\Delta}{N}}.
\]
Consequently, at most \(\lceil 2L\Delta\varepsilon^{-2}\rceil\) iterations are sufficient to produce an iterate satisfying \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient descent reaches gradient norm at most epsilon within order L times the initial objective gap divided by epsilon squared iterations.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\varepsilon}\leq \lceil 2L\Delta\varepsilon^{-2}\rceil\).

notation.meaning: initial objective gap to the stated lower bound
iterations until an epsilon-first-order point is found

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be bounded below by \(f_{\inf}\), and let a deterministic method generate \(x_0,x_1,\ldots\). Write \(\Delta_0=f(x_0)-f_{\inf}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A defining template for worst-case first-order bounds of descent methods; the exponent depends on the decrease law and the relationship between the step measure and gradient residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method belongs to the descent-method upper-bound family with parameters \((a,p,\kappa)\), where \(a>0\), \(p>0\), and \(\kappa>0\), if every nonterminal iteration satisfies \[f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\ge a\,s_k^p,\qquad \|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\kappa s_k.\] Its canonical first-order bound is the budget obtained by accumulating this decrease until some gradient norm is at most \(\epsilon\): \[N(\epsilon)\le\left\lceil\frac{\Delta_0\kappa^p}{a\epsilon^p}\right\rceil.\] The family consists of all methods and function classes for which uniform constants make these relations valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family comprises methods whose accepted steps produce a uniform decrease proportional to a positive power of a step measure and whose gradients are controlled by that measure. Its associated complexity scale is the initial objective gap divided by the per-iteration decrease forced while the gradient exceeds tolerance.
assumptions_latex: The constants \(a,p,\kappa\) are uniform over all admitted instances and iterations.
An iteration terminates successfully whenever \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min_{0\le k<N}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon\quad\text{for some}\quad N\le\left\lceil\frac{(f(x_0)-f_{\inf})\kappa^p}{a\epsilon^p}\right\rceil.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The family can be parameterized directly by a residual decrease condition \(f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\ge c\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^p\), with \(c=a/\kappa^p\).
special_cases_latex: For the common quadratic decrease law \(p=2\), the template yields an \(O(\epsilon^{-2})\) iteration bound.
immediate_consequences_latex: A sharper exponent requires a stronger uniform decrease law or additional structure.
The template also bounds the number of unsuccessful residual-large iterations if their total count is uniformly controlled by accepted iterations.
boundary_notes: The displayed rate is a family-defining template, not a claim that every algorithm called a descent method satisfies it.
Nonmonotone, stochastic, or inexact methods require modified decrease and probability conditions.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Methods for First-Order Criticality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity bound obtained by globally minimizing Lipschitz-Hessian cubic models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable, bounded below by \(f_{\inf}\), and have an \(M\)-Lipschitz Hessian. At iteration \(k\), let \(s_k\) globally minimize
\[
m_k(s)=f(x_k)+\nabla f(x_k)^{\mathsf T}s+\tfrac12s^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x_k)s+\tfrac{M}{6}\|s\|^3,
\]
and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+s_k\). There is a universal constant \(C>0\) such that an iterate with \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\) occurs within at most \(C\Delta\sqrt{M}\,\varepsilon^{-3/2}+1\) model evaluations, where \(\Delta=f(x_0)-f_{\inf}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact cubic second-order models improve the worst-case first-order stationarity exponent from epsilon minus two to epsilon minus three halves.
assumptions_latex: Each cubic model is globally minimized.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\varepsilon}=O(\Delta\sqrt{M}\,\varepsilon^{-3/2})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mathematical role and epsilon^{-3/2} first-order rate are plausible, but no citation supports the exact cubic coefficient, global-minimization hypotheses, universal-constant formulation, or model-evaluation count.
