knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable. At iterate \(x_k\), a method constructs a model \(m_k(s)\) using \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) and curvature information \(B_k\), possibly through matrix-vector products.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order information is used to generate steps, but successful termination is defined solely by approximate first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A second-order method for first-order criticality is an algorithm whose step decision is measurable with respect to information containing a curvature model \[m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top B_ks+r_k(s),\] where \(B_k\) represents exact or approximate Hessian information, while its target predicate is exclusively \[P_\epsilon^{(1)}(f,x)\equiv\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\epsilon.\] Its complexity is \(\mathcal C_A^{(1)}(\epsilon,\delta;\mathcal F)\) under a declared counter that separately identifies iterations, derivative evaluations, or curvature products.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This class uses Hessian or Hessian-approximation information in its local step model but measures success only by the gradient-norm tolerance. Consequently, a first-order termination claim must not be presented as a second-order stationarity guarantee.
assumptions_latex: The curvature information \(B_k\) is part of the algorithm's information set and influences the generated step or acceptance decision.
The target is \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\epsilon\), without a required eigenvalue condition.
The resource counter declares whether forming, factoring, or applying \(B_k\) is charged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_{A,\mathrm{curv}}^{(1)}(\epsilon,\delta;\mathcal F):=\inf\{N:\inf_{f,x_0}\Pr(\exists t,\ C_A(t)\le N,\ \|\nabla f(x_t)\|\le\epsilon)\ge1-\delta\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The classification is determined by the information used to form steps and the first-order target, not by the name of the update rule.
special_cases_latex: Trust-region Newton, cubic regularization, and Newton-CG can fall in this class when analyzed only until \(\|\nabla f\|\le\epsilon\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Curvature-enabled iteration bounds and curvature-product bounds are distinct statements.
No lower bound on \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\) follows from membership in this class.
boundary_notes: A method using only gradient differences does not automatically count as second-order unless the declared information model treats them as curvature access.
Guarantees imposing both gradient and Hessian-eigenvalue tolerances belong to second-order stationarity complexity.

notation.meaning: Exact or approximate curvature operator used in the local model.

review_flags: No inspected source supports this exact information-target classification.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-model complexity for a first-order target

children.title: First-Order Oracle Lower-Bound Family
children.top_down_role: Hard-instance limitations for smooth nonconvex first-order methods.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Oracle Lower-Bound Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-unrestricted deterministic first-order oracle lower bound for smooth nonconvex stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exists a universal constant \(c>0\) with the following property. For every \(L,\Delta,\varepsilon>0\) in the nontrivial accuracy regime and every deterministic algorithm whose query \(x_k\) depends only on preceding values and gradients, some dimension \(d\), some differentiable \(L\)-smooth function \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), and some initial point \(x_0\) satisfy \(f(x_0)-\inf f\leq\Delta\) while
\[
\|\nabla f(x_k)\|>\varepsilon\qquad\text{for all }k<cL\Delta\varepsilon^{-2}.
\]
Thus the \(O(L\Delta\varepsilon^{-2})\) descent-method rate is unimprovable in order over this oracle class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No deterministic first-order oracle method can uniformly improve the epsilon-squared denominator for finding stationary points of smooth nonconvex functions.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic and accesses only function values and gradients at queried points.
The hard-instance dimension may grow with the oracle budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\varepsilon}=\Omega(L\Delta\varepsilon^{-2})\) in the worst case.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is correctly framed as a lower complexity bound for the target leaf, but the claimed deterministic-oracle lower bound depends critically on the precise oracle model, nontrivial accuracy regime, resisting-oracle assumptions, and dimension growth. An authoritative theorem locator is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of differentiable functions, and let a first-order oracle return \(O_f(x)=(f(x),\nabla f(x))\). An algorithm's next query and output may depend on previous oracle responses and internal randomness but on no other information about \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Black-box smooth nonconvex optimization; the quantifier order distinguishes a minimax oracle lower bound from poor performance of one fixed method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(L(\epsilon,\delta;\mathcal F,\mathfrak A)\) is a first-order oracle lower bound if \[\forall A\in\mathfrak A\ \forall N<L(\epsilon,\delta;\mathcal F,\mathfrak A)\ \exists f\in\mathcal F:\Pr_A\!\left(\min_{0\le t\le N}\|\nabla f(x_t)\|>\epsilon\right)>\delta.\] Equivalently, no algorithm in \(\mathfrak A\) can uniformly produce an \(\epsilon\)-first-order stationary point with success probability at least \(1-\delta\) using fewer than \(L\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order oracle lower bound is a minimax impossibility statement: for every admitted black-box algorithm and every smaller query budget, some function in the class prevents the algorithm from finding a point with sufficiently small gradient at the required confidence.
assumptions_latex: Algorithms access the instance only through the declared first-order oracle and any allowed internal randomness.
The hard instance may depend on the algorithm and query budget but must belong to the fixed class \(\mathcal F\).
The dimension convention, initialization restriction, smoothness parameters, and initial objective-gap bound are included in \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{A\in\mathfrak A}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\inf\{N:\Pr_A(\min_{t\le N}\|\nabla f(x_t)\|\le\epsilon)\ge1-\delta\}\ge L(\epsilon,\delta;\mathcal F,\mathfrak A).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For deterministic algorithms and \(\delta=0\), every algorithm using fewer than \(L\) queries has a hard instance on which all queried gradients have norm greater than \(\epsilon\).
special_cases_latex: A dimension-dependent lower bound restricts the claim to dimensions large enough to embed the hard instance.
A randomized lower bound quantifies success probability over algorithmic randomness and any randomized oracle.
immediate_consequences_latex: An upper bound matching \(L\) in tolerance dependence is optimal only for the same function, oracle, dimension, and algorithm classes.
Restricting the algorithm class can only make the minimax lower bound no smaller.
boundary_notes: The definition itself supplies no rate such as a power of \(\epsilon\).
Access to Hessian-vector products, finite-sum indices, or higher derivatives changes the oracle class and may invalidate a first-order lower bound.

notation.meaning: Admitted class of adaptive first-order oracle algorithms.

review_flags: No inspected lower-bound source or exact locator was available.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimax first-order oracle lower bound

children.title: Second-Order Stationarity Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity families jointly controlling first-order residuals and negative curvature.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\subset C^2(\mathbb R^d)\), let \(X_0(f)\) be the admitted initializations, and let \(C_A(t)\) be a nondecreasing resource counter for an algorithm \(A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional unconstrained smooth nonconvex optimization with separate tolerances for gradient residual and negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\epsilon_g>0\) and \(\epsilon_H\ge0\), define \[P^{(2)}_{\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H}(f,x)\equiv\left[\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\epsilon_g\ \wedge\ \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\ge-\epsilon_H\right].\] The high-probability second-order stationarity complexity is \[\mathcal C_A^{(2)}(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H,\delta;\mathcal F)=\inf\left\{N:\inf_{f\in\mathcal F,x_0\in X_0(f)}\Pr(\exists t,\ C_A(t)\le N,\ P^{(2)}_{\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H}(f,x_t))\ge1-\delta\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second-order stationarity complexity is the smallest declared resource budget ensuring, uniformly and at the required confidence, an iterate with both small gradient and no Hessian eigenvalue below the allowed negative-curvature tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Every admitted objective is twice differentiable at every candidate output.
The norm, eigenvalue convention, initialization set, cost unit, and probability space are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_A^{(2)}=\inf\{N:\inf_{f,x_0}\Pr(\min_{C_A(t)\le N}\max\{\|\nabla f(x_t)\|/\epsilon_g,\,[-\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_t))]_+/\epsilon_H\}\le1)\ge1-\delta\},\] with the ratio form used only when \(\epsilon_H>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The Hessian condition is equivalent to \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq-\epsilon_H I\).
special_cases_latex: Setting \(\epsilon_H=0\) requires positive-semidefinite Hessian at the output.
A coupled convention may set \(\epsilon_H=\sqrt{L_H\epsilon_g}\), but that is a specialization rather than part of the definition.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every second-order stationary output is first-order stationary at tolerance \(\epsilon_g\).
Relaxing either tolerance or increasing \(\delta\) cannot increase the least feasible budget.
boundary_notes: Approximate second-order stationarity does not guarantee local minimality without additional landscape assumptions.
Nonsmooth and constrained problems require different first- and second-order residuals.
review_flags: No inspected source supplies the exact two-tolerance complexity definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate second-order stationarity complexity

children.title: Trust-Region Second-Order Bounds
children.top_down_role: Approximate second-order criticality guarantees for trust-region variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Second-Order Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation bound for trust-region methods targeting simultaneous approximate first- and second-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable and bounded below, with Lipschitz gradient and Lipschitz Hessian on the relevant level set. Consider a trust-region method whose quadratic models use \(\nabla f(x_k)\) and \(\nabla^2f(x_k)\), whose trial steps achieve a fixed fraction of Cauchy and negative-curvature model decrease, and whose acceptance and radius parameters are fixed away from their degenerate limits. Then constants \(C_1,C_2>0\), independent of \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H\), give
\[
N(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\leq C_1\varepsilon_g^{-2}+C_2\varepsilon_H^{-3}
\]
before some iterate satisfies \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\geq-\varepsilon_H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A suitably implemented trust-region method attains approximate second-order stationarity in order epsilon-gradient minus two plus epsilon-curvature minus three evaluations.
assumptions_latex: The gradient and Hessian are Lipschitz on the relevant level set.
Trial steps provide uniform Cauchy and negative-curvature decrease.
Standard trust-region acceptance and radius safeguards hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)=O(\varepsilon_g^{-2}+\varepsilon_H^{-3})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits, but the generic Cauchy and negative-curvature decrease conditions are insufficiently tied to a theorem establishing the simultaneous O(epsilon_g^{-2}+epsilon_H^{-3}) evaluation bound. The counted evaluation type also needs source support.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^d)\). At \(x_k\), define \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), \(H_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\), and the quadratic model \(m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top H_ks\) on \(\|s\|\le\Delta_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-derivative trust-region schemes whose subproblem solution or approximation detects both gradient-driven decrease and negative curvature; this is a family definition, not a universal numerical rate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region second-order bound is a uniform budget \(B_{\mathrm{TR}}(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\) for algorithms that select \(s_k\) satisfying \[\|s_k\|\le\Delta_k,\qquad m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)\ge\kappa_{\mathrm{md}}\max\{D_g(g_k,H_k,\Delta_k),D_H(H_k,\Delta_k)\},\] accept steps using the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio, and update \(\Delta_k\) by fixed safeguards. Here \(D_g\) and \(D_H\) are declared gradient and negative-curvature model-decrease benchmarks. The bound requires an iterate of cost at most \(B_{\mathrm{TR}}\) satisfying \(\|g_k\|\le\epsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(H_k)\ge-\epsilon_H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family consists of safeguarded trust-region methods whose trial steps capture a fixed fraction of both gradient and negative-curvature model decrease. A second-order bound is a uniform resource budget for reaching the joint gradient and Hessian-eigenvalue tolerances.
assumptions_latex: The objective is bounded below on the relevant level set and has the smoothness required to compare actual and quadratic-model reductions.
The trust-region radius update parameters and model-decrease fraction \(\kappa_{\mathrm{md}}>0\) are uniform.
The subproblem procedure can expose negative curvature when \(\lambda_{\min}(H_k)<-\epsilon_H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists k\text{ with }C_A(k)\le B_{\mathrm{TR}}(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H),\quad \|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon_g,\quad \nabla^2f(x_k)\succeq-\epsilon_HI.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The curvature condition may be stated as \(\lambda_{\min}(H_k)\ge-\epsilon_H\).
special_cases_latex: Exact trust-region subproblem minimization satisfies a stronger model condition than many fraction-of-decrease requirements.
Truncated conjugate-gradient variants need an explicit negative-curvature detection or complementary eigenvalue procedure.
immediate_consequences_latex: A bound counting outer iterations does not determine the number of inner Krylov products.
If only a Cauchy decrease condition is imposed, the definition generally supports first-order rather than second-order complexity.
boundary_notes: The functions \(D_g,D_H\) and the numerical rate must be specified by a sourced theorem before a quantitative bound is asserted.
Local convergence of trust-region Newton methods is distinct from global worst-case second-order complexity.

notation.meaning: Uniform fraction of benchmark model decrease.

review_flags: The hinted trust-region texts were not inspected; no exact source locator supports this complexity-family definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Trust-region second-order complexity family

children.title: Cubic-Regularization Second-Order Bounds
children.top_down_role: Approximate second-order criticality guarantees for cubic regularization.

knowledge_statements.title: Cubic-Regularization Second-Order Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint first- and second-order evaluation complexity of adaptive cubic regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be bounded below, twice continuously differentiable, and have an \(M\)-Lipschitz Hessian. Suppose a cubic-regularization method computes trial steps satisfying uniform approximate model-minimization and model-stationarity conditions, uses regularization parameters bounded above on successful iterations, and accepts steps by a fixed actual-to-predicted decrease test. Then constants \(C_g,C_H>0\), independent of the tolerances, satisfy
\[
N(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\leq C_g\varepsilon_g^{-3/2}+C_H\varepsilon_H^{-3}
\]
before an iterate obeys \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\geq-\varepsilon_H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adaptive cubic regularization reaches joint approximate second-order stationarity with gradient exponent three halves and curvature exponent three.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is bounded below and has an \(M\)-Lipschitz Hessian.
Cubic subproblems satisfy uniform approximate minimization conditions.
Acceptance and regularization updates use fixed nondegenerate parameters.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)=O(\varepsilon_g^{-3/2}+\varepsilon_H^{-3})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated exponents are plausible for adaptive cubic regularization and the kind fits the leaf, but no inspectable source defines the approximate model conditions, successful/unsuccessful iteration accounting, or hypotheses needed for the joint bound.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^d)\). At \(x_k\), a cubic-regularization method uses \[m_k(s)=f(x_k)+g_k^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top H_ks+\frac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|^3,\] with \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), \(H_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\), and \(\sigma_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth nonconvex methods using cubic regularization of a quadratic Taylor model and targeting approximate second-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A cubic-regularization second-order bound is a uniform cost budget \(B_{\mathrm{CR}}(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\) for methods whose accepted step \(s_k\) satisfies declared approximate model-optimality conditions, including sufficient model decrease and residual conditions of the form \[\|
abla m_k(s_k)\|\le\eta_k,\qquad \lambda_{\min}(
abla^2m_k(s_k))\ge-\zeta_k,\] with controlled \(\eta_k,\zeta_k\), and whose regularization parameters remain safeguarded. The budget guarantees an iterate satisfying \(\|
abla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x_k))\ge-\epsilon_H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family uses a quadratic Taylor model plus a positive cubic norm term. Its second-order complexity bound is a uniform budget for reaching both the gradient and negative-curvature tolerances when subproblems are solved to declared model-accuracy conditions and regularization parameters are controlled.
assumptions_latex: The Hessian has the continuity required to control third-order Taylor remainder on the relevant level set.
The regularization parameters satisfy uniform positive safeguards or a sourced adaptive-update bound.
The approximate cubic subproblem conditions are strong enough to capture gradient and negative-curvature decrease.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists k\text{ with }C_A(k)\le B_{\mathrm{CR}}(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H),\quad \|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon_g,\quad \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\ge-\epsilon_H.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Exact global minimization of \(m_k\) is the specialization \(\eta_k=\zeta_k=0\).
special_cases_latex: A fixed regularization parameter gives a nonadaptive cubic model when the necessary smoothness constant is known.
Adaptive cubic regularization updates \(\sigma_k\) according to agreement between actual and predicted reduction.
immediate_consequences_latex: Outer-iteration, full-Hessian, and inner linear-algebra complexities remain different cost measures.
First-order model residual alone does not automatically certify adequate negative-curvature treatment.
boundary_notes: No tolerance exponent is included because it depends on exact subproblem conditions, smoothness assumptions, and cost unit.
The definition excludes regularizers of degree other than three.

notation.meaning: First- and second-order cubic-subproblem accuracy tolerances.

review_flags: No inspected authoritative source or precise locator supports the exact family conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Cubic-regularization second-order complexity family

children.title: Newton–Krylov Second-Order Bounds
children.top_down_role: Matrix-free second-order criticality guarantees using curvature searches.

knowledge_statements.title: Newton–Krylov Second-Order Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Outer evaluation bound with randomized Krylov overhead for matrix-free negative-curvature certification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Assume the hypotheses and sufficient-decrease conditions yielding \(N=O(\varepsilon_g^{-2}+\varepsilon_H^{-3})\) successful Newton-type iterations, and suppose \(\|\nabla^2f(x)\|\leq U\) on the relevant level set. At each iteration, randomized Lanczos applied through Hessian-vector products either returns a vector \(v\) with \(v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x_k)v\leq-\varepsilon_H/2\) or certifies \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\geq-\varepsilon_H\), with joint failure probability at most \(\delta\), using
\[
O\!\left(\sqrt{U/\varepsilon_H}\,\log(dN/\delta)\right)
\]
products per curvature search. Hence curvature certification uses \(O(N\sqrt{U/\varepsilon_H}\log(dN/\delta))\) Hessian-vector products, apart from products used by the Newton linear solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomized Krylov searches provide matrix-free negative-curvature detection with square-root spectral dependence and logarithmic dimension-confidence overhead.
assumptions_latex: The Hessian norm is bounded by \(U\) on the visited level set.
Outer steps satisfy uniform gradient and negative-curvature decrease conditions.
Independent randomized Lanczos searches have total failure probability at most \(\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{Hv}=O(N\sqrt{U/\varepsilon_H}\log(dN/\delta))\) for curvature certification.

notation.meaning: Hessian-vector products used by curvature searches

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The matrix-free complexity-bound role fits, but the randomized Lanczos alternative, logarithmic factor, union-bound dependence on N, and exclusion of Newton-solve products require a precise source. The outer Newton-type iteration bound is assumed rather than stated with theorem-level hypotheses.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^d)\). At \(x_k\), a matrix-free method accesses \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\) and the linear operator \(v\mapsto H_kv\), where \(H_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)\), without forming \(H_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order stationarity bounds for Newton-type outer iterations using Krylov linear solves and curvature searches, with Hessian-vector products as a principal cost unit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A Newton–Krylov second-order bound is a pair \((B_{\mathrm{out}},B_{Hv})\) such that a matrix-free algorithm, using Krylov subspaces \[\mathcal K_j(H_k,g_k)=\operatorname{span}\{g_k,H_kg_k,\ldots,H_k^{j-1}g_k\},\] returns, with the stated confidence, an iterate satisfying \(\|g_k\|\le\epsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(H_k)\ge-\epsilon_H\) within at most \(B_{\mathrm{out}}\) outer iterations and \(B_{Hv}\) cumulative Hessian-vector products. The algorithm must declare residual stopping rules and a mechanism that either finds sufficient negative curvature or certifies its absence to tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Newton–Krylov second-order bound controls both outer iterations and cumulative Hessian-vector products for a matrix-free Newton method whose Krylov procedures solve Newton equations approximately and search for negative curvature.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm can evaluate gradients and exact or accuracy-controlled Hessian-vector products.
Krylov residual tolerances and curvature-detection thresholds are fixed functions of the requested stationarity tolerances.
Any randomized eigenvalue routine includes its failure probability in the total confidence budget.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C_{\mathrm{out}}\le B_{\mathrm{out}},\quad C_{Hv}\le B_{Hv},\quad \|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon_g,\quad \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\ge-\epsilon_H.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A single scalar budget may be formed as \(c_{\mathrm{out}}B_{\mathrm{out}}+c_{Hv}B_{Hv}\), but only after prices are declared.
special_cases_latex: Truncated conjugate gradients detects certain negative-curvature directions while approximately solving positive-curvature Newton systems.
Lanczos iterations can be used expressly to estimate the leftmost Hessian eigenvalue.
immediate_consequences_latex: An outer-iteration bound alone can conceal dimension- and conditioning-dependent Krylov work.
Matrix-free operation removes the requirement to store the full Hessian but not the cost of applying it.
boundary_notes: A standard conjugate-gradient residual test without adequate curvature certification does not establish second-order stationarity.
Finite-precision loss of Krylov orthogonality is outside an exact-arithmetic oracle bound unless explicitly modeled.

notation.meaning: Order-j Krylov subspace generated by the Hessian and gradient.

review_flags: The Newton-CG and Lanczos source hints were not inspected, so no exact complexity locator is available.
knowledge_statements.title: Matrix-free Newton–Krylov second-order complexity

children.top_down_role: Randomized second-order criticality guarantees without explicit Hessian formation.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Jin, Ge, Netrapalli, Kakade, and Jordan, How to Escape Saddle Points Efficiently
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Jin, Ge, Netrapalli, Kakade, and Jordan, How to Escape Saddle Points Efficiently

knowledge_statements.title: Perturbed First-Order Second-Order Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: High-probability second-order stationarity complexity of perturbed gradient descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be bounded below, with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(\rho\)-Lipschitz Hessian, and put \(\Delta=f(x_0)-\inf f\). Perturbed gradient descent with stepsize of order \(L^{-1}\), isotropic perturbations triggered when the gradient is small, and appropriately chosen perturbation radius and waiting time returns, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), an iterate \(x\) satisfying
\[
\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq\varepsilon,
\qquad
\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\geq-\sqrt{\rho\varepsilon},
\]
after \(\widetilde O(L\Delta\varepsilon^{-2})\) gradient evaluations, where the suppressed factors are logarithmic in the problem parameters, \(d\), and \(1/\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Perturbed gradient descent finds an epsilon-gradient point with no curvature below minus square root rho epsilon, at near-gradient-descent complexity.
assumptions_latex: The gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz and the Hessian is \(\rho\)-Lipschitz.
The objective is bounded below with finite initial gap \(\Delta\).
Perturbations are isotropic and independently sampled at prescribed trigger times.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N=\widetilde O(L\Delta\varepsilon^{-2})\) with success probability at least \(1-\delta\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed high-probability perturbed-gradient rate is appropriate to the leaf and mathematically plausible, but its validity depends on exact perturbation radius, trigger threshold, waiting time, accuracy regime, and logarithmic factors. No source is supplied for those theorem-specific details.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be twice differentiable. A perturbed first-order method uses gradients for ordinary updates and, when a trigger condition is met, replaces an iterate \(x_k\) by \(x_k+\xi_k\), where \(\xi_k\) is random.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized smooth nonconvex methods that seek approximate second-order stationary points without explicitly forming a Hessian; confidence and perturbation accounting are essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A perturbed first-order second-order bound is a budget \(B_{\mathrm{PFO}}(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H,\delta)\) for algorithms of the form \[x_{k+1}=x_k-\eta G_k\quad\text{or}\quad x_{k+1}=x_k+\xi_k,\] where the perturbation branch is activated by a declared small-gradient or stagnation trigger. The bound requires \[\Pr\!\left(\exists k:\ C_A(k)\le B_{\mathrm{PFO}},\ \|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon_g,\ \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\ge-\epsilon_H\right)\ge1-\delta.\] The cost includes all gradient or stochastic-gradient samples consumed during post-perturbation escape phases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This complexity family concerns randomized methods that normally take first-order steps but inject random perturbations near suspected saddles. The bound is the total declared first-order-oracle budget for reaching joint gradient and Hessian-eigenvalue tolerances with high probability.
assumptions_latex: The objective has the gradient and Hessian regularity required by the particular escape analysis.
The perturbation distribution, radius, trigger, escape horizon, and failure-probability allocation are fixed by the method.
The cost counter includes unsuccessful perturbations and every first-order-oracle call.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\Pr\bigl(\tau^{(2)}_{\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H}\le B_{\mathrm{PFO}}(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H,\delta)\bigr)\ge1-\delta.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Failure can equivalently be defined as the event that no qualifying iterate is visited before the budget is exhausted.
special_cases_latex: With exact gradients, \(G_k=\nabla f(x_k)\).
With stochastic gradients, the oracle variance and minibatch costs become part of the instance and resource models.
immediate_consequences_latex: The logarithmic or polynomial dependence on \(\delta\) cannot be omitted from a high-probability bound.
Avoiding explicit Hessian formation does not make the output condition first-order; the target still includes a Hessian-eigenvalue requirement.
boundary_notes: Random initialization alone is not the same mechanism as repeated perturbation at small-gradient iterates.
A saddle-escape event without subsequent certification of both tolerances is weaker than second-order stationarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Model Bounds for Second-Order Criticality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order criticality complexity for regularized Taylor models of degree greater than two.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix an integer \(p\geq2\). Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be bounded below and \(p\)-times continuously differentiable, with globally Lipschitz \(p\)-th derivative on the relevant level set. An adaptive regularization method using degree-\(p\) Taylor models plus a \((p+1)\)-power regularizer, with trial steps satisfying the standard approximate model-minimization and acceptance conditions, produces an iterate satisfying
\[
\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq\varepsilon_g,
\qquad
\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\geq-\varepsilon_H
\]
within
\[
O\!\left(\varepsilon_g^{-(p+1)/p}+\varepsilon_H^{-(p+1)/(p-1)}\right)
\]
successful and unsuccessful evaluations, with constants independent of the tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degree-p regularized Taylor models improve the tolerance exponents for joint first- and second-order criticality as p increases.
assumptions_latex: The \(p\)-th derivative is Lipschitz on the relevant level set.
Model steps and acceptance updates satisfy uniform adaptive-regularization conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N=O(\varepsilon_g^{-(p+1)/p}+\varepsilon_H^{-(p+1)/(p-1)})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The kind and joint exponents are plausible for degree-p adaptive regularization, but the formula requires a theorem matching the smoothness order, approximate minimization conditions, second-order termination measure, and inclusion of both successful and unsuccessful evaluations.

knowledge_statements.source_title: Higher-Order Model Bounds for Second-Order Criticality
knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(p\ge3\) and \(f\in C^p(\mathbb R^d)\). Denote the order-\(p\) Taylor polynomial at \(x_k\) by \(T_{p,k}(s)=f(x_k)+\sum_{j=1}^{p}D^jf(x_k)[s]^j/j!\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Methods using derivatives beyond the Hessian to reach a target that remains only second-order: small gradient and controlled negative Hessian curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A higher-order model second-order bound is a budget \(B_p^{(2)}(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H)\) for methods using regularized models \[m_k(s)=T_{p,k}(s)+\frac{\sigma_k}{p+1}\|s\|^{p+1},\qquad \sigma_k>0,\] with declared approximate model-solution and acceptance conditions. The budget guarantees an iterate satisfying \[\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon_g,\qquad \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x_k))\ge-\epsilon_H.\] Complexity must state whether one unit means an outer iteration, a simultaneous evaluation of derivatives through order \(p\), a tensor-vector contraction, or arithmetic work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: This family uses a Taylor model of order at least three plus an order-one-higher regularizer, while the output requirement remains approximate second-order stationarity. Its complexity is meaningful only after the higher-derivative access and cost model are declared.
assumptions_latex: Derivatives through order \(p\) exist, and the regularity controlling the order-\(p\) Taylor remainder is uniform on the relevant region.
Regularization parameters and model-solution accuracies satisfy uniform safeguards.
The implementation's higher-derivative oracle and contraction costs are explicitly specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists k\text{ with }C_p(k)\le B_p^{(2)}(\epsilon_g,\epsilon_H),\quad \|\nabla f(x_k)\|\le\epsilon_g,\quad \nabla^2f(x_k)\succeq-\epsilon_HI.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The order-\(p\) derivative term is the homogeneous polynomial \(D^pf(x_k)[s,\ldots,s]/p!\).
special_cases_latex: For \(p=2\), the model reduces to cubic regularization and is excluded here by the condition \(p\ge3\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A favorable outer-iteration exponent need not imply favorable arithmetic complexity because tensor operations can dominate.
Using derivatives of order above two does not change the stated second-order output certificate.
boundary_notes: Higher-order criticality conditions involving derivatives above the Hessian are outside this slot.
No quantitative tolerance exponent is asserted without an inspected theorem matching the oracle and smoothness conventions.

children.top_down_role: Confidence, initialization, dimension, and noise effects in randomized saddle escape.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb R^d)\), and let \(x\) be a reference point with \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\epsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\le-\gamma\) for \(\gamma>0\). A randomized procedure starts from \(X_0\sim\mu_x\) and generates \(X_t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local high-probability escape from a quantitatively negative-curvature region; success is defined geometrically or by objective decrease and is distinct from eventual convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a neighborhood radius \(r>0\) and decrease threshold \(\Delta>0\), define the escape event by \[E_t(x)=\left\{\|X_t-x\|>r\ \text{or}\ f(X_t)\le f(x)-\Delta\right\}.\] For a nondecreasing resource counter \(C(t)\), the probabilistic escape complexity is \[\mathcal C_{\mathrm{esc}}(\gamma,r,\Delta,\delta)=\inf\left\{N:\inf_{f\in\mathcal F}\inf_{x\in S_\gamma(f)}\Pr\bigl(\exists t,\ C(t)\le N,\ E_t(x)\bigr)\ge1-\delta\right\},\] where \(S_\gamma(f)\) is the declared set of small-gradient points with Hessian eigenvalue at most \(-\gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Probabilistic escape complexity is the least resource budget within which a randomized procedure, uniformly over the admitted strict-saddle points, leaves a prescribed neighborhood or attains a prescribed objective decrease with probability at least one minus the failure probability.
assumptions_latex: The saddle set \(S_\gamma(f)\), perturbation or initialization distribution \(\mu_x\), resource counter, and escape thresholds are specified before the worst case is taken.
All randomness from initialization, perturbations, and stochastic oracles is included in the probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_{\mathrm{esc}}=\inf\{N:\inf_{f,x\in S_\gamma(f)}\Pr(\tau_{\mathrm{esc}}(f,x)\le N)\ge1-\delta\},\qquad \tau_{\mathrm{esc}}:=\inf\{C(t):E_t(x)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If the analysis establishes that leaving the ball necessarily yields the stated decrease, the disjunctive event may be replaced by the objective-decrease event alone.
special_cases_latex: Random initialization complexity takes \(X_0\sim\mu\) once and counts the subsequent dynamics.
Perturb-and-run complexity conditions on a detected small-gradient iterate and samples a fresh local perturbation.
immediate_consequences_latex: The complexity may depend on dimension, confidence, curvature magnitude, perturbation radius, and noise parameters.
A per-saddle failure probability must be combined with the number of escape episodes when asserting a whole-run success probability.
boundary_notes: Leaving a neighborhood need not imply convergence to a local minimum.
At a degenerate saddle with no quantitative negative-curvature gap, this definition supplies no finite uniform escape guarantee.

notation.meaning: Declared small-gradient region possessing curvature at most minus the gap.
Resource cost at the first qualifying escape event.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Probability Escape Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local perturbed-gradient escape from a region containing a quantitatively strict saddle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and a \(\rho\)-Lipschitz Hessian. Suppose \(x\) satisfies \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\leq\varepsilon\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\leq-\sqrt{\rho\varepsilon}\). For a perturbed-gradient procedure using stepsize of order \(L^{-1}\) and an isotropic perturbation of the standard saddle-neighborhood scale, there are universal constants \(c,C>0\) such that, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), within
\[
T\leq C\frac{L}{\sqrt{\rho\varepsilon}}\log\!\left(\frac{d}{\delta}\right)
\]
iterations the procedure leaves the associated saddle neighborhood and achieves objective decrease at least \(c\varepsilon^{3/2}/\sqrt{\rho}\), up to theorem-specific logarithmic parameter corrections.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isotropic perturbation escapes a quantitatively strict saddle in finite time with prescribed confidence and a definite objective decrease.
assumptions_latex: The gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz and the Hessian is \(\rho\)-Lipschitz.
The starting region contains curvature at most \(-\sqrt{\rho\varepsilon}\).
The perturbation is isotropic at the theorem-prescribed radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(\tau_{\mathrm{esc}}\leq T)\geq1-\delta\) with \(T=O(L(\rho\varepsilon)^{-1/2}\log(d/\delta))\).

notation.meaning: first exit time from the saddle neighborhood

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the high-probability escape leaf, but the saddle neighborhood, perturbation scale, escape event, objective-decrease event, and omitted logarithmic corrections are theorem-specific. The displayed bound cannot be validated without an exact source and locator.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X_k)_{k\ge 0}\) be an \(\mathbb R^d\)-valued stochastic iterative process on a probability space, let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a measurable unstable region, and let \(I\subseteq U\) be an admissible initialization set. Define the exit time by \(\tau_U:=\inf\{k\in\mathbb N_0:X_k\notin U\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, discrete-time randomized dynamics near an unstable region; the definition concerns a tail guarantee and does not prescribe a particular perturbation mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(B:(0,1)\to\mathbb N_0\) is a uniform high-probability escape bound for \((X_k)\) from \(U\) over \(I\) if \(\mathbb P_x(\tau_U\le B(\delta))\ge 1-\delta\) for every \(x\in I\) and every \(\delta\in(0,1)\). Equivalently, \(\sup_{x\in I}\mathbb P_x(\tau_U>B(\delta))\le\delta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a stochastic iteration started at any admissible point in the unstable region, a high-probability escape bound assigns each failure probability between zero and one a finite iteration limit. The probability of remaining in the region beyond that limit must be at most the prescribed failure probability, uniformly over all allowed starting points. The bound is therefore a quantile bound on the exit-time random variable, rather than an expectation or an almost-sure asymptotic statement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall\delta\in(0,1),\qquad \sup_{x\in I}\mathbb P_x\!\left(\tau_U>B(\delta)\right)\le\delta.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For each \(x\in I\), the \((1-\delta)\)-quantile \(q_{1-\delta}(\tau_U\mid X_0=x):=\inf\{t:\mathbb P_x(\tau_U\le t)\ge1-\delta\}\) satisfies \(q_{1-\delta}(\tau_U\mid X_0=x)\le B(\delta)\).
special_cases_latex: If the process is initialized deterministically at \(x_0\), take \(I=\{x_0\}\).
A geometric tail estimate \(\sup_{x\in I}\mathbb P_x(\tau_U>t)\le Ce^{-ct}\) yields the admissible form \(B(\delta)=\left\lceil c^{-1}\log(C/\delta)\right\rceil\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For fixed \(\delta\), escape occurs by iteration \(B(\delta)\) on an event having probability at least \(1-\delta\).
If \(B\) is valid, then every integer-valued \(\widetilde B\) satisfying \(\widetilde B(\delta)\ge B(\delta)\) is also valid.
boundary_notes: The probability law includes every source of algorithmic and initialization randomness.
The definition does not imply a finite expected exit time unless additional tail information is available.
Leaving \(U\) need not mean reaching a local minimum or even decreasing the objective.

notation.meaning: First iteration at which the process leaves the measurable region U.
Probability conditional on the deterministic initialization X_0=x.
Iteration bound at failure probability delta.

knowledge_statements.title: Expected Escape-Time Analysis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tail-sum representation and exponential-tail bound for discrete escape times.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\tau\) be a nonnegative integer-valued stopping time representing the first exit from a specified unstable neighborhood. Then
\[
\mathbb{E}[\tau]=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\mathbb{P}(\tau>t).
\]
If constants \(C\geq1\) and \(a>0\) satisfy \(\mathbb{P}(\tau>t)\leq\min\{1,Ce^{-at}\}\) for every integer \(t\geq0\), and \(m=\lceil a^{-1}\log C\rceil\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}[\tau]\leq m+\frac{Ce^{-am}}{1-e^{-a}}
\leq \left\lceil\frac{\log C}{a}\right\rceil+\frac{1}{1-e^{-a}}.
\]
Thus a uniform exponential escape tail gives a finite quantitative mean residence time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected escape time equals the sum of survival probabilities, so an exponential survival tail yields an explicit finite expectation bound.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau\) is a nonnegative integer-valued stopping time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[\tau]\leq\lceil a^{-1}\log C\rceil+(1-e^{-a})^{-1}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: tail-sum formula for nonnegative integer-valued random variables and summation of a geometric tail

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X_k)_{k\ge0}\) be a stochastic process in \(\mathbb R^d\), let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be measurable, and define \(\tau_U:=\inf\{k\in\mathbb N_0:X_k\notin U\}\). For an initialization distribution \(\mu\) supported on \(U\), write \(\mathbb E_\mu\) for expectation under \(X_0\sim\mu\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, discrete-time stochastic dynamics; the object is the first moment of residence time, distinct from a prescribed-confidence tail bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The process has expected escape-time bound \(M\in[0,\infty)\) from \(U\) for initialization law \(\mu\) if \(\tau_U\) is integrable and \(\mathbb E_\mu[\tau_U]\le M\). It has a uniform expected escape-time bound over \(I\subseteq U\) if \(\sup_{x\in I}\mathbb E_x[\tau_U]\le M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected escape-time analysis studies the mean number of iterations spent in an unstable region before the process first exits. A finite bound requires integrability of the exit time, not merely almost-sure escape. The distributional version averages over the chosen initialization law, whereas the uniform version takes the worst conditional expectation over every admissible deterministic starting point. This average-time object does not itself control a small failure probability as sharply as a full tail estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathbb E_\mu[\tau_U]\le M<\infty,\qquad\text{or uniformly}\qquad \sup_{x\in I}\mathbb E_x[\tau_U]\le M.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Because \(\tau_U\) is nonnegative and integer valued, \(\mathbb E_\mu[\tau_U]=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\mathbb P_\mu(\tau_U>t)\); hence the bound is equivalent to \(\sum_{t\ge0}\mathbb P_\mu(\tau_U>t)\le M\).
special_cases_latex: For deterministic initialization \(x_0\), choose \(\mu=\delta_{x_0}\), giving \(\mathbb E_{x_0}[\tau_U]\le M\).
If \(\sup_{x\in I}\mathbb P_x(\tau_U>t)\le Ce^{-ct}\), then \(\sup_{x\in I}\mathbb E_x[\tau_U]\le C/(1-e^{-c})\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Markov's inequality gives \(\mathbb P_\mu(\tau_U>M/\delta)\le\delta\) for every \(\delta\in(0,1)\).
A finite expected escape time implies \(\mathbb P_\mu(\tau_U<\infty)=1\).
boundary_notes: Almost-sure finiteness alone does not guarantee finite expectation.
The expectation may depend strongly on the initialization law even when escape occurs almost surely from every point.
Exit from the selected region is not a certificate of local or global optimality.

notation.meaning: Expectation when the initial point has distribution mu.

knowledge_statements.title: Initialization-Measure Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-sure strict-saddle avoidance by gradient descent under absolutely continuous initialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d)\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(0<\alpha<1/L\), and define \(g(x)=x-\alpha\nabla f(x)\). Assume the strict saddle points of \(f\) are countable, and at each such point \(x^\star\), \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x^\star))<0\). For every probability measure \(\mu\) absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure,
\[
\mu\bigl(\{x_0:g^k(x_0)\to x^\star\text{ for some strict saddle }x^\star\}\bigr)=0.
\]
Hence gradient descent initialized from \(x_0\sim\mu\) converges to a strict saddle with probability zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With an absolutely continuous starting distribution, fixed-step gradient descent almost surely does not converge to any countable strict saddle.
assumptions_latex: Every saddle under consideration has a strictly negative Hessian eigenvalue.
The strict saddles are countable and initialization is absolutely continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}_{x_0\sim\mu}(g^k(x_0)\text{ converges to a strict saddle})=0\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: stable-manifold avoidance for a diffeomorphic gradient map plus countable union of null basins
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind matches initialization-measure dependence, and the stated countability and absolute-continuity conditions plausibly yield the conclusion. A precise strict-saddle avoidance theorem is required to validate the global diffeomorphism and stable-manifold/null-basin reasoning.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X_k)_{k\ge0}\) be a Markov process on \(\mathbb R^d\), let \(U\) be a measurable region, and let \(\tau_U:=\inf\{k\ge0:X_k\notin U\}\). Denote by \(K_t(x):=\mathbb P_x(\tau_U\le t)\) the conditional finite-time escape probability and let \(\mu\) be a probability measure supported on \(U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Random initialization in finite-dimensional smooth optimization; this definition isolates dependence on the starting distribution from subsequent algorithmic randomness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The initialization-measure escape profile of \(\mu\) is \(p_t(\mu):=\mathbb P_\mu(\tau_U\le t)=\int_U K_t(x)\,\mu(dx)\). The infinite-time avoidance mass is \(a_\infty(\mu):=\mathbb P_\mu(\tau_U=\infty)=\int_U\mathbb P_x(\tau_U=\infty)\,\mu(dx)\). Thus avoidance or escape depends on initialization through the measure assigned to pointwise basins and exceptional nonescaping sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialization-measure dependence is the functional dependence of finite-time escape and infinite-time avoidance probabilities on the law of the starting point. For each starting point, the dynamics determine a conditional escape probability. Integrating that probability against the initialization measure gives the overall escape probability. Similarly, the measure assigned to points from which the trajectory never exits determines the initialization-dependent avoidance mass. Consequently, a measure-zero exceptional set is irrelevant to an absolutely continuous initialization but may have positive or full probability under a singular or atomic initialization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[p_t(\mu)=\int_U\mathbb P_x(\tau_U\le t)\,\mu(dx),\qquad a_\infty(\mu)=\int_U\mathbb P_x(\tau_U=\infty)\,\mu(dx).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(S_\infty:=\{x\in U:\mathbb P_x(\tau_U=\infty)=1\}\) and the conditional nonescape probability is indicator-valued, then \(a_\infty(\mu)=\mu(S_\infty)\).

For two initialization laws \(\mu\) and \(
u\), their finite-time dependence is quantified by \(p_t(\mu)-p_t(
u)=\int_U K_t(x)\,(\mu-
u)(dx)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\mu\ll\lambda_d\) and \(S_\infty\) has Lebesgue measure zero, then \(\mu(S_\infty)=0\).
For deterministic initialization \(x_0\), \(p_t(\delta_{x_0})=K_t(x_0)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The bound \(|p_t(\mu)-p_t(\nu)|\le\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\) follows from \(0\le K_t\le1\).
Changing only the initialization law can change escape probability even when the transition mechanism is fixed.
boundary_notes: Absolute continuity must be stated relative to a specified reference measure.
A zero-measure stable set may still be reached after initialization; this definition concerns only its initial mass unless invariance is separately imposed.
Pointwise almost-sure escape does not automatically give a uniform finite-time bound.

children.title: Dimension-Confidence Tradeoff Regimes
children.top_down_role: Ambient-dimension and failure-probability effects in randomized guarantees.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For each dimension \(d\in\mathbb N\), let \((X_k^{(d)})\) be a randomized optimization process, let \(U_d\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be measurable, and define \(\tau_d:=\inf\{k\ge0:X_k^{(d)}\notin U_d\}\). Let \(I_d\subseteq U_d\) be the admissible initialization set and \(\delta\in(0,1)\) a failure probability.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Families of finite-dimensional randomized escape problems indexed jointly by ambient dimension and prescribed confidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dimension-confidence escape complexity is the extended-integer profile \(B_\star(d,\delta):=\inf\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\sup_{x\in I_d}\mathbb P_x(\tau_d>t)\le\delta\}\). A dimension-confidence regime is a specified subset \(R\subseteq\mathbb N\times(0,1)\) together with an asymptotic comparison \(B_\star(d,\delta)\in\Theta(\Phi(d,\delta))\), \(O(\Phi(d,\delta))\), or \(\Omega(\Phi(d,\delta))\), uniformly for \((d,\delta)\in R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dimension-confidence profile is the smallest iteration horizon that makes the worst-case probability of failing to escape no greater than the requested failure probability in dimension d. A tradeoff regime specifies which pairs of dimension and confidence are considered and compares this minimal horizon with a scale function of both variables. This separates dimension dependence from confidence amplification and prevents a bound valid only for fixed dimension or fixed confidence from being presented as a joint uniform result.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B_\star(d,\delta)=\inf\left\{t\in\mathbb N_0:\sup_{x\in I_d}\mathbb P_x(\tau_d>t)\le\delta\right\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Using conditional quantiles, \(B_\star(d,\delta)=\sup_{x\in I_d}q_{1-\delta}(\tau_d\mid X_0=x)\), up to the integer convention at distributional jumps.

A bound \(B_\star(d,\delta)=O(\Phi(d,\delta))\) uniformly on \(R\) means that constants \(C\) and an admissible threshold exist such that \(B_\star(d,\delta)\le C\Phi(d,\delta)\) throughout the stated asymptotic portion of \(R\).
special_cases_latex: A logarithmic confidence cost has the form \(\Phi(d,\delta)=g(d)\log(1/\delta)\).
A dimension-free regime satisfies \(\sup_d B_\star(d,\delta)<\infty\) for each fixed admissible \(\delta\).
immediate_consequences_latex: For fixed \(d\), \(B_\star(d,\delta)\) is nonincreasing as \(\delta\) increases.
Any claimed joint rate must state whether hidden constants are independent of both \(d\) and \(\delta\).
boundary_notes: The ambient dimension need not equal an effective unstable-subspace dimension.
The profile depends on the region, initialization class, process, and cost convention, all of which must remain fixed within a comparison.
An asymptotic rate outside its declared regime is not implied.

notation.meaning: Minimal worst-case escape horizon at dimension d and failure probability delta.
Comparison scale for the joint complexity profile.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dimension-confidence scaling of a Gaussian isotropic perturbation along any fixed direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v\in\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfy \(\|v\|=1\), and draw an isotropic perturbation \(\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,r^2I_d/d)\). For every \(0<\delta<1\), the Gaussian small-ball inequality gives
\[
\mathbb{P}\!\left( |v^{\mathsf T}\xi|\geq r\delta\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2d}}\right)\geq1-\delta.
\]
Thus the perturbation component available along a prescribed negative-curvature eigendirection has characteristic scale \(r/\sqrt d\); demanding failure probability \(\delta\) guarantees the conservative component scale \(r\delta/\sqrt d\). This quantifies one source of dimension dependence in randomized saddle-escape bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An isotropic Gaussian perturbation has directional magnitude of order radius divided by square root dimension, with an explicit confidence correction.
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is a fixed unit vector in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{P}(|v^{\mathsf T}\xi|\geq r\delta\sqrt{\pi/(2d)})\geq1-\delta\).

children.title: Confidence Dependence

knowledge_statements.title: Confidence Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-restart amplification of a probabilistic saddle-escape routine.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose one execution of a randomized escape routine costs at most \(T\) oracle calls and, from every admissible initialization, succeeds with probability at least \(p\in(0,1)\). Run \(r\) independent executions and accept the first successful output. The probability that all executions fail is at most \((1-p)^r\). Hence failure probability at most \(\delta\in(0,1)\) is guaranteed by \[r\ge \left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{-\log(1-p)}\right\rceil.\] The resulting oracle cost is at most \(rT\), and therefore depends logarithmically on \(1/\delta\) when \(p\) is bounded away from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent restarts reduce failure probability geometrically, so confidence level 1−δ costs at most T times a number of trials proportional to log(1/δ).
assumptions_latex: \(p\in(0,1)\) is a uniform lower bound on single-run success probability.
The random choices in distinct executions are independent.
Each execution uses at most \(T\) oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r=\left\lceil\log(1/\delta)/[-\log(1-p)]\right\rceil\) executions suffice, with total cost at most \(rT\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The restart calculation and logarithmic confidence dependence are mathematically correct, and complexity_bound fits the leaf. However, the record has no citation supporting its probabilistic escape setting, independence convention, or oracle-cost interpretation.

children.title: Joint Tradeoff Regimes
children.top_down_role: Regimes balancing dimension-sensitive costs against confidence requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Tradeoff Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension–confidence cost under independent restart amplification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For dimension \(d\), let a base escape routine have success probability at least \(p_d\in(0,1)\) and oracle cost at most \(T_d\). Independent repetition to overall failure probability at most \(\delta\in(0,1)\) requires no more than \[N(d,\delta)=T_d\left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{-\log(1-p_d)}\right\rceil\] oracle calls. If \(p_d\le 1/2\), then \(-\log(1-p_d)\) lies between \(p_d\) and \(2p_d\); consequently the amplified cost is, up to universal constants and rounding, \(T_d p_d^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\). Thus dimension affects confidence cost through both \(T_d\) and \(p_d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The joint dimension–confidence cost is the per-run dimension-dependent cost multiplied by the repetitions needed to overcome the dimension-dependent failure probability.
assumptions_latex: At dimension \(d\), each run succeeds with probability at least \(p_d\in(0,1)\).
Runs are independent and each costs at most \(T_d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(d,\delta)\le T_d\left\lceil\log(1/\delta)/[-\log(1-p_d)]\right\rceil\), with order \(T_dp_d^{-1}\log(1/\delta)\) when \(p_d\le 1/2\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The amplification formula and the comparison p_d <= -log(1-p_d) <= 2p_d for p_d <= 1/2 are correct. A source is still required to connect the abstract dimension-dependent quantities p_d and T_d to a recognized saddle-escape complexity regime.

children.title: High-Dimensional Confidence Limits
children.top_down_role: Scalability boundaries caused by simultaneous dimension growth and stringent confidence targets.

knowledge_statements.title: High-Dimensional Confidence Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restart cost when single-run escape probability vanishes exponentially with dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p_d\) be the success probability of one independent escape attempt in dimension \(d\). If \(p_d\le e^{-cd}\) for some \(c>0\), then achieving success probability at least \(1-\delta\) requires \[r\ge \frac{\log(1/\delta)}{-\log(1-p_d)}\ge \frac{1-p_d}{p_d}\log(1/\delta).\] Consequently, \[r\ge (1-e^{-cd})e^{cd}\log(1/\delta).\] Thus independent restarting cannot provide polynomial dependence on \(d\) at fixed confidence whenever the base success probability is exponentially small and the cost of each attempt is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If one escape attempt succeeds only with exponentially small probability in dimension, restart amplification itself requires exponentially many attempts at fixed confidence.
assumptions_latex: Overall failure probability must not exceed \(\delta\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(r\ge (1-e^{-cd})e^{cd}\log(1/\delta)\), so restart complexity is exponential in \(d\) for fixed \(\delta\).

notation.meaning: success probability of one dimension-d escape attempt

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The lower bound on the number of restarts follows correctly from p_d <= exp(-cd), and failure_boundary fits the terminal container. The exponentially small base-success regime and its relevance to a concrete escape model are uncited, so the mathematical scope cannot be validated as stated.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of smooth functions, \(\mathcal A\) a class of admissible oracle algorithms, \(\mathcal O\) a fixed oracle model, and \(S_\varepsilon(f)\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) the target set at accuracy \(\varepsilon>0\). For \(A\in\mathcal A\), let \(T_\varepsilon(A,f)\) be the number of oracle calls before its first output in \(S_\varepsilon(f)\), with value \(\infty\) if no such output occurs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case oracle complexity over explicitly fixed smoothness, method, target, and information classes; deterministic and randomized variants require separate quantifiers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The minimax complexity of the method class is \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal A,\mathcal F}(\varepsilon):=\inf_{A\in\mathcal A}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_\varepsilon(A,f)\). A rate \(\Phi(\varepsilon)\) is optimal for \((\mathcal A,\mathcal F,\mathcal O,S_\varepsilon)\) if positive constants \(c,C\), independent of \(\varepsilon\), satisfy \(c\Phi(\varepsilon)\le\mathcal C_{\mathcal A,\mathcal F}(\varepsilon)\le C\Phi(\varepsilon)\) throughout the declared accuracy regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method-class complexity optimality bound compares the best worst-case performance achievable by any method in a declared algorithm class with a common rate. The upper bound requires an admissible method that succeeds on every function in the problem class within the stated number of oracle calls. The lower bound requires that every admissible method encounter some function in the class on which fewer calls cannot guarantee the target. Optimality is meaningful only after the oracle, success criterion, smoothness constants, initialization information, randomization convention, and charged operations are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal C_{\mathcal A,\mathcal F}(\varepsilon)=\Theta(\Phi(\varepsilon)).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The upper half is \(\exists A^\star\in\mathcal A\ \forall f\in\mathcal F:\ T_\varepsilon(A^\star,f)\le C\Phi(\varepsilon)\).
The deterministic lower half is \(\forall A\in\mathcal A\ \exists f_A\in\mathcal F:\ T_\varepsilon(A,f_A)\ge c\Phi(\varepsilon)\).
special_cases_latex: For first-order stationarity, \(S_\varepsilon(f)=\{x:\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\}\).
For approximate second-order stationarity, \(S_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(f)=\{x:\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon_g,\ \lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\ge-\varepsilon_H\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Matching upper and lower rates exclude a uniformly better accuracy exponent within the declared method and problem classes.
Changing the oracle or target set defines a different minimax quantity and can change the optimal rate.
boundary_notes: For randomized algorithms, expected, high-probability, and distributional lower bounds are distinct notions.
Dimension may grow with accuracy in a hard-instance construction and must be stated.
Constants may depend on fixed smoothness or initial-gap parameters only when the regime explicitly permits it.

children.title: First-Order Hard Instances

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Hard Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic first-order oracle lower bound for smooth nonconvex stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(L>0\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(0<\varepsilon<\sqrt{L\Delta}\). For every deterministic algorithm whose query \(x_t\) depends only on preceding function values and gradients, there exist a sufficiently large dimension \(d\), an \(L\)-smooth function \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\), and an initial point \(x_0\) satisfying \(f(x_0)-\inf_x f(x)\le\Delta\), such that fewer than \(cL\Delta\varepsilon^{-2}\) first-order oracle queries do not guarantee an iterate \(x_t\) with \(\|\nabla f(x_t)\|\le\varepsilon\), where \(c>0\) is a universal constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Some smooth nonconvex functions force every deterministic first-order method to use order LΔ/ε² oracle calls before guaranteeing ε-first-order stationarity.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm is deterministic and accesses only function values and gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case first-order oracle complexity is at least \(cL\Delta\varepsilon^{-2}\) in sufficiently large dimension.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is an appropriately typed first-order oracle complexity lower bound, but its exact quantifiers, unrestricted deterministic algorithm class, dimension requirement, parameter range, and universal-constant claim require a specific lower-bound theorem citation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of differentiable functions on Euclidean spaces, let \(\mathcal A_1\) be a class of algorithms whose query decisions use only earlier first-order oracle replies \(\mathcal O_1(f,x)=(f(x),\nabla f(x))\), and fix a stationarity tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case finite-dimensional smooth nonconvex optimization under a first-order oracle; the dimension and smoothness parameters belong to the declared instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(A\in\mathcal A_1\) and integer \(T\ge1\), a function \(f_A\in\mathcal F\) is a \((T,\varepsilon)\) first-order hard instance if, for the query sequence \(x^{(0)},\ldots,x^{(T-1)}\) generated by \(A\) on \(f_A\), one has \(\|\nabla f_A(x^{(t)})\|>\varepsilon\) for every \(0\le t<T\). A family is method-class hard at scale \(T(\varepsilon)\) if such an instance exists for every \(A\in\mathcal A_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order hard instance is a smooth objective whose function values and gradients do not permit a specified first-order method to produce an epsilon-stationary query point before a prescribed number of oracle calls. A hard family for a method class reverses the quantifiers: every admissible method must have at least one instance, possibly method-dependent, that delays stationarity for that long. The definition concerns information available through the first-order oracle and does not claim that the same fixed function defeats every possible algorithm unless that stronger quantifier is explicitly imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall A\in\mathcal A_1\ \exists f_A\in\mathcal F\ \forall t<T(\varepsilon):\quad \|\nabla f_A(x_A^{(t)})\|>\varepsilon.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(T_\varepsilon(A,f):=\inf\{t:\|\nabla f(x_A^{(t)})\|\le\varepsilon\}\), hardness is \(T_\varepsilon(A,f_A)\ge T\).
special_cases_latex: For deterministic zero-respecting methods, the admissible query subspace may be restricted by the supports revealed by previous gradients.
For randomized methods, hardness may instead require \(\mathbb P(T_\varepsilon(A,f_A)\ge T)\ge p\) or \(\mathbb E[T_\varepsilon(A,f_A)]\ge T\); these are separate variants.
immediate_consequences_latex: A method-class hard family with scale \(T(\varepsilon)\) gives the lower bound \(\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_1}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_\varepsilon(A,f)\ge T(\varepsilon)\).
The construction delays first-order criticality but need not delay approximate local minimality under a stronger oracle.
boundary_notes: The oracle transcript, initialization rule, dimension scaling, and smoothness constants must be fixed in the class definition.
A hard instance for one algorithm is not automatically hard for the entire method class.
Counting iterations and counting oracle calls coincide only when each iteration makes exactly one charged query.

notation.meaning: Oracle returning the function value and gradient at a query.
The t-th query generated by algorithm A.
First query index attaining epsilon-first-order stationarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Method Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle lower bound for gradient stationarity with Lipschitz Hessian information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix \(L_2>0\), \(\Delta>0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\). In the deterministic zero-respecting second-order oracle model, there are sufficiently high-dimensional twice continuously differentiable functions \(f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) with \(L_2\)-Lipschitz Hessian and \(f(x_0)-\inf_x f(x)\le\Delta\) for which fewer than \[c\Delta L_2^{1/2}\varepsilon^{-3/2}\] oracle queries cannot guarantee an iterate satisfying \(\|
abla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\). Here one oracle query returns \(f(x)\), \(
abla f(x)\), and \(
abla^2 f(x)\), and \(c>0\) is universal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even Hessian-based zero-respecting methods may require order Δ√L₂/ε³ᐟ² oracle calls to guarantee ε-first-order stationarity on Hessian-Lipschitz functions.
assumptions_latex: The method is deterministic and zero-respecting in the second-order oracle model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At least \(c\Delta L_2^{1/2}\varepsilon^{-3/2}\) second-order oracle queries are required in the worst case.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed epsilon^{-3/2} scaling is plausible for a suitably defined second-order oracle class, but the zero-respecting restriction, smoothness assumptions, dimension dependence, and parameter range must be checked against an authoritative theorem.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of twice continuously differentiable functions, \(\mathcal A_2\) a class of algorithms accessing \(\mathcal O_2(f,x)=(f(x),
abla f(x),
abla^2f(x))\), and define \(S_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(f):=\{x:\|

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(L(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\) is a deterministic second-order method-class lower bound if every \(A\in\mathcal A_2\) has an instance \(f_A\in\mathcal F\) for which none of its first \(L(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)-1\) oracle queries belongs to \(S_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(f_A)\). Equivalently, \(\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_2}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(A,f)\ge L(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order method lower bound is a worst-case information limitation for algorithms allowed to observe function values, gradients, and Hessians. It states that every method in the declared class has some smooth instance on which an approximate second-order stationary point cannot be reached before the specified number of charged oracle queries. The lower bound applies to named algorithm families only when their steps, auxiliary calculations, and information access satisfy the declared oracle model. It is not merely a poor convergence example for one Newton-type update.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{A\in\mathcal A_2}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}T_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(A,f)\ge L(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The explicit quantifier form is \(\forall A\in\mathcal A_2\ \exists f_A\in\mathcal F\ \forall t<L:\ x_A^{(t)}\notin S_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(f_A)\).
special_cases_latex: Setting \(\varepsilon_H=\infty\) reduces the success condition to first-order stationarity, though the algorithm retains second-order information.
A one-parameter convention may set \(\varepsilon_H=c\varepsilon_g^{1/2}\), producing a lower bound expressed only in \(\varepsilon_g\).
immediate_consequences_latex: No algorithm in \(\mathcal A_2\) can possess a smaller uniform worst-case oracle bound on \(\mathcal F\) than \(L\).
A matching upper bound establishes method-class optimality for the specified target and oracle.
boundary_notes: Exact Hessian access differs from Hessian-vector products and inexact derivative oracles.
The definition does not bound arithmetic cost of solving a Newton, trust-region, or regularized subproblem.
Randomized lower bounds require an explicit success probability or expected-query convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper bound on the attainable guarantee constant for second-order methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle lower-complexity limitation for second-order methods on objectives with Lipschitz-continuous Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the objective \(f\) of Definition 4.3.1 have an \(L_f\)-Lipschitz-continuous Hessian, and let a second-order method \(\mathcal M\) satisfy Assumption 4.3.2. Suppose that, for every starting point satisfying \(\|x_0-x^*\|_{(2)}\le\rho_0\), after generating \(k\) test points the method guarantees \[\min_{0\le i\le k}\bigl(f(x_i)-f(x^*)\bigr)\le \frac{L_f\rho_0^3}{C_{\mathcal M}(k)}.\] Then, whenever \(k=3m+2\) for an integer \(m\) with \(0\le m\le n/4-1\), one has \(C_{\mathcal M}(k)\le36(k+1)^{3.5}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any second-order method satisfying the stated information rule and uniform error guarantee on an initial radius rho_0 cannot have guarantee constant C_M(k) larger than 36 times (k+1) to the power 3.5 at iteration counts k=3m+2, provided 0≤m≤n/4−1.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_{\mathcal M}(k)\le36(k+1)^{3.5}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity, minimizer, value, and radius of the cubic-chain instance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact solution properties of the hard-instance family used in second-order method lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(n\ge 2\), \(2\le k\le n\), and \(f_k\) as defined by the cubic-chain construction, \(f_k\) is uniformly convex and has the unique global minimizer \(x_*\) given by \[x_*^{(i)}=(k-i+1)_+,\qquad i=1,\ldots,n,\] where \((\tau)_+=\max\{\tau,0\}\). Moreover, for \(x_0=0\), \[f_k^*=f_k(x_*)=-\frac{2}{3}k,\qquad R_k^2=\|x_0-x_*\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^{k}i^2<\frac{(k+1)^3}{3}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cubic-chain function is uniformly convex and has a unique minimizer whose ith coordinate is the positive part of k minus i plus one. From the zero initial point, the optimal value is minus two k over three, and the squared distance to the minimizer is the sum of the first k squares, strictly less than one third of (k+1) cubed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_k\text{ is uniformly convex},\quad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f_k(x)=\{x_*\},\quad x_*^{(i)}=(k-i+1)_+;\quad \text{for }x_0=0,\ f_k^*=-\frac{2}{3}k,\ \|x_0-x_*\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^{k}i^2<\frac{(k+1)^3}{3}

children.title: Local-Minimum Oracle Lower Bounds
children.top_down_role: Information limitations for locating approximate local minima.

knowledge_statements.title: Local-Minimum Oracle Lower Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimax query lower bound for approximate second-order local-minimum certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of twice differentiable functions on \(\mathbb R^d\), and let an oracle return \(f(x)\), \(
abla f(x)\), and \(
abla^2f(x)\). Define \(N_{\mathcal F}(\varepsilon,\gamma,\delta)\) as the least number of queries allowing an algorithm to output \(x\) satisfying \[\|
abla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon,\qquad \lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x))\ge-\gamma\] with probability at least \(1-\delta\), uniformly over \(f\in\mathcal F\). An oracle lower bound \(B\) means \(N_{\mathcal F}(\varepsilon,\gamma,\delta)\ge B(d,\varepsilon,\gamma,\delta)\); it applies only to the stated function, oracle, and algorithm classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local-minimum oracle lower bound is a minimax query bound for producing a point with small gradient and nearly positive-semidefinite Hessian at prescribed confidence.
assumptions_latex: Each query returns the function value, gradient, and Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A valid lower bound has the form \(N_{\mathcal F}(\varepsilon,\gamma,\delta)\ge B(d,\varepsilon,\gamma,\delta)\) under an explicitly fixed oracle model.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record only defines minimax query complexity and the phrase 'oracle lower bound B'; it does not state any lower bound for locating approximate local minima. It therefore does not fill the Local-Minimum Oracle Lower Bounds terminal and is not a complexity_bound record.
