knowledge_statements.statement_title: Oracle Lower Bound for Approximate Local Minimization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of functions on \(\mathbb R^d\), let \(\mathcal A_{\mathcal O}\) be algorithms using an oracle \(\mathcal O\), and fix \(r>0\) and \(\varepsilon\ge0\). Define \(\operatorname{Loc}_{r,\varepsilon}(f):=\{x:f(x)\le\inf_{\|y-x\|\le r}f(y)+\varepsilon\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information-based worst-case complexity for producing a point with an explicit neighborhood-value guarantee; this target is stronger and more literal than derivative stationarity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For success level \(p\in(0,1]\), a query scale \(L(r,\varepsilon,p)\) is a local-minimum oracle lower bound if every possibly randomized \(A\in\mathcal A_{\mathcal O}\) has an instance \(f_A\in\mathcal F\) such that, after fewer than \(L(r,\varepsilon,p)\) oracle calls, \(\mathbb P\bigl(\widehat x_A\in\operatorname{Loc}_{r,\varepsilon}(f_A)\bigr)<p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local-minimum oracle lower bound states that limited oracle information cannot guarantee finding an approximate local minimum, defined by objective comparison throughout a radius-r neighborhood, before a prescribed number of queries. The probability is taken over the algorithm's randomness and any randomized oracle. The adversarial instance may depend on the algorithm. The radius, value tolerance, success probability, problem class, dimension rule, and oracle replies are part of the definition, since changing any of them changes the information problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall A\in\mathcal A_{\mathcal O}\ \exists f_A\in\mathcal F:\quad q<L(r,\varepsilon,p)\Longrightarrow \mathbb P\!\left(\widehat x_A^{(q)}\in\operatorname{Loc}_{r,\varepsilon}(f_A)\right)<p.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(Q_A(f)\) is the first query budget at which the success probability reaches \(p\), then the lower bound is \(\inf_A\sup_f Q_A(f)\ge L(r,\varepsilon,p)\).
special_cases_latex: With \(\varepsilon=0\), \(\operatorname{Loc}_{r,0}(f)\) consists of points minimizing \(f\) throughout their closed radius-\(r\) neighborhoods.
For deterministic algorithms and oracles, take \(p=1\); failure means the output is not in \(\operatorname{Loc}_{r,\varepsilon}(f)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A lower bound for this neighborhood-value target need not equal a lower bound for approximate second-order stationarity.
Increasing \(r\) or decreasing \(\varepsilon\) weakens the target set and can only make the success requirement harder.
boundary_notes: Without a positive radius, every point satisfies the value comparison at \(r=0\).
Second-order necessary conditions do not characterize this target for arbitrary nonconvex functions.
The definition must not be conflated with identifying the globally best local minimum.

notation.meaning: Points whose value is within epsilon of every point in a radius-r neighborhood.
Output of algorithm A after q oracle queries.

review_flags: No source was verified for this particular neighborhood-value target and oracle lower-bound formulation.

children.title: Sharp Complexity Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Method and regularity classes with sharp complexity classifications.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\theta\in\Theta\) collect accuracy, smoothness, dimension, confidence, and initial-gap parameters. For a fixed problem class \(\mathcal F_\theta\), method class \(\mathcal A\), oracle \(\mathcal O\), cost model, and target set, let \(\mathcal C(\theta)\) denote the corresponding minimax complexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameter-dependent worst-case classifications in a fixed smooth nonconvex information model; sharpness is always relative to a declared regime and uniformity convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A subset \(R\subseteq\Theta\) is a sharp complexity regime with scale \(\Phi:R\to(0,\infty)\) if constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), independent of every parameter varying in \(R\), satisfy \(c\Phi(\theta)\le\mathcal C(\theta)\le C\Phi(\theta)\) for all \(\theta\in R\). The pair \((R,\Phi)\) is the resulting sharp complexity classification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sharp complexity regime is a specified region of parameter space on which matching lower and upper bounds characterize minimax complexity up to constant factors. The constants must be uniform over every parameter declared variable in the regime, although they may depend on quantities explicitly held fixed. A classification is therefore not just an accuracy exponent: it records the method class, function regularity, oracle, target certificate, dimension and confidence scaling, and charged cost. Different regimes may possess different sharp scales without contradiction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[\forall\theta\in R,
\qquad c\Phi(\theta)\le\mathcal C(\theta)\le C\Phi(\theta).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The defining relation is \(\mathcal C(\theta)=\Theta_R(\Phi(\theta))\), where the subscript records uniformity on \(R\).
Sharpness consists of a method attaining \(C\Phi\) on the whole class and a hard-instance lower bound of \(c\Phi\) against every method in the declared class.
special_cases_latex: An accuracy-only regime may be \(R=\{\varepsilon:0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0\}\).
A joint regime may impose \(d\ge d_0(\varepsilon)\) and \(0<\delta\le\delta_0\), allowing hard-instance dimension and confidence to scale with accuracy.
immediate_consequences_latex: Within \(R\), no admissible method improves the order \(\Phi\) uniformly, and at least one admissible method attains it.
A result sharp in oracle calls need not be sharp in arithmetic operations or wall-clock cost.
boundary_notes: Polylogarithmic gaps do not satisfy constant-factor sharpness unless they are absorbed into the declared scale.
Bounds obtained under different smoothness normalizations or success criteria do not form a matching pair.
Sharpness on \(R\) makes no assertion outside \(R\).

notation.meaning: Tuple of all parameters varied by the classification.
Minimax complexity in the fixed information and cost model.

review_flags: A precise source for the stated uniform sharp-regime convention was not inspected.
knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Complexity Classification Regime

children.title: Upper-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Method and regularity classes equipped with established complexity upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform oracle upper bounds over a fixed problem and method class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a problem class, \(\mathcal A\) an algorithm class, and \(S_\varepsilon(f)\) the accepted criticality set. A function \(U(\varepsilon,\theta)\) is an oracle upper bound in parameter regime \(R\) if there exists \(A\in\mathcal A\) such that, for every \((\varepsilon,\theta)\in R\) and every \(f\in\mathcal F\), algorithm \(A\) outputs some \(x\in S_\varepsilon(f)\) using at most \(U(\varepsilon,\theta)\) oracle calls. For randomized methods the guarantee must additionally state whether the bound is deterministic, expected, or holds with prescribed probability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper-bound regime specifies where one method uniformly reaches the chosen criticality criterion within a stated number of oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: The problem class \(\mathcal F\), algorithm class \(\mathcal A\), and oracle are fixed.
The accepted output set \(S_\varepsilon(f)\) is specified.
The parameter vector \(\theta\) and regime \(R\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(A\in\mathcal A\) with worst-case oracle cost at most \(U(\varepsilon,\theta)\) throughout \(R\).

notation.meaning: parameter regime where the bound holds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quantifier structure is a reasonable abstract characterization of an oracle upper bound, but it is closer to a definition than an instantiated complexity bound. A complexity-framework source and an explicitly fixed model are needed before deciding whether this generic formulation adequately fills the terminal.

children.title: Lower-Bound Regimes
children.top_down_role: Oracle and method classes equipped with corresponding complexity lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform minimax oracle lower bounds over a fixed problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a function class \(\mathcal F\), an algorithm class \(\mathcal A\), an oracle, and accepted sets \(S_\varepsilon(f)\). A function \(L(\varepsilon,\theta)\) is an oracle lower bound in regime \(R\) if, for every \(A\in\mathcal A\) and every \((\varepsilon,\theta)\in R\), there exists \(f\in\mathcal F\) such that \(A\) cannot guarantee an output in \(S_\varepsilon(f)\) before making at least \(L(\varepsilon,\theta)\) oracle calls. For randomized algorithms, the quantifiers must include the required success probability or expected-cost convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower-bound regime specifies parameter values where every permitted algorithm encounters a problem requiring at least the stated number of oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: The classes \(\mathcal F\) and \(\mathcal A\), the oracle, and \(S_\varepsilon(f)\) are fixed.
The parameter vector \(\theta\) belongs to a specified regime \(R\).
Randomized guarantees use a fixed probability or expectation convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(A\in\mathcal A\) has a worst-case instance requiring at least \(L(\varepsilon,\theta)\) oracle calls throughout \(R\).

notation.meaning: parameter regime where the lower bound holds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The minimax quantifiers are broadly appropriate, but the record defines a lower-bound regime rather than supplying a concrete complexity bound. A cited framework and fixed oracle, function, algorithm, and success conventions are required to validate its role in this terminal.

children.title: Sharp Matching Classes
children.top_down_role: Classes where available upper and lower complexity rates coincide at the relevant resolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Sharp Matching Classes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion for oracle upper and lower bounds to match sharply.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(N^*(\varepsilon,\theta)\) be the minimax oracle complexity for fixed problem, oracle, algorithm, and success conventions. Suppose throughout a regime \(R\) that \[cL(\varepsilon,\theta)\le N^*(\varepsilon,\theta)\le CU(\varepsilon,\theta)\] for constants \(c,C>0\) independent of \((\varepsilon,\theta)\). The upper- and lower-bound classes match sharply on \(R\) when \(U(\varepsilon,\theta)=\Theta(L(\varepsilon,\theta))\) uniformly on \(R\). In that case \(N^*(\varepsilon,\theta)=\Theta(U(\varepsilon,\theta))=\Theta(L(\varepsilon,\theta))\), so the complexity order cannot be improved within the fixed model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper and lower bounds form a sharp matching class when their ratio stays bounded by constants uniformly throughout the stated parameter regime.
assumptions_latex: Upper and lower bounds concern the same function, oracle, algorithm, and success models.
Their constants are uniform over the regime \(R\).
Both bound functions are positive on \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(U=\Theta(L)\) uniformly on \(R\), then \(N^*=\Theta(U)=\Theta(L)\) on \(R\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sharp-matching criterion is internally correct, and property fits the leaf. No source is supplied for the minimax framework or the uniform-Theta convention, so the record remains unsupported candidate knowledge.

children.title: Unmatched Complexity Gaps
children.top_down_role: Classes retaining a separation between known upper and lower complexity results.

knowledge_statements.title: Unmatched Complexity Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of available upper and lower bounds to determine minimax order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L(\varepsilon,\theta)\le N^*(\varepsilon,\theta)\le U(\varepsilon,\theta)\) be valid lower and upper oracle bounds under identical conventions. An unmatched complexity gap occurs on a regime \(R\) if \[\sup_{(\varepsilon,\theta)\in R}\frac{U(\varepsilon,\theta)}{L(\varepsilon,\theta)}=\infty.\] The gap may be polynomial, logarithmic, dimensional, or confidence-dependent. It does not by itself establish that either bound is suboptimal: closing it requires either a smaller valid upper bound, a larger valid lower bound, or a separation showing that the compared models are not equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complexity gap remains when the known upper-to-lower-bound ratio is unbounded; this alone does not identify which bound can be improved.
assumptions_latex: Both bounds use identical oracle, problem, algorithm, and success conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An unbounded ratio \(U/L\) prevents a sharp minimax complexity classification on \(R\).

notation.meaning: known upper and lower complexity bounds

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unbounded-ratio criterion correctly describes failure of constant-factor matching under identical models, and failure_boundary fits the terminal. A source is required for this complexity-gap framework and its intended regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Taxonomy of Smooth Criticality Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) be \(C^2\), let \(C_1(f):=\{x:
abla f(x)=0\}\), let \(C_2(f):=\{x:
abla f(x)=0,\ 
abla^2f(x)\succeq0\}\), and let \(M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\) and \(M_{\mathrm{glob}}(f)\) denote its local and global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A definitional classification of limitations in smooth unconstrained finite-dimensional criticality theory, not a claim that the listed mechanisms are exhaustive for nonsmooth or constrained problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A smooth criticality failure boundary is a tuple \((\mathcal F,\mathcal D,\mathcal O,\mathcal Q)\) for which a desired implication or guarantee \(\mathcal Q\) fails on some \(f\in\mathcal F\). It is classified as geometric when a criticality implication such as \(C_i(f)\subseteq M(f)\) fails; dynamical when an iteration has a positive-probability nonescaping or convergent exceptional set; numerical-oracle when inexact information makes the certificate undecidable at the stated tolerance; and adjacent-class when \(f\), its domain, or its noise model lies outside the smooth unconstrained assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The failure-boundary taxonomy records exactly which ingredient prevents a smooth criticality conclusion. Geometric failures invalidate an implication from first- or second-order stationarity to local or global quality. Dynamical failures concern the behavior of a chosen iteration even when the landscape has an unstable direction. Numerical-oracle failures arise because finite or corrupted derivative information cannot resolve the required sign or tolerance. Adjacent-class boundaries occur when constraints, nonsmoothness, stochastic objectives, manifolds, or other altered problem structures require different notions of stationarity. A single example may occupy more than one class, so the taxonomy is a labeled cover rather than a disjoint partition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak B=\mathfrak B_{\mathrm{geom}}\cup\mathfrak B_{\mathrm{dyn}}\cup\mathfrak B_{\mathrm{oracle}}\cup\mathfrak B_{\mathrm{adj}},\] where membership records the mechanism by which the declared conclusion \(\mathcal Q\) fails.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A geometric first-order boundary is witnessed by \(C_1(f)\nsubseteq M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\); a second-order-to-global boundary is witnessed by \(C_2(f)\nsubseteq M_{\mathrm{glob}}(f)\).
special_cases_latex: A strict saddle whose stable set has positive initialization probability is both a dynamical and initialization-measure boundary.
A point with \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\) smaller than Hessian-oracle error is a numerical-oracle boundary for negative-curvature certification.
immediate_consequences_latex: A valid theorem must exclude every boundary mechanism relevant to its claimed conclusion through explicit hypotheses.
Failure of one implication does not invalidate weaker conclusions, such as stationarity alone.
boundary_notes: The classes may overlap and are not asserted to be logically exhaustive beyond the declared smooth unconstrained setting.
The taxonomy itself supplies no convergence or complexity guarantee.
Constrained and nonsmooth stationarity require normal-cone or generalized-derivative definitions rather than direct reuse of \(C_1\) or \(C_2\).

notation.meaning: Geometric, dynamical, oracle, and adjacent-class failure categories.

review_flags: This synthesized taxonomy requires an authoritative source supporting its categories and scope; none was verified.

children.title: Stationarity Without Solution Quality
children.top_down_role: Logical separations among stationarity, local minimality, and global quality.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d	o\mathbb R\) be differentiable and bounded below, let \(f_\star:=\inf_x f(x)\), and define \(C_1(f):=\{x:
abla f(x)=0\}\). If \(f\in C^2\), also define \(C_2(f):=\{x:
abla f(x)=0,\ 
abla^2f(x)\succeq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logical separations in finite-dimensional smooth nonconvex optimization; local minimality and global objective quality are treated as different targets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(x\) exhibits stationarity without solution quality if it satisfies a declared stationarity certificate but fails a declared quality condition. First-order local-quality separation means \(x\in C_1(f)\setminus M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\). Second-order global-quality separation means \(x\in C_2(f)\) and \(f(x)-f_\star>\Delta\) for a stated \(\Delta\ge0\). A function class exhibits the separation if it contains at least one such pair \((f,x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity without solution quality is the existence of a point that passes a derivative-based criticality test but does not satisfy the optimization property being sought. For first-order stationarity, failure of local quality means that the point is not a local minimizer. For second-order stationarity, a point may be locally minimizing yet have an objective value more than a specified gap above the global infimum. The definition requires the quality criterion and gap to be stated explicitly because local minimality, global minimality, and objective approximation are inequivalent in nonconvex problems.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[C_1(f)\setminus M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\ne\varnothing\quad\text{or}\quad \exists x\in C_2(f):f(x)-f_\star>\Delta.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The absence of first-order local-quality separation is precisely \(C_1(f)\subseteq M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\).
The absence of second-order \(\Delta\)-global-quality separation is \(\sup_{x\in C_2(f)}(f(x)-f_\star)\le\Delta\), when the supremum is well defined.
special_cases_latex: A differentiable local maximum or saddle with zero gradient is a first-order separation witness.
A strict but nonglobal local minimizer is a second-order-to-global separation witness when its Hessian is positive semidefinite.
immediate_consequences_latex: A convergence theorem whose conclusion is only \(\|\nabla f(x_k)\|\to0\) supplies no local- or global-quality guarantee without additional landscape assumptions.
Eliminating strict saddles does not by itself eliminate poor local minima.
boundary_notes: If \(f_\star=-\infty\), a finite global objective gap is not defined.
Approximate stationarity requires separate tolerances and may create additional ambiguity.
For convex differentiable functions, first-order stationarity does imply global minimality, so this separation is specifically nonconvex.

notation.meaning: Set of local minimizers of f.
Declared maximum acceptable global objective gap.

review_flags: The exact combined local- and global-quality separation formulation lacks an inspected supporting source.
knowledge_statements.title: Stationarity–Quality Separation

children.title: First-Order Stationarity False Positives

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Stationarity False Positives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stationary point that is a strict local maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(f(x)=-x^2\), and let \(x_*=0\). Then \(f'(x_*)=0\), so \(x_*\) satisfies exact first-order stationarity and every tolerance condition \(|f'(x_*)|\le\varepsilon\) with \(\varepsilon\ge0\). At the same time, \(f(x)<f(x_*)\) for every \(x\ne x_*\), making \(x_*\) a strict global maximum rather than a local minimum. Thus first-order stationarity does not certify minimization for smooth nonconvex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For f(x)=−x², the origin has zero derivative but is a strict global maximum, so first-order stationarity does not certify solution quality.
assumptions_latex: The problem is unconstrained minimization on \(\mathbb R\).
First-order stationarity means \(f'(x)=0\), with tolerance relaxation \(|f'(x)|\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_*=0\) passes the first-order stationarity test but is not a local minimizer.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. A point \(x\) is first-order stationary when \(\nabla f(x)=0\), and it is an \(\varepsilon\)-first-order stationary point when \(\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\). Let \(M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\) denote the local minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact and approximate first-order tests for smooth unconstrained minimization; the false-positive label is relative to local-minimum acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An exact first-order stationarity false positive is a point \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) such that \(
abla f(x)=0\) but \(x
otin M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\). At tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), an \(\varepsilon\)-false positive is a point satisfying \(\|
abla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) while failing the separately declared local-quality condition, such as \(x
otin M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order stationarity false positive is a point accepted by a zero-gradient or small-gradient test even though it is not a local minimizer. Exact false positives include differentiable local maxima and saddles because both can have zero gradient. The approximate version depends on a gradient tolerance and a separately specified notion of quality; without that quality predicate, the phrase false positive is undefined. The definition describes a logical limitation of the test and does not assert that any particular algorithm converges to the offending point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{FP}_1(f):=\{x:\nabla f(x)=0\}\setminus M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The first-order test has no exact false positives precisely when every critical point is a local minimizer: \(\{x:\nabla f(x)=0\}\subseteq M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\).
A witness satisfies \(\nabla f(x)=0\) and, for every \(r>0\), there exists \(y\) with \(\|y-x\|<r\) and \(f(y)<f(x)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(t)=-t^2\), the point \(t=0\) is a stationary strict local maximum and hence a false positive.
For \(f(u,v)=u^2-v^2\), the origin is a stationary saddle and hence a false positive.
immediate_consequences_latex: A stopping rule based only on a small gradient cannot certify local minimality over arbitrary smooth nonconvex functions.
Additional curvature or landscape assumptions are required to exclude maxima and saddles.
boundary_notes: A nonglobal local minimizer is not a false positive when the acceptance target is merely local minimality.
Boundary-constrained optima need not have zero gradient; this unconstrained definition does not apply directly.
Numerical gradient error must be incorporated into the tolerance before classifying an approximate point.

notation.meaning: Set of exact first-order false positives relative to local minimality.

review_flags: The mathematical definition is standard, but the supplied local-minima locator was not inspected to verify exact support.

children.title: Second-Order Stationarity False Positives

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Stationarity False Positives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A degenerate second-order stationary point that is not a local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be given by \(f(x)=x^3\), and let \(x_*=0\). Then \(f'(x_*)=0\) and \(f''(x_*)=0\ge0\), so \(x_*\) satisfies exact second-order stationarity for unconstrained minimization. Nevertheless, \(x_*\) is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum: every neighborhood of \(x_*\) contains points where \(f(x)<f(x_*)\) and points where \(f(x)>f(x_*)\). Hence positive-semidefinite second-order stationarity is not sufficient for local minimality in the degenerate case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For f(x)=x³, the origin has zero gradient and a positive-semidefinite Hessian but is not a local minimum, giving a degenerate second-order false positive.
assumptions_latex: The problem is unconstrained minimization on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_*=0\) passes the exact second-order stationarity test but is not a local minimizer.

notation.meaning: the one-dimensional Hessian at the tested point

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. Define \(C_2(f):=\{x:\nabla f(x)=0,\ \nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\}\), and let \(M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\) and \(M_{\mathrm{glob}}(f)\) be its local and global minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact smooth unconstrained second-order stationarity; local-minimum and global-quality false positives are distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A local-quality second-order false positive is \(x\in C_2(f)\setminus M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\). For \(\Delta\ge0\) and finite \(f_\star:=\inf f\), a global-quality second-order false positive is \(x\in C_2(f)\) with \(f(x)-f_\star>\Delta\). The first arises from insufficiency of second-order necessary conditions; the second may be an actual but suboptimal local minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order stationarity false positive passes both the zero-gradient test and the positive-semidefinite-Hessian test while failing the intended solution-quality requirement. Relative to local minimality, degenerate higher-order behavior can make a second-order stationary point nonminimizing. Relative to global quality, even a genuine strict local minimum may be a false positive if its objective gap exceeds the accepted threshold. These two meanings must not be merged, because one concerns failure of local sufficiency and the other concerns the absence of a global guarantee.

Certifying positive-definite curvature can establish strict local minimality but still does not establish global quality.

children.title: Approximation-Tolerance Ambiguity
children.top_down_role: Finite-accuracy neighborhoods containing geometrically different point types.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-Tolerance Ambiguity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed approximate second-order tolerances need not distinguish minima from saddles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For tolerances \(\varepsilon_g\ge 0\) and \(\varepsilon_H>0\), call \(z\in\mathbb R^2\) approximately second-order stationary when \(\|\nabla f(z)\|\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(z))\ge-\varepsilon_H\). Choose \(0<\eta\le\varepsilon_H\) and \(f_\eta(x,y)=\frac{\eta}{4}(x^2-1)^2+\frac{\eta}{2}y^2\). The strict local minima \((\pm1,0)\) and the saddle \((0,0)\) all satisfy this approximate condition: their gradients vanish, while the saddle has minimum Hessian eigenvalue \(-\eta\). Thus one finite-accuracy criticality neighborhood can contain geometrically different exact point types.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any fixed positive curvature tolerance can classify both strict local minima and a saddle as approximate second-order stationary points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(-1,0),(0,0),(1,0)\}\) satisfies the same approximate second-order test although \((0,0)\) is a saddle and \((\pm1,0)\) are strict local minima.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-accuracy derivative certificates in smooth unconstrained finite-dimensional optimization; ambiguity is relative to declared geometric classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The tolerance pair \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\) is geometrically ambiguous for \((f,G_1,G_2)\) if \(A_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(f)\cap G_1\ne\varnothing\) and \(A_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(f)\cap G_2\ne\varnothing\). More generally, a certificate is ambiguous on a function class \(\mathcal F\) if identical acceptance inequalities admit points with different declared quality labels for some \(f\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximation-tolerance ambiguity occurs when one finite-accuracy stationarity test accepts points belonging to geometrically or qualitatively different classes. For example, the same gradient and curvature tolerances may accept a neighborhood of a local minimum and also a flat saddle, a point near a maximum with weak curvature, or a globally poor local minimum. The ambiguity belongs to the certificate at the stated tolerances and function class; it is not merely uncertainty about numerical representation. Tightening tolerances removes the ambiguity only if the relevant geometric classes are separated by corresponding derivative margins.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[A_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(f)\cap G_1\ne\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad A_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(f)\cap G_2\ne\varnothing.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(q:\mathbb R^d\to\{1,2\}\) is a quality label, ambiguity means that \(q\) is not constant on \(A_{\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H}(f)\).
For first-order testing alone, take \(\varepsilon_H=\infty\), so the acceptance set is \(A_{\varepsilon_g}(f)=\{x:\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon_g\}\).
special_cases_latex: If a local minimum and a saddle both satisfy \(\|\nabla f\|\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f)\ge-\varepsilon_H\), the second-order tolerance is ambiguous.
When \(\varepsilon_g=\varepsilon_H=0\), ambiguity reduces to coexistence of geometrically distinct exact second-order stationary points.
immediate_consequences_latex: An algorithm terminating anywhere in the acceptance set cannot infer the geometric label from the inequalities alone.
Uniform derivative margins separating the classes are sufficient additional data for choosing unambiguous tolerances.

Oracle error and stopping tolerance are distinct quantities, though their combined effect may enlarge the effective acceptance set.

knowledge_statements.title: Spurious Local Minima
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unconstrained finite-dimensional definition relative to global objective value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\). A point \(x_{\mathrm{sp}}\in\mathbb R^n\) is a spurious local minimum if there exists \(r>0\) such that \(f(x_{\mathrm{sp}})\le f(x)\) whenever \(\|x-x_{\mathrm{sp}}\|<r\), but \(x_{\mathrm{sp}}\) is not globally minimizing. Equivalently, its global suboptimality gap \(\Delta_{\mathrm{sp}}=f(x_{\mathrm{sp}})-\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\) is strictly positive. If \(f\) is differentiable, every such point is stationary, although stationarity alone does not reveal the positive gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spurious local minimum minimizes nearby objective values but has value strictly above the global infimum.
assumptions_latex: For the stationarity assertion, \(f\) is differentiable at \(x_{\mathrm{sp}}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{\mathrm{sp}}\) is locally minimizing and \(f(x_{\mathrm{sp}})-\inf_x f(x)>0\); differentiability implies \(\nabla f(x_{\mathrm{sp}})=0\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be \(C^2\), let \(C(f):=\{x:\nabla f(x)=0\}\), and let a strict critical point mean a critical point whose Hessian has no zero eigenvalue. For a saddle-escape statement, let \(\gamma>0\) denote the required uniform negative-curvature margin.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional unconstrained landscapes where Hessian degeneracy, missing spectral margins, or nonisolated critical sets invalidate strict-saddle or isolated-critical-point hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A critical point \(x\in C(f)\) is geometrically degenerate if \(\det
abla^2f(x)=0\). A class-level degenerate-geometry failure occurs when a desired conclusion requires isolated nondegenerate critical points or the margin \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x))\le-\gamma\) at every nonminimizing critical point, but the class contains an \(f\) with either a singular critical Hessian, a nonisolated critical set, or \(\inf_{x\in C(f)\setminus M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)}[-\lambda_{\min}(

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A degenerate-geometry failure occurs when the curvature or isolation assumptions needed by a criticality or escape conclusion break down. Pointwise Hessian degeneracy means that a critical point has at least one zero-curvature direction. At class level, failure may appear as nonisolated critical manifolds, nonminimizing points with no negative Hessian eigenvalue, or negative-curvature magnitudes that approach zero so that no uniform strict-saddle margin exists. These cases are grouped by the loss of robust local geometry, not by the behavior of any one algorithm.

Failure of a uniform strict-saddle margin means \(\forall\gamma>0\ \exists x\in C(f)\setminus M_{\mathrm{loc}}(f)\) with \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))>-\gamma\).
special_cases_latex: A continuum of critical points often has tangent directions in the Hessian kernel.
A flat saddle with \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) is a degenerate failure because it has no negative-curvature certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat-Saddle Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A degenerate saddle invisible to Hessian negative-curvature tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) defined by \(f(x,y)=x^4-y^4\). At \(z=(0,0)\), one has \(\nabla f(z)=0\) and \(\nabla^2 f(z)=0\), so no Hessian eigenvalue gives a negative-curvature direction. Nevertheless, every neighborhood of \(z\) contains points \((t,0)\) with \(f(t,0)>f(z)\) and points \((0,t)\) with \(f(0,t)<f(z)\). Hence \(z\) is a saddle, and any avoidance or escape condition requiring a uniformly negative Hessian eigenvalue fails at this flat saddle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The origin of the quartic difference is a saddle whose gradient and Hessian both vanish, defeating negative-curvature detection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((0,0)\) is a saddle with \(\nabla f(0,0)=0\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f(0,0))=0\).

notation.meaning: The degenerate critical point at the origin.

children.title: Vanishing Spectral-Gap Failures
children.top_down_role: Poor separation among negative, null, and positive curvature modes.

knowledge_statements.title: Vanishing Spectral-Gap Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A saddle family whose positive and negative curvature both approach zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), let \(f_\mu(x,y)=\frac{\mu}{2}x^2-\frac{\mu}{2}y^2\). The origin is a strict saddle and \(\nabla^2 f_\mu(0,0)=\operatorname{diag}(\mu,-\mu)\). Its eigenvalues are separated from the null-curvature threshold by only \(\mu\). As \(\mu\downarrow0\), both the negative-curvature magnitude and the separation between the negative and positive modes vanish. Consequently, no family-uniform constant \(\gamma>0\) can satisfy \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2 f_\mu(0,0))\le-\gamma\), so uniform strict-saddle and finite-time escape estimates based on such a gap do not apply.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict saddles may have arbitrarily weak positive and negative curvature, eliminating any uniform spectral-gap constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda(\nabla^2 f_\mu(0,0))=\{-\mu,\mu\}\), and no positive curvature-gap bound holds uniformly as \(\mu\downarrow0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\text{A family }\{(f_k,x_k)\}_{k\ge1}\text{ has a vanishing spectral-gap failure if }\nabla f_k(x_k)=0,\quad 0<\operatorname{gap}_0(H_k)<\infty,\quad\text{and}\quad\inf_{k\ge1}\operatorname{gap}_0(H_k)=0.\] Equivalently, there are indices \(k_j\) and nonzero eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\in\sigma(H_{k_j})\) such that \(\lambda_j\to0\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence or family of twice-smooth objectives and critical points has a vanishing spectral-gap failure when the smallest absolute value among the nonzero Hessian eigenvalues approaches zero. At a fixed numerical scale, a critical point is spectrally unresolved when it has a nonzero Hessian eigenvalue whose magnitude does not exceed that scale. Consequently, negative or positive curvature modes cannot be separated uniformly from null modes by one positive constant.

children.title: Nonisolated Critical-Set Failures
children.top_down_role: Failure of isolated-critical-point arguments on stationary manifolds and singular sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonisolated Critical-Set Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A stationary set with intersecting manifolds and a singular crossing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) be \(f(x,y)=x^2y^2\). Since \(\nabla f(x,y)=(2xy^2,2x^2y)\), its critical set is \(\mathcal C=\{(x,y):x=0\}\cup\{(x,y):y=0\}\). Thus every critical point is nonisolated, and \(\mathcal C\) is the union of two smooth one-dimensional manifolds meeting singularly at the origin. No neighborhood of any point in \(\mathcal C\) contains that point as its unique stationary point. Therefore arguments requiring isolated critical points, disjoint isolating neighborhoods, or pointwise local linearization cannot be applied without replacing the point by a critical-set analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective has two intersecting axes of stationary points, so isolated-critical-point arguments fail everywhere on its critical set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{crit}(f)=\{x=0\}\cup\{y=0\}\), and no point of this critical set is isolated.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly has two intersecting axes of nonisolated critical points and fits the leaf. No authoritative source is supplied, and the assertion that pointwise local linearization cannot be applied is broader than justified; only arguments requiring isolation are directly excluded by the example.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable. Its critical set is \(\operatorname{Crit}(f)=\{x\in U:\nabla f(x)=0\}\). A point \(x_\star\in\operatorname{Crit}(f)\) is isolated in this set if some \(r>0\) satisfies \(B_r(x_\star)\cap\operatorname{Crit}(f)=\{x_\star\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth unconstrained optimization; the definition covers stationary manifolds and singular stationary sets without assuming regularity or constant dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[x_\star\text{ exhibits a nonisolated critical-set failure if }x_\star\in\operatorname{Crit}(f)\text{ and }\forall r>0,\ \bigl(B_r(x_\star)\setminus\{x_\star\}\bigr)\cap\operatorname{Crit}(f)\ne\varnothing.\] Equivalently, there is a sequence of distinct critical points \(x_j\ne x_\star\) with \(x_j\to x_\star\). A region \(V\subseteq U\) has this failure when it contains such a point. The critical set may locally be a positive-dimensional embedded manifold, a union of intersecting strata, or an otherwise singular set; smooth manifold structure is not part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A critical point has a nonisolated critical-set failure when every neighborhood of it contains another, distinct critical point. Equivalently, distinct critical points converge to it. The definition includes smooth stationary manifolds as well as intersecting or singular stationary sets and records precisely when arguments requiring a unique stationary point in a neighborhood cannot be applied.

equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\exists\{x_j\}\subseteq\operatorname{Crit}(f)\setminus\{x_\star\}:\quad x_j\to x_\star.\]
\[x_\star\in\operatorname{Crit}(f)'\,,\] where \(S'\) denotes the set of accumulation points of \(S\).

An error bound of the form \(\|x-x_\star\|\le c\|\nabla f(x)\|\) cannot hold at other critical points converging to \(x_\star\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nearly Stationary Plateaus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrarily large regions can pass weak gradient and curvature tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(R>0\) and tolerances \(\varepsilon_g>0\), \(\varepsilon_H\ge0\), choose \(0<\delta\le\varepsilon_g\) and define \(f_\delta(x)=\delta x\) on \(\mathbb R\). Throughout the interval \(P_R=[-R,R]\), one has \(|f_\delta'(x)|=\delta\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(f_\delta''(x)=0\ge-\varepsilon_H\). Thus every point of an arbitrarily long interval satisfies the usual approximate first- and second-order inequalities, although \(f_\delta'(x)\ne0\) everywhere and the objective has no stationary point. Small derivative signals alone therefore provide neither localization nor proximity to an exact critical point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrarily long interval can satisfy approximate gradient and curvature tests even though it contains no stationary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_R\subseteq\{x:|f_\delta'(x)|\le\varepsilon_g,\ f_\delta''(x)\ge-\varepsilon_H\}\), but \(\{x:f_\delta'(x)=0\}=\varnothing\).

No source or specific locator supports this plateau counterexample or its general interpretation.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(f\in C^2(U)\), and fix tolerances \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H\ge0\) and a geometric scale \(r>0\). For a nonempty connected set \(P\subseteq U\), write \(\operatorname{diam}(P)=\sup_{x,y\in P}\|x-y\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth unconstrained optimization; both first-order signal and total Hessian magnitude are required to be weak over an extended connected region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[P\text{ is an }(r,\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\text{-nearly stationary plateau of }f\text{ if }P\text{ is connected},\quad \operatorname{diam}(P)\ge r,\quad \sup_{x\in P}\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon_g,\quad \sup_{x\in P}\|\nabla^2f(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon_H.\] The plateau is nontrivial when \(r>0\). A sequence \((P_k)\) is asymptotically stationary and flat at scale \(r\) if \(\operatorname{diam}(P_k)\ge r\) while the corresponding tolerances \(\varepsilon_{g,k}\to0\) and \(\varepsilon_{H,k}\to0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nearly stationary plateau is a connected region of prescribed positive diameter on which both the gradient norm and the Hessian operator norm are uniformly small. A sequence of such regions is asymptotically stationary and flat when their diameters remain bounded below while both tolerances tend to zero. This distinguishes an extended weak-signal region from a single approximate critical point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{diam}(P)\ge r,\qquad \sup_{x\in P}\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon_g,\qquad \sup_{x\in P}\|\nabla^2f(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon_H.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The two uniform signal conditions are equivalent to \(P\subseteq\{x\in U:\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\varepsilon_g,\ \|\nabla^2f(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\varepsilon_H\}\).
special_cases_latex: When \(\varepsilon_g=\varepsilon_H=0\), \(f\) has zero gradient and zero Hessian throughout \(P\).
For a line segment \(P=[a,b]\subseteq U\), the geometric condition becomes \(\|a-b\|\ge r\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every point of \(P\) is an \(\varepsilon_g\)-first-order stationary point.
Every Hessian eigenvalue at every \(x\in P\) lies in \([-\varepsilon_H,\varepsilon_H]\), so neither strong positive nor strong negative curvature is present there.
boundary_notes: Small gradient alone does not satisfy this definition when curvature is large.
Small gradient and Hessian at one point do not define a plateau unless an extended connected set satisfies the uniform bounds.
The definition does not impose a bound on objective-value variation beyond what the derivative conditions express.

notation.meaning: Euclidean diameter of the plateau set

review_flags: No inspected authoritative source states this exact three-parameter plateau definition; the thresholds and connectedness convention require sourcing.
knowledge_statements.title: Quantified nearly stationary plateau

children.title: Dynamical Avoidance Failures
children.top_down_role: Regimes where stable-manifold conclusions fail or provide no practical escape guarantee.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure of dynamical avoidance at an undesirable invariant set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(T:X\to X\) be an iteration map, let \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\), and let \(S\subseteq X\) be a closed invariant set consisting of undesirable stationary states, so \(T(S)\subseteq S\). Let \(\mu\) be the initialization probability measure and \(B(S)=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(T^k(x),S)\to0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic discrete-time dynamics with random initialization; the definition separates probabilistic convergence failure from lack of finite-time escape control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((T,\mu)\) has a dynamical avoidance failure for \(S\) if at least one of the following holds: \[\mu(B(S))>0;\] or there exist a neighborhood \(N\supseteq S\) and a measurable set \(A\subseteq N\setminus S\) with \(\mu(A)>0\) such that the exit time \(\tau_N(x)=\inf\{k\ge0:T^k(x)\notin N\}\) is infinite on a positive-measure subset of \(A\), or is finite almost surely on \(A\) but has no finite uniform bound there. The first clause negates almost-sure avoidance; the second records trapping or practically uncontrolled escape even without convergence to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dynamical avoidance fails for an undesirable invariant stationary set when the initialization distribution assigns positive probability to points whose iterates converge to that set. It also fails in the finite-time sense when a positive-probability collection of nearby initial points never exits a chosen neighborhood, or exits eventually but with no finite uniform escape-time bound. The definition therefore distinguishes an almost-sure avoidance statement from a usable finite-time escape guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mu(B(S))>0\quad\text{or}\quad \exists N\supseteq S,\ A\subseteq N\setminus S:\ \mu(A)>0\ \text{and}\ \bigl(\mu(\{x\in A:\tau_N(x)=\infty\})>0\ \text{or}\ \sup_{x\in A}\tau_N(x)=\infty\bigr).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Almost-sure avoidance fails exactly when \(\mu(X\setminus B(S))<1\).
special_cases_latex: If \(S=\{x_\star\}\), then \(B(S)=\{x:T^k(x)\to x_\star\}\).
If \(A\) is positively invariant and \(A\subseteq N\), then \(\tau_N(x)=\infty\) for every \(x\in A\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The assertion \(T^k(x_0)\not\to S\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(x_0\) is false whenever \(\mu(B(S))>0\).
When \(\sup_{x\in A}\tau_N(x)=\infty\), no deterministic iteration bound valid for all \(x\in A\) certifies departure from \(N\).
boundary_notes: This definition does not require \(S\) to be a strict saddle set.
A zero-measure stable set is not an avoidance failure under an absolutely continuous initialization, though it can become one under a singular initialization measure.
Unbounded uniform exit time does not imply that any individual orbit remains forever.

notation.meaning: basin of convergence to the undesirable invariant set
first exit time of the orbit from the neighborhood

review_flags: The node combines two distinct avoidance-failure notions, and no inspected source supports this exact disjunctive definition.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of dynamical avoidance at an undesirable invariant set

children.title: Noninvertible Iteration Maps
children.top_down_role: Discrete maps outside the local-invertibility regime used by standard avoidance arguments.

knowledge_statements.title: Noninvertible Iteration Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gradient descent can collapse space when its step reaches a reciprocal curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\alpha>0\) and let \(f(x)=x^2/(2\alpha)\) on \(\mathbb R\). The gradient-descent iteration map is \(T(x)=x-\alpha f'(x)=0\) for every \(x\). Its derivative is \(T'(x)=0\), so \(T\) is neither locally injective nor locally invertible at any point. Indeed, every set containing the origin has the whole line as its one-step preimage. Consequently, measure-zero pullback and stable-manifold arguments that require the iteration map to be a local diffeomorphism cannot be transferred to this stepsize-curvature regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a reciprocal-curvature step, gradient descent maps every point to zero and loses all local invertibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T(x)=0\) and \(T'(x)=0\) for all \(x\in\mathbb R\), so \(T\) is nowhere locally invertible.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits the noninvertibility leaf, and the constant gradient-descent map is computed correctly. The claimed boundary for measure-zero pullback and stable-manifold arguments lacks an authoritative source and inspectable locator.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Noninvertibility of an optimization iteration map
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and let \(T:X\to\mathbb R^n\) be continuously differentiable. The associated deterministic iteration is \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\). For gradient descent on \(f\in C^2(X)\), \(T_\alpha(x)=x-\alpha\nabla f(x)\) and \(DT_\alpha(x)=I-\alpha\nabla^2f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth discrete-time maps; local singularity and global failure of one-to-one invertibility are distinguished.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The iteration map \(T\) is locally noninvertible at \(x\in X\) when \[\det DT(x)=0.\] It is noninvertible on a set \(V\subseteq X\) when the restriction \(T|_V\) is not a bijection from \(V\) onto \(T(V)\), or its inverse on \(T(V)\) is not continuously differentiable. A local-invertibility-regime failure near an invariant set \(S\) occurs when every neighborhood \(V\supseteq S\) contains a point \(x\) with singular \(DT(x)\). For gradient descent, local singularity occurs precisely when \(1/\alpha\) is an eigenvalue of \(\nabla^2f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth iteration map is locally noninvertible at a point when its Jacobian is singular. It is noninvertible on a region when its restriction is not one-to-one and onto its image or lacks a continuously differentiable inverse. The local-invertibility regime fails near an invariant set when singular Jacobians occur in every neighborhood of that set. For a gradient-descent map, singularity means that the Hessian has eigenvalue equal to the reciprocal stepsize.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\det DT(x)=0,\quad\text{or more generally}\quad T|_V\text{ has no }C^1\text{ inverse on }T(V).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For square \(DT(x)\), local singularity is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rank}DT(x)<n\).
For \(T_\alpha(x)=x-\alpha\nabla f(x)\), \(\det DT_\alpha(x)=0\) is equivalent to \(1/\alpha\in\sigma(\nabla^2f(x))\).
special_cases_latex: A constant map is noninvertible wherever the domain contains more than one point.
A projection map \(T(x)=Px\) with \(\operatorname{rank}P<n\) is locally noninvertible at every point.
immediate_consequences_latex: At a point with \(\det DT(x)=0\), no local \(C^1\) diffeomorphism representation exists.
Preimages of null sets need not retain the regularity properties used in avoidance arguments that assume a diffeomorphism.
boundary_notes: A nonsingular Jacobian at every point guarantees local invertibility, not necessarily global injectivity.
Noninvertibility alone does not imply convergence, cycling, divergence, or attraction to a saddle.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the iteration map at x
gradient-descent iteration map with stepsize alpha

review_flags: The local inverse-function criterion is standard, but no inspected source ties it to the exact optimization-avoidance boundary asserted by this node.
knowledge_statements.title: Noninvertibility of an optimization iteration map

children.title: Aggressive-Stepsize Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Step regimes producing altered stability, cycles, or divergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggressive-Stepsize Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic gradient descent cycles at the stability boundary and diverges beyond it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\frac{\lambda}{2}x^2\) with \(\lambda>0\), and apply constant-step gradient descent \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha f'(x_k)=(1-\alpha\lambda)x_k\). If \(\alpha=2/\lambda\), every initialization \(x_0\ne0\) produces the two-cycle \(x_k=(-1)^k x_0\). If \(\alpha>2/\lambda\), then \(|1-\alpha\lambda|>1\) and \(|x_k|=|1-\alpha\lambda|^k|x_0|\to\infty\). Thus excessive stepsizes destroy convergence even for a smooth strongly convex quadratic, producing cycling at the boundary and divergence beyond it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a positive quadratic, gradient descent cycles at step two over curvature and diverges for larger steps.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha=2/\lambda\) gives a nontrivial two-cycle, while \(\alpha>2/\lambda\) gives \(|x_k|\to\infty\).

source_refs.source_title: Constrained Optimization and Lagrange Multiplier Methods
source_refs.locator: 2.3.1 Stepsize Analysis for the Method of Multipliers p. 126

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, assume \(
abla f\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on an invariant region \(D\subseteq U\), and consider \(T_\alpha(x)=x-\alpha
abla f(x)\) with \(\alpha>0\). At a critical point \(x_\star\), the linearized multipliers are \(1-\alpha\lambda_i(
abla^2f(x_\star))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constant-step deterministic gradient descent on a region with a known gradient-Lipschitz scale; aggressiveness is defined relative to the standard curvature scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The iteration has an aggressive stepsize on \(D\) when \[\alpha L\ge2.\] More locally, it is spectrally aggressive at a critical point \(x_\star\) when there exists a positive Hessian eigenvalue \(\lambda_i>0\) such that \(|1-\alpha\lambda_i|\ge1\), equivalently \(\alpha\lambda_i\ge2\). Strict inequality gives a linearly expanding multiplier, while equality gives the boundary multiplier \(-1\). This definition identifies a regime in which directions that are stable for sufficiently small positive steps can become neutral or unstable and in which monotone-descent conclusions based on \(\alpha<2/L\) are outside their stated range.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constant-step gradient descent is in an aggressive regime on a region when the stepsize times the gradient-Lipschitz constant is at least two. At a critical point, the step is spectrally aggressive when some positive-curvature Hessian direction has linearized multiplier of magnitude at least one. Equality marks a neutral sign-flipping boundary, and strict inequality makes that direction linearly expanding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\alpha L\ge2,\quad\text{or locally}\quad\exists\lambda_i(\nabla^2f(x_\star))>0:\ |1-\alpha\lambda_i|\ge1.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(\lambda_i>0\), \(|1-\alpha\lambda_i|\ge1\) is equivalent to \(\alpha\lambda_i\ge2\).
The region-wide threshold is \(\alpha\ge2/L\) when \(L>0\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\lambda x^2\) with \(\lambda>0\), the recurrence is \(x_{k+1}=(1-\alpha\lambda)x_k\), and aggressiveness begins at \(\alpha\lambda=2\).
At \(\alpha\lambda=2\), the scalar multiplier equals \(-1\), allowing a period-two sign alternation.
immediate_consequences_latex: A positive-curvature critical direction with \(\alpha\lambda_i>2\) is linearly unstable.
The usual global descent condition based on a strict inequality \(0<\alpha<2/L\) does not cover the aggressive regime.
boundary_notes: The threshold depends on the selected Lipschitz or local curvature bound; an overestimate of \(L\) may label a harmless step aggressive.
Aggressiveness permits altered stability, cycles, or divergence but does not assert that all such behavior occurs for every objective.

notation.meaning: linearized multiplier in a Hessian eigenvector direction

review_flags: No inspected source was available for the exact naming and combined global/local definition of aggressive-stepsize dynamics.

children.title: Singular Initialization Measures
children.top_down_role: Starting distributions concentrated on stable sets or invariant subspaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Initialization Measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A singular starting law may concentrate entirely on a saddle's stable set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x,y)=\frac12x^2-\frac12y^2\) and apply gradient descent with \(0<\alpha<1\). Its update is \(T(x,y)=((1-\alpha)x,(1+\alpha)y)\). The line \(S=\{(x,0):x\in\mathbb R\}\) is invariant, and every trajectory initialized in \(S\) converges to the strict saddle \((0,0)\). If the initialization law \(\nu\) satisfies \(\nu(S)=1\), then convergence to this saddle has probability one, even though \(S\) has two-dimensional Lebesgue measure zero. Almost-sure avoidance under an absolutely continuous initialization law therefore need not extend to singular laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distribution supported on a saddle's stable line makes gradient descent converge to that saddle with probability one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu\bigl(\{(x_0,y_0):T^k(x_0,y_0)\to(0,0)\}\bigr)=1\), although \(S\) is Lebesgue-null in \(\mathbb R^2\).

notation.meaning: Invariant stable line of the saddle.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind fits, and the singular law supported on the invariant stable line produces saddle convergence with probability one as stated. No source or locator supports the extension boundary from absolutely continuous to singular initialization laws.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singular initialization concentrated on an exceptional dynamical set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be Borel, let \(\mathcal L^n\) denote Lebesgue measure, let \(T:X\to X\) be measurable, and let \(\mu\) be the probability law of the initial point \(x_0\). Let \(E\subseteq X\) be a measurable exceptional set, such as a stable set or a proper invariant subspace.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional random initialization for deterministic dynamics; singularity is measured relative to ambient Lebesgue measure and relevance requires mass on the exceptional set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The initialization law \(\mu\) is singular with respect to ambient volume if \[\mu\perp\mathcal L^n,\quad\text{i.e.}\quad\exists N\subseteq X\text{ measurable}:\ \mathcal L^n(N)=0\ \text{and}\ \mu(N)=1.\] It is an avoidance-adverse singular initialization for \(E\) when, additionally, \(\mathcal L^n(E)=0\) and \(\mu(E)>0\). It is fully concentrated on \(E\) when \(\mu(E)=1\). If \(E\) is positively invariant, \(T(E)\subseteq E\), then initialization in \(E\) keeps every subsequent iterate in the exceptional set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An initialization probability measure is singular relative to ambient volume when all of its mass lies on a Lebesgue-null measurable set. It is adverse to an avoidance conclusion for a particular exceptional set when that set has zero ambient volume but positive initialization probability. Full concentration means probability one. Typical examples are distributions supported on a lower-dimensional stable set or invariant subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\exists N:\ \mathcal L^n(N)=0,\ \mu(N)=1;\qquad\text{and, for an adverse set }E,\quad\mathcal L^n(E)=0<\mu(E).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\mu\perp\mathcal L^n\) means that \(\mu\) and \(\mathcal L^n\) are mutually singular measures.
Full exceptional-set concentration is \(\operatorname{supp}\mu\subseteq E\) up to \(\mu\)-null sets.
special_cases_latex: A Dirac law \(\delta_{x_0}\) is singular with respect to \(\mathcal L^n\).
A probability law supported on a proper linear subspace of \(\mathbb R^n\) is singular with respect to \(\mathcal L^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A Lebesgue-null exceptional set need not have zero probability under \(\mu\).
If \(\mu(E)=1\) and \(T(E)\subseteq E\), then \(\mu(\{x_0:T^k(x_0)\in E\ \forall k\})=1\).
boundary_notes: A measure can be singular without charging the particular stable or invariant set relevant to an avoidance theorem.
A distribution having a density with respect to lower-dimensional surface measure can still be singular relative to ambient Lebesgue measure.

notation.meaning: mutual singularity of the initialization law and ambient volume

review_flags: Measure singularity is standard, but no inspected source supports the node-specific linkage to saddle-avoidance failures.
knowledge_statements.title: Singular initialization concentrated on an exceptional dynamical set

children.title: Asymptotic but Arbitrarily Slow Escape
children.top_down_role: Saddle avoidance without useful finite-time control.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic but Arbitrarily Slow Escape
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing negative curvature prevents a uniform finite escape-time bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), consider \(f_\mu(x,y)=\frac12x^2-\frac{\mu}{2}y^2\) and gradient descent with fixed \(0<\alpha<1\). Then \(y_k=(1+\alpha\mu)^k y_0\). For \(0<|y_0|<r\), the first index \(\tau_r\) satisfying \(|y_{\tau_r}|\ge r\) obeys \(\tau_r=\left\lceil\log(r/|y_0|)/\log(1+\alpha\mu)\right\rceil\). Each initialization with \(y_0\ne0\) eventually escapes, but \(\tau_r\) is unbounded as \(\mu\downarrow0\) or \(|y_0|\downarrow0\). Hence asymptotic saddle avoidance alone supplies no uniform finite-time guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trajectories eventually leave a quadratic saddle, yet escape time becomes arbitrarily large as negative curvature or initial displacement vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\tau_r=\left\lceil\frac{\log(r/|y_0|)}{\log(1+\alpha\mu)}\right\rceil\), which has no uniform upper bound over \(\mu>0\) and \(0<|y_0|<r\).

notation.meaning: First time the unstable coordinate reaches radius r.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, and the escape-time expression and lack of a uniform bound are correct under the stated parameters. No authoritative source or specific locator supports the finite-time saddle-escape boundary.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Eventual escape without a uniform finite-time bound
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(T:X\to X\) be a discrete-time map on a metric space \(X\), let \(S\subseteq X\) be an invariant stationary set, let \(N\supseteq S\) be a neighborhood, and let \(A\subseteq N\setminus S\) be a specified class of initial points. Define \(\tau_N(x)=\inf\{k\ge0:T^k(x)\notin N\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic discrete-time local dynamics; escape is measured from one fixed neighborhood and uniformly over a stated initialization class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dynamics has asymptotic but arbitrarily slow escape from \(N\) on \(A\) when \[\forall x\in A,\quad \tau_N(x)<\infty,\qquad\text{and}\qquad \sup_{x\in A}\tau_N(x)=\infty.\] Equivalently, every admissible orbit eventually leaves \(N\), but for every integer \(K\ge1\) there is an initial point \(x_K\in A\) whose first \(K\) iterates remain in \(N\). For a probability law \(\mu\), a probabilistic version requires \(\tau_N<\infty\) almost surely while \(\mu(\tau_N>K)>0\) for every \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Escape is asymptotic but arbitrarily slow when every admissible initial point eventually leaves the selected neighborhood, yet the exit times are unbounded over the admissible class. Thus avoidance holds pointwise but no finite iteration count works uniformly. In the probabilistic version, exit occurs almost surely while every finite time horizon has a positive-probability tail of trajectories that have not yet escaped.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\tau_N(x)<\infty\ \forall x\in A,\qquad \sup_{x\in A}\tau_N(x)=\infty.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\forall K\in\mathbb N\ \exists x_K\in A:\quad T^k(x_K)\in N\quad(0\le k\le K).\]
Probabilistically, \(\tau_N<\infty\) almost surely and \(\mu(\tau_N>K)>0\) for every \(K\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) contains points arbitrarily close to a stable manifold boundary, their exit times may form an unbounded family while remaining finite individually.
For a singleton \(A\), the condition cannot hold because one finite exit time is automatically a uniform bound.
immediate_consequences_latex: No finite \(K\) guarantees escape by time \(K\) for every \(x\in A\).
Pointwise nonconvergence to \(S\) does not supply a uniform local escape complexity bound.
boundary_notes: The condition excludes genuinely trapped points because every \(\tau_N(x)\) must be finite.
The definition depends on both \(N\) and \(A\); shrinking either can change whether uniform escape holds.
Unbounded exit time alone does not specify a tail rate or expected escape time.

notation.meaning: first time the orbit exits N

review_flags: No inspected source states this exact deterministic and probabilistic escape-time definition in the saddle-avoidance setting.
knowledge_statements.title: Eventual escape without a uniform finite-time bound

children.title: Recurrent Dynamical Failure Modes
children.top_down_role: Nonconvergent local dynamics near stationary regions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonstationary recurrence near a stationary region
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((X,d)\) be a metric space, let \(T:X\to X\) be continuous, and let \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\). A point \(x\) is recurrent if there is a strictly increasing sequence \(k_j\to\infty\) such that \(T^{k_j}(x)\to x\). Let \(S\subseteq X\) be a stationary set and \(N\supseteq S\) a neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic discrete-time dynamics; the failure requires recurrent nonfixed behavior remaining in or repeatedly returning to a stationary neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A recurrent dynamical failure mode near \(S\) is present when there exists \(x\in N\setminus S\) such that \[\exists k_j\uparrow\infty:\quad T^{k_j}(x)\to x,\qquad\text{and}\qquad T(x)\ne x.\] It is locally trapped when \(T^k(x)\in N\) for every \(k\ge0\). A periodic orbit of least period \(p\ge2\) is a special recurrent failure. More generally, recurrence may be nonperiodic; the defining feature is repeated return arbitrarily close to a nonfixed state rather than convergence to one stationary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recurrent dynamical failure near a stationary set occurs when a nonstationary initial point in its neighborhood returns arbitrarily close to itself along an unbounded sequence of iterations and is not fixed by the iteration map. The failure is locally trapped if the entire orbit remains in the neighborhood. Periodic cycles of length at least two are included, but recurrence need not be periodic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\in N\setminus S,\quad T(x)\ne x,\quad\exists k_j\uparrow\infty:\ d(T^{k_j}(x),x)\to0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Recurrence is equivalent to \(x\in\omega(x)\), where \(\omega(x)\) is the omega-limit set of the orbit.
For a periodic point of least period \(p\ge2\), one may take \(k_j=jp\).
special_cases_latex: A two-cycle consists of distinct points \(x,y\) satisfying \(T(x)=y\) and \(T(y)=x\).
An invariant quasiperiodic orbit can be recurrent without containing a periodic point.
immediate_consequences_latex: The orbit of a recurrent nonfixed point cannot converge to a different fixed point.
A trapped periodic orbit with period \(p\ge2\) prevents convergence of that orbit to the stationary set \(S\).
boundary_notes: Bounded nonconvergent motion is not automatically recurrent at its initial point.
Repeated visits to \(N\) alone are weaker than recurrence, which requires return near the same nonfixed state.
The definition does not classify chaoticity, stability, or the measure of the recurrent basin.

notation.meaning: omega-limit set of the orbit starting at x

review_flags: Topological recurrence is standard, but no inspected source supports its exact use as this optimization failure class.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonstationary recurrence near a stationary region

children.title: Cycling Dynamics
children.top_down_role: Periodic or nearly periodic local behavior near stationary regions.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycling Dynamics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A boundary stepsize creates an exact nonstationary period-two orbit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\frac{\lambda}{2}x^2\) with \(\lambda>0\), use gradient descent with \(\alpha=2/\lambda\). The update map is \(T(x)=x-\alpha f'(x)=-x\). Hence every \(x_0\ne0\) generates the exact cycle \(x_0,-x_0,x_0,-x_0,\ldots\), whose least period is two. Moreover, \(f(x_k)=f(x_0)\) for all \(k\), while neither point of the cycle is stationary. Thus bounded iterates and nonincreasing-objective conclusions that rely on a strict stepsize inequality can fail at its boundary through persistent cycling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the quadratic stability boundary, every nonzero gradient-descent trajectory is an exact two-cycle with constant objective value.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample kind is appropriate for Cycling Dynamics, and the exact period-two orbit at the quadratic stability boundary is correct. No source or locator supports the example or the associated convergence-theory boundary.

children.title: Recurrent Orbits
children.top_down_role: Repeated returns to local regions without convergence to a stationary point.

knowledge_statements.title: Recurrent Orbits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recurrence obstructs convergence whenever the recurrent point is not fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a metric space, let \(T:X\to X\) be continuous, and define \(x_k=T^k(x_0)\). The orbit is recurrent at \(x_0\) if there exists a strictly increasing sequence \(k_j\to\infty\) such that \(x_{k_j}\to x_0\). If \(T(x_0)\ne x_0\), such an orbit cannot converge: otherwise continuity and convergence would give both \(x_k\to x_\star\) with \(T(x_\star)=x_\star\) and the recurrent subsequence \(x_{k_j}\to x_0\), forcing \(x_0=x_\star\), contrary to nonfixedness. Thus nonfixed recurrence lies outside fixed-point convergence theory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a continuous iteration repeatedly returns near a nonfixed starting point, its orbit cannot converge to a fixed point.
assumptions_latex: \((X,d)\) is a metric space and \(T:X\to X\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sequence \((T^k(x_0))_{k\ge0}\) does not converge.

notation.meaning: The kth iterate from the initial point.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, and nonfixed recurrence for a continuous iteration map indeed precludes convergence. However, no source or locator is supplied, and the statement includes a proof-style contradiction argument that should be removed when the sourced record is revised.

children.title: Aperiodic Recurrence
children.top_down_role: Nonperiodic recurrent behavior within local iteration dynamics.

knowledge_statements.title: Aperiodic Recurrence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes bounded, nonperiodic recurrence of a deterministic iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:X\to X\) be continuous on a metric space and let \(x_{k+1}=T(x_k)\) have a precompact orbit. The orbit exhibits aperiodic recurrence when its omega-limit set \(\omega(x_0)\) is infinite, every neighborhood of some \(z\in\omega(x_0)\) is visited infinitely often, and the orbit is neither convergent nor eventually periodic. Thus boundedness and recurrent returns alone do not imply convergence to a critical point, even when every accumulation point satisfies a prescribed criticality condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orbit may revisit neighborhoods indefinitely while remaining bounded, nonconvergent, and nonperiodic; recurrence alone therefore does not establish convergence to one critical point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\omega(x_0)\) may be infinite although the orbit is recurrent and all its accumulation points satisfy criticality.

notation.meaning: omega-limit set of the orbit starting at x_0

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record fits the aperiodic-recurrence failure-boundary container, but the proposed characterization is not presented as a standard named definition, and recurrence of a point already follows from its membership in the omega-limit set under the usual definition. The further optimization claim concerning critical accumulation points needs a source specifying the relevant algorithm and criticality condition.

children.title: Convergence-Theory Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of stationarity conclusions when local trajectories remain recurrent.

knowledge_statements.title: Convergence-Theory Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates subsequential criticality and asymptotic regularity from full-sequence convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(f\equiv0\) and define \(x_k=(\cos(\log(k+1)),\sin(\log(k+1)))\). Then \(f(x_{k+1})=f(x_k)\), \(\nabla f(x_k)=0\), the sequence is bounded, and \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert\to0\). Nevertheless, \(x_k\) does not converge and its accumulation set is the unit circle. Hence descent, vanishing steps, boundedness, and criticality of every accumulation point do not by themselves imply convergence of the entire iterate sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even bounded critical iterates with constant objective values and vanishing successive differences can fail to converge; an additional structural convergence mechanism is necessary.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R\) is the constant-zero smooth function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_{k+1}-x_k\rVert\to0\) and \(\nabla f(x_k)=0\) for all \(k\), but \(\{x_k\}\) does not converge.
