knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure classes for an inexact local criticality oracle
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. At a query point \(x\), a numerical oracle returns \((\widetilde g,\widetilde H)\) for \((g,H)=(\nabla f(x),\nabla^2f(x))\), with certified or assumed error bounds \(\|\widetilde g-g\|\le\delta_g\) and \(\|\widetilde H-H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\delta_H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth criticality assessment with deterministic norm-bounded oracle errors; the classes concern reliability of first- and second-order certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For requested tolerances \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H>0\), a numerical-oracle failure occurs if the available outputs and error bounds do not determine the truth of \(\|g\|\le\varepsilon_g\) or \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\ge-\varepsilon_H\). The first-order classification is unresolved when \[\bigl|\|\widetilde g\|-\varepsilon_g\bigr|\le\delta_g,\] and the curvature classification is unresolved when \[\bigl|\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\varepsilon_H\bigr|\le\delta_H.\] False acceptance means the computed tests pass while at least one exact test fails; false rejection is the converse. These classes include conditioning, finite-precision, approximation, and inaccurate-information mechanisms through their induced error radii.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact numerical oracle fails at a requested criticality scale when its returned gradient or Hessian, together with the known error radius, cannot determine whether the exact first- or second-order test holds. Classification is unresolved when the computed quantity lies within one error radius of the relevant threshold. A false acceptance passes the computed test although an exact test fails, while a false rejection fails the computed test although the exact tests hold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bigl|\|\widetilde g\|-\varepsilon_g\bigr|\le\delta_g\quad\text{or}\quad\bigl|\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\varepsilon_H\bigr|\le\delta_H.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The exact gradient norm is confined to \([\max\{0,\|\widetilde g\|-\delta_g\},\|\widetilde g\|+\delta_g]\); classification is unresolved when this interval crosses \(\varepsilon_g\).

The exact minimum eigenvalue is confined to \([\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)-\delta_H,\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\delta_H]\); classification is unresolved when this interval crosses \(-\varepsilon_H\).
special_cases_latex: When \(\delta_g=\delta_H=0\), ambiguity from oracle error disappears.
A gradient-only oracle has no basis for certifying the second-order condition unless additional curvature information is supplied.
immediate_consequences_latex: Robust acceptance requires \(\|\widetilde g\|+\delta_g\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)-\delta_H\ge-\varepsilon_H\).
Robust rejection follows if \(\|\widetilde g\|-\delta_g>\varepsilon_g\) or \(\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\delta_H<-\varepsilon_H\).
boundary_notes: The definition assumes valid deterministic error bounds; stochastic confidence intervals require an explicit probability level.
An unresolved classification is not itself a false certificate.
The taxonomy does not prescribe how the approximate derivatives are computed.
review_flags: No inspected source states this complete oracle-failure taxonomy with both ambiguity intervals and false-decision classes.

children.title: Ill-Conditioned Eigenvalue Detection
children.top_down_role: Weak curvature obscured by spectral sensitivity and numerical error.

knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Eigenvalue Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gives the perturbation threshold below which Hessian eigenvalue signs are uncertifiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\) be the exact Hessian and let \(\widetilde H=H+E\) with \(\lVert E\rVert_2\le\delta\). Weyl's inequality gives \(\lvert\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)-\lambda_{\min}(H)\rvert\le\delta\). Consequently, \(\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)<-\delta\) certifies negative curvature of \(H\), while \(\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)>\delta\) certifies positive definiteness. If \(\lvert\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)\rvert\le\delta\), numerical information at this error level cannot determine the sign of the exact smallest eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computed smallest eigenvalue is sign-reliable only when its distance from zero exceeds the spectral-norm error in the Hessian approximation.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) and \(\widetilde H\) are real symmetric matrices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign of \(\lambda_{\min}(H)\) is uncertifiable from \(\widetilde H\) whenever \(\lvert\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)\rvert\le\delta\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ill-conditioned detection of a minimum-eigenvalue threshold
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex:
Let \(H\in\mathbb S^n\) be a symmetric Hessian or curvature matrix, let \(\widetilde H=H+E\) be its computed approximation, assume \(\|E\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leawdelta\), and fix a negative-curvature threshold \(-\varepsilon_H\) with \(\varepsilon_H\ge0\). The exact classification compares \(\lambda_{
min}(H)\) with \(-\varepsilon_H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric finite-dimensional eigenvalue detection under an operator-norm perturbation bound; ill-conditioning is relative to a specified classification threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimum-eigenvalue detection is ill-conditioned at \((H,\varepsilon_H,\delta)\) when the spectral margin does not exceed the admissible perturbation: \[\bigl|\lambda_{\min}(H)+\varepsilon_H\bigr|\le\delta.\] From computed data it is unresolved when \[\bigl|\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\varepsilon_H\bigr|\le\delta.\] In either formulation, perturbations allowed by the error model can place the minimum eigenvalue on opposite sides of the threshold, so the sign of the threshold test is not robust. For detecting any negative curvature, set \(\varepsilon_H=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Detection of whether the smallest eigenvalue lies below a prescribed negative-curvature threshold is ill-conditioned when the distance from that eigenvalue to the threshold is no larger than the admissible matrix perturbation. With only a computed matrix, classification is unresolved when its smallest eigenvalue lies within the error radius of the threshold. Ordinary negative-curvature detection is the special case with threshold zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bigl|\lambda_{\min}(H)+\varepsilon_H\bigr|\le\delta\quad\text{or, from computed data,}\quad\bigl|\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\varepsilon_H\bigr|\le\delta.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The computed-data uncertainty interval \([\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)-\delta,\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\delta]\) contains \(-\varepsilon_H\).

The robust-detection margin ratio \(\kappa_{\mathrm{det}}=\delta/|\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\varepsilon_H|\) satisfies \(\kappa_{\mathrm{det}}\ge1\), with an infinite value when the denominator is zero.
special_cases_latex: For \(\varepsilon_H=0\), the unresolved regime is \(|\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)|\le\delta\).
If \(\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\delta< -\varepsilon_H\), negative curvature beyond the threshold is robustly detected.
immediate_consequences_latex: Robust nonnegative-threshold certification requires \(\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)-\delta\ge-\varepsilon_H\).
When the uncertainty interval crosses the threshold, neither side of the classification is certified by the stated error bound alone.
boundary_notes: Eigenvector sensitivity is not required for this eigenvalue-threshold definition.
For nonsymmetric matrices, eigenvalue perturbations need not obey the same operator-norm interval and this definition does not apply unchanged.
A small spectral gap between two nonminimal eigenvalues is distinct from a small margin to the classification threshold.

notation.meaning: real symmetric n by n matrices

review_flags: No inspected source was available for this exact threshold-relative definition and condition ratio.
The ambient-context text contains the intended symbol \(\delta\); source verification should also normalize any transcription artifacts.

children.title: Premature Krylov Termination
children.top_down_role: Restricted searches ending before unstable modes become visible.

knowledge_statements.title: Premature Krylov Termination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that a restricted Krylov search can entirely miss an unstable eigendirection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1)\) and start a symmetric Krylov search with \(q=e_2\). For every \(m\ge1\), the generated space \(\mathcal K_m(H,q)=\operatorname{span}\{q,Hq,\ldots,H^{m-1}q\}\) equals \(\operatorname{span}\{e_2\}\). Its minimum Ritz value is \(1\), although \(\lambda_{\min}(H)=-1\). Thus termination based only on the current restricted spectrum can falsely report absence of negative curvature when the starting vector has no component in an unstable invariant subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Krylov method started orthogonally to the negative eigenspace can report only positive Ritz values and completely miss genuine negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min_{v\in\mathcal K_m,\,\lVert v\rVert=1}v^{\mathsf T}Hv=1\) for every \(m\), while \(\lambda_{\min}(H)=-1\).

notation.meaning: order-m Krylov subspace generated by H and q

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two-dimensional example is correct and its counterexample content kind fits the terminal container: the starting vector lies in the positive invariant eigenspace, so every generated Krylov space misses the negative eigendirection. No authoritative Krylov or Ritz-value source is supplied.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Premature termination of a Krylov curvature search
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), let \(q_1\ne0\), and define \(\mathcal K_m(H,q_1)=\operatorname{span}\{q_1,Hq_1,\ldots,H^{m-1}q_1\}\). Let \(Q_m\) have orthonormal columns spanning this Krylov space and let \(\theta_m=\lambda_{\min}(Q_m^THQ_m)\) be its smallest Ritz value. Fix a curvature threshold \(-\varepsilon_H\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact-arithmetic symmetric Krylov subspace detection of negative curvature; finite-precision and stochastic variants are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Termination at iteration \(m\) is premature for threshold \(-\varepsilon_H\) when the restricted search reports no threshold-violating curvature but the full matrix has such curvature: \[\theta_m\ge-\varepsilon_H\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lambda_{\min}(H)<-\varepsilon_H.\] Equivalently, every unit vector currently visible in \(\mathcal K_m(H,q_1)\) has Rayleigh quotient at least \(-\varepsilon_H\), although some unit vector in \(\mathbb R^n\) has a smaller Rayleigh quotient. A stopping rule commits this failure when it accepts the first inequality as a global curvature certificate without an independent residual, probability, or iteration guarantee sufficient for the second inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Krylov curvature search terminates prematurely when the smallest Rayleigh quotient found in its current Krylov subspace is above the negative-curvature threshold even though the full symmetric matrix has an eigenvalue below that threshold. The searched subspace has not yet exposed the unstable direction, but the stopping rule treats its restricted Ritz value as a global certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\lambda_{\min}(Q_m^THQ_m)\ge-\varepsilon_H>\lambda_{\min}(H).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\min_{v\in\mathcal K_m,\ \|v\|=1}v^THv\ge-\varepsilon_H,\qquad \min_{v\in\mathbb R^n,\ \|v\|=1}v^THv<-\varepsilon_H.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(q_1\) is orthogonal to an invariant eigenspace containing all eigenvectors below the threshold, no Krylov power generated from \(q_1\) can reveal those modes in exact arithmetic.
At \(m=n\), premature termination is impossible when \(\mathcal K_n(H,q_1)=\mathbb R^n\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The restricted Ritz test yields a false second-order stationarity certificate.
A direction \(v\) with \(v^THv<-\varepsilon_H\|v\|^2\) exists outside the curvature detected by the terminated search.
boundary_notes: Slow convergence of a Ritz value without actual termination is not yet a termination failure.
This definition does not prescribe a particular Lanczos stopping criterion.
Loss of orthogonality and roundoff require a separate finite-precision error model.

notation.meaning: mth Krylov subspace generated by H and the starting vector
smallest Ritz value in the current Krylov subspace

review_flags: No inspected source supports this exact failure definition and stopping-rule interpretation.

children.title: Finite-Difference Curvature Noise
children.top_down_role: Truncation, cancellation, and evaluation noise in curvature approximation.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Difference Curvature Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies truncation and evaluation-noise errors in centered directional curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\) be a unit vector and suppose \(\lvert D^4f(x+td)[d,d,d,d]\rvert\le M\) for \(\lvert t\rvert\le h\). If evaluations satisfy \(\widetilde f(y)=f(y)+e(y)\) with \(\lvert e(y)\rvert\le\eta\), then the centered estimator \(\widehat c_h=(\widetilde f(x+hd)-2\widetilde f(x)+\widetilde f(x-hd))/h^2\) obeys \(\lvert\widehat c_h-d^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x)d\rvert\le Mh^2/12+4\eta/h^2\). Decreasing \(h\) therefore eventually amplifies evaluation noise rather than improving curvature accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centered curvature differences balance an order-squared truncation error against evaluation noise amplified by the inverse square of the step.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is four times directionally differentiable along \(x+td\) for \(\lvert t\rvert\le h\).
\(\lVert d\rVert=1\) and the fourth directional derivative is bounded by \(M\).
Each function evaluation has absolute error at most \(\eta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert\widehat c_h-d^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x)d\rvert\le Mh^2/12+4\eta/h^2\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f\in C^2(U)\), let \(x\in U\), let \(v\in\mathbb R^n\) with \(\|v\|=1\), and suppose an evaluated gradient is \(\widetilde g(y)=\nabla f(y)+e(y)\) with \(\|e(y)\|\le	ea\). For \(h>0\), define the forward-difference Hessian-vector estimate \(D_hv=[\widetilde g(x+hv)-\widetilde g(x)]/h\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward finite differences of noisy gradients in finite-dimensional smooth optimization; the definition separates truncation and evaluation-noise scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the Hessian is \(M\)-Lipschitz along \([x,x+hv]\). The finite-difference curvature error scale is \[\mathcal E(h)=\frac{M}{2}h+\frac{2\eta}{h}.\] Curvature detection at threshold scale \(\gamma>0\) is noise dominated when \(\mathcal E(h)\ge\gamma\). It is sign unresolved for the directional curvature \(v^T\nabla^2f(x)v\) when \[\left|v^TD_hv\right|\le\mathcal E(h),\] because the error allowance reaches both signs. The first term records truncation and the second records amplification of gradient-evaluation error and cancellation by division by \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward finite-difference Hessian-vector estimate formed from noisy gradients has a curvature-error scale consisting of a truncation term proportional to the differencing interval and a noise-amplification term inversely proportional to it. Detection at a requested curvature scale is noise dominated when this total error is at least that scale. The directional sign is unresolved when the computed curvature magnitude does not exceed the error allowance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal E(h)=\frac{M}{2}h+\frac{2\eta}{h}\ge\gamma,\quad\text{or for sign ambiguity}\quad |v^TD_hv|\le\mathcal E(h).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The error decomposition is \(D_hv-\nabla^2f(x)v=r_{\mathrm{tr}}+r_{\mathrm{noise}}\) with \(\|r_{\mathrm{tr}}\|\le Mh/2\) and \(\|r_{\mathrm{noise}}\|\le2\eta/h\).
special_cases_latex: With exact gradients, \(\eta=0\) and only the truncation scale \(Mh/2\) remains.
With nonzero \(\eta\), taking \(h\to0\) makes the noise term \(2\eta/h\) unbounded.
immediate_consequences_latex: A smaller differencing interval does not monotonically improve the worst-case error when \(\eta>0\).
A robust negative-curvature declaration requires the computed directional curvature to lie below the threshold by more than \(\mathcal E(h)\).
boundary_notes: Central differences have a different truncation order and are not covered by this formula.
Function-value finite differences require a different noise-amplification model.
The constants depend on the norm convention and the stated deterministic error bound.

notation.meaning: forward-difference estimate of the Hessian-vector product
Hessian Lipschitz constant along the differencing segment
combined truncation and noise error scale

children.title: Inexact-Derivative Failures
children.top_down_role: Gradient or curvature errors overwhelming the requested criticality scale.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact-Derivative Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relates derivative-oracle errors to attainable first- and second-order criticality tolerances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(\lVert\widetilde g-
abla f(x)Vert\le\delta_g\) and \(\lVert\widetilde H-
abla^2f(x)Vert_2\le\delta_H\). If an inexact oracle reports \(\lVert\widetilde gVert\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)\ge-\varepsilon_H\), then only \(\lVert
abla f(x)Vert\le\varepsilon_g+\delta_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(
abla^2f(x))\ge-(\varepsilon_H+\delta_H)\) are certified. Requested criticality below the corresponding oracle-error scale is therefore not justified without stronger error control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate derivatives certify true criticality only after their error bounds are added to the reported gradient and curvature tolerances.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is twice differentiable at \(x\).
The gradient error is at most \(\delta_g\).
The Hessian spectral-norm error is at most \(\delta_H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reported \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\)-criticality implies at best true \((\varepsilon_g+\delta_g,\varepsilon_H+\delta_H)\)-criticality.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative error overwhelming a requested criticality scale
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. At \(x\in U\), let \(g=\nabla f(x)\), \(H=\nabla^2f(x)\), and let approximations satisfy \(\widetilde g=g+e_g\) and \(\widetilde H=H+E_H\). Fix target tolerances \(\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic norm-bounded first- and second-derivative errors for approximate smooth criticality certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inexact-derivative failure at scales \((\varepsilon_g,\varepsilon_H)\) occurs when the derivative uncertainty is at least as large as the margin separating a computed test from its exact threshold: \[\|e_g\|\ge\bigl|\|\widetilde g\|-\varepsilon_g\bigr|\quad\text{or}\quad\|E_H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\ge\bigl|\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\varepsilon_H\bigr|.\] A false acceptance is realized when \(\|\widetilde g\|\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)\ge-\varepsilon_H\), while \(\|g\|>\varepsilon_g\) or \(\lambda_{\min}(H)<-\varepsilon_H\). The definition is scale-relative: the same absolute errors may be harmless for loose tolerances and fatal for tighter ones.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact-derivative failure occurs when gradient or Hessian error is large enough to cross the margin between a computed criticality quantity and its requested threshold. A false acceptance passes both computed first- and second-order tests even though at least one corresponding exact test fails. Failure is therefore relative to the requested criticality tolerances, not merely to whether derivative error is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|e_g\|\ge\bigl|\|\widetilde g\|-\varepsilon_g\bigr|\quad\text{or}\quad\|E_H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\ge\bigl|\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\varepsilon_H\bigr|.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Gradient classification is unresolved when \(\varepsilon_g\in[\max\{0,\|\widetilde g\|-\|e_g\|\},\|\widetilde g\|+\|e_g\|]\).
Curvature classification is unresolved when \(-\varepsilon_H\in[\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)-\|E_H\|_{\mathrm{op}},\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)+\|E_H\|_{\mathrm{op}}]\).
special_cases_latex: If \(E_H=0\), only first-order misclassification remains possible through \(e_g\).
If \(e_g=0\), first-order stationarity is exact but the curvature certificate may still fail.
immediate_consequences_latex: Robust acceptance requires \(\|\widetilde g\|+\|e_g\|\le\varepsilon_g\) and \(\lambda_{\min}(\widetilde H)-\|E_H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\ge-\varepsilon_H\).
Without error bounds smaller than the threshold margins, a computed approximate criticality declaration is not certified.
boundary_notes: This definition does not specify whether errors arise from approximation, sampling, roundoff, or stale information.
Biased stochastic errors require probability-qualified bounds when deterministic bounds are unavailable.
Large derivative error need not cause a wrong decision when the exact quantities lie far from the thresholds.
review_flags: No inspected source states this exact margin-based definition of inexact-derivative failure.

children.title: Adverse Noise Regimes
children.top_down_role: Noise regimes that invalidate concentration or fail to excite unstable directions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let an oracle at \(x\inbR^n\) return \(G(x,awxi)=\nabla f(x)+\zeta(x,\xi)\), where \(\xi\) is random. Near a strict saddle \(x_\star\), let \(U_-\) denote the negative-eigenspace of \(\nabla^2f(x_\star)\), and let \(P_-\) be the orthogonal projector onto \(U_-\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional stochastic first-order or perturbation oracles; the taxonomy isolates bias, concentration failure, and failure to excite unstable directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A noise model is adverse at \(x\) if at least one of the following holds. Bias-adverse: \[\|\mathbb E[\zeta(x,\xi)]\|\text{ is not negligible relative to the requested gradient tolerance}.\] Concentration-adverse: the required moment or tail control is absent, for example \(\mathbb E\|\zeta(x,\xi)\|^2=\infty\), so a finite-variance concentration premise fails. Excitation-adverse near \(x_\star\): \[\mathbb E\|P_-\zeta(x_\star,\xi)\|^2=0,\] equivalently \(P_-\zeta(x_\star,\xi)=0\) almost surely, so the noise injects no component into any unstable direction. A model may belong to more than one class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oracle-noise model is adverse when its bias is not small relative to the requested stationarity tolerance, when it lacks the moment or tail control required by a concentration argument, or when it has zero variance in every negative-curvature direction at a strict saddle. These classes are not mutually exclusive. The final class captures noise that exists but cannot excite an unstable direction needed for stochastic escape.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\|\mathbb E\zeta\|\text{ is tolerance-scale significant},\quad\text{or}\quad\mathbb E\|\zeta\|^2=\infty,\quad\text{or}\quad\mathbb E\|P_-\zeta\|^2=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Excitation degeneracy is equivalent to \(P_-\zeta=0\) almost surely when \(\mathbb E\|P_-\zeta\|^2\) is defined.
If \(\Sigma=\mathbb E[(\zeta-\mathbb E\zeta)(\zeta-\mathbb E\zeta)^T]\), excitation degeneracy includes \(P_-\Sigma P_-=0\).
special_cases_latex: Noise supported entirely on the nonnegative eigenspace \(U_-^\perp\) is excitation-adverse.
A centered finite-variance distribution may avoid the bias and infinite-variance classes while still being excitation-adverse.
immediate_consequences_latex: An unbiased-oracle premise fails in the bias-adverse class.
A finite-variance concentration result cannot be invoked when \(\mathbb E\|\zeta\|^2=\infty\).
A perturbation supported in \(U_-^\perp\) cannot directly displace an iterate along \(U_-\).
boundary_notes: Heavy tails do not preclude all concentration results; the failure is relative to the assumptions of the chosen result.
Nonzero total variance does not guarantee variance in an unstable subspace.
The phrase tolerance-scale significant requires a numerical threshold before the bias class becomes operational.

orthogonal projector onto the negative eigenspace

knowledge_statements.title: Adverse stochastic-oracle noise regimes

children.title: Biased Noise
children.top_down_role: Oracle noise with systematic directional or magnitude distortion.

knowledge_statements.title: Biased Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies persistent oracle bias as a barrier to true stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a stochastic gradient oracle satisfy \(G(x,\xi)=
abla f(x)+b(x)+\zeta(x,\xi)\), where \(\mathbb E[\zeta(x,\xi)\mid x]=0\). Then its mean field is \(\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid x]=
abla f(x)+b(x)\). Any method driven toward a zero of this mean field may converge to \(x_\star\) satisfying \(
abla f(x_\star)=-b(x_\star)\), so \(\lVert
abla f(x_\star)Vert\) can be as large as the persistent bias. Unbiased-noise stationarity conclusions therefore fail unless the bias vanishes or is explicitly controlled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Persistent gradient bias shifts the oracle's equilibrium away from true stationary points, leaving a residual gradient comparable to the bias.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A mean-oracle equilibrium can satisfy \(\nabla f(x_\star)=-b(x_\star)\ne0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mean-field calculation is correct and the failure-boundary kind fits persistent bias. The statement nevertheless makes a stochastic-optimization convergence-boundary claim without an authoritative oracle or biased stochastic-approximation source.

children.title: Heavy-Tailed Noise
children.top_down_role: Noise regimes lacking the concentration behavior used by standard escape analyses.

knowledge_statements.title: Heavy-Tailed Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses Cauchy noise to delimit variance-based and exponential concentration arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_i=g+\xi_i\), where the \(\xi_i\) are independent standard Cauchy variables. For every sample size \(m\ge1\), the average \(m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mG_i\) has the same distribution as \(g+\xi_1\). Hence averaging does not reduce its deviation probability, its variance is undefined, and bounds derived from finite variance or sub-Gaussian tails are inapplicable. Heavy-tailed oracle noise therefore requires additional moment assumptions, truncation, clipping, or robust mean estimation before usual concentration-based criticality guarantees can be asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With Cauchy oracle noise, sample averaging does not concentrate at all, so variance-based and sub-Gaussian criticality guarantees fail.
assumptions_latex: The variables \(\xi_i\) are independent standard Cauchy random variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^mG_i\overset{d}=g+\xi_1\) for every \(m\ge1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Cauchy stability counterexample is correct and appropriately demonstrates failure of averaging and variance-based concentration. An authoritative probability or robust stochastic-optimization locator is still required.

children.title: Degenerate Excitation Noise
children.top_down_role: Noise distributions that fail to activate relevant unstable directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Excitation Noise
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes noise that cannot excite an unstable curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\) have a unit eigenvector \(v\) with \(Hv=\lambda v\) and \(\lambda<0\). Let perturbations \(\xi_k\) have covariance \(\Sigma\succeq0\). If \(v^{\mathsf T}\Sigma v=0\), then \(v^{\mathsf T}(\xi_k-\mathbb E\xi_k)=0\) almost surely. Thus centered perturbations contain no component along the negative-curvature direction, and any saddle-escape argument requiring positive excitation in every unstable direction is inapplicable. A sufficient nondegeneracy condition is a uniform lower covariance bound on the unstable subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Noise with zero covariance along a negative eigendirection cannot perturb iterates in that direction, invalidating saddle-escape arguments based on isotropic excitation.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is symmetric and \(Hv=\lambda v\) with \(\lambda<0\) and \(\lVert v\rVert=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v^{\mathsf T}(\xi_k-\mathbb E\xi_k)=0\) almost surely, so the unstable direction is not excited.

notation.meaning: local Hessian or symmetric curvature matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-variance implication is valid only after explicitly assuming the perturbations have finite second moments and defining the displayed covariance for each relevant perturbation, or assuming a common covariance. The link to saddle-escape excitation assumptions also lacks an authoritative source, so the reliable mathematical version and its hypotheses cannot yet be fixed from the supplied evidence.

children.title: Concentration-Guarantee Failures
children.top_down_role: Probabilistic guarantee boundaries caused by unsuitable oracle-noise structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Concentration-Guarantee Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Delimits finite-horizon concentration guarantees under repeated stochastic oracle calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that \(E_k\) denotes correctness of a stochastic oracle at iteration \(k\), with \(\mathbb P(E_k^c)\le\delta_k\). For every finite horizon \(K\ge1\), the union bound yields \(\mathbb P(\bigcap_{k=1}^K E_k)\ge1-\sum_{k=1}^K\delta_k\). Consequently, summable failure budgets with \(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\delta_k<1\) are sufficient for a positive uniform infinite-horizon guarantee obtained from these marginal bounds alone. By contrast, if the events \(E_k\) are independent and \(\mathbb P(E_k)=1-\delta\) for a fixed \(\delta\in(0,1)\), then \(\mathbb P(\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}E_k)=0\). Thus a fixed per-iteration confidence level does not, by itself, support uniform correctness over indefinitely many independent calls.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-horizon union bound accumulates the per-iteration failure probabilities. Summable budgets suffice for a uniform bound, whereas a fixed failure probability over independent repeated calls gives zero probability of perpetual correctness.
assumptions_latex: \(E_k\) is the oracle-correctness event at iteration \(k\), and \(\mathbb P(E_k^c)\le\delta_k\).
For the fixed-confidence failure example, the events \(E_k\) are independent and satisfy \(\mathbb P(E_k)=1-\delta\) for some \(\delta\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(K\ge1\), \(\mathbb P(\bigcap_{k=1}^K E_k)\ge1-\sum_{k=1}^K\delta_k\); under independent fixed failure probability, \(\mathbb P(\bigcap_{k=1}^{\infty}E_k)=0\).

notation.meaning: upper bound on the failure probability at iteration k
fixed per-iteration failure probability in the independent example

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary of the smooth unconstrained criticality problem class
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let the reference class \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{su}}\) consist of deterministic problems \(\min_{x\in U}f(x)\), where \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is open and \(f\in C^2(U)\). Its first- and second-order criticality quantities are \(\nabla f(x)\) and \(\nabla^2f(x)\), and feasibility imposes no constraints beyond \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal boundary definition for neighboring optimization classes that invalidate at least one ambient assumption of smooth unconstrained Euclidean criticality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A problem belongs to an adjacent problem-class boundary of \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{su}}\) when it is obtained by relaxing or replacing at least one defining condition of \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{su}}\) so that the canonical criticality object changes. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjacent problem-class boundary is reached when a problem relaxes or replaces a defining assumption of deterministic twice-smooth unconstrained Euclidean optimization and thereby changes the appropriate stationarity mapping or local geometry. Constraints, nonsmoothness, manifolds, stochastic information, and composite or variational structure are representative mechanisms. In such a neighboring class, zero Euclidean gradient alone is not the canonical universal stationarity condition.

For an unconstrained nonsmooth function, a generalized condition may be \(0\in\partial f(x)\).
On a smooth Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), first-order criticality uses \(\operatorname{grad}_{\mathcal M}f(x)=0\).

knowledge_statements.title: General Constrained Stationarity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates unconstrained criticality from KKT and tangent-space optimality conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(c_i(x)=0\) and \(g_j(x)\le0\), with continuously differentiable data. Under an appropriate constraint qualification, a local minimizer \(x_\star\) admits multipliers satisfying stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and complementarity. Thus \(\nabla f(x_\star)=0\) is generally neither necessary nor the correct constrained certificate. For example, minimizing \(f(x)=x\) over \(x\ge0\) has the local and global minimizer \(x_\star=0\), although \(f'(x_\star)=1\). Second-order tests must likewise restrict Lagrangian curvature to feasible critical directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At constrained minimizers the objective gradient may be nonzero; KKT multipliers, feasible tangent directions, and restricted Lagrangian curvature replace unconstrained conditions.
assumptions_latex: The objective and constraint functions are continuously differentiable.
A constraint qualification appropriate to the selected KKT theorem holds at the local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Constrained stationarity is expressed by a KKT system, not generally by \(\nabla f(x_\star)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: KKT Stationarity for a Smooth Nonlinear Program
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f,c_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable, let \(\mathcal E\) and \(\mathcal I\) be finite disjoint index sets, and consider \(\min_x f(x)\) subject to \(c_i(x)=0\) for \(i\in\mathcal E\) and \(c_i(x)\ge 0\) for \(i\in\mathcal I\). Define \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\sum_{i\in\mathcal E\cup\mathcal I}\lambda_i c_i(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition marks the boundary between unconstrained smooth criticality and general finite-dimensional smooth nonlinear programming. It defines first-order KKT stationarity; it does not assert that multipliers exist at every local minimizer without a constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A feasible point \(x^\star\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a KKT-stationary point of the nonlinear program if there exists \(\lambda^\star\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal E|+|\mathcal I|}\) such that \(
abla_x\mathcal L(x^\star,\lambda^\star)=0\), \(\lambda_i^\star\ge 0\) for every \(i\in\mathcal I\), and \(\lambda_i^\star c_i(x^\star)=0\) for every \(i\in\mathcal I\). Feasibility means \(c_i(x^\star)=0\) for \(i\in\mathcal E\) and \(c_i(x^\star)\ge 0\) for \(i\in\mathcal I\). Equivalently, with \(\mathcal A(x^\star)=\mathcal E\cup\{i\in\mathcal I:c_i(x^\star)=0\}\), stationarity is \(
abla f(x^\star)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal A(x^\star)}\lambda_i^\star
abla c_i(x^\star)\), where active inequality multipliers are nonnegative and inactive inequality multipliers are zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is KKT-stationary when objective descent is blocked to first order by a signed combination of active constraint normals. Concretely, there must be multipliers for which the Lagrangian gradient vanishes, inequality multipliers are nonnegative, and every inequality multiplier is complementary to its constraint slack. Equality multipliers are unrestricted in sign. The definition includes primal feasibility and therefore concerns a primal-dual pair, not merely a zero of the Lagrangian gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and every \(c_i\) are continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(x^\star\).
\(\mathcal E\) and \(\mathcal I\) are finite, and the inequalities use the convention \(c_i(x)\ge 0\).
\(x^\star\) is feasible for all equality and inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\text{ is KKT-stationary}\iff \exists\lambda^\star:\ \nabla_x\mathcal L(x^\star,\lambda^\star)=0,\ \lambda_{\mathcal I}^\star\ge0,\ \lambda_i^\star c_i(x^\star)=0\ (i\in\mathcal I)\), together with primal feasibility.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(0=\nabla f(x^\star)-\sum_{i\in\mathcal A(x^\star)}\lambda_i^\star\nabla c_i(x^\star)\), with \(\lambda_i^\star\ge0\) on \(\mathcal A(x^\star)\cap\mathcal I\).

Using the normal cone generated by the active smooth constraints when the relevant constraint qualification holds, stationarity can be written \(-\nabla f(x^\star)\in N_\Omega(x^\star)\), subject to the corresponding normal-cone sign convention.
special_cases_latex: If \(\mathcal E=\mathcal I=\varnothing\), the definition reduces to \(\nabla f(x^\star)=0\).
For equality constraints only, \(\lambda^\star\) is unrestricted in sign and complementarity is vacuous.
If an inequality is inactive, \(c_i(x^\star)>0\) forces \(\lambda_i^\star=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Under LICQ at a local minimizer, a multiplier satisfying these conditions exists and is unique.
KKT stationarity alone is not sufficient for local minimality in a general nonconvex problem.
boundary_notes: Without a constraint qualification, a local minimizer may fail to admit normalized KKT multipliers; Fritz John stationarity is the nearby weaker notion.
Second-order constrained criticality additionally restricts the Hessian of the Lagrangian on a critical or tangent subspace and is not part of this definition.
Nonsmooth objectives or constraints require generalized derivatives and lie outside this smooth KKT formulation.

notation.meaning: Active constraint index set at a feasible point.
Vector of equality and inequality Lagrange multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Simple Convex-Set Stationarity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States first-order stationarity for smooth optimization over a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let \(f\) be continuously differentiable near \(C\). A point \(x_\star\in C\) is first-order stationary for minimizing \(f\) over \(C\) exactly when \(\langle
abla f(x_\star),y-x_\starangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\). Equivalently, \(-
abla f(x_\star)\in N_C(x_\star)\), or \(x_\star=P_C(x_\star-\alpha
abla f(x_\star))\) for any \(\alpha>0\). The unconstrained equation \(
abla f(x_\star)=0\) follows only when the normal cone is trivial, as at an interior point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Over a closed convex set, stationarity is a variational inequality, normal-cone inclusion, or zero projected-gradient residual—not necessarily a zero gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\langle
abla f(x_\star),y-x_\starangle\ge0\) for all \(y\in C\) if and only if \(-
abla f(x_\star)\in N_C(x_\star)\), equivalently \(x_\star=P_C(x_\star-\alpha
abla f(x_\star))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationarity over a Closed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, let \(f\) be continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(C\), and consider \(\min_{x\in C}f(x)\). Define \(N_C(x)=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\langle v,y-x\rangle\le0\ \forall y\in C\}\) for \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition covers a smooth objective constrained only by membership in a simple closed convex set. Convexity of the feasible set is essential for the global variational inequality, while convexity of the objective is needed only when stationarity is to certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x^\star\in C\) is stationary for minimizing \(f\) over \(C\) if \(\langle
abla f(x^\star),y-x^\starangle\ge0\) for every \(y\in C\). With the stated normal-cone convention, this is equivalent to \(-
abla f(x^\star)\in N_C(x^\star)\). It is also equivalent, for every fixed \(\alpha>0\), to the projected-gradient fixed-point relation \(x^\star=P_C(x^\star-\alpha
abla f(x^\star))\), where \(P_C(z)=\arg\min_{y\in C}\|y-z\|\). The projected-gradient residual \(G_\alpha(x)=\alpha^{-1}(x-P_C(x-\alpha
abla f(x)))\) therefore vanishes exactly at stationary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible point is stationary over a closed convex set when the gradient has nonnegative inner product with every feasible displacement from that point. Equivalently, the negative gradient is a normal to the set, or one projected-gradient step of any positive length leaves the point fixed. This definition allows the objective to be nonconvex: in that case stationarity is necessary at a local minimizer but is not by itself an optimality certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
\(f\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(C\).
\(x^\star\in C\), and \(P_C\) denotes the unique Euclidean projection onto \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\text{ is stationary}\iff \langle\nabla f(x^\star),y-x^\star\rangle\ge0\ \forall y\in C\iff-\nabla f(x^\star)\in N_C(x^\star)\iff G_\alpha(x^\star)=0\) for any \(\alpha>0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x^\star=P_C(x^\star-\alpha\nabla f(x^\star))\) for any, equivalently every, \(\alpha>0\).
\(-\nabla f(x^\star)\in N_C(x^\star)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), stationarity is exactly \(\nabla f(x^\star)=0\).
If \(x^\star\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(N_C(x^\star)=\{0\}\), so stationarity again reduces to a zero gradient.
For \(C=\mathbb{R}_+^n\), stationarity gives \(\nabla_i f(x^\star)\ge0\), \(x_i^\star\ge0\), and \(x_i^\star\nabla_i f(x^\star)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every local minimizer over convex \(C\) satisfies the variational inequality.
If \(f\) is convex on \(C\), the variational inequality is necessary and sufficient for global optimality.
The norm \(\|G_\alpha(x)\|\) is a computable first-order criticality measure.
boundary_notes: For a nonconvex feasible set, the inequality against every \(y\in C\) can be stronger than local first-order stationarity; tangent or limiting normal cones are then required.
Positive semidefiniteness of a projected Hessian is a separate second-order condition.
The projection equivalence uses Euclidean projection onto a closed convex set and need not hold in this form for nonconvex sets.

notation.meaning: Convex-analytic normal cone with outward-normal sign convention.
Unique Euclidean projection onto the closed convex set.

source_refs.locator: Section 2.1, Proposition 2.1.2 and equation (2.1), together with the projection characterization in Proposition 2.1.3, pp. 191-197

children.title: Nonsmooth-Composite Stationarity Interface
children.top_down_role: Generalized derivatives and composite criticality belong to nonsmooth optimization.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be continuously differentiable and let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous. Set \(\Phi(x)=f(x)+g(x)\) and let \(\partial g(x)\) denote the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition treats finite-dimensional nonsmooth composite optimization. The basic inclusion permits nonconvex \(f\) and nonconvex \(g\); the proximal fixed-point equivalence stated below is restricted to proper closed convex \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A point \(x^\star\in\operatorname{dom}g\) is composite stationary for \(\Phi=f+g\) if \(0\in
abla f(x^\star)+\partial g(x^\star)\), equivalently if there exists \(v^\star\in\partial g(x^\star)\) satisfying \(
abla f(x^\star)+v^\star=0\). Its stationarity residual is \(\operatorname{dist}(0,
abla f(x)+\partial g(x))\). If \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, then for every \(\alpha>0\) stationarity is equivalent to \(x^\star=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha g}(x^\star-\alpha
abla f(x^\star))\), and hence to vanishing of \(G_\alpha(x)=\alpha^{-1}(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha g}(x-\alpha
abla f(x)))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite point is stationary when the negative smooth gradient is a generalized subgradient of the nonsmooth term. The distance from zero to the resulting sum is the intrinsic inclusion residual. When the nonsmooth term is closed and convex, this inclusion is exactly the fixed-point condition for the proximal-gradient map, so its residual gives a single-valued criticality measure.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(\operatorname{dom}g\).
\(g\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and \(x^\star\in\operatorname{dom}g\).
The proximal equivalences additionally assume that \(g\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\text{ is composite stationary}\iff0\in\nabla f(x^\star)+\partial g(x^\star)\); for convex \(g\), this is also equivalent to \(G_\alpha(x^\star)=0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(-\nabla f(x^\star)\in\partial g(x^\star)\).
For proper closed convex \(g\), \(x^\star=\operatorname{prox}_{\alpha g}(x^\star-\alpha\nabla f(x^\star))\) for any \(\alpha>0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g\equiv0\), the inclusion reduces to \(\nabla f(x^\star)=0\).
If \(g=\delta_C\) for a closed convex set \(C\), then \(\partial g=N_C\), recovering convex-set stationarity.
If \(f\equiv0\), stationarity is \(0\in\partial g(x^\star)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: An \(\varepsilon\)-stationary point may be defined by \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x))\le\varepsilon\).
For convex \(g\), \(\|G_\alpha(x)\|\) vanishes exactly at composite stationary points.
boundary_notes: Clarke, convex, proximal, and limiting subdifferentials are not interchangeable outside their respective regularity regimes.
For nonconvex \(g\), the displayed proximal map may be set-valued and its fixed points need not characterize the limiting-subdifferential inclusion without additional hypotheses.
Stationarity does not imply local or global minimality for a nonconvex composite objective.

notation.meaning: Limiting subdifferential unless convexity is explicitly imposed.
Minimizer of \(g(y)+\|y-z\|^2/(2\alpha)\) in the convex specialization.

review_flags: No inspected source hint supported the exact limiting-subdifferential composite inclusion and its convex proximal fixed-point specialization.
A source from variational analysis or composite optimization is required before promotion.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Stationarity Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity for finite-dimensional, proper lower-semicontinuous objectives using the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\). The point \(x\) is limiting-stationary when \[0\in\partial F(x),\] where \(\partial F(x)\) is the Mordukhovich limiting subdifferential. Its stationarity residual is \(r(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))\); thus exact stationarity is equivalent to \(r(x)=0\), while \(r(x)\leq\varepsilon\) defines \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity. If \(F\) is continuously differentiable near \(x\), then \(\partial F(x)=\{\nabla F(x)\}\), so this definition reduces to \(\nabla F(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonsmooth stationarity means that the limiting subdifferential contains zero; its distance from zero measures approximate stationarity and recovers the gradient criterion for smooth objectives.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is stationary exactly when \(0\in\partial F(x)\), equivalently \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial F(x))=0\).

notation.meaning: Limiting subdifferential of F at x.
Distance from zero to the limiting subdifferential.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.4 Nonsmooth Functions p. 33

children.title: Composite Stationarity Interface
children.top_down_role: Boundary leading to criticality notions for composite objective structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Stationarity Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity for a smooth term plus a proper lower-semicontinuous nonsmooth term.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(F(x)=f(x)+g(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), where \(f\) is continuously differentiable near \(x\) and \(g\) is proper and lower semicontinuous. The composite first-order stationarity condition is \[0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x).\] Equivalently, for any \(\gamma>0\), define \(G_\gamma(x)=\gamma^{-1}\bigl(x-\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x-\gamma\nabla f(x))\bigr)\). If \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex, then \(G_\gamma(x)=0\) is equivalent to the displayed inclusion. When \(g\) is the indicator of a closed convex set, this becomes constrained variational stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth-plus-nonsmooth objective, stationarity is the inclusion of zero in the gradient plus subdifferential; under convexity, it is equivalent to a zero proximal-gradient mapping.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper and lower semicontinuous; proximal equivalence additionally requires \(g\) closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\in\nabla f(x)+\partial g(x)\), and under convexity of \(g\), this is equivalent to \(G_\gamma(x)=0\).

notation.meaning: Proximal mapping of the scaled function gamma g.

children.title: Generalized-Derivative Ownership
children.top_down_role: Placement of subdifferential and related derivative frameworks in nonsmooth optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Derivative Ownership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assigns stationarity predicates to the regularity class of the objective rather than to a smooth surrogate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be finite at \(x\). The stationarity object must be owned by the regularity class of \(F\): use \(\nabla F(x)\) when \(F\) is differentiable, \(\partial_C F(x)\) for locally Lipschitz Clarke stationarity, and \(\partial F(x)\) for limiting stationarity of a proper lower-semicontinuous function. These notions satisfy \(\partial F(x)\subseteq\partial_C F(x)\) under local Lipschitz continuity, so \(0\in\partial F(x)\) implies \(0\in\partial_C F(x)\), but the converse need not hold. Consequently, the chosen generalized derivative is part of the certificate and cannot be omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective’s regularity determines the valid derivative notion. Limiting stationarity is generally stronger than Clarke stationarity, so every certificate must name its generalized derivative.
assumptions_latex: For Clarke stationarity and the inclusion comparison, \(F\) is locally Lipschitz near \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The certificate must specify whether \(0=\nabla F(x)\), \(0\in\partial F(x)\), or \(0\in\partial_C F(x)\) is asserted.

children.title: Smooth-Certificate Transfer Limits
children.top_down_role: Limits on carrying smooth stationarity certificates into nonsmooth or composite settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth-Certificate Transfer Limits
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth gradient certificate does not automatically certify stationarity of a nonsmooth objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A vanishing gradient of a selected smooth component does not certify stationarity of the full nonsmooth objective. For example, let \(F(x)=f(x)+|x|\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), with \(f(x)=(x-1)^2\). At \(x=1\), one has \(
abla f(1)=0\), but \[\partial F(1)=\{1\},\qquad 0
otin\partial F(1).\] Hence the smooth certificate \(\|
abla f(x)\|=0\) cannot be transferred to \(F\) without incorporating the nonsmooth term. Transfer is valid at a point only when the applicable sum rule yields \(0\in
abla f(x)+\partial g(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero gradient for the smooth component can coexist with nonstationarity of the full composite objective; the nonsmooth subdifferential must be included.
assumptions_latex: Stationarity is interpreted using the limiting subdifferential.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(x=1\), \(\nabla f(1)=0\) but \(0\notin\partial F(1)\).

children.title: Manifold-Quotient Geometry Interface
children.top_down_role: Intrinsic gradients, Hessians, retractions, and quotient degeneracy belong to manifold optimization.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: First- and Second-Order Criticality on a Riemannian Quotient
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((\mathcal M,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold on which a Lie group \(G\) acts smoothly, freely, properly, and isometrically. Let \(\mathcal Q=\mathcal M/G\), let \(\pi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal Q\) be the quotient map, and let \(F:\mathcal M\to\mathbb R\) be smooth and \(G\)-invariant, so that \(F=\bar F\circ\pi\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition covers intrinsic criticality on a smooth Riemannian quotient. It excludes singular orbit spaces arising from nonfree actions and distinguishes horizontal quotient directions from vertical directions that merely change representatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in\mathcal M\), define the vertical space \(\mathcal V_x=\ker D\pi(x)\) and horizontal space \(\mathcal H_x=\mathcal V_x^\perp\). The orbit \([x]=\pi(x)\) is first-order stationary if \(\operatorname{grad}\bar F([x])=0\). Equivalently, the horizontal lift of this gradient vanishes: \(\operatorname{grad}F(x)=0\), since invariance makes \(\operatorname{grad}F(x)\in\mathcal H_x\). The orbit is second-order stationary if it is first-order stationary and \(\langle\eta,\operatorname{Hess}\bar F([x])[\eta]\rangle\ge0\) for every \(\eta\in T_{[x]}\mathcal Q\); equivalently, the horizontal Hessian quadratic form at \(x\) is nonnegative on every \(\xi\in\mathcal H_x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quotient critical point is an entire orbit, not a selected representative. Its intrinsic gradient vanishes when the horizontal lift of the quotient gradient vanishes on the total space. Second-order stationarity tests curvature only in horizontal directions, because vertical directions move along the same orbit and do not represent distinct quotient points.
assumptions_latex: The action of \(G\) on \(\mathcal M\) is smooth, free, proper, and isometric.
\(F\) is smooth and invariant under the action, so \(F(g\cdot x)=F(x)\) for every \(g\in G\).
The quotient carries the Riemannian metric induced by the horizontal distribution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([x]\text{ is first-order stationary}\iff\operatorname{grad}\bar F([x])=0\iff\operatorname{grad}F(x)=0\); second-order stationarity additionally requires \(\operatorname{Hess}\bar F([x])\succeq0\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\langle\operatorname{grad}F(x),\xi\rangle=0\) for every \(\xi\in\mathcal H_x\).
At a stationary orbit, \(\langle\xi,\operatorname{Hess}F(x)[\xi]\rangle\ge0\) for every horizontal \(\xi\), interpreted through the quotient connection.
special_cases_latex: If \(G\) is trivial, then \(\mathcal Q=\mathcal M\) and the definition is ordinary Riemannian stationarity.
For an embedded submanifold of Euclidean space, \(\operatorname{grad}F(x)\) is the tangent projection of the ambient gradient.
Vertical zero modes caused solely by symmetry are removed from the quotient second-order test.
immediate_consequences_latex: All representatives \(g\cdot x\) describe the same stationary quotient point.
A retraction-based criticality map must be defined on tangent or horizontal directions and be compatible with the quotient representation.
boundary_notes: If the action is not free, the orbit space may be stratified rather than a smooth manifold, and this definition does not apply globally.
Positive semidefiniteness on the full tangent space of the total manifold can contain symmetry-induced degeneracy not present on the quotient.
Retractions and vector transports are algorithmic geometric structures; they are not part of the stationary-point definition itself.

notation.meaning: Vertical tangent space to the group orbit through x.
Metric-orthogonal horizontal complement of the vertical space.
Orbit of x and corresponding point of the quotient manifold.

review_flags: None of the inspected source hints addressed Riemannian quotient gradients, horizontal lifts, and quotient Hessians.
An authoritative manifold-optimization source is required to verify the precise horizontal-Hessian equivalence and conventions.

children.title: Manifold Geometry Interface
children.top_down_role: Boundary leading to intrinsic optimization over smooth manifolds.

knowledge_statements.title: Manifold Geometry Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Embedded-manifold representation of intrinsic first- and second-order criticality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb{R}^N\) be a smooth embedded Riemannian submanifold with the induced metric, and let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable. For any smooth extension \(\bar f\) near \(x\in\mathcal M\), \[\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_x\nabla\bar f(x),\] where \(P_x\) is the orthogonal projection onto \(T_x\mathcal M\). Thus intrinsic first-order stationarity is \(P_x\nabla\bar f(x)=0\). Intrinsic second-order stationarity additionally requires \(\langle\eta,\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[\eta]\rangle_x\geq0\) for every \(\eta\in T_x\mathcal M\); an ambient Euclidean Hessian alone does not express this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an embedded manifold, the Riemannian gradient is the tangent projection of an extension’s Euclidean gradient; second-order stationarity is tested only along tangent directions.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\subset\mathbb{R}^N\) is a smooth embedded submanifold with induced metric.
\(\bar f\) is a smooth local extension of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=P_x\nabla\bar f(x)\), with stationarity characterized intrinsically on \(T_x\mathcal M\).

notation.meaning: Tangent space of the manifold at x.
Orthogonal projection onto the tangent space.

children.title: Quotient Geometry Interface
children.top_down_role: Boundary leading to optimization over equivalence classes and quotient spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Geometry Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationarity of an invariant objective represented through horizontal lifts on a smooth Riemannian quotient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Lie group \(G\) act freely, properly, and isometrically on a Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), and let \(\pi:\mathcal M\to\mathcal M/G\) be the quotient map. If \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb{R}\) is smooth and \(G\)-invariant, there is a unique \(\tilde f:\mathcal M/G\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(f=\tilde f\circ\pi\). For \(x\in\mathcal M\), the horizontal lift of \(\operatorname{grad}\tilde f([x])\) equals the horizontal projection of \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\). Therefore \[[x]\text{ is stationary for }\tilde f\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0,\] because invariance makes \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\) horizontal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a free proper isometric symmetry, an invariant objective descends to the quotient, and quotient stationarity is represented by the horizontal gradient of any representative.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) acts freely, properly, and isometrically on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The horizontal lift of \(\operatorname{grad}\tilde f([x])\) is \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)\), and quotient stationarity is representative-independent.

notation.meaning: Orbit of x in the quotient manifold.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The quotient representation is plausible under the stated free, proper, isometric action, but no citation supports quotient smoothness, the descended metric, horizontality of the invariant gradient, or the representative-independent stationarity equivalence.

children.title: Intrinsic Stationarity Ownership
children.top_down_role: Placement of intrinsic gradients, Hessians, and retraction-based criticality.

knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic Stationarity Ownership
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First- and second-order stationarity are defined by the Riemannian metric and tangent geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal M,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle)\) be a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold and let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable. A point \(x\in\mathcal M\) is intrinsically first-order stationary exactly when \[\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0.\] It is intrinsically second-order stationary when it is first-order stationary and \[\langle\eta,\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[\eta]\rangle_x\geq0\quad\text{for every }\eta\in T_x\mathcal M.\] Both predicates are coordinate-independent. Consequently, ambient gradients, coordinate gradients, or unconstrained Euclidean Hessians are valid certificates only after conversion to these intrinsic objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Manifold stationarity belongs to the Riemannian gradient and Hessian on the tangent space, not to unprojected ambient or coordinate derivatives.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: First-order stationarity is \(\operatorname{grad}f(x)=0\); second-order stationarity additionally requires positive semidefiniteness of \(\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\) on \(T_x\mathcal M\).

notation.meaning: Riemannian gradient of f at x.
Riemannian Hessian of f at x.

children.title: Symmetry-Degeneracy Boundary
children.top_down_role: Limits of Euclidean critical-point classification under quotient symmetries.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry-Degeneracy Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous symmetries force null Hessian directions before quotienting, invalidating isolated nondegeneracy tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a positive-dimensional Lie group \(G\) act smoothly on \(\mathcal M\), and let \(f:\mathcal M\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice continuously differentiable and \(G\)-invariant. If \(x\) is stationary, then every tangent vector \(v\in T_x(G\cdot x)\) to the group orbit satisfies \[\operatorname{Hess}f(x)[v]=0.\] Hence, whenever \(T_x(G\cdot x)\neq\{0\}\), the Hessian on \(T_x\mathcal M\) is singular and \(x\) cannot be a nondegenerate isolated critical point on the unreduced manifold. Nondegeneracy can instead be required only transversely to the orbit, or equivalently on a regular quotient when one exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous invariance creates orbitwise zero Hessian directions, so unreduced critical points are degenerate; nondegeneracy must be tested transverse to symmetry or on the quotient.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a positive-dimensional Lie group acting smoothly on \(\mathcal M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_x(G\cdot x)\subseteq\ker\operatorname{Hess}f(x)\), so nontrivial orbit directions force unreduced Hessian degeneracy.

notation.meaning: Tangent space to the orbit at x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure phenomenon belongs in this container, but no source is supplied and the statement invokes a gradient and Hessian without explicitly equipping the manifold with a Riemannian metric. An authoritative source must also establish the orbit-tangent kernel claim under clearly stated regularity assumptions.

children.title: Stochastic Nonconvex Boundary
children.top_down_role: Sampling assumptions, stochastic convergence, and variance-reduction mechanisms belong to stochastic optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Nonconvex Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates deterministic smooth criticality from stochastic-oracle assumptions and probabilistic convergence guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x)=\mathbb{E}[f(x,\xi)]\), and suppose an algorithm observes random vectors \(g(x,\xi)\) rather than \(
abla F(x)\). A deterministic conclusion such as \(\min_{0\leq k<K}\|
abla F(x_k)\|\leq\varepsilon\) does not follow merely by replacing exact gradients with samples. Such a conclusion requires explicit oracle hypotheses, for example \(\mathbb{E}[g(x,\xi)\mid x]=
abla F(x)\) and a conditional variance bound, together with a probabilistic or expected accuracy criterion. Sampling complexity, martingale arguments, batch growth, and variance reduction therefore lie outside a deterministic smooth-landscape certificate unless separately supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sample gradients cannot simply replace exact gradients in deterministic criticality results; oracle bias, variance, accuracy mode, and sampling complexity require separate stochastic analysis.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm accesses a stochastic oracle \(g(x,\xi)\) rather than \(\nabla F(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Deterministic smooth convergence guarantees do not transfer without stated stochastic-oracle and probabilistic-convergence assumptions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role matches the immutable node and the deterministic-versus-stochastic distinction is reasonable, but no source supports the oracle assumptions, convergence-mode distinction, or allocation of sampling-complexity mechanisms to stochastic analysis.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stochastic First-Order Stationarity for a Smooth Expected Objective
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((\Xi,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \(\ell:\mathbb R^n\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) be measurable in its second argument and differentiable in its first, and define \(F(x)=\mathbb E_\xi[\ell(x,\xi)]\). Assume differentiation and expectation may be interchanged, so \(\nabla F(x)=\mathbb E_\xi[\nabla_x\ell(x,\xi)]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition separates stationarity of the deterministic expectation objective from probabilistic guarantees for a random algorithmic output. It concerns smooth, unconstrained, finite-dimensional nonconvex optimization and does not prescribe a sampling or variance-reduction algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A deterministic point \(x^\star\in\mathbb R^n\) is first-order stationary for the stochastic objective if \(
abla F(x^\star)=0\), and it is \(\varepsilon\)-stationary if \(\|
abla F(x^\star)\|\le\varepsilon\). If an algorithm returns a random vector \(X\), then \(X\) is mean-square \(\varepsilon\)-stationary when \(\mathbb E\|
abla F(X)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2\), and it is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-stationary in probability when \(\mathbb P(\|
abla F(X)\|\le\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\). A stochastic-gradient oracle \(G(x,\xi)\) is unbiased with variance bounded by \(\sigma^2\) if \(\mathbb E[G(x,\xi)\mid x]=
abla F(x)\) and \(\mathbb E[\|G(x,\xi)-
abla F(x)\|^2\mid x]\le\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity belongs to the expected objective: its exact gradient must vanish. Because stochastic algorithms return random points, approximate stationarity must specify how randomness is quantified, such as an expected squared gradient norm or a high-probability gradient bound. Unbiasedness and bounded variance describe an oracle and are separate assumptions rather than components of stationarity itself.
assumptions_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E[\ell(x,\xi)]\) is finite and continuously differentiable on the region under consideration.
The interchange \(\nabla F(x)=\mathbb E[\nabla_x\ell(x,\xi)]\) is valid.
Expectations defining mean-square stationarity and oracle variance are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(x^\star	ext{ is stationary}\iff
abla F(x^\star)=0\); random-output approximations are specified by either \(\mathbb E\|
abla F(X)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2\) or \(\mathbb P(\|
abla F(X)\|\le\varepsilon)\ge1-\delta\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Exact stationarity is \(\mathbb E_\xi[\nabla_x\ell(x^\star,\xi)]=0\) when gradient-expectation interchange holds.
For deterministic \(X=x\), mean-square \(\varepsilon\)-stationarity reduces to \(\|\nabla F(x)\|\le\varepsilon\).
special_cases_latex: For a finite sum, \(F(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x)\) and \(\nabla F(x)=m^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^m\nabla f_i(x)\).
If \(\sigma=0\), the oracle returns the exact gradient almost surely.
When \(F\) is convex, exact first-order stationarity also certifies global optimality; this implication generally fails in the nonconvex regime.
immediate_consequences_latex: A bound on \(\mathbb E\|\nabla F(X)\|^2\) is a convergence-quality statement about the algorithm's output distribution, not about individual samples.
Variance reduction changes the oracle error behavior but not the definition \(\nabla F(x^\star)=0\).
boundary_notes: The sample gradient \(\nabla_x\ell(x,\xi)\) need not vanish at a stationary point of the expectation.
Biased oracles, heavy-tailed noise, constraints, and nonsmooth regularizers require modified assumptions or criticality measures.
Expected-norm, expected-squared-norm, and high-probability criteria are distinct and should not be interchanged without quantitative conversion.

notation.meaning: Random point returned by an algorithm.

review_flags: The inspected hints did not provide a source supporting the combined definitions of expectation stationarity, random-output criteria, and unbiased bounded-variance oracles.
A current stochastic nonconvex optimization reference is required before promotion.

children.title: Global Landscape-Topology Interface
children.top_down_role: Mountain-pass principles, sublevel-set topology, barrier crossing, and global basin structure belong to global optimization or Morse theory.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sublevel-Set Connectivity and the Minimax Barrier
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a path-connected topological space and let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. For \(a\in\mathbb R\), define the closed sublevel set \(L_a=\{x\in X:f(x)\le a\}\). For \(x,y\in X\), let \(\Gamma(x,y)=\{\gamma\in C([0,1],X):\gamma(0)=x,\gamma(1)=y\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition records global connectivity and barrier information that cannot be read from the gradient and Hessian at one point. It is topological and variational, and it does not by itself assert the existence of a critical point at the minimax level.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The minimax connection level between \(x\) and \(y\) is \(c_f(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(x,y)}\max_{t\in[0,1]}f(\gamma(t))\). The associated barrier height is \(B_f(x,y)=c_f(x,y)-\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\ge0\). Equivalently, \(c_f(x,y)=\inf\{a\in\mathbb R:x\text{ and }y\text{ lie in the same path-connected component of }L_a\}\). Thus two points occupy distinct sublevel basins below level \(a\) precisely when they lie in different path components of \(L_a\); their first connection level is the least height at which those components merge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The global landscape between two points is measured by the smallest possible highest objective value along a continuous path joining them. Subtracting the larger endpoint value gives the barrier height. The same quantity is the first sublevel at which the two points become path-connected, so it records a change in global basin connectivity rather than a local derivative condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is continuous, so every path maximum \(\max_{t\in[0,1]}f(\gamma(t))\) exists.
The topology on each \(L_a\) is the subspace topology inherited from \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c_f(x,y)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(x,y)}\max_t f(\gamma(t))=\inf\{a:x,y\text{ belong to one path component of }L_a\}\), and \(B_f(x,y)=c_f(x,y)-\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(c_f(x,y)\le a\) exactly when paths from \(x\) to \(y\) exist whose objective height is arbitrarily close to, and under suitable attainment equal to, \(a\).
The merge-level formulation identifies \(c_f(x,y)\) through the filtration \((L_a)_{a\in\mathbb R}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(x\) and \(y\) already lie in the same path component of \(L_{\max\{f(x),f(y)\}}\), then \(B_f(x,y)=0\).
If every joining path exceeds \(\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\), then \(B_f(x,y)>0\).
For two local minima in distinct low sublevel components, \(c_f(x,y)\) is their basin merge level.
immediate_consequences_latex: The family of path components of \(L_a\) can change only through global level-set events as \(a\) increases.
Local equality of gradients and Hessians at two points does not determine \(c_f(x,y)\) or \(B_f(x,y)\).
boundary_notes: A mountain-pass critical point at level \(c_f(x,y)\) requires additional compactness and geometric hypotheses; it is not included in this definition.
Path components and connected components can differ in general topological spaces; this record consistently uses path connectivity.
The minimax infimum need not be attained by a path without compactness or coercivity assumptions.
Morse-theoretic conclusions require smoothness and nondegeneracy beyond the continuity assumed here.

notation.meaning: Closed objective sublevel set at height a.
Continuous paths joining x to y.
Barrier height above the higher endpoint.

review_flags: No inspected source hint supported the minimax-path and sublevel-component equivalence in the required global topological scope.
A source in critical point theory, mountain-pass theory, or topological data analysis is required before promotion.

children.title: Global Landscape Interface
children.top_down_role: Boundary leading to global basin, barrier, and critical-level organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Landscape Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local criticality data alone do not determine global optimality or global landscape structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a twice continuously differentiable nonconvex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), the local conditions \(\nabla f(x)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) do not imply that \(x\) is globally minimizing. For example, for \(f(t)=(t^2-1)^2+t/2\), each local minimizer satisfies the usual second-order local conditions, while the two wells have unequal objective values and only the lower one is globally minimizing. Global conclusions require additional landscape structure, such as convexity, an invexity property, a strict-saddle-plus-benign-minima theorem, or an independently verified global lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First- and second-order local criticality cannot determine global optimality in a general nonconvex landscape; additional global structure or bounds are necessary.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is twice continuously differentiable and may be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(x)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) alone do not imply \(f(x)=\inf_y f(y)\).

notation.meaning: The Euclidean Hessian is positive semidefinite.

children.title: Sublevel-Set Topology
children.top_down_role: Topological organization of objective sublevel sets across critical levels.

knowledge_statements.title: Sublevel-Set Topology
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological data attached to objective sublevel sets and their changes across critical values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). For \(a\in\mathbb{R}\), the sublevel set at height \(a\) is \[L_a(f)=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq a\}.\] Sublevel-set topology is the filtered family \(\{L_a(f)\}_{a\in\mathbb{R}}\), considered through properties such as emptiness, compactness, connected components, homotopy type, or homology, together with inclusion maps \(L_a(f)\hookrightarrow L_b(f)\) for \(a\leq b\). These are global properties of \(f\); derivatives at one point do not determine them without additional hypotheses linking critical levels to topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sublevel-set topology studies the nested sets below each objective height and how their connectivity or topological type changes as the height increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_a(f)\subseteq L_b(f)\), and the resulting filtration encodes global topological information about the objective.

notation.meaning: Sublevel set of f at height a.
